events.title: US stock market hits all-time high as investors bet big on AI
events.summary: The benchmark S&P 500 is up 14 percent this year despite elevated oil prices and US government debt sell-off. The United States stock market has hit an all-time high as excitement around artificial intelligence continues to fuel a buying frenzy on Wall Street. The S&P 500, the benchmark stock index, closed 0.58 percent higher on Tuesday, topping the previous peak reached in mid-August. list 1 of 4 Christa Pike lawyers say she is speaking one week after failed execution list 2 of 4 Fans flood Buenos Aires ahead of Messi’s final international match list 3 of 4 ‘We are desperate’: Venezuela’s power cuts fuel growing public anger list 4 of 4 Electric car bursts into flames at charging station in Turkiye The Nasdaq Composite, which is more heavily weighted towards tech stocks, also hit a record high, finishing up 0.45 percent. Tech stocks were among the top performers, with each of the “Magnificent Seven” apart from Meta closing higher. Amazon led the pack with a 1.95 percent gain, followed by Microsoft and Tesla, which rose 0.78 percent and 0.51 percent, respectively. Apple and Alphabet both rose 0.22 percent, while Nvidia gained 0.14 percent. Meta, which has risen more than 20 percent since the launch last month of its new AI assistant, Muse, fell 0.41 percent. Other big movers in tech included Marvell Technology, which rose 5.81 percent, and Cisco, which gained 4.54 percent. Keith Lerner, chief investment officer and chief market strategist at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta, Georgia, said the market rally should be seen as a “technology and AI surge”. “Every bull market has a dominant theme, and technology and AI remain this market’s dominant theme,” Lerner told Al Jazeera. “Technology and communication services were the only two S&P 500 sectors to rise last month, while the other nine declined.” Wall Street has shrugged off a host of challenges facing the US economy amid hyperscalers’ multibillion-dollar investments in AI. Despite the energy crunch caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran and a sell-off of US government bonds partly driven by ballooning government debt, the market is well on track to record its fourth consecutive year of double-digit returns. The S&P 500 has risen 14 percent so far in 2026, while the Nasdaq Composite is up 18.78 percent. Lerner at Truist Advisory said the market rally had the potential to continue through the end of 2026 given historical trends and expectations for strong corporate earnings. “We do not expect a straight line higher for markets,” Lerner said. “Still, the fourth quarter of midterm-election years has produced an average gain of 7 percent and has been positive 84 percent of the time since 1950.” Lerner said that rising interest rates posed the biggest risk to the upward trend. “Still, on balance, the weight of the evidence suggests this bull market still has more upside potential,” he said. Asian stock markets fell on Wednesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong slumping in morning trading. The Nikkei 225 in Tokyo, Kospi in Seoul and Hang Seng Index in Hong Kong were down 0.79 percent, 1.36 percent and 0.71 percent, respectively, as of 02:30 GMT. Oil prices, which have been elevated since the start of the war on Iran, rose on Wednesday as traders weighed the fallout of fighting between forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis. Brent crude futures for December delivery stood at $101.45 a barrel as of 02:30 GMT, up 0.87 percent.

events.title: Oman evacuates injured crew from attacked tanker in Strait of Hormuz
events.summary: India’s Foreign Ministry says 11 out of 12 injured crew members on board the On Peace are Indian nationals. Oman’s air force has evacuated 10 crew members of a Panamanian-flagged oil tanker following an attack in the Strait of Hormuz. The On Peace tanker was struck 9 nautical miles (about 17km) off the Omani port city of Limah on Tuesday, according to the Omani Ministry of Defence. The attack set off a fire on board the vessel. list 1 of 3 Is Iran charging a toll to allow oil traffic through Hormuz? list 2 of 3 Hormuz ship attacks surge: Are increased oil exports sustainable? list 3 of 3 What new measures is Iran taking to counter US economic pressure? “The crew members were transported to the Khasab hospital in Musandam governorate and received medical treatment,” the ministry said in a statement on X. No group has claimed the attack so far. It comes as security in the Strait of Hormuz continues to deteriorate amid the United States and Israel’s war on Iran. India’s foreign ministry, the Ministry of External Affairs, said at least 12 of the ship’s 19 crew members were injured when a projectile hit the vessel as it transited the strait. Seventeen of the 19 crew members were Indian nationals, it said, as were 11 of the injured. “The continuing incidents of attacks on shipping in the region remain a cause of deep concern for India,” the ministry said. “We reiterate our call for an immediate cessation of such attacks in the interests of peace and stability in the region.” India is one of the largest contributors of sailors to merchant shipping worldwide. The Indian government said in July that at least 10 Indian seafarers had been killed since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February. Another attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz in September also killed an Indian sailor. Iran effectively closed the waterway after the US-Israel war began on February 28. It has frequently attacked commercial vessels that do not use its designated route in the waterway, and has said it wants to charge ships for passage. At least seven other incidents involving tankers have been reported in the past week, according to Marisks, a shipping intelligence service. Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to pre-war levels in recent weeks. The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to provisional data from Kpler, a data firm. Still, prices remain high, with Brent crude futures rising to $101.51 a barrel on Tuesday, compared with $72.48 the day before the war began.

events.title: Abu Dhabi to refresh Tamm app as it pursues AI-native government goal
events.summary: Abu Dhabi plans to launch the latest version of the Tamm app in December as it pursues its goal of becoming the world’s first fully AI-native government, a senior executive has said. The refreshed Tamm 5.0 app, which would be introduced at the Gitex Global technology exhibition in Dubai, promises "increasingly intelligent" services, Department of Government Enablement director general Ruba Al Hassan told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Those services are to also be more "proactive and personalised", but they still have to remain "simple and trusted", said Ms Al Hassan, who oversees strategic affairs and future foresight at the department. Tamm currently has about 4.7 million users, having grown by more than 1.5 million in just a year. About 90 per cent of its transactions are finalised within a day, the latest data from the DGE shows. Tamm 5.0 would be "another step" in the evolution from a digital government to an AI-native government, "moving towards a model where government increasingly understands context ... anticipates needs and helps people achieve things more easily", Ms Al Hassan said. The DGE did not reveal the specific changes to Tamm or new services that are to be introduced. "It’s time for the next phase, which is about making the experience even more seamless and reducing the effort required from residents, businesses and visitors," she added. The DGE remains "focused" on its goal of transforming the capital's government services into a fully AI-native platform by next year, Ms Al Hassan said. The agency is "moving with urgency, but building responsibly", she added. "We are already seeing that tangible progress across government, not only through individual AI applications, but through the foundations that make AI-native government possible," she said, referring to data, infrastructure, digital services, workforce capability and governance. "The question is not whether we can deploy AI faster, it’s whether we can create lasting value at scale, so we believe we are on the right path to do that." Abu Dhabi is boosting tech use across the emirate under its digital strategy, which focuses on five key enablers – one of them being the use of AI across public services. Despite the persisting challenges – especially issues involving AI models going rogue and compromising other websites – the DGE is seeking to ensure the safety and reliability of such systems. "We’re seeing a lot of noise in the global AI conversation. New models are constantly coming out, capabilities are getting better quickly and everyone’s focused on what might happen in the future," Ms Al Hassan said. "Our focus is slightly different. We’re interested in where AI delivers practical value today ... we also believe trust is critical. People need confidence that AI is being used responsibly, transparently and with clear human accountability." Educating users is also a key part of the DGE's mandate, she said. "As AI improves, the value of human judgment actually also increases. People need to know how to work effectively with AI, challenge AI outputs and make better decisions," she said. "When it comes to AI, the skill won’t be coding, it will be maintaining judgment." 'Most powerful generation' Meanwhile, Omar Al Olama, Minister of State for AI, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, described the present generation as the "most powerful in human history", while calling for more responsible use of AI. "The reason ... is because you have the intelligence of every single generation, every single human that has lived, that has actually produced something that has lasted ... the content and knowledge are at your fingertips," he told the conference. "And you don't just have raw knowledge. You're actually able to leverage intelligence to do something with it through agentic AI," he added, referring to the class designed to make autonomous decisions and act with minimal human supervision. "This is the time for a new ambitious generation ... people might not believe in your ideas, to wield these tools to create something that others can't see or don't believe is possible. It's a calling."

events.title: Incredible or catastrophic? Jaguar unveils its polarising electric car
events.summary: The Type 01's launch event was attended by celebrities including actor Florence Pugh Published 7 October 2026, 01:01 BST Two years ago, Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) relaunched Jaguar into a blizzard of controversy. Its bizarre teaser ad was described as "woke" and its "Barbie pink" concept car was ridiculed. Now, the first of its new models has appeared in public for the first time. The all-electric Type 01, unveiled in New York, represents a radical new direction for the classic brand . The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type. But it marks a gamble for JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy. The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles. The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered". However, it comes at a hefty price tag, with a minimum cost of £130,000 ($172,426). In the US, the Type 01 has a starting price of $130,500. Under normal circumstances, the launch of a car like this might generate few headlines. But in this case the attention has been much greater, and for good reason. In 2024 Jaguar unveiled its new identity to the public. The first step was a surreal advert, showing models in a range of bizarre and brightly coloured outfits. There was a new Jaguar logo - but no cars in sight. Two weeks later, Jaguar's denim-clad design chief Gerry McGovern took to a Miami stage to unveil a pair of radical concept cars , resplendent in Miami Pink and London Blue colour schemes. "Jaguar has no desire to be loved by everybody," he quipped. The pink concept car unveiled in 2024 The event was meant to herald Jaguar's future as a luxury all-electric marque , but it triggered a furious backlash in the press and on social media. Critics claimed JLR was betraying its heritage in favour of going "woke". Even the colour chosen for the launch was derided as "Barbie pink", as culture wars erupted around it. The reception appeared to catch JLR by surprise. The reinvention of Jaguar as a luxury electric brand was part of a wide-ranging strategy set out by the company in early 2023, in which it pledged to invest £15bn in new models and technologies. How Jaguar lost its way - long before that polarising advert Published 8 December 2024 'Trust and reserve judgement' on rebrand, says Jaguar Published 23 November 2024 At the time, Jaguar itself was struggling. The badge, which was once an intrinsic part of Swinging Sixties British cool, had lost its lustre. Where in the past it had supplied E-Types to Brigitte Bardot and Steve McQueen, it now struggled to sell upmarket saloons and SUVs to middle-ranking corporate executives, who generally preferred Audis and BMWs. "Jaguar's core demographic, despite the uproar, gave up on the brand years ago, so they effectively had nothing to lose," explains Matthias Schmidt of Schmidt Automotive Research. The Type 01's design has been met with mixed reactions from car enthusiasts The unveiling of the Type 01 on Tuesday was met with mixed reactions, with some on social media criticising the new car. "Looks like a Cybertruck and a Bentley Continental had an illegitimate child," Facebook user Ken Katch said, referring to the Tesla pick-up, known for its divisive design. Craig Kinnersley, who runs a luxury car consultancy, wrote on LinkedIn that it is an "unmitigated catastrophe" that looks like a hearse and lacks any "memorable Jaguar flourish". Car journalist Steve Fowler said the Type 01 "looks incredible" and makes him "proud to be British". "Not everyone will like it - that's fine. Not everyone has to!" he wrote on X. Alistair Weaver from vehicle sales platform Edmunds said Jaguar deserved some credit for the Type 01's looks, despite it being "polarising". "If Jaguar designed a car that looked like anything else, it would have had no hope," Weaver told the BBC. But the firm faces an uphill battle in the US, where EVs are becoming less popular , he added. JLR wound down production of its old Jaguar models in 2024 and 2025. The "woke" row, while it possibly made life briefly uncomfortable for the company's leadership, did at least keep the Jaguar name in the public consciousness at a time when it was selling very few cars. "It brought Jaguar from the back pages to the front pages, given that it was dying in a crowded international market," says Schmidt. "Everyone is now talking about what would have been another boring product." The GT is expected to be the first of three new electric designs from Jaguar.

events.title: Trump set to talk to Russia's Putin 'very soon' about plague-related death in Siberia
events.summary: Trump said the call with Putin was scheduled “very soon,” a day after offering U.S. assistance to Russia. The CDC said it was closely monitoring reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia but saw no indication of a broader threat to the U.S. U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday stateside that he was set to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the death of a laboratory worker from a suspected case of plague in Siberia. Trump said the call was scheduled for "very soon" when asked by a reporter about the timing at a White House press gaggle. Asked separately what U.S. intelligence agencies were saying about the incident, Trump said, "So far, we are in very deep discussions. We'll be able to report about it probably tomorrow." Trump's, who has said in the past that Putin is someone he can work with despite tensions over Moscow's war in Ukraine, on Monday offered U.S. help to Russia over the deadly plague incident. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC, said in a post on X Wednesday that it "is aware of and closely monitoring reports of a suspected case of pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia that resulted in a death." The U.S. public health agency said the circumstances surrounding the case remain unconfirmed. Pneumonic plague can spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact, the CDC said. However, the CDC said that "at this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States," adding that it and its interagency partners were prepared and would continue to closely monitor the situation. The World Health Organization has told CNBC that it assesses the risk to the general public as low, based on available information.

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Redmond explains how VMs die, but not when you can expect that to happen Microsoft extends the Outlook naughty step with two more file types 11 hours ago Classic Outlook clings to stale search results as Microsoft works on a fix 12 hours ago Windows 11 market share creeps upwards as cost of staying on Windows 10 set to double 1 day ago Flight delayed? So are these codec updates 4 days ago AWS turns its best practice framework into an agent that recommends cloudy reconfigs 4 days ago Microsoft has updated the lifecycle of an Azure instance, without offering any information on how long it takes for an instance type to expire. Redmond’s “enhanced lifecycle” landed in late September in a post that explains the four phases in the life of a cloudy VM: Current – VMs are recommended for new deployments, are available in many regions, and receive standard maintenance and support; Extended – Still supported, but may be subject to usage quotas and unspecified “changes to purchasing options and pricing.” Microsoft recommends planning a move to Current VMs. End of Life – VMs are still supported but are only available to existing customers and you may not be able to get more of the instances you want. Once VMs reach this stage, Microsoft wants you “actively” working to shift workloads onto Current or Extended VMs. Retired – Unsupported but not quite dead. Microsoft says VMs in this phase are no longer available and have been “deallocated” – Azure-speak for not having an IP address and being dormant, with data preserved. Customers can’t provision the instance types. Microsoft’s post explains that the company defined this lifecycle because it is “committed to helping you navigate these infrastructure transitions and take advantage of the next wave of innovation.” The post includes many mentions of “modernization” – the process of moving to Current Azure instance types. “As Azure continues to advance, our commitment is to make change predictable, transparent, and supported through clear lifecycle guidance, early visibility, and practical help to modernize with confidence,” the post states. The mention of “predictable” change led The Register to wonder if the lifecycle has a predictable cadence that means users can expect that instance types will remain in “Current” status for a certain number of years. We asked Microsoft if its Azure instance lifecycles are timed, and a spokesperson sent the following comment: “As Azure continues to innovate, we regularly evolve our infrastructure to give customers access to newer technologies and capabilities. As part of our updated Azure Virtual Machines lifecycle, we will continue to provide customers with advance notice when select older-generation VM series enter the End of Life stage. We’re giving customers time, guidance and resources to plan their transition to the current VM generations, while continuing to support Azure VMs through their lifecycle in alignment with the policies we published.” The spokesperson added that Microsoft customers are “notified directly about their specific VM retirements.” For what it’s worth, Microsoft publishes retirement announcements for Azure services . The company has also previously revealed it runs Azure servers for six years. It is unclear if the new Azure lifecycle is tied to that hardware retirement schedule. What is clear is that Microsoft wants Azure customers to regularly consider moving to its latest instance types. That’s a reasonable suggestion given that newer VMs will likely use more powerful processors. There’s also plenty of upside for Microsoft because more recent silicon typically offers more cores per die, and better performance-per-watt. Microsoft therefore gets greater processor density with lower energy consumption, which lowers its operating costs. Let’s see if Redmond’s lifecycle tweaks also see it pass on those savings.

events.title: Australia top court rules against coal mine expansion, citing climate harm
events.summary: Campaigners say ruling sets a ‘binding national precedent’ requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered. Australia’s highest court has ruled against the expansion of a major coal mine, finding that planning authorities had failed to ensure that emissions of planet-warming greenhouse gases would be “minimised to the greatest extent practicable”. Environmental campaigners called Wednesday’s court decision the first climate case to reach the country’s highest court. They said it set a “binding national precedent” requiring climate damage be weighed when fossil fuel projects are considered. list 1 of 3 Australia’s Great Barrier Reef hit by record bleaching as oceans warm list 2 of 3 World’s ‘fossil fuel obsession’ threatens billions of lives: Amnesty list 3 of 3 South Africa to Australia: Why coal profits are surging during Iran war In the ruling, three of the High Court’s five judges found that the expansion of the Mount Pleasant mine in New South Wales must be halted. Planning authorities, they said, were obliged to consider granting consent only with conditions ensuring that all greenhouse gas emissions were minimised, and had not done so in this case. The case was brought by retired science teachers Wendy Wales and Tony Lonergan, who had fought for years to halt the planned mine expansion in Australia’s rural coal-digging heartland. “Today the High Court has said what we have always known,” Wales said in a statement. “We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and then pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us and won’t be felt by us.” The mine’s operator, Mach Energy, had sought to extend the life of the open-cut mine in the Hunter Valley by more than 20 years, to 2048, and to nearly double its annual output. Mach is owned by Droxford International, a subsidiary of Indonesia’s Salim Group. Mach argued that coal exported and burned overseas could not be clearly linked to environmental effects felt near the mine. The company’s proposal was initially approved by the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission. But environmental campaigners disagreed, saying every ounce of greenhouse gas released into the atmosphere made bushfires, floods and drought more likely. “Today, the highest court in the country agreed that those decisions have to account for the damage they cause,” said Lonergan. “This isn’t the end of coal overnight. But it is the end of coal mine approvals that look the other way on climate.” Australia is one of the world’s largest fossil fuel exporters, ranking among the top sellers of both coal and liquefied natural gas. Anita O’Hart, a lawyer for Wales and Lonergan’s community group, said the “historic” ruling was expected to affect how future fossil fuel projects are handled. “The High Court has confirmed that planning authorities cannot ignore the chain of causation from a project’s emissions through to real, local climate harm,” she said. “This ruling will be applied by courts and planning authorities across Australia, and it will be studied internationally as one of the most significant domestic climate law decisions in the world.” Mach Energy said it was “disappointed with the outcome” but accepted the court’s decision. “We will continue to actively pursue all available options to ensure the long-term continuity of the Mount Pleasant operation,” the company said in a statement.

events.title: Trump isn't ‘completely wrong’: Hormuz disruption is Asia’s problem, says Singapore's foreign minister
events.summary: Trump isn’t “completely wrong” that Asia has a major stake in keeping Hormuz open., said Vivian Balakrishnan. Freedom of navigation through global waterways is “non-negotiable” and existential for Singapore, he noted. SINGAPORE — U.S. President Donald Trump isn’t “completely wrong” in suggesting that the disruption to energy flows via the Strait of Hormuz is Asia's problem, Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said. Asian economies are among the biggest customers of energy shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Arabian Sea, making any prolonged disruption particularly consequential for the region. Trump has said that Asian economies should shoulder more of the burden of keeping the waterway open rather than relying predominantly on U.S. protection. "We don't use the strait. We don't need it. Europe needs it. Korea, Japan, China, [and] a lot of other people," he said earlier this year. Balakrishnan, however, cautioned against viewing the issue simply through the lens of who buys the oil, stressing the importance of maintaining freedom of navigation through international waterways. He made the remarks to CNBC on Wednesday at Milken Institute's Asia Summit in Singapore. For Singapore, that principle is “non-negotiable,” Balakrishnan said, citing the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the rights of transit passage and freedom of navigation. “This, for us, is an existential question, and it's a matter of principle, matter of international law,” Balakrishnan said. Iran’s attempts to assert greater control over traffic through Hormuz also go beyond the revenues it could generate from tolls and fees, he said. From Tehran’s perspective, the ability to charge vessels could effectively establish its right to determine which ships are allowed through, giving Iran what Balakrishnan described as a potential “veto right” over Hormuz. That power could provide Tehran with “greater leverage right now than even a potential nuclear weapon from an Iranian point of view,” he said. Balakrishnan added he does not expect the U.S. or Gulf states to tolerate a situation in which Iran had such a veto over the waterway, suggesting tensions could persist even if oil continues flowing. “I think there will be a lot of pushing and shoving the next few months,” he said, adding that he did not see “a quick diplomatic off-ramp” to the conflict. In April, Balakrishnan had warned that a U.S.-China conflict in the Pacific could make the disruption seen in the Strait of Hormuz look like a "dry run," underscoring the vulnerability of global trade to critical maritime chokepoints. Balakrishnan has maintained that Singapore would “refuse to choose” between Washington and Beijing, instead acting according to its own long-term national interests, while stressing that the city-state would uphold freedom of navigation through the Strait of Malacca and would not participate in efforts to close, interdict or impose tolls on the waterway.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Late veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft remembered for wit and generosity Late veteran news anchor Richard Morecroft is being remembered as a consummate professional and "a great Australian". The 70-year-old died "at a time of his choosing", a statement on Instagram said, after he received a cancer diagnosis earlier this year. "We are devastated to lose such a warm, generous and caring human and hope that all those who knew him, if only through their TV screens, will remember him fondly," the statement said. Morecroft graced television screens for decades as an ABC 7PM NSW anchor for almost 20 years, BTN presenter and host of Letters and Numbers on SBS. Doogue (left) and Morecroft presenting the news together. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Geraldine Doogue worked with Morecroft as co-host on The National in 1985, when her late husband Ian Carroll changed the half-hour 7PM television bulletin to an hour-long news and current affairs program. Doogue told 702 ABC Sydney that she was shocked by his death and said his professionalism was a big part of his legacy. "He was just terribly good to me and to my late husband ... during that really tumultuous year," she said. "I mean, he was very much for it. Richard, once he was in, he was in. He was a very loyal, he contributed massively." Veteran news anchor and television presenter, Richard Morecroft, is being remembered in tributes. ( Supplied: Instagram ) Doogue said he had a strong sense of what "an ABC authority ought to be" and modelled it "effortlessly". "He had quite a wit about him, but he fundamentally felt his role, I think, was to be that face of the ABC while he was doing this," she said. He also hosted wildlife and educational programs and wrote about nature and the environment. Morecroft eventually moved to the NSW south coast, which Doogue said he called "his cathedral", with his partner of 36 years, Alison Mackay. "He had this whole side in him that was artistic, very much involved with the natural world," she said. "He just thrived in that environment and gave enormously to [and was] very generous to all sorts of charities." Australian Story ABC presenter and friend, Leigh Sales, told ABC 702 Sydney Mornings she first saw Morecroft on TV while watching Behind the News at school in the 1980s. Sales says Morecroft spoke with her just after she started working at the ABC. Sales said when she moved from Brisbane to Sydney as a young reporter at 22, he checked in with her to see how she was settling in. Sales is often seen speaking with young journalists and producers, helping to foster the next generation. "I try really hard to be a good listener and to not be just telling people, 'Well, here's how I do it'," she said. "The other thing that I feel like I learned from him is it doesn't matter if you're the star, you muck in like one of the team and you're not better than anyone else." Richard Morecroft at the 2025 Sculpture in the Valley festival with festival director Stuart McCreery. ( ABC News: ABC Illawarra/Rory Macdonald ) Former ABC presenter Keith Conlon, who met Morecroft when they worked together at a student radio station in Adelaide in the 1970s, said his fellow broadcaster was always a "lovely, warm person". "We kind of invented community radio on the run, and Richard was one of those people who came through the door — he was an arts student [at University of Adelaide]," he said. "He wasn't one of those 'out there' types … Very articulate, very intelligent. Conlon said originally, Morecroft expressed interest in potentially becoming a teacher or an actor, but that it made sense he turned to news reading. "If you're a newsreader, you are in a way acting. You only run the gamut from A to B but you've got to try to lift that news off the page and give things a different nuance," he said. Conlon said Morecroft had "a twinkle in his eye". ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) Conlon said he was "delightful" with "a twinkle in his eye". "He had a beautiful voice — just that lovely tone, but much more than that, he had a considered way of talking," he said. "He loved the language, he loved the sense of what we were talking about, and he was dedicated to doing those things right. He was a perfectionist. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a statement that Morecroft was a "great Australian". "Combining a consummate professionalism with an unyielding humanity, Richard was a figure of absolute trust, a warm and familiar presence who guided us through the good times and bad," he said. "He loved the arts and was deeply passionate about our natural environment.

events.title: Pakistan provides fuel aid to 9 million low-income people as Middle East war drives up prices
events.summary: Pakistan’s government is providing fuel subsidies to over 9 million low-income people as the U.S.-Iran war drives up energy prices ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan’s government has provided fuel subsidies to more than 9 million low-income people as the U.S.-Iran war drives up energy prices, officials said Tuesday. Information Technology Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja said the program was designed to ease the burden on millions of people as regional geopolitical tensions drove up global fuel prices. “We have ensured the process remains seamless and agile for citizens,” Khawaja said, describing it as Pakistan’s first nationwide use of technology to deliver targeted fuel subsidies. Rising petrol and diesel prices have added pressure on a cash-strapped nation already grappling with high inflation, pushing up transportation, food and other living costs and raising fears of anti-government protests. The program, approved by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif last month, offers fuel discounts to eligible motorcycle riders, rickshaw operators and owners of small cars, many of whom depend on their vehicles for work and daily travel. The subsidies were announced after Jamaat-e-Islami, Pakistan’s major Islamist political party, threatened to march on Islamabad to pressure the government to cut taxes on petrol and diesel. Fuel prices in Pakistan have risen by more than 50% since the war between the United States and Iran began earlier this year, adding to pressure on households already struggling with the cost of living. Sharif’s government says the subsidies are intended to help low-income motorists buy gasoline at prewar prices. events.title: Kenya confirms its first Ebola case and death in a man who traveled from Congo
events.summary: A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend has become Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak NAIROBI, Kenya -- A Kenyan citizen who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi over the weekend became Kenya’s first confirmed case of Ebola and the country’s first death from the disease in the fast-moving outbreak , authorities said Tuesday, sparking urgent contact-tracing efforts to try to contain the spread of the virus. The man had been residing in Congo for the past seven years and fell ill about a month ago. He was treated at various hospitals before traveling by road to Kampala, Uganda, where he boarded a flight to the Kenyan capital, arriving on Saturday afternoon, Health Minister Aden Duale said. Health authorities in Kenya have placed the country’s border points on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases. Duale said that the man had been isolated and treated at Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for the Ebola virus and died late Monday. Ebola is highly contagious and spreads in the human population through contact with bodily fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The current outbreak was declared in mid-May, months after it had been spreading in a remote part of eastern Congo. At least 8,400 cases have been recorded, including more than 4,000 deaths, according to government data, making it the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history. Kenya has never had an outbreak of Ebola, according to the Kenya Medical Research Institute. The country hosts a United States-funded isolation center for American citizens exposed to Ebola to quarantine for 21 days before traveling back to the U.S. The isolation facility faced legal battles and deadly protests by locals who feared it was exposing them to the virus. Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in mid-May. Uganda has recorded 20 cases and France one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August. Duale said that 28 contacts of the man who had returned on Saturday, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers on the flight and four crew members, who traveled on the same plane from Uganda, were being traced. The contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released after testing negative for the virus, said the ministry’s director-general, Dr. Patrick Amoth. After the man arrived in Nairobi, his relatives took him in a private vehicle to Nairobi Hospital, where he was immediately isolated. He was buried on Tuesday afternoon in accordance with recommended public safety protocols. The minister said that Kenya had tested 267 samples at five laboratories across the country since May before this first case was detected. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Tuesday commended the “rapid identification, isolation and testing of the patient” and said a high-level team had been dispatched to Kenya to offer support. In Congo, where the outbreak has spread to seven provinces, conditions are difficult. Responders have faced attacks on health teams, misinformation about the virus, a failure by locals to report symptoms and rebel violence that has limited access to treatment centers. While cases have slowed in Ituri province, the epicenter, the outbreak is spreading in emerging hot spots in North Kivu and South Kivu provinces. “It is like fighting a megafire. Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations,” Stéphanie Hoffmann with Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said in a statement. The World Health Organization has warned that it could surpass the deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, which erupted more than a decade ago and killed more than 11,000 people in West Africa. events.title: Paramount and Warner Bros are now one Hollywood giant: Skydance
events.summary: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros CHICAGO -- It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood behemoth. The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together under a new name : Skydance. HBO Max, titles ranging from “Harry Potter” to “Sinners” and networks such as CNN now also find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of “Top Gun” and “The Godfather.” All are under the helm of billionaire David Ellison and his new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz . “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said. “We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.” Ellison’s Skydance bought Paramount for $8 billion last year before setting its sights on Warner. What followed erupted into a tumultuous, roughly yearlong fight over the storied Hollywood giant. Including billions of dollars in debt, the acquisition amounts to nearly $111 billion. The now-combined Skydance marks one of the biggest tie-ups in media and entertainment history, further concentrating power in an industry already run by just a handful of big players. Politics also loomed over much of the process. The Ellison family has notably held a long relationship with Republican President Donald Trump, who said Tuesday that Skydance is “going to be a great company.” The early days of Paramount's quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war. Months after disclosing it was open to selling all or part of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix in December. But Paramount said it also had made offers that Warner management “never engaged meaningfully” with. It soon launched a hostile counterbid . The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Netflix bowed out after Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share. Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement in late February. Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner's future. From awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known. In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors and other professionals announced their “unequivocal opposition” to the Paramount-Warner merger. An open letter — which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams — warned of fewer jobs and “less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.” Others lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon, the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise — who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower, with the words “the future is paramount and the future looks pretty great from here.” Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison. The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, “Remarkably Bright Creatures” actor Sally Field — who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal — stressed that “unique storytelling matters” and “we can’t let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged.” Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix's studio and streaming deal was on the table, with a particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters. Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). And over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration also chimed in about hopes for a new owner. Days after Paramount launched its hostile bid for Warner, Trump said CNN spread “poison and lies” and that it was “imperative” the network be sold. The White House took aim again at CNN in March, over the network's coverage of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.” Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. On Tuesday, he told reporters that the company had "not talked to any political leader of any party about news — other than to say that we want to be in the truth business and we want be in the trust business.

An application is expected to be made to the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel soon. The landowner where Goolwa's first McDonald's could be built has pushed back against local opposition, saying residents have a "democratic right" to choose what to eat or drink. Mick McArdle's commercial property at Hutchinson Street is under contract to the fast-food giant, subject to approval of a development application expected to be lodged with the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel soon. But it has faced vocal opposition, first from a volunteer group dedicated to protecting Goolwa's culinary and cultural heritage, and then from Alexandrina Council, which recently voted to oppose establishing chain-based fast-food outlets in the seaside town. The property is under contract and a development application is expected soon. ( 891 ABC Adelaide: Caroline Horn ) "I don't think that people should have the right to take away other people's democratic right to choose what they eat or drink," Mr McArdle said. "A lot of people actually like the idea of having a McDonald's here. Alexandrina Council last month voted in favour of Cr Peter Oliver's motion, which stated that 38 food outlets in the area, including restaurants, cafes, supermarkets and service stations, already offer food. The motion passed, but not unanimously. It followed lobbying by Cittaslow Goolwa, a volunteer group of about 250 members. Goolwa was the first Australian town to be accredited by Cittaslow International in 2007, a European movement that promotes quality of life and sustainability in towns and cities, and handed a "slow town" status . Cittaslow Goolwa vice-president Christine Putland said recently that the town already sold takeaway hamburgers and did not need to rely on a "multinational company" to create more . "Even if the franchises might be more local or state-based, it is still not growing out of the community," she said in August. A Cittaslow delegation travelled to Goolwa from Italy in 2007 to present the council with a certificate. ( Website: Cittaslow Goolwa ) But Mr McArdle, who has lived in the town since 1978 and runs an automotive repair business on the site, said a significant portion of the town's population of more than 8,000 wanted a McDonald's because it would give young people work, and create more competition for takeaway food. "Competition has to be good for the people in Goolwa; competition keeps the prices at a reasonable level," Mr McArdle said. "And one of the service stations where you come into town has golden fried chicken, pizzas, the whole lot. He acknowledged he had a vested interest in the situation, but pointed out members of Cittaslow Goolwa involved with food outlets did as well. "At the end of the day, if the development application ticks all the boxes as far as zoning and all that sort of stuff, then why should they [McDonald's] not be able to go in there?" Mr McArdle said. Advocates for Goolwa's heritage attractions say the site of a former automotive repair business has been targeted for a McDonald's. Alexandrina Council Mayor Keith Parkes said there were "definitely people in the town" who backed a McDonald's but "the vast majority didn't". "It would be interesting to know whether the people that are in favour are long-term residents or fairly new residents to the area," he said. He agreed that a McDonald's would require local staff. "However, the small businesses in the town at the moment and around the place, struggle to get staff as it is, particularly in the hospitality area," Mr Parkes said. Aside from a McDonald's at the top of the Fleurieu Peninsula at Aldinga, there is only one other McDonald's on the peninsula, which is located 17 kilometres to Goolwa's west at Victor Harbor. "It will be very interesting, when eventually all the information comes out in the open, just where we stand with who's for and who's against it, and their reasons," Mr Parkes said. He reiterated that any development application requiring a change of use for the site would not go to the council for consideration. It would go to the Fleurieu Development Assessment Panel — an independent body established under the Planning, Development and Infrastructure Act 2016.

events.title: Politicians slam Trump’s suggestion that Iran ‘take’ San Diego, Los Angeles
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Both Democrats and Republicans have expressed outrage at Trump’s remarks that cities could be sacrificed in the Iran war. Members of the Republican Party have joined Democrats in questioning remarks made by United States President Donald Trump about the California cities of Los Angeles and San Diego. Much of the backlash came on Tuesday, a day after Trump told a midterm rally in Nebraska that Americans should be willing to make sacrifices to gain victory in the US-Israeli war against Iran. list 1 of 3 US pulls bombers from UK base: Is Iran manoeuvring Trump’s war plans? list 2 of 3 Trump blames Democrats and Ukraine for soaring US fuel prices, not Iran war list 3 of 3 Trump jokes about letting Iran bomb Los Angeles and San Diego Those sacrifices, he implied, could include the destruction of American cities, in case of an Iranian attack. “It’s a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” Trump said, seemingly in reference to the knock-on effects of the war, including rising fuel and fertiliser prices. “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. This is a very small price to pay, and it’s going to be over with very soon.” Trump has downplayed the impact of the war – now in its eighth month – despite polling that shows the conflict is widely unpopular in the US. He has also repeatedly promised the war would end soon, though no lasting ceasefire has been reached so far. The fallout from his Nebraska remarks was swift. Gavin Newsom, an outspoken critic of Trump and the Democratic governor of California, said the president was “deranged”. “This is not only madness. This is dangerous,” Newsom said in a video on the social media platform X, in which he called for Congress to rein in Trump’s behaviour. Newsom, a possible contender in the 2028 presidential race, has clashed repeatedly with Trump. Last year, the two faced off over Trump’s decision to deploy federal troops to California, as part of an effort to support a crackdown on undocumented immigration in the Los Angeles area. In December, a federal judge ruled that the deployment had been illegal and ordered its end. Newsom, who opposed the deployment, cited that conflict in his remarks about Trump’s Nebraska rally. “The president of the United States – the same one who sent in the National Guard into Los Angeles, sent 700 active duty Marines to the second largest city in the United States of America – just invited Iran to take out Los Angeles and San Diego,” Newsom said. He added that Trump’s remarks should convince those who “didn’t think the November election mattered” to vote in the upcoming midterms. Some from Trump’s own party have also expressed shock at his remarks. Jim Desmond, a Republican running in a competitive race for the House of Representatives near San Diego, was among those who distanced themselves from Trump’s statement. “I vehemently disagree with President Trump’s comments. America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond wrote on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” US Representative Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans and is running for re-election in northern California, also called Trump’s comments “unhelpful”. But the White House has dismissed criticism of the remarks, calling it part of a “media freakout” that “is not rooted in reality”. “He was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped,” White House Director of Communications Steven Cheung wrote on social media. “America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” California has the largest population and economy of any state in the US. Because of its population, it also has the most seats in the House of Representatives, at 52. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are up for grabs in November’s midterms, along with a third of the Senate. Also on the ballot are key state and local races. With Republicans’ control of Congress on the line, the results of the midterms are expected to weigh heavily on the final two years of Trump’s second term.

events.title: Licence granted for controversial mineral sands mine
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Avonbank Mineral Sands Project near Horsham granted licence by Victorian regulator WIM Resource dug a test pit, which it then grew barley and lentil crops on. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) Resources Victoria has approved a mining licence for the Avonbank Mineral Sands Project in Dooen, near Horsham. The WIM Resource-operated mine was granted a 20-year licence to dig up materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy projects. WIM Resource says construction could start in late 2027, with the mine to be operational by 2029, pending finances, construction and environmental approvals. Victoria's mining regulator has granted a 20-year licence for a controversial mineral sands mine near Horsham in Victoria's west. Resources Victoria granted the licence to the WIM Resource Avonbank project in Dooen, 15 kilometres north-east of Horsham, licensing the company to mine heavy mineral sands including zircon, titanium and rare earth elements. The mine site will cover about 3,400 hectares, with the Chinese-backed company planning to mine around the clock for materials used in everyday technology and renewable energy infrastructure. The company said construction could begin late next year, with mining starting in 2029, pending finances and other construction and environmental approvals. "This is a major moment for Avonbank, but just as importantly, it is a major moment for the Wimmera Southern Mallee," said the WIM Resource executive team of Eddy Wu and Michael Winternitz in a statement. The company plans to operate the mine for 36 years, digging up 12.75 million tonnes of heavy mineral concentrate. It has done so in the face of stiff opposition from residents and the local council, which has previously labelled the company's attitude to community concerns "disgusting". "Going by my phone calls … I think there's some people absolutely devastated in the community," said Horsham Rural City Council Mayor Brian Klowss. Brian Klowss says the community remains unhappy with the mining company's plans. ( Supplied: Rural Press Club of Victoria ) The Victorian government's mining regulator said it approved the company's licence after determining it had an "appropriate program of work", which it could finance and complete. However, it rejected the company's request for a 38-year-licence. The Horsham Rural City Council has previously raised numerous concerns about the proposed mine, including dust issues, and concerns with use of the nearby intermodal freight hub and rehabilitation prospects of the land. Resources Victoria said mineral handling procedures, real-time onsite monitoring and the mine's operating hours would be finalised as part of the work plan assessment. The mine site is near Dooen, a rural village in the Wimmera region. ( Supplied: WIM Resource ) "This outcome is as a result of diligent assessment work by numerous agencies and departments at both the state and Commonwealth level," said Resources Victoria director for regulatory operations, Laura Helm. But Cr Klowss said many in the community felt their voices had not been heard, and that he was "dubious" about the site's rehabilitation plans. He said while some concerns had been considered, questions remained about real-time air monitoring and a potential mining licence for the nearby freight hub. "They're devastated about what it's going to do to our community," he said. Cr Klowss said he was told to expect a licensing decision in January, and that former planning minister Lily D'Ambrosio and current minister Sonya Kilkenny would not speak to council about the mine. "I'm actually probably curious to know why the decision was made now," he said. The ABC has contacted the Victorian government for a response. Victorian Farmers Federation (VFF) president Ryan Milgate said the licensing approval on the eve of an election was fundamentally at odds with the VFF's call for a pause on new critical minerals projects. The mine site will cover about 3,400 hectares. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The Avonbank mine is one of 10 mineral sands projects planned for the Wimmera-Mallee and across the New South Wales border. WIM Resource said it estimated the project, when complete, would support 1,000 full-time local jobs, and that it would continue to work with traditional owners, councils, landowners, businesses and the broader community. The company also said it would provide a $40 million community benefit fund, progressively funded over the life of the mine, that would provide long-term investment for communities across the region. WIM Resource says the mine will support the community.

events.title: Trillions are being ‘wasted’ on the AI boom, Arthur Hayes says. He’s betting on what comes next
events.summary: Humanity is “wasting multi-trillion dollars” on AI data center build-up, according to former BitMEX CEO Arthur Hayes. A key test could come in late 2027 or 2028, when new data center capacity is delivered and customers face their compute commitments. Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies could benefit from the excess liquidity that follows a bailout, Hayes said. Former BitMEX CEO Arthur Hayes is betting that the artificial intelligence boom will eventually produce a familiar outcome: too much investment, a crash and, ultimately, a bailout that sends crypto higher. Hayes, co-founder and chief investment officer of crypto investment firm Maelstrom, said in response to questions from CNBC at the Gamma Prime Investing Conference in Singapore that humanity is "wasting multi-trillion dollars" on building AI data centers. The massive data center buildout would ultimately make computing power "extremely cheap and extremely plentiful," Hayes said. The bet runs against the massive investment pouring into AI infrastructure, as technology companies race to secure the computing power needed to develop and run increasingly advanced AI models. Hayes sees that buildout eventually becoming overcapacity, setting the stage for a downturn that he expects will ultimately benefit crypto. "If you study financial history and you study every single major technological rollout, it always is overbuilt. There always is a crash, and there always is a bailout," Hayes said. Investors who position for those bailouts stand to benefit, Hayes said, pointing to the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis and other episodes over the past two decades. "Thankfully, we have bitcoin and other crypto to soak up that excess liquidity, and so we know the asset that's going to perform the best when the bailout comes," Hayes said, adding that "you just have to be patient." SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic are among the end users driving demand for computing power, and none of them makes money, Hayes said. Once the data centers currently under construction are completed, infrastructure providers will seek payment for the compute those companies have committed to, he said. That could come in late 2027 or 2028, when much of the new data center capacity is delivered, according to Hayes. The bull case is that AI becomes "so useful" over the next 12 months that demand grows enough for AI companies to become profitable, Hayes said. Some companies supplying the AI boom are already making money, Hayes said, pointing to memory chipmakers and Nvidia. The question for investors is whether they are paying the right multiple for those companies' forward earnings, he added. Hayes also said he does not like betting on falling prices or shorting AI companies, calling it "not really a great investment opportunity," but added that major technological rollouts have historically been overbuilt. The abundance of computing power created by the AI buildout is also behind Hayes' latest crypto venture, Flop, an AI-agent payments project expected to launch in the first quarter of 2027. Cheaper and more plentiful computing power would allow AI agents to proliferate, Hayes said. His new project, Flop, aims to create a spot market for computing power, where participants are rewarded with Flop tokens for providing GPUs and performing AI inference. There is currently no payments network for AI agents, Hayes said. Flop aims to create a spot market for compute. "If agents can convert a currency directly into compute, which is what they eat and consume, then they will use this currency," Hayes said. "That's our bet."

events.title: Yemeni forces launch offensive to retake Houthi-held al-Waziiya in Taiz
events.summary: The mountainous district is key to control of Mocha, the Red Sea port the Houthis seized last month. Houthis, Saudi-led forces claim victories as Yemen fighting rages on Forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have launched an operation to capture a strategic mountainous district from the Houthis as part of a wider push to retake the Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The offensive on the district of al-Waziiya in Taiz governorate on Tuesday came as Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s government, intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile targeting the city of Khamis Mushait. list 1 of 3 Pakistan, Turkiye join Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means list 2 of 3 Saudi Arabia says East-West pipeline pumping 5.8 million bpd list 3 of 3 Yemen’s government is on the attack against the Houthis. What has changed? The operation is part of the “Dawn of Yemen” offensive that was announced on Sunday by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014. The media centre of Yemen’s army said in a post on X that the Homeland Shield Forces, a pro-government military faction, have begun “a large-scale operation” to retake al-Waziiya. “The armed forces have secured strategic hills overlooking the al-Mansoura area, amidst a mass retreat by the Houthi militia,” it said, citing a military source. The Houthis, however, denied the claim, saying they had successfully repelled the Yemeni government advance in al-Waziiya. The mountainous district is located west of Taiz, east of the Red Sea port of Mocha. The Houthis had seized Mocha and areas around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait – a strategic maritime corridor – in a lightning offensive last month. “These are the mountains that the Houthis took control of prior to the takeover of the city of Mocha,” Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said, reporting from Sanaa. “If the Yemeni government is serious about taking over the city of Mocha, they cannot do so unless they take over the region in the district of al-Waziiya,” he added. The fighting came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait. Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the coalition, said the Houthi missile threats originated from Houthi-held Sanaa and the governorates of Saada and Amran. “The coalition continues to neutralise the threat posed by ballistic and surface-to-surface missiles and to destroy their launch sources,” he added. Earlier on Tuesday, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz airport in Jazan and Najran airport, near the Yemen border, were hit in attacks that wounded three people. The attacks caused injuries of “varying severity” and material damage, and the injured have been taken to hospital, the authority said. The Houthis said late on Monday that their forces targeted sites across southern Saudi Arabia, including airports and military sites. The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, has confirmed its participation in the Yemeni government offensive to retake all Houthi-held territory, saying 100 of its fighter jets are providing air support. Pakistan and Turkiye have also agreed to activate “deterrence measures” under their mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia and rapidly deploy forces to the Gulf kingdom to counter attacks by the Houthis.

events.title: Everything we know about the suspected plague case in Russia so far
events.summary: This undated photo released in 2019 by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, shows the institute workers in a lab. The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East via AP On October 2, an Irkutsk lab employee died from pneumonia. There's confusion over what illness the woman died from, with conflicting reports out of the region. The World Health Organization says the US is at "very low risk" of being exposed to the plague. After a technician at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia died, Russian officials are attempting to calm global concerns. Daria Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, died on October 2 after being hospitalized days earlier for pneumonia in Shelekhov, a nearby town . The World Health Organization told the Associated Press on October 6 that the plague presents a "very low" risk to the broader European region. That doesn't mean we know everything — or really, much of anything — as of now. While there's no confirmation of a plague outbreak so far, conflicting reports about how the alleged "patient zero" got infected, whether she was infected at work, and Russia's current safety protocols have given some medical experts pause. "It's an odd situation that needs more transparency and requires more information for clarity," Dr. Nahid Bhadelia, the founding director of the Boston University Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases, told Business Insider. Here's everything we know so far. What happened to Darya Shipilova? As of now, not much is known about Shipilova's cause of death. Still, independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikala said she was hospitalized on September 29. A friend told CNN that Shipilova died on October 2. Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, said that testing Shipilova found "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" and that she died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology." People of Baikal , an independent regional news outlet, reported that Shipilova was "deeply anxious about ever infecting anyone if something happened," according to one of her colleagues at the institute. Other colleagues called her "responsible" and described the anti-plague institute as "a serious facility" in terms of safety measures. Did she die of pneumonic plague? Reports from Russian exiled publications — ones forced to operate outside Russia or use decentralized reporting methods — speculate whether Shipilova died from the pneumonic plague. The Moscow Times , an independent publication located in Amsterdam, reported unconfirmed claims that Shipilova may have broken a test tube containing plague bacteria at the institute before she fell ill. It also reported, citing Russian Telegram channel Mash, that she was hospitalized with pneumonia symptoms and placed on a ventilator before her death. Russian authorities had not publicly confirmed either account. Why has this case raised an alarm? Reports from Russian state media and independent publications have often clashed, leading to more questions than answers. "The scenario, to me, doesn't fit together," Bhadelia said. If the reports of a broken test tube were true, an anti-plague institute should have several safety measures in place, such as protective equipment, ventilation, and clear treatment protocols. "She needs to have broken a test tube, have a breach in her personal protective equipment, not reported the incident, not gotten the antibiotic prophylaxis, just gone home under no one's observation, shown up at a local district hospital, and exposed 200 people," Bhadelia added. That explanation, however, is at odds with another report from the People of Baikal. There were also confusing reports about Russia's safety protocols. Rospotrebnadzor said authorities identified and monitored 197 people who had contact with Shipilova. It said that two people tested positive for COVID-19 and two others for rhinovirus. Everyone else who was tested showed no signs of other infectious agents. "It could be that we just don't have the perfect information, that there might be some media sensationalism in the regional media, or there may be something else going on that we don't know," Bhadelia said. Still, the current risk is nowhere near a COVID-19-level threat. What is pneumonic plague — and how does it spread? Yersinia pestis, or plague , is a bacterial infection that progresses very quickly, Bhadelia said. Patients with pneumonic plague can sometimes develop symptoms in under 24 hours. It can be fatal if left untreated. Luckily, when caught early, treatment is also pretty straightforward: A course of antibiotics. In July 2025, an Arizona man contracted pneumonic plague from two ill cats. He was medically evaluated after two days of abdominal pain, chest pain, and dry cough. He died eight hours after admission. However, all 46 people exposed to him recovered after taking antibiotics. Bhadelia said it points to one of the biggest mysteries of the Russia case so far: If Shipilova was reportedly experienced, knew she was exposed, and reported it, why wouldn't she be under quarantine and quickly treated with medication? "Early identification and post-exposure prophylaxis is one of the ways that this could be avoided," she said. Is there any risk to people in the US? The WHO says the risk outside Russia is "very low," and there is no evidence of cases in the US or beyond the Irkutsk area. What we're missing from Russia Bhadelia, who is also the founding director of the Biothreats Emergence, Analysis, and Communications Network, said the organization is trying to provide the most up-to-date information on the pneumonic plague in Russia. It's not easy. For one, Russia is notorious for clamping down on the free press, particularly after the start of the Ukraine war . Additionally, some early reports of the plague, including from pro-Kremlin sources such as REN TV , appeared inaccessible when Business Insider checked on October 6. Some of the official reports from Rospotrebnadzor have also been vague. For example, the agency said it tested Shipilova and found no connection to plagues attached to her work. However, Bhadelia said it's unclear exactly what she was tested for. "We should find out what the results were of what she was negative for, even if they don't know what she's positive for," she said. For onlookers, the situation carries some parallels to the COVID-19 pandemic . Over six years later, WHO still hasn't confirmed the origin of COVID-19, which Bhadelia said could be contributing to the panic. "Transparency is important," she said. "We've learned from the COVID lesson that this can spin out to be much bigger." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Former CIA official with Top Secret clearance admits to $194 million fraud, including 298 gold bars and four luxury South Florida properties
events.summary: A former senior federal official pleaded guilty Tuesday to defrauding the government of about $194 million, using invented classified programs to buy 298 gold bars, four luxury South Florida properties, watches and two BMWs. David J. Rush of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud in federal court in Alexandria, after reaching a tentative plea deal in September . Under the final agreement, he owes at least $195.4 million in restitution. The fraud caused $193.6 million in losses, according to court documents, and $1.8 million in private charter flights he billed to the government. Rush held senior executive posts and a TS/SCI clearance at an agency the filings call “Government Agency 1.” CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the CIA referred the case to the FBI after an internal investigation “identified potential crimes.” “David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions,” Ratcliffe said. “Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche, according to the DOJ announcement. “The Trump Administration is committed to rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, including by prosecuting those who foolishly defraud American taxpayers.” $145 million billed for “consulting” Court documents say that Rush made up two programs beginning around October 2025. The first was a fake Special Access Program that supposedly required buying luxury real estate in South Florida. His job let him identify requirements and approve resources for them, which effectively made him his own approving official, the court documents read. Rush held fake briefings to admit contractors to the made-up program, in a process known as a “read-in,” and told the contractors the work was highly classified—and had one sign an NDA. When an agency contracting official questioned the spending, Rush said the official had no “need to know.” Between November 2025 and March 2026, Rush had a government contractor send about $145 million to 0701 Holdings LLC, a company set up at his direction that billed for “consulting.” That money was then used to buy two Palm Beach homes for $21.9 million and $27 million, a $13.65 million Palm Beach parcel and a $40 million parcel in Hobe Sound. Rush planned to resell the properties for profit, the documents continue. He called one guesthouse “super unique and cool” but questioned whether buying it would “hamstring us when we’re selling.” 298 gold bars For the second program, Rush told a subcontractor’s executive that a sensitive assignment for about six people allowed the use of gold, diamonds or cryptocurrency. The subcontractor bought 298 gold bars at a cost to the government of $46,361,721, including fees, and delivered them in Pelican cases to a safe in Rush’s Loudoun County office. On May 19, FBI agents found all 298 bars at Rush’s home, their serial numbers matching the subcontractor’s records. They also found about $2.1 million in cash, €104,795 and more than 30 watches, including several Rolexes. Rush reached his position partly by lying about his background, the documents read. He claimed to be a combat veteran and military pilot with a bachelor’s degree from a university in South Carolina and a doctorate from one in New York. However, the court documents say he graduated from neither, and never flew for the military. He left the Navy reserves in 2015, but claimed 392 hours of military leave from his civilian job starting in 2021. In the statement of facts, Rush also admitted that in late 2025 he gave a foreign government official information about a U.S. clandestine human source. As part of his agreement, Rush will forfeit the gold, cash, 35 watches, two 2026 BMW Alpina XB7s, $38.65 million seized from the LLC’s account, and properties in Palm Beach and on Jupiter Island. He faces up to 20 years in prison at his Jan. 28, 2027, sentencing. The Justice Department said its investigation is continuing, and the Director of National Intelligence has asked the Inspector General for the Intelligence Community to investigate. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Sudan’s al-Burhan rejects talks, vows to retake all territory from RSF
events.summary: At least 10 civilians were killed in West Kordofan and 5,500 displaced in Blue Nile as clashes widened on Tuesday. Sudan's army advances in North Kordofan as RSF drone attacks intensify Sudan’s military chief, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, has promised to seize “every inch” of territory under the control of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), rejecting negotiations to end three and a half years of war. Al-Burhan made the comments on Tuesday while addressing a gathering in Village 5, located in the northern Sudanese locality of Merowe, according to the Sudan News Agency. list 1 of 2 Why do Sudan’s humanitarian truces keep failing and who is to blame? list 2 of 2 Sudan’s historical famine echoes through latest hunger crisis He said the “military option” would continue until the RSF was removed from Sudan. The Sudanese army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023 after leaders of the groups fell out over plans to integrate the paramilitary force into Sudan’s army. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million , according to UN and international estimates. Al-Burhan’s pledge to continue fighting came as 10 civilians were killed and several others were wounded in an attack by the RSF in Sudan’s West Kordofan state, according to a local charity group. In a statement, the Dar Hamar Emergency Committee accused the RSF of multiple violations against civilians in Abu Ajal village in the southeastern countryside of En Nahud. The RSF has been massing in West Kordofan as Sudan’s army advances towards the cities of En Nahud and Al Khuway after gains in neighbouring North Kordofan. In Sudan’s Blue Nile state, more than 5,500 people were displaced from villages over three days amid deteriorating security, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Tuesday. Meanwhile, an envoy of US President Donald Trump said Sudanese parties must take the lead in talks to end the war. In a post on X on Monday, Massad Boulos, the US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, said peace could be achieved “through an inclusive Sudanese-owned and Sudanese-led national dialogue, transition toward a civilian-led government”. The US State Department said last month that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the RSF, nor their respective leaders “represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan”.
