events.title: Read the memo from Skydance’s product chief after Paramount and WBD joined forces
events.summary: Skydance's chief product officer addressed the Paramount and WBD teams in a memo after the merger. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Skydance's product chief addressed the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery teams after the merger. Dane Glasgow sent a memo to staffers on Tuesday about working together going forward. He said the team would help keep Skydance on the "cutting edge" as technology reshapes storytelling. The product chief at the newly dubbed Skydance is ready to get the ball rolling — and encouraging employees to do the same — on the heels of Paramount Skydance's merger with Warner Bros. Discovery . "The leaders who will have the greatest impact here are the ones with a bias for action under ambiguity. They let the best idea win, full stop," Dane Glasgow, chief product officer at Skydance , told staffers Tuesday in a memo that was obtained by Business Insider. Glasgow told the Paramount and WBD teams that he recognized the months leading up to the merger had been "challenging" and that he appreciated their "resilience" and "steadfast commitment." "I'm very excited about what we are going to build — an organization where technical craft matters, where the best ideas win and where we can move at a pace that matches our ambition," he said. Glasgow also nodded to CEO David Ellison's remarks about the merger, saying technology was "reshaping how stories are created, distributed and experienced" and that the team would help keep the company "on the cutting edge of that work." Paramount Skydance's $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery was completed on Tuesday, creating a new media behemoth called Skydance . Skydance's properties now include Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Studios, HBO, CBS,  CNN, and more , as well as valuable intellectual properties such as DC Comics and Harry Potter. Read the full memo Glasgow sent Skydance employees below: Team, I want to take a moment to welcome you all to the new Product & Tech team at Skydance! For more than a century, Paramount and Warner Bros. have operated as two legendary companies that have built new worlds, delighted audiences, and shared stories that have redefined our industry. As we expand our horizons, I want to make sure we all take this moment to celebrate the work we've done to reach such a historic moment. As a team, we're bringing together some of the best product, technology, operations and production service professionals in the business. We will build and deliver next generation products and services that leverage our combined expertise to bring richer entertainment experiences and capabilities to our team's key customers: creatives, consumers, advertisers, content and distribution partners, and employees. I also recognize that the last few months have been challenging, especially as many of you have been on the forefront of our companies' ongoing transformations. I deeply appreciate your resilience and your steadfast commitment to delivering for our stakeholders every single day. And I specifically want to thank Avi Saxena, Dave Duvall, James Crossland and Tyler Whitworth for their leadership on the WBD side — I look forward to continuing to work with you all and bringing our teams even closer together. As we get started, I also wanted to share my initial views as they relate to leadership, culture and ways of working: 1. On culture: We're bringing together two organizations that each have a lot to be proud of, and a lot to learn from one another. Let's go into this assuming best intent with genuine curiosity about how each other works. We will listen and ask each other questions, sharing information and flagging areas of disagreement or misalignment openly and constructively. 2. On how we work: We will always start with a hypothesis and move quickly to build prototypes and internal builds to test our assumptions. We will be early testers of our own products and ensure that our fast and iterative process results in high-quality experiences for our customers. We'll continuously provide feedback and encourage our people to stay curious as we explore new ways of doing things. And we'll hold two things in tension at once: patience with each other as we blend two cultures, and a sense of urgency to correct processes that only serve to slow us down. 3. On leadership: The leaders who will have the greatest impact here are the ones with a bias for action under ambiguity. They let the best idea win, full stop. They're transparent in both directions: honest with their teams about what's happening, and quick to surface concerns upward before they become bigger problems. They keep the customer at the center of every decision they make. They are willing to roll up their sleeves and demonstrate both their technical prowess and managerial expertise. And they own the outcome and hold a high standard for what we deliver and how we deliver it. As David mentioned earlier today, technology is reshaping how stories are created, distributed and experienced, and this team will play an important role in keeping Skydance on the cutting edge of that work. We each have established roadmaps coming into the fourth quarter, and I am excited to keep our momentum going. As we share organizational updates with you in the coming weeks and months, I ask that you stay focused on your current priorities and responsibilities. As decisions are made, we will share them deliberately and thoughtfully as we build a world-class, high-performing organization and culture. If you have questions, please visit the Skydance Integration Hub, which will serve as a go-to source for updates, FAQs, and other information as we progress through this transition. A replay of today's Town Hall will also be available there. In the coming weeks, I will spend time across our locations listening and learning from many of you. We'll find opportunities for our team to create and collaborate — not just among ourselves, but with our partners across the organization, including DTC, Studios, Finance, Advertising Sales and many others. I'm very excited about what we are going to build — an organization where technical craft matters, where the best ideas win and where we can move at a pace that matches our ambition. Thank you for the work that got us here, and for everything we'll achieve as we continue to power our climb together - let's go! Cheers! Dane Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Musk’s SpaceX in talks to borrow US$40 billion to buy Nvidia chips
events.summary: SpaceX is seeking to raise about US$10 billion (S$12.8 billion) in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips. SpaceX is seeking US$40 billion, led by Apollo Global Management, to buy Nvidia chips, showing huge demand for AI computing power. The plan includes US$10 billion in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt, with the deal expected to close in 2027. The report highlights rising costs and heavy AI spending, while SpaceX shares fell and Nvidia’s stock rose after the news. Elon Musk’s SpaceX is in talks with banks and investors to raise US$40 billion (S$51.1 billion) of debt to buy chips from Nvidia, sources familiar with the matter said, underscoring the insatiable demand among AI developers for more computing power. Pacific Investment Management is one of the investment managers looking at the deal, said the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the talks are private. SpaceX’s fund-raising discussions are in an early stage and could end without a deal being completed, they said. Musk’s AI, satellite and rocket conglomerate is seeking to raise about US$10 billion in bank loans and US$30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips, the Financial Times reported earlier, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. Apollo Global Management is leading the financing, in a deal that is expected to close in 2027, the newspaper said. Tech companies and artificial intelligence model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to build and lease giant data centres full of chips to power AI systems. The worldwide expansion of computing capacity has sent the costs of everything from land to chips and power-generation equipment soaring, touching off a series of massive financing deals. Nvidia, SpaceX and Apollo did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Times’ report. SpaceX shares erased gains in postmarket trading following the FT’s report, falling 1.2% in US postmarket trading to $169.79. Nvidia’s stock rose fractionally. In September , Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by the end of 2026 . It was the most detailed timetable that the trillionaire has given yet for expansion plans for the Memphis-area cluster. Colossus 2 now has 110,000 Nvidia GB200 chips and 440,000 GB300s, Musk said in a post on X. A further 220,000 GB300s are due to be operational next week, with another 220,000 expected in November, he said. An additional 220,000 may come online late December “if we get lucky”, he said. Musk’s xAI has recruited multiple Wall Street firms to test its Grok chatbot, including Apollo and Morgan Stanley. Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source US$500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure. The coalition – which also includes Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group and KKR & Co. – said at the time that they would “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers”. Executives indicated that it will focus on debt financing to provide access to compute for Nvidia’s largest customers and signalled that there were already many deals in the works that would qualify towards this commitment. events.title: South Sudan’s aid crisis deepens as food stocks run low
events.summary: More than one million people could lose life-saving aid by October as funding shrinks and arrivals from Sudan continue. Renk, South Sudan – The arrivals begin before dawn. Women carry children and plastic bags; men walk with almost nothing. Every week, about 3,000 refugees and returnees cross into South Sudan from Sudan. Many arrive hungry, exhausted and with little or no money. But the food assistance they depend on is also running out. More than one million vulnerable people could lose access to life-saving food and nutrition assistance by October unless additional resources are secured, according to the World Food Programme (WFP). In Malakal, one of the agency’s key logistics hubs in the Upper Nile state, food stocks have fallen from 10,000 metric tonnes at this time last year to less than 300 tonnes now. The drop comes as humanitarian agencies face shrinking resources while needs continue to rise, WFP says. WFP assistant executive director Matthew Hollingworth visited Renk and Malakal in Upper Nile and Pigi county in Jonglei state this month, where he witnessed firsthand the pressures facing communities already struggling with conflict, displacement, hunger and climate shocks. Hollingworth told Al Jazeera that the war in Sudan had driven up prices and put additional pressure on a country already stretched by the influx of refugees. “The war in Sudan has been catastrophic for the north of this country. Prices have gone so much higher due to the complexity of importing goods from Sudan,” he said. “Moreover, the influx of refugees [comes] to a country that is really stretched when it comes to helping them.” In Renk, Hollingworth saw the effects of drought alongside areas still affected by flooding. “It all comes at the time when the international community has a lot less to give, and we don’t have the same resources we used to have,” he told Al Jazeera. “On the other side, the government of South Sudan has to consider the issue of illegal checkpoints that prevent us from being able to get everywhere. We need to reach vulnerable people across the country.” Peter Maker, a displaced person in Pigi, said insecurity and the arrival of people displaced from other areas had made it difficult to farm or find work. “We face major challenges due to national insecurity and an influx of people from other areas. Our main issues are insecurity and lack of access to farmland,” he told Al Jazeera. “Although I am able-bodied and qualified to work, insecurity prevents me from travelling for opportunities or farming safely outside, leaving us heavily reliant on the UN and aid.” Maker said longer-term solutions were needed and warned that further cuts or blockages to assistance would be devastating. He attributed much of the local suffering to political leadership and divisions between communities, while saying people currently survive by sharing resources, relying on God and receiving occasional aid. Renk, in Upper Nile state near the border with Sudan, has become a major entry point for people fleeing the war that erupted there in April 2023. More than 1.4 million refugees and returnees have crossed into South Sudan since the war erupted in Sudan in 2023, according to the World Food Programme. Many arrive after journeys marked by checkpoints, extortion and violence, with little idea of what comes next. Zainab Musa, a mother of six staying at a transit centre in Renk, recently crossed from Sudan. She said conditions were difficult and there was little food. “The humanitarian situation is hard and there is nothing to eat, just hunger,” she told Al Jazeera. “I thought of moving from the border at Jodha to the transit centre to look for help.” Musa said she planned to travel to her grandfather in Bunj, in Maban county, in Upper Nile. The transit centres in Renk were not designed for the scale of arrivals they are now receiving. Families wait for onward transport to Malakal or other parts of South Sudan, while some remain for months. The WFP has been forced to reduce rations and cut support as funding has dried up. In August, the WFP and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) warned that more than 650,000 refugees and asylum seekers were at risk of losing food assistance. They said food and nutrition assistance for the most vulnerable 240,000 refugees was expected to run out in September without additional funding. Nura Mohammed Ahmed, a Sudanese refugee, said hunger and a lack of adequate nutrition were already taking a heavy toll at the transit centre. Malakal has hosted families displaced by conflict and disaster for years. The former Protection of Civilians site, redesignated as an internally displaced people’s settlement earlier this year, hosts nearly 40,000 displaced people across more than 6,000 households. Many have been displaced for years. But basic services are also coming under pressure.

events.title: NSW coalmine climate ruling a massive shake-up to Australia's oil and gas
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts High Court rules in favour of climate group in Hunter Valley coalmine case Tony Lonergan and Wendy Wales from the Hunter Valley community group which faught the case rally outside the High Court of Australia in Canberra. ( Supplied: Zoe Lonergan ) A landmark ruling in the High Court has found planning authorities are required to consider the emissions caused by burning fossil fuels overseas when approving projects. Three of the five judges found in favour of a Hunter Valley residents' group, which halted the Mount Pleasant mine expansion last year in the New South Wales Court of Appeal. The High Court case centred around the open-cut coalmine near Muswellbrook, which was approved for expansion by NSW planning authorities in 2022, before being halted through the community-led court battle last year. The extension of the Mount Pleasant coalmine would add roughly twice Australia's total annual greenhouse gas emissions to the atmosphere. ( Supplied: Nearmaps ) MACH Energy, which operates the mine and brought the High Court case, wants to extract a total of 444 million tonnes of coal from the site, almost doubling the amount currently produced each year, until 2048. Because the thermal coal is for export, the more than 870 million tonnes of carbon dioxide-equivalent emissions caused by its combustion will occur in other countries. They are known as scope 3 emissions and are not accounted for in Australia's greenhouse gas inventory. Residents from the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) have fought to block the expansion on the grounds that those "downstream" emissions will also cause climate-related harms locally and should have been considered as part of the planning process. In July 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal agreed that the project's global emissions would cause local climate change impacts and that the Independent Planning Commission's 2022 approval did not take this into account. MACH Energy wants to extract more than 440 million tonnes of coal from the site. ( Supplied: Climate Media Centre ) MACH Energy's appeal to the High Court sought to overturn that NSW Court of Appeal decision on the basis that scope 3 emissions from the project should be considered at a global scale through pre-existing obligations under the Paris Agreement. Three of the five High Court judges dismissed that appeal, finding that the NSW Independent Planning Commission needed to "consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions". Decision could impact other projects The case is expected to have national implications for the way fossil fuel project approvals take global emissions into account. Legal experts say the case is the first time the High Court has dealt with questions about who is responsible for greenhouse gas emissions and the harm they cause, and whether local planning authorities have a duty to consider how fossil fuel projects contribute to the climate crisis. In a week of floods and droughts across Australia, the government extended the life of one of the world's largest gas facilities. Anita O'Hart, the principal lawyer who fought the case for the resident's group, said it was a historic ruling for Australian environmental law "and for the communities who have been fighting for accountability in the fossil fuel approvals process". "The High Court has confirmed that planning authorities cannot ignore the chain of causation from a project's emissions," she said. "The Independent Planning Commission was required to consider those impacts, and that obligation is now binding across the NSW planning system." MACH Energy released a statement on its website acknowledging the court decision, which it said it would carefully review. "We advanced this appeal to obtain clarity on important questions regarding the scope of mandatory considerations in environmental decision-making," the company said. "Clear legal principles benefit proponents, regulators, communities and environmental organisations alike. The High Court has now provided that guidance." MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant coal mine can continue operating until the end of 2032. ( 7.30 Report ) The company noted that a permit provided by the NSW government in August would allow the mine to continue operating for another six years. "Our focus now is on working constructively with regulators, governments, local communities and other stakeholders to understand the practical implications of today's High Court decision" the MACH Energy statement said.

events.title: Why Darwin could become 'a major interconnection point' for global data
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Darwin could host multiple international subsea cables amid NT government's digital infrastructure push Topic: Urban Development and Planning The developments have been pitched for the Darwin suburb of Fannie Bay. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Development applications show Google and Inligo Networks want to connect subsea fibre-optic cables to infrastructure in Darwin's Fannie Bay. Telecom analysts and the government say the NT capital city is optimally placed to serve markets in south-east Asia and Australia's southern states. Darwin is becoming a "network ecosystem" of subsea cables, terrestrial cables and data centres, Mr Tan says, which has been embraced by the NT government. As data centres and fibre-optic cable networks proliferate globally, planning documents show two international subsea cables could soon dock in the Darwin suburb of Fannie Bay. An application lodged with the Development Consent Authority shows tech giant Google plans to connect its "Bosun" subsea cable to infrastructure on the corner of Atkin Drive and Conacher Street. Subsea cables are fibre-optic wires which run along the ocean floor, transmitting data to onshore landing stations and facilitating intercontinental internet traffic. The planning application does not detail what the telecom infrastructure at the site will be. The proposed development is located near the Darwin Ski Club, at the corner of Atkin Drive and Conacher Street. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) If approved, Bosun will travel through telecommunication conduits — connected to the Fannie Bay site — to Christmas Island , where there is onward connectivity to Singapore. Bosun forms part of Google's Connect Australia initiative , a network of fibre-optic cables connecting Darwin and Perth to the east coast and trans-Pacific cable networks. On the parcel of land directly opposite the proposed Bosun site, multinational subsea cable company Inligo Networks is building Darwin's first "open" cable landing station. According to designs published by Inligo, the station will comprise a single-storey building and is set to harbour part of Inligo's Asia Connect Cable System (ACC-1). Designs for the building planned by Inligo Digital Australia's open cable landing station at Fannie Bay. ( Supplied: Inligo ) Once complete, ACC-1 will connect Darwin to four Indonesian cities, East-Timor, Singapore, the Philippines, Guam and the US mainland. It will also connect to Inligo's Unite Cable System — a network linking Darwin, Adelaide and Melbourne, granted major project status under the former NT government. The facility's "open" status means it will be accessible to multiple telecommunication companies and service providers looking to use one of the cables for their networks. Darwin is on track to host five international subsea cables in the coming years, with major tech firms seeking to exploit the city's proximity to south-east Asia and the Pacific. The NT's first international subsea cable, Vocus's Darwin-Jakarta-Singapore Cable system (DJSC), went online in July 2023 following a government investment of nearly $8 million. The lot is typically used by Darwin Ski Club patrons for overflow parking. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Hawaiki Nui 1, a subsea cable stretching from Singapore to Sydney via the Indo-Pacific, is being developed by digital infrastructure company BW Digital. Meanwhile, Meta's gargantuan Project Waterworth is on track to stretch around the world — from the United States' east to west coast — will also connect to Australia via Darwin. Marvin Tan, a senior research analyst from telecom research group TeleGeography, said Darwin is optimally placed to serve markets in south-east Asia and Australia's southern states. Marvin Tan says Darwin's geographic proximity to south-east Asia means it can service international markets wanting to bypass the South China Sea. ( Supplied ) "Traditionally, cables reached the eastern parts or the western parts of Australia, but now you can simply tap into Darwin and the terrestrial network to reach both," he said. Mr Tan also noted Australia's geopolitical stability and robust legal system, which he said make it an optimal location for data centres and, subsequently, subsea cable development. Google plans to connect its Bosun subsea cable to infrastructure in Fannie Bay. ( Supplied: FYFE/Google Earth ) Darwin specifically gives international proponents of data centres and subsea cables an opportunity to bypass the South China Sea. "Instead of going from Singapore to Japan and the United States, you can go south to Darwin and then back to the US, like with Project Waterworth and ACC-1," Mr Tan said.

events.title: US judge authorises fund to subpoena New York Fed for documents related to Radiant World
events.summary: Investment fund Mariner Atlantic Multi-Strategy LLC has filed a criminal complaint in Switzerland against iron ore trader Radiant World. NEW YORK – A US judge on Oct 6 authorised an investment fund that filed a criminal complaint in Switzerland against iron ore trader Radiant World to subpoena payments records from the US Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Clearing House Interbank Payments System. US District Judge John Cronan in Manhattan said Mariner Atlantic Multi-Strategy LLC’s requested subpoenas were not unduly intrusive or burdensome because they sought seemingly “easy-to-collect payments records related to specific accounts and a specific timeframe”. He also said subpoenas were appropriate because it was not otherwise possible for Mariner to obtain the records it sought, and Swiss courts were “receptive” to assistance from their US counterparts. Radiant World did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside business hours. REUTERS

events.title: Big Red Bash says 2027 will be the outback festival's last hurrah
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Big Red Bash organisers say 2027 is final year of the Birdsville festival Thousands of caravans lined up around the stage, beside the Big Red sand dune in 2024. ( Supplied: Matt Williams ) The Big Red Bash will be held one last time in Birdsville in 2027. The outback festival has been a major tourism drawcard for 13 years. The festival site is still underwater, but organisers are confident the site will be dry by mid next year. The Big Red Bash has been a major event in outback Queensland for more than a decade, but organisers say next year will be the festival's last hurrah. "To make a call like this after 13 years, it's a very hard thing to do," festival founder Greg Donovan said. "We built this festival over many years; we built it from our heart, but this decision is one we've had to make with our head. It's so sad to know next year will be our last one. Flooding in front of the Big Red sand dune in 2026. ( Supplied: Ben Fullagar ) "Our family and many other people put their hearts and souls into making this the great event that it is." Birdsville is 1,500 kilometres west of Brisbane, where Queensland, South Australia and the Northern Territory meet. Mr Donovan said that while event costs had increased in recent years, expense wasn't the main challenge. The event was cancelled this year after widespread flooding inundated the site at the Big Red sand dune. Big Red sand dune surrounded by water in May, 2026. ( ABC Western Qld: Heidi Sheehan ) In 2025, a scaled-back version was held, with a John Williamson concert at Big Red. In 2023 and 2024, rainfall caused havoc for organisers and festival-goers. "All of those challenges add up ... maybe it's time to bow out graciously and celebrate what has been an amazing festival," Mr Donovan said. The Big Red site is still flooded after significant rainfall across outback Queensland and the Northern Territory earlier this year. But Mr Donovan is confident the site will dry over the summer months, based on the Bureau of Meteorology's evaporation data. Rain and mud made things difficult for the festival organisers and attendees in 2023 and 2024. ( ABC Western Qld: Peter Quattrocelli ) The festival has attracted crowds of between 8,000 and 12,000 people in previous years, cementing it as one of the most significant tourism drawcards for outback Queensland. Locals believe its absence will be a major blow for outback tourism, as tourists often stop in small towns to boost the western Queensland tourism economy. "It's a bit devastating for us out here; it's something we look forward to to boost our economy," Diamantina Shire Council Mayor Francis Murray said. "It's going to have an effect on our businesses that are already doing it tough, that's for sure" Birdsville business owner Jenna Brook said the Big Red Bash had helped put Birdsville on the world stage. "It brings a huge number of people to Birdsville and surrounding towns that wouldn't come," Ms Brook said. The Nutbush dance record attempt is a fixture at the Big Red Bash. ( ABC Western Queensland: Heidi Sheehan ) "To lose that is a huge hit to businesses. The final Big Red Bash will be held in July 2027 with artists including Missy Higgins, Hoodoo Gurus, Jessica Mauboy, Leo Sayer, The Living End, Birds of Tokyo and Shannon Noll. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Company's Project Glasswing and Cyber Verification Program metamorphose into triple tier threat hunting club Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says 5 hours ago Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it 1 day ago Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what 1 day ago Anthropic's super bug-hunting model Mythos is hardcore good at math, as latest vuln under attack shows 3 days ago OpenAI alerts 100+ orgs that its 'misaligned models' attempted to break in - or worse 4 days ago Only a week after warning about the perils of competitor Z.ai's GLM-5.3 model and its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Anthropic has expanded its Cyber Verification Program (CVP) – or rather, reconfigured it. "For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs: Project Glasswing and the CVP," the AI biz said . "Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems." Project Glasswing and CVP launched in April 2026 alongside the debut of Mythos, the company's highly capable and equally hyped frontier model. Project Glasswing gave partners early access to Mythos so they could scour their systems for vulnerabilities before attackers beat them to it. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity was not particularly impressed with CVEs identified by Project Glasswing, noting that fewer than 0.5 percent of the 225 Anthropic-linked vulnerabilities he tracked were being exploited in the wild. And Anthropic's own warning last month about the risks posed by GLM-5.3 somewhat undermines the idea that there's anything special about its own Mythos model. Even so, Anthropic says that its security program has allowed its partners to spot at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026. And the biz claims that its own open source scanning efforts revealed an additional 5,500 verified vulnerabilities between April and October. "Of these verified vulnerabilities, more than 33,000 have so far been rated as critical- or high-severity," Anthropic said. "This is likely an undercount, as it is based on survey data from only a subset of Glasswing partners. As such, we expect the true impact to be at least five times higher." When these might get patched is unclear. The company's own figures indicate that of 5,674 true positive vulnerabilities, 3,014 are high severity, and 1,522 are critical severity, yet only 516 have been patched. Given industry boasting about the cybersecurity prowess of AI models, generating a fix, testing it, and deploying it ought to be nearly automatic at this point. But the gap between identification and remediation suggests there's a lot of slack in the system that needs to be ironed out. Two programs into one with three tiers Now Anthropic's two programs, one intended for organizations and one for individual security professionals, have been merged and reconfigured into three tiers. The AI biz has not explained why, but its stated intent is to tie model capabilities to specific tasks: Defense Access, Red Team Access, and Specialized Access. Depending on the tier, participants will encounter more or fewer blocks on security-related tasks. As a measure of program participation value, Anthropic said that based on five attempts at 10 CyScenarioBench challenges, those without CVP access got blocked on every attempt. Defense Access is intended for security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government organizations that focus on system defense. In this tier, Claude Opus 5.5 faced refusals in 46 of 50 attempts and succeeded four times. Red Team Access is for penetration testing and offensive cyber evaluation, and participants will still face model refusals for model interactions that would cause physical harm or mass disruption.

events.title: Elon Musk’s ex-wife says he is someone who ‘thrives on chaos’
events.summary: Justine Musk said her former husband "thrives on chaos" and that "everything is life and death" in his narrative. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Justine Musk said Elon Musk "thrives on chaos" and lives with intense urgency. Justine Musk compared Elon to someone who invents a parachute after jumping from a cliff. Current and former xAI workers have previously described constant "fire drills" under Musk. For Elon Musk, chaos may be more than a management style: His ex-wife says it’s where he feels comfortable. Justine Musk described the billionaire’s appetite for intensity in a teaser posted Tuesday for Kara Swisher’s interview with her and filmmaker Alex Gibney ahead of the release of Gibney’s documentary “MUSK.” “I once described him as somebody who can, like, jump off the edge of a cliff and, you know, invent a parachute on the way down,” Justine Musk told Swisher about her ex-husband, “Like, I think he thrives on chaos.” Justine Musk, an author and the mother of Vivian Jenna Wilson , said the Tesla CEO's language often casts challenges as existential emergencies, with an element of performance. “Everything is life and death,” she said. “And I think he really lives like that. He really lives with that pitch of intensity.” That description echoes inside Elon Musk's companies. At xAI, current and former employees told Business Insider that  Musk’s growing involvement  led to abrupt shifts in priorities, intensive “war rooms,” and a group chat of more than 300 engineers. Researchers would interrupt ongoing work to address concerns he flagged. “Because the company is so small, everything is a fire drill,” one former worker previously told Business Insider. Musk’s willingness to make sweeping changes and quickly reverse some of them predates his AI startup. After slashing Twitter’s workforce following his 2022 takeover, he said that some cuts had gone too far. Justine Musk said her former husband's intensity can draw others in before they recognize what’s happening. "He brings it with him, and he has a way of sucking you into it, and at first it can look a lot like excitement," Justine Musk said. “I always assume that there’s a method to his madness, you know, a lot of sleight of hand sometimes." The hum of the kidney dialysis machine that Onasis Munoz is connected to suddenly stops. The fluorescent lights overhead flicker out, and his room at a clinic in Valencia, Venezuela, is plunged into darkness. It is not the first time a power cut has interrupted one of the three weekly sessions Munoz needs to do the work his failing kidneys can no longer do, filtering waste and excess fluid from his blood. For years, electricity would go out every couple of days across parts of Venezuela's Carabobo state. But in recent months, Munoz said, the outages have grown to be daily, lasting around seven hours. The clinic's emergency batteries have since been depleted, and its backup generator no longer works. He explained that the frequent power failures have disrupted his treatment. His health has slumped as a result. "I arrive home, exhausted, as if I had run a marathon," the 34-year-old said. But often there is no electricity there either, and recent weeks have been sweltering. "I can't switch on the air conditioning. I cannot rest because of the heat and the mosquitoes. There's no relief," Munoz said. Across Venezuela, the prolonged outages are riling locals, as the electricity supply to homes, businesses and essential services becomes unstable. Some of the cuts are deliberate, as the government of interim President Delcy Rodriguez rations electricity. The resulting frustration has spilled onto the streets, where demonstrators hold "cacerolazos" – a traditional form of protest that involves banging pots and pans. Some have gone as far as blocking roadways and setting tyres on fire. The electricity crisis has also raised concerns about how the government is managing the country's vast oil supply, a key source of income for the country. "We are desperate. We cannot understand how a country so rich in resources can be practically left in the dark," said Patricia Cueva, a lawyer from Maracaibo, the capital of oil-rich Zulia state. "We cannot rest. We cannot work. Our children cry." A recent study by ANOVA Policy Research, a consultancy firm, found that 62.8 percent of Venezuelan households – or nearly two out of every three families – experienced daily electricity cuts in 2026, compared with 37.1 percent in 2024. Only 6.9 percent reported a continuous supply of electricity. The energy crisis has its roots in multiple causes. Previous governments have blamed foreign sanctions for weakening Venezuela's economy. The Rodriguez administration, meanwhile, has cited the climate phenomenon El Niño for the crisis. Some 90 percent of Venezuela's electricity is generated by hydropower, making the system vulnerable to extreme heat and drought. But energy specialist Nelson Hernandez is among the Venezuelans pointing a finger at the government for this year's surge in outages. Hernandez acknowledges that climate conditions can have an impact on electricity production. But he underscored that Venezuela's electricity crisis is not a "random event". "Practically the entire crisis stems from the systematic neglect of the infrastructure," he told Al Jazeera, pointing to what he called "profound failures" in management, lack of strategic planning and ageing technology. He also signalled that shifting government policies towards oil extraction plays a key role. Venezuela sits on the largest proven oil reserves in the world. Much of the oil industry was nationalised, but that started to change in January, after the US conducted a military operation to abduct and imprison Venezuela's then-President Nicolas Maduro. Since then, relations between Washington and Caracas have shifted. Under pressure from US President Donald Trump, Rodriguez – Maduro's former vice president – has implemented reforms to allow greater foreign investment in the country's oil sector. Trump, meanwhile, has eased restrictions on the oil's export and expanded the US role in the industry. The result has been an uptick in output. Oil production in Venezuela has risen by almost 30 percent this year, from 924,000 barrels per day in January to 1.201 million in August, according to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC). As Venezuela revives its dilapidated oil industry, Hernandez says increased production is putting pressure on an already strained electricity system. "Because electricity supplies to oil fields cannot be rationed without jeopardising oil production, the burden of adjustment and the power cuts fall directly on the residential and commercial sectors," he said. Hernandez estimates the oil industry requires around 1,600 megawatts or more for extraction, pumping, transportation and refining.

events.title: He manages one of the most successful soccer clubs in the world and is the elite leader every CEO wants to talk to. So why has Mikel Arteta decided to go public on having his own DNA mapped?
events.summary: Mikel Arteta tells me he is not a fan of the word pressure, an external force that may make leaders freeze. He prefers to talk about expectation, desire, and fulfilling tasks. “It’s about putting a lot of focus on leading yourself,” he says. “And making very clear who you want to be, what you want to accomplish in life, what is your purpose, what drives you, what is your passion, and then making sure that you create your ecosystem around you to achieve.”   Arsenal, the English Premier League champions he manages, used to be the “bridesmaid club”, missing out again and again in the battle for the most lucrative title in world soccer. They were “chokers” who did not have what it takes to be truly elite.  Last year, that changed, as Arsenal won the title for the first time in 22 years. “We showed very important values not only in sport, but in life,” Arteta said at the time. “Perseverance, to be resilient, to be composed in moments when people are doubting. And to be vulnerable.” Fans were in tears as they celebrated on the streets of North London, Arsenal’s home.  Leading a squad of 24 soccer players through the roller-coaster of sport is not the same as running a global business. Traits, though, are similar. Arteta is known for strict discipline and for a management approach that follows the “aggregation of marginal gains” rule. Every incremental improvement may appear insignificant, but together they are the difference between winning and the alternative, which in Arteta’s world is not much of an alternative. As Bill Shankly, one of the all-time great managers in English football, once said: “If you are first, you are first. If you are second, you are nothing.”  For Arteta, health is a “foundational” part of elite level leadership. Which is why he agreed to have his whole genome (the DNA make up of his body) sequenced, to better understand how his body works and the possible future health risks.  “You have to lead—whether it is your family or your club,” he told me. “You had better look after yourself and you had better lead yourself first.  “In order to do that, the foundation is your health. I think without that, there is nothing underneath. Your energy, your well-being, your capacity to basically connect with people emotionally, and to be able to handle all the situations, challenges, and the amount of work and stress that we go through daily at work.”  Arteta partnered with the global healthcare company Bupa , which offers genome sequencing to, the firm says, “better understand how genetics and lifestyle may shape health.”  Mikel Arteta for Bupa Genomics campaign. Bupa “Mikel now has those insights to share with a doctor if he needs them in the future,” said Melvin Samsom, group chief medical officer at Bupa.  “His results have prompted him to look more closely at his nutrition and choices that support his long-term health. A genetic test is the starting point. We combine genomic insights with clinical guidance and preventive care so people can understand what their results mean and take informed steps to look after their health, whether that means acting on a risk today or having useful information to draw on later.”  Arteta, who had a serious heart condition when he was young, said having the test gave him peace of mind and helped with conversations with his family about the future and living healthily. I asked him about “going public” with such personal information (the test revealed an increased likelihood of coeliac disease and a level of lactose intolerance).  “[Arteta’s] results have prompted him to look more closely at his nutrition and choices that support his long-term health. A genetic test is the starting point” Melvin Samsom, group chief medical officer at Bupa “I think we talk publicly about a lot of things that are not as relevant as health, and we focus so much on success and success related to your professional life,” he said.  “I think we need to have a space to talk about your personal life, about your family, about your health, about how you feel about yourself, the kind of changes that you go through in your life. I don’t feel the same way as five years ago, 10 years ago, 15 years ago—and I noticed that. I want to be able to recognize what is happening in my body, and I need support in order to do that because I don’t know.  “I want to have the best people around me, to guide me. And suddenly, when I get up in the mornings and I feel like I need more sleep or my big toe, because of my arthritis and all my years playing football, is hurting, [this is] one of the things that can help me to go through the day better, because the last thing that I want is to find limitations at my age, at 45.  “Whether it’s to play with my children or to go out on the pitch and run with the boys and be passionate about what I do and be active and be demanding [about] the way they have to look after themselves, but then don’t do it myself.  “So, we decided to open that door. I’m far from perfect. There are things happening in my body that I know now that I didn’t know before—it is my responsibility to get things done and try to improve them.”  Arteta reveals that his children regularly admonish him—“Daddy! Too much cheese!”—and that, since the genome results and some changes in eating and sleeping routines, he is already feeling healthier. And that affects how he leads.  “We are in front of a lot of people every single day,” he said. “They have an expectation for you to produce, to inspire, to guide them, and we had better be in the best possible way.  “I put health as the foundation. Why? Because I think it’s very difficult to feel emotionally good with yourself if physically you’re not at your best, or you are not doing the things that can help you to be your best. If you are fatigued because you are not eating the right way, or if you are in pain. Pain inhibits your muscles, inhibits your brain because you don’t feel good, and then that has other consequences.”  “Face those challenges that life brings us, that an opponent can bring or a situation or contest—just be prepared and face it” Mikel arteta, manager of English Premier League team, arsenal Many C-suite leaders talk about the stress of handling volatility, and about keeping calm despite the challenges around them whether that is geopolitics or the race towards the AI-enabled future. Try compressing all of those pressures into 90 minutes and a game where all the outcomes are uncertain, and plausibly existential for the person in charge (soccer managers are regularly sacked).  “We live in an environment that is extremely unpredictable, and actually enjoying that unpredictability, it’s a joy, you know?” Arteta said when I asked him about handling rapid-change environments. “Every day is new. events.title: Froyo's made a comeback. But at £12 a tub will it last?
events.summary: Froyo has made a return with several stores opening across the UK this year Kiersten Paterno was one of the many people willing to queue up to an hour to treat herself to some frozen yoghurt. "It was a 45-minute wait for my turn but the whole experience of choosing your flavours and customising it with different toppings was a big part of the appeal for me," the 19-year-old student says. Froyo was a huge trend in the UK in the late 2000s and early 2010s and was most popular in London. Chains like Snog had 10 stores in the capital at its peak and other brands like AngelBerry had shops in Bristol and Brighton. And this year it's made a comeback, driven by nostalgia, social media and its perception as a healthier dessert choice. Several brands such as Go Greek, Myka and Yo-Chi launched in London, while Frurt, which operates mainly in the north west of England and Yorkshire, has opened new stores, including one in Leicester. These companies saw hundreds of customers queueing to create their own dessert pot, despite it not being a particularly cheap treat, with tubs costing as much as £12. Kiersten Paterno, 19, values froyo as it's nostalgic and can be healthy Kiersten says she was initially attracted to the dessert as she could manage portion size and sweetness level. "I could control how sweet I wanted it to be through the toppings. It feels healthier overall as it's a dessert I can enjoy without feeling like I've overindulged." She admits it can be pricey but says she doesn't mind spending a little more as an occasional treat. Research suggests the froyo market is steadily growing. Market Data Forecast estimates that the European frozen yoghurt market is worth £434m in 2026, up from £419m last year. Australian brand Yo-Chi opened a Notting Hill branch in August and blew up quickly on social media for its range of toppings and "third space" feel. "Sweet treat culture is huge. People aren't spending a fortune on big things, but a little thing like that, they're happy to," says Bethan Clarke, Yo-Chi campaign manager. There were long queues outside Yo-Chi on its launch day While Yo-Chi would "never call ourselves healthy" - froyo is usually lower in calories and fat than ice cream, but may also contain more added sugar - Clarke says the fact that it is customisable means that people are in control of their own portion sizes and sugar levels. Social media trends like "2026 is the new 2016" are helping froyo's virality. "People are coming back to re-experience childhood a little bit," says Clarke. Ella Light, who also works for Yo-Chi, says she's been surprised by the mix of people coming into the store. "I was kind of expecting to see the Gen Z girlies coming in, [but] this morning there was a group of builders!" 2010s throwbacks with a modern twist Snog was the big name in froyo in the 2010s But how likely is the current froyo craze to survive? After all, it was huge in the 2010s but by the end of that decade was all but dead. Vhari Russell, founder of Food Marketing Experts, says: "Market over-saturation played a role in the initial disappearance of froyo, as well as the natural cycle of dying trends." Market leader Snog faced increasing competition from the likes of Yog, Yoomoo and Pinkberry, while consumers also realised that the dessert may not have been the healthier option they initially thought it was. "But now 2010s throwbacks coupled with a modern twist are seeing huge appetite across the market," says Russell. Will £12 for a tub eventually start to put people off though? Russell doesn't believe so, as she calls it an "affordable luxury". Going out for a froyo can be "an experiential moment" as much as anything, she adds. "For many people, they don't smoke or have expensive lifestyles, so froyo isn't viewed as food, it's viewed as an experience." Not interested in queuing for two hours? Here's how to make your own If the price of froyo seems unreasonable or if you can’t justify queueing for hours, BBC Food have five different froyo variations you can make at home. events.title: Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture
events.summary: Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture. The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful. Ikea already offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year The new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with its own secondhand online marketplace which launches in the UK this week. The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally. The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future. “The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream. “The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.” The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK. Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card. The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items. In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is now expanding into homewares and electronics , as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sites such as Vinterior . The US secondhand site eBay recently bought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn (£900m). Preloved items now make up about a 10th of global fashion sales . There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items. AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.

events.title: Braid-creator Jonathan Blow on making the 'biggest puzzle game ever'
events.summary: For ten years, Jonathan Blow has been working with a small team on what he believes is "the biggest puzzle game ever made". The American developer is renowned as one of the fathers of the modern indie game movement, creating the genre-defining puzzle-platformer Braid in 2008. Now, a decade on from his last project, The Witness, The Order of the Sinking Star is due to be released on Thursday - a game with roughly 1,500 puzzles that he estimates could take around 500 hours to complete. So why make something the majority of players may never get even halfway through, let alone finish? "Some people decide what to make based on what's practical or what makes business sense," Blow says. "It's never been the way that I think." "I sort of make bad business decisions in a sense...because I let the design dominate that process. But then because we did that, we always have something unique," he says. The game's blurb likens itself to a "game design supercollider" - four worlds viewed from overhead, built on the mechanics of four pre-existing free puzzle games from other designers (with their permission to do so). These ideas are then "smashed together" to create brand-new brainteasers. For example, one world's mechanics, based on those from the free 2014 game Mirror Isles by Alan Hazelden, sees players use mirror reflections to swap places across islands. When combined with the system of another free game created by Hazelden, Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes - where players throw stones into water to create paths - brand-new puzzle opportunities suddenly arise. How an AI was tricked into breaking its own rules Taking a risk on making something more experimental is what appears to ultimately drive Blow, who says that as the industry has grown, the culture for developers has also changed. "Somewhere along the way...this idea that the best designers were trying to always make new experiences...just sort of got dropped by the wayside," he says. The outspoken designer is renowned for his frank takes on the industry - previously calling social media games such as Farmville "evil" and World of Warcraft's quest design "unethical". In December 2025, Hazelden publicly distanced himself from Blow - writing in a post on Bluesky , external that he was "dismissive of diversity efforts" and "pro-MAGA". Blow, who has not responded to these critiques publicly, tells me he instead decided to "sit down and focus on the games". "What the players want from developers is good games," he says. "They don't want us to be arguing, especially with each other, about political stances." Blow says the industry faces an uncertainty in how it approaches AI Blow says he is sceptical of AI, which was "not part of the pipeline at all" for Order of the Sinking Star, even though he recognises it as an "advancement" and an "interesting technology". Of the benefits often cited by those who use the tech, such as increased productivity, he asks: "If you're saying you're ten times as productive and it's been 3 years, you should have been able to do thirty years of work." "So where's this output of 30 years of work?" Despite rejecting the tech, Blow says the industry faces an "uncertain time" in how it deals with AI, particularly with newer creators who may rely too heavily on it to code rather than learning the "weird glyphs" themselves. "A danger is that not many people know how to program in the future," he says. "And if AI can't really do everything, then the supply of programmers might not be enough to make good stuff." In 2008 Jonathan Blow released the genre-defining puzzle platformer Braid, the post-release of which is documented in the film Indie Game: The Movie Blow's refusal to compromise on any aspect of the Order of the Sinking Star transcends its core design. The developer decided to make his own programming language, Jai, from scratch. He then used this, alongside a custom engine, to make the game. A game's engine is a piece of software that packs everything needed to craft a playable experience - including graphics rendering, physics simulation and scripting - into one place for creators. Some developers turn to pre-built game engines such as Unity or Unreal Engine, rather than taking on the considerable challenge of building an engine from scratch. For Blow, creating his own engine in this language meant he could build something "tuned and authored very specifically" to what he wanted to make. It is yet another reason he gives for why this project, which started as a simple "design experiment", has taken ten years to finish. "I do want the next project after this to be less on hard mode, or really it was nightmare mode, because we did so many things on hard mode at the same time," he reflects. "But it's also been rewarding in a certain way. Because otherwise, what else are you in the industry for?

events.title: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns Equinor
events.summary: Anders Opedal said Equinor would have to take "a hard view" about future investments in the UK if it were to reject new drilling Oil giant Equinor has warned it may shun further investments in the UK if new oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw are not approved. "The question will be: is the UK investable in the future? I hope it will not come to that," said Anders Opedal, boss of the Norwegian state oil company which is part owner of the sites. He told the BBC the company would "have to take a hard view about it" if a decision was made to reject new drilling. The warning comes as the UK government is set to decide whether or not to grant final approval to extract oil and gas at Rosebank and Jackdaw, despite a ban pledged in Labour's election manifesto. The government said any decision would take into account all relevant evidence. Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035. The UK already relies on Norway for half of its gas needs, and the Norwegian government has continued to issue new licences for oil and gas exploration in its own North Sea waters. Equinor has predicted production will remain at current levels until the middle of the next decade. Opedal said he remained confident that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's talk of a "pragmatic approach to oil and gas" meant both projects would get approved but he said the current limbo was "an uncomfortable position to be in". He said that the UK could produce more of its own oil and gas. "It's a political choice," he said. "The North Sea oil and gas industry started on the UK side. We learned from the UK and it's actually the same geology on both sides of the border - several fields actually cross it." Rosebank is the United Kingdom's largest undeveloped oil and gas field, located in the North Atlantic about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands and is thought to hold up to 500 million barrels of oil and gas. Opedal told the BBC the exploration licence for the site was originally granted 25 years ago. "The licence was awarded in 2001, the discovery was made in 2004 and the final investment decision in 2023," he said. Both Rosebank and Jackdaw were initially given the go-ahead by the former Conservative government but were delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact. Following a public consultation on the sites, which closed in August, the final decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh. Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank. Adura has previously said that if approval comes soon, Jackdaw could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete". Tessa Khan, executive director of Uplift, an organisation that wants the UK to move away from fossil fuel production, said new drilling at Rosebank "won't cut our bills" and was a "bad deal for Britain". "It's overwhelmingly oil for export – but it will make Equinor and its part-owner, the Norwegian government, richer, while Britain is left with high energy bills and a declining workforce." Khan said Labour's "climate credibility is also on the line". A government spokesperson said the North Sea remained a "vital national asset", adding that "oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come - alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis". "Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process," the spokesperson added. events.title: Christa Pike lawyers say she is speaking one week after failed execution
events.summary: The 50-year-old has regained consciousness and is receiving care nearly one week after being sent to the hospital following a botched lethal injection. Lawyers for Christa Pike say she is awake and able to speak after her botched execution attempt by the state of Tennessee on September 30. Tuesday’s statement marks the first public indication that Pike’s condition has improved after she was transported to a Nashville hospital after receiving two doses of pentobarbitol, lethal injections intended to end her life. list 1 of 3 Tennessee prisons official resigns after Christa Pike’s failed US execution list 2 of 3 Christa Pike unconscious, on ventilator after botched execution: Lawyers list 3 of 3 Christa Pike seeks firing squad, not lethal injection: Inside US executions Her failed execution has sparked debate about the use of the death penalty in the United States. Pike is thought to be the first person to have survived such an injection in the country. “Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care,” Pike’s lawyers said in a statement. “Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.” The statement also expresses gratitude to medical workers who the lawyers say have “treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her”. Pike’s lawyers had previously stated that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. They described her arms as “swollen, burned and blistered” by the failed execution. Pike was convicted and sentenced to die in 1996 for her participation in the murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18 years old. Two co-defendants received lesser sentences. Pike’s defence lawyers had pointed to her mental health struggles in their attempts to commute her sentence. But the Slemmer family had advocated for the death penalty, pointing to the violent nature of the 19-year-old’s murder. Accounts of Pike’s failed execution describe her kicking off the sheet covering her body and, at one point, appearing to snore. She reportedly expressed feeling pain as the lethal injections were administered. The incident has brought attention to the prevalence of botched executions in the US criminal justice system. Critics have argued that botched executions — defined as those that deviate from established procedures through unforeseen issues, delays or administrative incompetence — can cause unnecessary pain and suffering for those being put to death. Citing the researcher Austin Sarat, the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit, estimates that 3 percent of executions in the US from 1890 to 2010 were botched.

events.title: ATO won't budge on credit card ban after meeting with business groups
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ATO won't budge after snap meeting over credit card ban New regulation has put a ban on card surcharges. ( Adobe Stock ) Business groups have accused the ATO of having "double standards" for refusing to accept credit card payments from November 30. The tax office said it was not appropriate for it to absorb the surcharge fees itself because that would effectively transfer the cost to the taxpayer. The ATO has stood firm on its decision, despite calling a special forum for frustrated small business groups to discuss the changes. The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) will not budge on its decision to stop accepting credit card payments from December 1, after holding a snap crisis meeting with business groups angered by the move. Australia's tax chief convened a meeting with business groups this morning to the discuss the changes in the wake of widespread backlash. But the ATO has indicated it is not going to reverse the credit card ban, according to a spokesperson from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), which attended the meeting. "We will continue to seek to have the ban overturned," the ACCI spokesperson said. The ABC has approached the ATO for comment. Last week the tax office announced it would stop accepting credit card payments at the end of next month. That step came in response to the Reserve Bank of Australia's reforms to scrap card surcharges from October 1, which the bank said was "in the public interest" and would save customers about $1.6 billion a year. The ATO said it would continue accepting credit cards until November 30 to allow for a transition period, saying it was untenable beyond that point. Small business owners say they have been expected to absorb the fees of card transactions themselves, and have lost the option of using credit card payments to the ATO as a cash flow method. Some feared the sudden change would mean they needed to source cash quickly to begin paying by debit instead, or they would be forced to go into arrears with the ATO, and that could result in enforcement against their businesses, including possible closure. Earlier Andrew McKellar, chief executive of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI), had called for the ATO's credit card ban to be reversed. "There is a clear double standard here. Government is telling small business to absorb the hit from the surcharge ban and its cost, while the tax office is saying a different set of rules applies to it," he said. "Small business is the backbone of the economy. They are doing it tough, with rising costs and a fourth interest rate increase last week." Master Builders CEO Denita Wawn said the surcharge card ban and other regulatory decisions were made "without consultation" and showed a "lack of practical understanding of the impact of decisions being made by this government". "It's quite incredulous," she told News 24 yesterday afternoon. The ABC understands business groups were frustrated by the meeting, and it was unclear who had made the decision to end credit card payments, and when. In a statement on October 2, taxation commissioner Rob Heferen said the ATO "would have preferred to continue accepting credit cards" but credit card companies declined to offer a rate that was low enough. "The costs associated with accepting credit card payments are significant, with merchant fees estimated to be almost $200 million annually and expected to continue increasing over time," he said in the statement. "It is not tenable for the ATO to absorb the costs associated with accepting credit cards on an ongoing basis. Small business have criticised the ATO over its credit card ban. ( ABC News: Nassim Khadem ) Opposition Leader Angus Taylor called for the government to "instruct" the ATO to reverse their decision. "This is a government that says to small businesses, 'You've got to absorb the surcharges,' and then the Australian Tax Office says, 'We're not going to accept credit card payments because we can't accept the surcharges,'" Mr Taylor said. "The hypocrisy of this government knows no bounds." Other entities have also signalled they will stop accepting credit card payments, including StrataPay, some private schools, local councils, and rental payment platforms. The ATO has said credit card payments make up only 2.3 per cent of payments to the tax office. It said "more than 60 per cent of credit card payments by value were made by privately owned and wealthy groups, and public and multinational businesses", while about 5 per cent of all small businesses used credit cards to pay their taxes.

If you buy a lot of cat litter, Amazon will probably infer that you have cats, or if you buy a lot of anti-acne skin products, then Amazon might guess you’re prone to breakouts. Even if we know that Amazon customizes our shopping experiences based on our purchase history, it still comes as a surprise to see all of these personal details laid out in a convenient list. Especially when those details get uncomfortably intimate. One Threads user came across this section of her Amazon settings where you can see who the shopping giant thinks you are, and alongside more benign assumptions like “Shops from women’s departments” and “Probably owns a Shark robot vacuum,” she found that Amazon assumes she “has flat buttocks.” “I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless,” an Amazon customer, @fangirlinmegan, wrote on Threads . “I mean it ain’t wrong but damn did you have to call me out like that?” In less than a day, the post garnered over a million views, including many from users who were curious what their own Amazon profiles might reveal. Here’s how you find out. On desktop, you can find this page by hovering over where Amazon says “Hello, [your name]” in the upper right corner. Then click “Account” under the “Your Account” section. Under the “Ordering and shopping preferences” section, click “Your Shopping preferences.” From here, you can add in information of your own, like your shoe size, interests, and dietary preferences. But we’re not here to tell Amazon that it should stop selling you beef jerky since you’re a vegetarian. We’re here to see if Amazon thinks you have “flat buttocks.” When you scroll to the bottom of the page, you’ll see a blue hyperlinked option that says “Manage your information.” Once you click that, you’ll see what dirt Amazon has on you. On the mobile app, you can get here by clicking the hamburger icon from the bottom menu bar, then navigating to Account > Shopping preferences > About you. For me, Amazon has gleaned that I am someone who “practices photography,” “plays collectible card games,” and is “invested in the Apple ecosystem.” This is all true. Amazon has even flattered me by noting that I “read diverse non-fiction,” to which I say — why yes, I am indeed an open-minded intellectual with a thirst for knowledge. Thank you for noticing. Other colleagues of mine found that Amazon correctly noted their interests in vinyl records and ceramics, as well as a penchant for “natural materials” in home decor and clothing that “prioritizes comfort.” None of us had anything as affronting as “has flat buttocks,” but the Threads user noted that this was likely because she had purchased “butt scrunch leggings.” Tech companies know too much about us, and it’s jarring to realize just how closely they’re paying attention to how we use their platforms. events.title: "You suck": Emmer unloads on Senate Republicans
events.summary: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is saying out loud what House Republicans have been grumbling about for much of the year: They're fed up with the Senate. Why it matters You won't ever hear Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) or Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) talk about their Senate counterparts like this. "There are no Democrats. There are no Republicans. They are just senators," Emmer told donors last week at a closed-door fundraiser Axios attended for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.). Emmer said Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) "is doing the job that he thinks he's supposed to do. There's a certain fraternity sorority that is the U.S. Senate." The intrigue: Emmer had a blunt message for senators who repeatedly say they can't pass House GOP priorities: "Don't just keep telling me 'Don't have the votes. Don't have the votes.' You suck." Emmer said he once thought as a House member that he should stay out of the filibuster debate. Now, he thinks his colleagues should "get rid of the darn filibuster." A Senate GOP aide retorted that what would "suck" would be losing the majority and that Republicans should be targeting Democrats instead of attacking their own side. Driving the news: Emmer's comments are the most critical yet from a House GOP leader, but sum up the mood inside the conference. More than a dozen Republicans paralyzed the House floor this summer in an effort to force Senate action on the SAVE America Act, the GOP's signature election bill that's become a major source of tension between the two chambers. "We're frustrated with the Senate," Emmer told Axios in an interview after the fundraiser. "We feel like we've been doing everything we were hired to do, and a lot of it goes over to the Senate and it just sits there." House Republicans put their votes "up on the board," Emmer argued, while senators "try to avoid" taking tough votes. The big picture: House GOP leaders often say they've "done their job" when asked about unfinished business. But there's a clear implication in that phrase: The Senate hasn't. Johnson has pointed to the backlog across the Capitol — including when he defended sending the House home early last month by noting that hundreds of House-passed bills were awaiting Senate action. The speaker blames Democrats for that, but his complaints have put the spotlight on Senate GOP leadership. Zoom in: Congressional Republicans spent much of the summer on completely different wavelengths over reconciliation 3.0 , which doesn't require any Democratic votes. Johnson pushed the Senate to take up the House's reconciliation framework, declaring in July that the Senate would pass it before leaving for August recess. "That'd be news to me," Thune said at the time about Johnson's floated timeline. The Senate left town without any action on reconciliation 3.0. "They can say all day long, you know, 'It's going to be hard.' Everything's hard. Give me a lecture about how hard things are. That's what I do every day. They've got to figure out a way to get it done," Scalise told Axios of his colleagues in the Senate in July. The bottom line: Emmer stopped short of saying Senate Republicans have been a bigger obstacle to the GOP agenda than Democrats. But he said two things frustrate lawmakers in the House when it comes to Senate Republicans: 1) They don't say what changes would get them to yes; and 2) they don't put themselves on the record when the answer is no. "Put your money where your mouth is. Put your vote up on the board, and let's see where you really are," Emmer told Axios.
