events.title: House GOP leaders admit redistricting fell short
events.summary: House GOP leaders are now openly acknowledging that their mid-decade redistricting push didn't work out as well as they'd hoped. Why it matters: Republicans kicked off the redistricting wars hoping new maps would give them a bigger cushion against the historical headwinds facing the president's party. That advantage is looking a lot smaller than they envisioned. Driving the news: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios that Republicans won't win all 13 seats they'd hoped to gain from new maps. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," Emmer told Axios aboard a plane Thursday between campaign stops in North Carolina and Virginia. Emmer echoed House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), who told Axios last month that Republicans were unlikely to sweep all 13. Zoom in: Emmer said he'd be "surprised" if Republicans sweep all five newly drawn seats in Texas and "shocked" if they win all four in Florida . But he said Republicans are certain to pick up newly drawn seats in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee. At a fundraiser for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) on Thursday, Emmer told donors that Republicans could also offset losses with pickups in Maine and potentially North Carolina, Ohio, New Mexico and Washington. Even assuming Republicans lose five seats because of redistricting in California and Utah, pickups elsewhere give the party a path to come out ahead, Emmer told donors. State of play: Redistricting still gave Republicans an edge, just smaller than they once thought. The Cook Political Report now projects Republicans will net around four seats from redistricting alone, down from the double-digit gains Republicans once hoped to squeeze from new maps. Democrats' maps in California and Utah — in response to a new Texas map — offset the GOP gains. Some newly drawn Republican pickup opportunities have become more competitive than expected. The bottom line: Democrats need to net just three seats to win the House, and the broader battlefield is moving in their direction. Cook shifted 15 House races toward Democrats last month, while Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 11 races toward Democrats days later. Many of the most competitive races are now in districts President Trump carried in 2024.

events.title: Ukraine says South Korean exports helped ease Russia's drone-strike crisis
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South Korea exports eased Russia fuel crisis caused by drone strikes, Ukraine says Fuel shipped from South Korea to Russia has caused a diplomatic dispute. ( Reuters: Kim Soo-hyeon ) More than 176,000 tonnes of petroleum products were shipped from South Korea to Russia in July and August. The supplies from South Korea made up 31 per cent of Russian fuel imports in August. Relations between South Korea and Ukraine are strained. Russia has imported fuel from South Korean ports, easing the impact of a fuel crisis caused by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, Ukraine's top sanctions official says. More than 176,000 tonnes of petroleum products from South Korean ports in July and August were imported by Russia, Ukraine's top sanctions official Vladyslav Vlasiuk said on Tuesday. The supplies from South Korea made up 31 per cent of Russian fuel imports in August, according to Mr Vlasiuk, citing what he said were reports that tankers, including ones under Western sanctions, were used for the deliveries. "These shipments began precisely when Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were reducing processing volumes and creating a fuel shortage within Russia," Mr Vlasiuk, presidential commissioner for Ukrainian sanctions policy, wrote on Facebook. His comments come amid a diplomatic row between Seoul and Kyiv that erupted last month when President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, a step that Seoul says was meant to stay secret. Ukraine has used long-range drones to attack Russian oil refineries and depots this year in what Kyiv has described as an effort to impose greater costs on its enemy, with no end in sight more than four years since Russia's full-scale invasion. Seoul says it continues to support efforts to end war in Ukraine. ( Reuters: Kim Soo-hyeon ) The strikes prompted Russia to impose a ban on diesel and gasoline exports, while restricting fuel purchases in some regions hit hard by the fuel crunch. "In effect, imports from South Korea helped Russia offset the impact of losing its own refining capacity," Mr Vlasiuk said, citing "available data" and "reports" as sources in his post. Earlier on Tuesday, the Guardian news agency reported that it had analysed port records and ship-tracking data, determining that the volumes were loaded at South Korean ports onto seven tankers, some of which are under UK and EU sanctions. Mr Vlasiuk provided the same figures as those in the Guardian. In response to the Guardian article, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said "the Korean government supports and actively participates in global efforts to end the war in Ukraine and achieve peaceful recovery". It said that its government was strictly enforcing export controls against Russia by expanding the scope beyond strategic items to include "non-strategic items … that carry a high risk of diversion for military use." Relations between South Korea and Ukraine have been under strain for weeks. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung threatened unspecified measures against Ukraine on Friday unless Kyiv acknowledged a confidentiality agreement that Seoul says covered the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers. Seoul has said it wants an apology. Ukraine denies there was a confidentiality agreement, but its foreign minister has said that Kyiv wants to mend ties with South Korea. events.title: The next step in factory automation: Machines that adapt with AI
events.summary: Discover what’s coming to Microsoft Ignite, Nov 17-20, 2026. Register now. Physical AI in manufacturing: From intelligent machines to coordinated operations There are nearly 5 million industrial robots operating in the world’s factories today, a number that grew nearly 10% in a single year. Almost all of them execute instructions written in advance by someone who anticipated the conditions they would meet. That approach has defined industrial automation for six decades. Physical AI is moving intelligence into the work of manufacturing itself. Robots, vehicles, production systems, and connected infrastructure can now perceive changing conditions, reason over context, and act within defined boundaries. Automation delivered precision, productivity, and safety by executing known instructions. Physical AI extends that foundation by helping systems respond to more variation in the conditions around them. At the International Manufacturing Technology Show (IMTS) 2026, standing on the main stage in Chicago, Illinois, I framed the opportunity around a practical question: how do manufacturers turn intelligence that works in one machine or process into a capability they can deploy, govern, and improve across the enterprise? Physical AI closes the loop between intelligence and action Physical AI is intelligence operating in the physical world through machines, systems, and people. It works through a continuous loop: Perceive : Read machines, environments, and operational signals. Reason : Interpret that context and determine the next best action. Act : Execute through machines, systems, and people, then use the result as feedback for the next cycle. Connected operations gave people visibility. Industrial AI added reasoning over patterns and outcomes. Physical AI closes the loop by acting in the physical world, measuring the result, and improving the next cycle. When AI moves from recommending on a screen to acting in the physical world, value and risk both become physical. Operating limits, identity and security, observability, validated fallback, and human approval and override must be designed into the system. Physical AI is creating value across the industrial lifecycle Manufacturers are already applying these capabilities from engineering through live operations. At the engineering end, KUKA is making industrial robots easier to program and deploy. With iiQWorks.Copilot, users can describe a task, generate code, simulate the workflow, and deploy it. For simple tasks, programming can be up to 80% faster. Krones is using AI agents and physically accurate digital twins to speed filling simulations. Runs that took three or four hours can now take five minutes or less. In live operations, ARUM is bringing the same shift into the machining center. TTMC Brain turns a conversation into a machining program and reduces numerical control programming from 177 steps to two. ABB is applying live industrial data to predictive maintenance and real-time optimization. Across its customer base, ABB reports up to 20% higher critical-asset reliability and up to 60% less unplanned downtime. These examples address two constraints on scaling automation: the engineering effort needed to deploy it and the reliability needed to keep it running. What physical AI changes for operations leaders In my conversations with manufacturers, the challenge is increasingly orchestration. A successful machine or workcell is only the first step. Leaders have to connect that capability to the way the enterprise operates, decides, and scales. Physical intelligence changes three enterprise models: The operating model moves from site automation to network coordination . Lines, plants, fleets, and field environments can operate as one connected system. The decision model moves from manual planning to agent-assisted operations . People set intent, policy, approval, and override while agents interpret context and coordinate work within those boundaries. The technology model moves from disconnected tools to one governed environment . Data, controls, platforms, and cross-vendor systems must work together across cloud and edge. Those shifts depend on two connected loops. One accelerates physical systems innovation: teams simulate conditions, train and adapt models, validate behavior and failure modes, and iterate before deployment. The other operationalizes physical intelligence: teams orchestrate work, execute across machines and people, govern what happens, and optimize performance across systems and fleets. Agentic orchestration connects the two. Operational feedback returns real-world conditions, interventions, failures, and outcomes to the next simulation and validation cycle. Repeatability matters more than any single deployment. A successful machine or workcell becomes an enterprise capability when its data, integration, governance, and operating model can be reused across lines, plants, and fleets. Otherwise, the organization scales exceptions instead of capability. AI governance in manufacturing belongs in the operating architecture Identity, policy, monitoring, security, and accountability must travel with the capability from one machine or site to the next. Operational, engineering, and business context must inform the same decisions across cloud and edge. For global manufacturers, that architecture must also support sovereignty, data residency, and operational technology security across sites and regions. Leaders need visibility into what the system can do, why it acted, and when a person must approve, intervene, or override. A consistent trust model lets teams deploy, manage, observe, and improve capabilities across mixed environments without rebuilding the controls at every site. For more on Microsoft’s industrial AI platform, read Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Global Industrial AIoT Platforms . Manufacturers do not need to automate an entire plant to begin. A practical starting point is one operational problem where the outcome matters and the boundaries are clear. Choose a workflow with measurable value, such as quality inspection, maintenance triage, machine programming, or process optimization. Map the data and operating context required to make a sound decision. Define what the system may recommend, what it may execute, and where a person must approve or intervene. Then design the deployment so that the successful pattern can be reused across another line, site, or fleet. For examples of how manufacturers can scale high-value use cases, read Step into the Factory of the Future . Physical AI will be measured in the operation: faster engineering, safer work, more reliable assets, and systems that improve under clear human authority. Start with one consequential workflow. Define its boundaries. Build so success can repeat. Turn shop-floor signals into coordinated action across your factory.

events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Melius , an AI platform for generating ad campaigns, images, and videos, announced on Tuesday that it raised a total of $25 million in funding, including a $20 million Series A led by CRV and a $5 million seed round led by General Catalyst. While the startup claims to have hit more than $1 million in annualized revenue within two months of coming out of stealth in July, co-founder Joowon Kim (pictured on right) admits that Melius didn’t hit it out of the park initially. When the New York-based company first launched over a year ago, Kim and his co-founders, Young Kim (pictured on left) and Arnav Ramu (pictured center) set out to build an AI-powered performance marketing tool. The three knew each other from working as engineers at Ramp, the corporate spending and finance software company. More than six months after building the product, the co-founders decided their original idea didn’t “have legs,” Joowon Kim told TechCrunch. Instead of helping marketers manage and optimize ad spend, the team chose to focus on what it saw as a much larger opportunity: building the tools that generate the creative assets and campaigns themselves. “We scrapped the entire codebase; we burned all of it,” Kim said. Melius quickly went to work on an entirely new product. Nearly a year after its initial launch, it revealed a platform that it describes as an “agents lab for creative work.” Melius is far from the only startup helping ad agencies, marketers, and brands generate creative assets and campaigns with AI. Competitors include rapidly growing Higgsfield, which was valued at $5.4 billion in August, as well as other small startups, including Krea and Flora AI. Kim isn’t concerned about the competition. He acknowledged that Higgsfield, a three-year-old company that has hit over $700 million in annualized revenue, “is growing like mad,” but according to Kim, the size of the market is so large that it can support multiple competitors. “There are a lot of players, which is pretty exciting,” he told TechCrunch. “That means there are customers to be won and there is demand in this space.” As for why former Ramp engineers are building an ad-generation product, Kim, who describes himself as a social media influencer, says he has been passionate about making short videos since elementary school and once dreamed of becoming a famous YouTuber. “I tried my best to make vlogs,” he said. “My dad was great at using FinalCut Pro, but I wasn’t.” Those early vlogs never quite took off, but his fascination with making digital media remained. Now, with Melius, he’s building the tool he always wanted: a platform where anyone, including seasoned creative directors, can turn their ideas into reality using plain language. events.title: Chart: A look at the S&P 500's remarkable and defiant trip to a new record
events.summary: S&P 500 surpassed its August peak on Tuesday. Stocks recovered despite the Iran war’s oil shock, rising borrowing costs and the Fed’s first rate hike. The market rally was also boosted by a few stocks tied to the AI hype, highlighting investors’ appetite for ambitious tech stocks. The S&P 500 rose to an all-time intraday on Tuesday, touching 7844.52 and surpassing its August 13 intraday peak when it hit 7,830. The benchmark also closed for the first time over 7,800. The recovery comes after months of oil shocks, rising borrowing costs and the possible start of a Federal Reserve rate hiking cycle. The record rally comes just a day after the 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5.3%, reaching levels not seen since 2002. In mid September, the Fed raised its benchmark rate for the first time in over three years and indicated more were to come. Oil had crossed $100 a barrel in early March for the first time since 2022 as the Iran conflict disrupted energy supplies moving through the Strait of Hormuz. After falling below $70 a barrel, it slingshot back above $100 in early September. "At the end of the day, oil and bond yields can be correlated, but so is the stock market and profits. And if the profits are there, which they have been, the stock market is going to be resilient, even if the economy is a bit more mixed," Shawn Snyder, economic strategist at Potomac Fund Management, told CNBC. Unlike prior records this year, this latest run has been narrowly lead by a few stocks tied to the AI hype and deemed unfettered by adverse macroeconomic headwinds. "When traders take a breather from the noise surrounding them — much of it negative in recent months — and look closer at what's happening in the markets, it becomes clear the U.S. stock market is the best place to park their money compared with other locations. It's hard to argue against the mostly positive risk-reward ratio we've seen over multiple decades," said JJ Kinahan, Cboe Global Markets senior vice president of retail and alternative investments. The so-called Magnificent 7 namely, Nvidia , Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta , Microsoft and Tesla make up more than 34% of the market cap of the S&P 500 . "When you consider that much girth among a small handful of stocks, it's apparent how much these stocks' daily movements dictate the direction of the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, both of which are in record territory again today," Kinahan said. With tech companies investing heavily in data centers and computing infrastructure demand for chips and equipment has gone up. Earlier this year, Amazon said it expected about $200 billion in capital expenditures across its businesses in 2026, citing opportunities including AI, chips and robotics. Investor appetite for ambitious technology bets also became evident in June, when SpaceX raised $75 billion in the largest IPO ever and began trading on June 12. The debut became another milestone where investors continued backing growth companies despite higher energy prices and borrowing costs. Looking ahead, however, Potomac Fund Management's Snyder cautioned that the "weakening" market breadth may last longer if inflation shows no signs of easing, or if there's no clear signal that the Federal Reserve is achieving its mandate. The central bank is slated to release its minutes from the September meeting on Wednesday. The market "can look relatively calm, but there are still things going on underneath the surface that may not be so calm," Snyder said. Correction: The 10-year Treasury yield on Monday surpassed 5.3% to reach highs not seen since 2002. An earlier version misstated the year.

events.title: Cramer says these blue-chip stocks are among the best ways to invest in the AI boom
events.summary: Jim Cramer said established tech giants with strong businesses and multiple ways to benefit from AI are some of the best places to invest in the boom. He remains diversified but is overweight AI, arguing those stocks offer more opportunities for growth as higher rates weigh on much of the rest of the market. CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that some of the best ways to invest in the artificial intelligence boom are established tech giants with multiple opportunities to capitalize on the technology. The " Mad Money " host acknowledged concerns about stretched AI valuations and comparisons with the dotcom bubble. Rather than backing away from a trade that continues to drive much of the market's gains , Cramer said he favors blue-chip companies with strong businesses and management teams that can find new ways to benefit from AI. "Because I think that a lot of things can possibly go right, I want to stick with the AI data center plays," Cramer said. He pointed to Meta and Microsoft as two examples. Cramer's CNBC Investing Club owns both stocks. While Meta shares had a rocky start to 2026, Cramer said he trusted CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his team to figure out how to monetize its AI spending, which the Facebook and Instagram parent is expected to do with Muse . The stock now trades around $738. "I didn't think, 'what a bunch of chowderheads, they don't have anything AI,'" Cramer said. "I thought that Mark Zuckerberg and his dream team are brilliant and they'll figure something out." Cramer had a similar view of Microsoft when shares traded at a 52-week low of $350 in June. "I didn't think their best times were behind them," Cramer said, despite at times expressing frustration in the stock's performance. Ultimately, though, Cramer retained the Club's shares because of his trust in the veteran leadership team of CEO Satya Nadella and CFO Amy Hood. "I thought, 'They're going to figure out this Copilot, and with their Azure web services business they're going to make a ton of money.'" Shares now trade around $529, as the market has grown more confident in Microsoft's plan for Copilot. Also, in late July, the performance and guidance for Azure also surpassed Wall Street expectations , leading to a stock rally. Cramer also highlighted Advanced Micro Devices and Intel in semiconductors, Marvell Technology in chips and fiber, and CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks in cybersecurity. The strategy looks particularly attractive to Cramer as higher interest rates make growth harder to find elsewhere. AI-related companies, by contrast, are among the relatively few businesses that can continue delivering strong growth in this environment, he said. "When I query about 80% of the S&P 500 about what can possibly go right, I can't even think of anything for most of them," Cramer said. "Sure, that can change when the war ends. Until then, though, the AI-related stocks give you the most opportunity for something to go right." That doesn't mean the AI trade is without risk. Cramer acknowledged that enthusiasm can become excessive. He also stressed, "I want to be diversified, and I certainly run a diversified" portfolio for the Investing Club. Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of META, MSFT, INTC, CRWD, PANW. events.title: Watchdog identifies 'psychological harm' at world's largest lithium mine
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Talison Lithium on notice after WorkSafe finds psychological distress among Greenbushes workers The Greenbushes mine has been described as a toxic workplace. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) WorkSafe has found poor workplace culture and conditions at Talison's Greenbushes Lithium Mine have left workers exposed to significant psychological harm. Staff say excessive demands, poor resourcing and work areas contaminated with animal faeces contributed to a toxic workplace culture. Talison says it is fast-tracking changes to workplace culture and safety. The owner of the world's largest lithium mine has been put on notice after a probe by Western Australia's work safety watchdog found a toxic workplace culture and psychologically distressed workforce. WorkSafe issued an improvement notice to Talison Lithium in August after survey responses indicated workers were exposed to psychosocial hazards at its Greenbushes mine, 240 kilometres south of Perth. Talison Lithium employs more than 1,500 workers at its Greenbushes site. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) The survey identified excessive work demands, inadequate resourcing and poor work conditions as factors in an environment causing significant psychosocial harm to staff. Reported issues included inadequate toilet facilities and working areas contaminated by animal faeces. Current and former staff who have spoken to the ABC described a toxic workplace culture. One worker, speaking anonymously due to the risk to their ongoing employment, said they felt morally distressed by what they witnessed at work and raised concerns over the independence of Talison's internal complaints process. "Employees go externally when they feel they've exhausted everything internally," they said. Workers also reported tiredness, nervousness or anxiety, low mood or depression, hopelessness and feelings of worthlessness. Greenbushes provides about 20 per cent of the world's lithium, which is considered crucial for the global energy transition. In an email sent to staff and seen by the ABC, Talison chief executive Rob Telford apologised to workers whose experience had fallen short of expectations of a respectful and safe workplace. "Let me be clear, any behaviour that undermines this, including bullying, aggression, intimidation, and any form of harassment, sexual or otherwise, has absolutely no place at Talison," Mr Telford wrote. Rob Telford says the findings of a psychosocial survey are deeply concerning. ( ABC South West WA: Jon Daly ) WorkSafe ordered Talison to complete the review of measures to manage psychosocial hazards at Greenbushes mine and consult with workers by November 20. It has ordered the review to consider interaction between job demands, worker control, role clarity, organisational change, consultation, leadership behaviours, reporting arrangements and workplace conditions. A Talison spokesperson said work had begun on improving the workplace culture before the improvement notice was issued. "Improvements have been implemented across a number of areas including clearer expectations for respectful workplace behaviour, increased team capacity, stronger systems and a sitewide program to improve facilities," they said in a statement. "Further work is planned, leveraging work that others in the industry have successfully trialled, but we have prioritised initiatives to support improving the felt experience of our workforce." The spokesperson acknowledged the findings of the psychosocial safety survey and improvement notice, and said the safety of its workforce was its priority. "[We are] working closely with our workforce and the regulator to address the matters which have been raised," the spokesperson said. The demand for lithium is being driven by batteries and electric cars. ( ABC South West: Ruslan Kulski ) "Any improvements we can make on the advice of the regulator to ensure our people continue to be treated with respect, feel safe at work, and can perform at their best, remains a focus for us. "This includes working with the regulator to fast-track changes and expedite a safety plan that was already in the process of being implemented." The spokesperson said employees were encouraged to raise concerns through a range of channels and that concerns were taken seriously. Australian Manufacturing Workers Union state secretary Steve McCartney said WorkSafe needed to take stronger action. "The feedback I'm getting is that it sounds pretty toxic, and the company is doing little or nothing to deal with it, except the review that has been there for quite some time," he said.

events.title: CDC: Monitoring Russian plague risk, "prepared" for any threat
events.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it is monitoring reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia and says it is prepared for any threat that emerges. Why it matters: Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous form of plague and is almost always fatal unless if left untreated. The latest: President Trump told reporters Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to discuss the suspected plague case and would speak with him "very soon." Asked what U.S. intelligence was saying about the situation, Trump said officials were in "very deep discussions" and that "we'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow." Catch up quick: Darya Shipilova , a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, died after reports that she may have been exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. Russian authorities say testing has not linked her death to plague or to pathogens she handled at work. However, at least five hospitals in the area remain in quarantine and almost 200 people who had contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical observation as a precaution. What they're saying: "We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available," the CDC said in an X post Tuesday. "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely." Context: The CDC said the plague is a dangerous bacterial disease that can be treated with antibiotics, especially when caught early. Pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact. The CDC says "rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals" are important for keeping people safe. State of play: The concerns have drawn attention on social media and from government officials and the White House. President Trump acknowledged Monday that he is aware of the situation. "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday, but said he hadn't spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about it yet. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." The Department of Health and Human Services and the State Department are also monitoring the situation. What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia Tuesday to share more information about Shipilova's death, per Reuters . ​Rubio told reporters: "I ​think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously ⁠share more information with the world." Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump.

Her most daring look this year had detachable sleeves. Florence Pugh is no stranger to making a fashion statement. events.title: Trump hedges on paying back government for ads that already aired
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he and his political action committee will pay for controversial television ads that praised him and had been funded by the U.S. government. The White House later clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service ads moving forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. Trump's announcement came after continued backlash to the ads, which had run in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election. A new Trump ad began airing on Tuesday. President Donald Trump hedged Tuesday when asked whether he would reimburse the U.S. government for previously aired television advertisements that praised him, saying, "We'll decide." The ads cost the federal government nearly $10 million before Trump on Monday announced that he and his political action committee will pay for the segments in the face of criticism that they are propaganda and aimed at helping Republican political candidates. The White House later Monday clarified that the super PAC — MAGA Inc. — will pay for what it calls public service announcements going forward, and not for the ads that have already aired. The prior airings reportedly were funded from a pool of up to $20 million set aside by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security . Asked whether he would reimburse the government for the costs of ads already aired, Trump told reporters, "The ads were really good." "They were promotion for the country, done by many presidents before," he said. "So we'll decide." Trump's latest comments on the furor came hours after a new ad aired. That ad was labeled as paid for by the U.S. government. The ad features video clips of Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussing the U.S. capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year. "Nicolás Maduro had his chance ... until he didn't," Hegseth says in the ad. "He effed around and he found out." Another clip in the ad shows Rubio warning, "Don't play games with [President Trump] in office." The ads have been running in the weeks leading up to November's midterm election . Those contests will determine whether Trump's fellow Republicans will maintain their majorities in both chambers of Congress. The White House and MAGA Inc. did not immediately reply when asked whether the super PAC would cover the cost of the new ad or whether the buy had already been placed before Trump's announcement and would remain taxpayer-funded. "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.," Trump said. AdImpact has tracked roughly $9.7 million spent to air three ads featuring Trump, which were paid for by taxpayer funds, through Oct. 5. Trump's announcement that he would pay for the ads came three days after The New York Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that "Trump personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads praising him and his presidency." Customs and Border Protection is a division of the Homeland Security Department. Sen. Maggie Hassan , D-N.H., in a Sept. 24 letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, wrote, "The advertisement does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions against the use of appropriated funds as part of 'a general propaganda effort designed to aid a political party or candidates.'" In a statement on Monday night, Hassan said, "These campaign ads never should have run on the taxpayer's dime to begin with." "They were clearly wrong and clearly illegal, which is why the President should also immediately repay the taxpayers for the amount already spent on these ads," Hassan said. "There's a lesson here: We can't underestimate the difference that citizens can make in our country when they speak out and hold their leaders to account," she said. On Tuesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., called for the Government Accountability Office and Office of Special Counsel to investigate the ads. events.title: Trump says Iran could ‘take out’ LA. Its missiles can’t reach that far.
events.summary: A US Air Force B-2 Spirit bomber is pictured at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri, following the Operation Midnight Hammer Iranian bombing raid, June 22, 2025. 509th Bomb Wing Trump raised a hypothetical strike on Los Angeles and San Diego at a Nebraska rally. Iran has no nuclear program or weapons. Tehran remains a proliferation risk, but not an imminent nuclear threat, program watchers say. Iran cannot strike Los Angeles or San Diego with a nuclear weapon, regardless of President Donald Trump's offhand comments on the campaign trail. Iran has no known nuclear weapons and no known missiles capable of reaching either California city. Tehran is roughly 7,500 miles from California, far beyond the approximately 1,200-mile range of Iran's longest-range ballistic missiles, according to the Defense Intelligence Agency. The nonpartisan Arms Control Association, which tracks nuclear proliferation around the world, said it's hard to tell how Iran's missile program could recover after being damaged by US strikes . The bombed sites have not been inspected by experts, though uranium for the program likely remains buried deep within rubble. "Iran is still a proliferation risk, but its nuclear program is not an imminent threat," Kelsey Davenport, the group's director for nonproliferation policy, told Business Insider. Trump raised the prospect of an Iranian strike on California in offhand remarks at a Republican rally in Nebraska on Monday, as he defended the war against Iran as "a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe." "They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego," Trump said. Iran has long-range conventional missiles and drones capable of striking US troops and infrastructure across the Middle East. Throughout Operation Epic Fury, Iranian strikes killed six troops in Kuwait in March, and other strikes have seriously damaged US military facilities throughout the Middle East. But those systems are only capable of regional strikes, and are not nuclear weapons. The United States has struck Iranian uranium-enrichment facilities twice since last May, including at the start of Operation Epic Fury . Before those strikes, Iran was moving closer to the ability to produce a nuclear weapon, but had not produced one. Davenport said that while the remaining amounts of uranium are unknown, military strikes alone cannot erase Iranian nuclear knowledge. "Iran will have the capabilities to build a bomb, regardless of how the war ends," she said. If Iran, or any other adversary, eventually acquired a nuclear weapon and a missile capable of delivering it across the ocean, locations most likely to be at risk might be major cities and sensitive military sites, though such an escalation would be unprecedented for any country, and unlikely, Davenport said. She pointed out the inherent dangers of escalation, also known as mutually-assured destruction. Using a nuclear weapon could invite nuclear retaliation , a primary reason those weapons have not been used since World War II. "That's an escalatory spiral states are not going to be eager to climb," Davenport said. And, countries frequently still carry out major conventional attacks without crossing the nuclear threshold. Israel, the US, and Russia are all nuclear powers that have attacked adversaries without using nuclear weapons. For more than a decade, Iran has also relied on asymmetric tools against the United States and its partners, including cyberattacks . Iranian government-linked hackers have targeted US banks, universities, businesses, and government agencies. A group linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps previously claimed responsibility for hacking systems that controlled US water treatment facilities. events.title: Russia plague: How great is the global risk? Maybe low, but infectious disease experts want more data
events.summary: Health and Wellness From booksmaxxing to looksmaxxing: Why the trends concern mental health experts Psychology and Relationships Worried about interrupting someone’s scrolling? Here’s what experts think Spend Why someone else’s credit card debt can make you anxious How to Talk to People Stop saying 'let me know if you need anything,' says psychologist—how to talk to a friend who's struggling Raising Successful Kids Parents who are really good at handling tantrums do 5 things—their kids become more emotionally intelligent, says psychologist Last week, an employee who worked at a Russian anti-plague institute died, possibly from an unspecified form of plague . This led to the quarantine of nearly 200 people in Russia's Irkutsk region, located in eastern Siberia, according to local news outlets. Following these reports, concerns are circulating about what exactly caused the death and quarantine — and just how worried the rest of the world should be. The World Health Organization says the incident presents a low risk globally of pathogen spread, and a moderate risk for the nearby area, Dr. Nahid Bhadelia , founding director of Boston University's Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases, told CNBC's "Squawk On the Street" on Tuesday. But some infectious disease experts say it's impossible to determine the risk yet, citing a lack of transparency from Russian authorities. "The risk to the wider public is uncertain ... I wouldn't call it low, medium or high because we don't know the information to answer that," says Dr. Raj Panjabi , a Harvard University physician and former White House Biosecurity Director to President Joe Biden. Typically, when a pathogen causes a death or quarantine, local public health authorities test the pathogen and share the genetic code sequencing so it can be analyzed and risk levels can be assessed by infectious disease experts internationally. Russian authorities have not yet publicly shared those details. Allegations of a plague outbreak spread after local government official Alexei Tsydenov, head of the nearby Republic of Buryatia, said in an Oct. 2 post on Russian social media platform VK that a woman in the Irkutsk region "may" have died of plague. After initially saying on Sunday that the laboratory staffer died from "pneumonia of unknown [cause]," Russian public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor reportedly said Tuesday that beyond Covid-19 and a virus that causes the common cold, "no other infectious disease pathogens were detected" among people tested so far. Yet the alleged size of the reported quarantine suggests an infection that could be more serious than what's being shared publicly, says Panjabi. "There's a mismatch between the words and the actions, and that's what makes us concerned. And a lack of transparency about the lab results, which is what's needed right now," he says. How worried should the rest of the world be? If Russia does have a plague outbreak, the rest of the world could have low cause for concern. Pneumonic plague , which can cause pneumonia or pneumonia-like symptoms, can lead to hospitalization or death — but it's treatable with antibiotics when identified early, Panjabi says. If a different form of pathogen is circulating in the Irkutsk region, you'd need more information than is currently available to determine your potential risk. You can track your need to worry by asking yourself three questions as data becomes available, Panjabi suggests. The answers can help you gauge the level of global concern, and gain knowledge on how the pathogen is progressing: Is there an escalation in new cases, or are more people falling sick? Are quarantines and restrictions being put in place for schools and workplaces? Do lab results reveal that this pathogen is something we haven't seen before? More broadly, to embrace uncertainty during any infectious disease outbreak or concern, Panjabi suggests prioritizing your "locus of control" with an exercise he recommends in his upcoming book, " Safer: A Playbook—Turning Fear into Action and Crisis into Community ." Draw a circle on a piece of paper and, inside the circle, write down everything you can't control surrounding a major global health event. You can't control the number of cases, or market volatility, for example. The goal of the activity is to remind yourself of what's out of your hands so you can shift your focus to what you actually can change, says Panjabi. "You don't need control over the whole situation to feel steadier. What we need sometimes is just control over the next meaningful step," he says. "And being able to shift the locus of control in this way is one way to do that." events.title: Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says
events.summary: The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI, the two leading US AI model makers, is no contest when it comes to assessing which one gives you more value for your subscription money, according to industry research firm SemiAnalysis. Following changes to OpenAI's $200 per month subscription plan that effectively halved its value, SemiAnalysis looked at the various subscription plans offered by AI companies, because that's still the main way that individuals and small businesses buy AI services. AI subscriptions are heavily subsidized – customers get far more tokens for their money than they would paying metered API rates. And SemiAnalysis argues that it's necessary to delve into subscription pricing to evaluate AI shops financially because subscription usage consumes a disproportionate amount of company compute resources. Claude subscriptions, the biz claims, take up about 42 percent of Anthropic's inference compute while generating just 10 percent of its revenue. And those subscriptions provide considerable value. "Anthropic is an overwhelmingly better deal, offering ~5x the API-equivalent value across the board," SemiAnalysis claims in reference to mid-tier models GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. "You could argue that this is unfair for [OpenAI] because 6.1 Sol is much cheaper per token than Opus 5.5, but the gap is still massive even if you switch to comparing the number of tokens." OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. SemiAnalysis' calculation relies on measuring token output rates, converting those into tokens per 5-hour usage window and per month, and then computing the API-equivalent value. Company researchers contend that API-equivalent value is the best figure for capturing the value of a subscription plan, though they allow that other measures like raw token volume may be more appropriate in some instances. API-based comparisons can be slow to account for the rapidly shifting capabilities of models that come to market. The debut of a new open source model, for example, can alter what's possible at a given price. For those with access to subscription plans, the subsidized prices clearly offer real value, so much so that there's an underground market for reselling tokens from pooled subscription accounts in many parts of the world. But there are other ways to measure AI value. Artificial Analysis, for example, tracks cost per task – the estimated dollar cost of completing a specific task. By that yardstick, GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72) is far more affordable than Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98), at least for those paying API rates. But that ratio may not be true for different tasks – benchmark performance may not reflect your workload. As measured by tokens, Claude Pro ($20 per month) provides 2.9 billion tokens per month, compared to ChatGPT ($20/mo) at 1 billion tokens per month, according to SemiAnalysis. But models may use more or fewer tokens than others for the same task, and when the output is functional, like code, AI output may achieve a similar result across different models but with differing degrees of efficiency. Anticipating AI costs gets more complicated for businesses, which can't count on subscription subsidies and may not have experience with AI cost management. In a July report, McKinsey said 93 percent of enterprises exceeded their AI budgets. "I think all businesses are seeing their AI costs rise," said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of AI agent biz Skydive, in an interview with The Register. Since the beginning of the year, he said, AI has been getting better at solving certain business problems, and companies have started deploying AI more widely, then noticing their token bills going through the roof. "The labs typically subsidize their prosumer plans with subscription pricing massively," said Amin. "And I think it's part of their marketing funnel because more people are able to use the tools, get familiar with the tools, and then bring those tools to work." But for larger companies, he said, two problems arise. You have more employees than can fit on a subsidized plan and, at scale, costs add up fast. "A huge way that enterprises solve this is being able to make a workload work well on the frontier and then quickly switch it to an open source model that they control and that they can serve at a much lower fraction of the cost," he said. "And so for us internally we were able to drop our AI costs 75 percent plus just by moving them all to Skydive Glide, which is our model router that for the given workload tries to find an equivalent open source model that can handle that workload without a quality drop. And so today we run a lot of our workloads on GLM-5.3 Flash." Amin said that companies adept at AI cost management maintain evaluation benchmarks that reflect their workloads. Companies use those metrics to test new models as they come out in whatever AI harness they're using, to ensure consistency. Looking ahead, he said, he expects companies will trust more of that work to service providers. "So what this means is that if you deploy an agent on top of us, we capture in the background the data of how that agent's actually running in production," he said. "And then we use that to construct the eval data set on the fly." ® Updated Oct 6 at 2322 GMT to clarify that Skydive is the platform that sells the agents, while Anything is the umbrella parent company.

events.title: Anduril lands $2.9 billion Navy submarine shipyard contract days after Luckey joins Pentagon weapons group
events.summary: Anduril landed a $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy to support submarine production. The company said it will build components for the Virginia-class submarine. Co-founder Palmer Luckey, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk were named to the Pentagon's Project Meridian. Anduril won an up to $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy on Tuesday to boost submarine production, days after co-founder Palmer Luckey was named to a Pentagon future weapons task force. The company is also investing $3.7 billion to scale a new shipyard at Sparrows Point, outside Baltimore, Maryland, slated to start operations in 2030 and create about 3,100 jobs. Anduril said the 2 million-square-foot facility will build components for the Virginia-class submarine. Some parts, including torpedo tubes, will be manufactured at a 160,000-square-foot facility in Orange County, California. "This is about putting more food on the table and being able to meet the requirements that our country has to produce more submarines," said Anduril President and Chief Strategy Officer Chris Brose in a press briefing. President Donald Trump thanked Luckey by name in comments Tuesday afternoon to mark the investment, calling him a "friend" and "very brilliant guy." The deal comes days after the Department of Defense tapped Luckey to join a new initiative called Project Meridian to identify and develop capabilities for future U.S. conflicts, raising questions over defense tech's growing sway in Washington as the companies compete for government contracts. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk are also part of the project. Both SpaceX and Anduril are actively working with the U.S. government. Department of Defense Chief Technology Officer Emil Michael addressed Luckey's involvement with the Pentagon in comments to CNBC on Tuesday, dismissing any concerns about a potential conflict of interest. "There's really nothing to see here," he said. Michael said the collection of academics, former military and industry leaders in Project Meridian is "exactly the right kind of mix that you want" to prepare for any future conflict. Defense tech companies and their leaders have seen their influence grow in Washington in recent months as Trump seeks to bolster U.S. military capabilities, including shipbuilding. Marc Andreessen , whose venture firm Andreessen Horowitz pours billions into defense tech firms, including Anduril, was named to the Pentagon's defense policy board this summer, alongside Thiel Capital's Blake Masters. Google unveils latest AI model, but Wall Street wants a breakout personal agent Former LinkedIn chief Roslansky to leave Microsoft, following other exec departures SpaceX launches Google AI chips into orbit in push toward space-based data centers Trump's AI lunch included every major tech company. Except Apple Anduril is widely known for building autonomous drones and crafts. Over the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was reportedly in talks to build drone boats on the site. Brose said the facility will focus on the Virginia-class submarine program, illustrating a push into conventional shipbuilding by the growing defense contractor. "Our goal here is to be a critical, and hopefully, over time, much larger and growing part of the supply chain for our lead shipbuilders," He said. "And over time, we hope that'll grow up to very large sections of the ship." Trump made several references to autonomous submarines and drones during his remarks. The massive Virginia-class vessels are built by General Dynamics Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries. This summer, General Dynamics won a $76.6 billion Navy award to build submarines. "This is an opportunity to really reimagine how a shipyard is built and how this work is done, and that's just not something that our current industrial base has the luxury of doing," Brose said. CORRECTION: This headline has been updated to reflect that co-founder Palmer Luckey was named to the Pentagon's Project Meridian. An earlier version misstated his title.

events.title: Programmable Memory Controller Eases Adoption of New DRAM Techniques (ETH Zürich, CISPA, NYU)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at ETH Zürich, CISPA , and New York University published a technical paper titled “Terracotta: Enabling the Adoption of New DRAM Techniques via a Flexible DRAM Interface and Memory Controller.” “DRAM continues to limit the performance, energy efficiency, and robustness of modern systems. Many prior works propose DRAM techniques that support in-DRAM computation, improve memory access latency and parallelism, and enhance DRAM maintenance and reliability. However, adopting each new technique requires repeated modifications to the rigid DRAM interface and memory controller, hindering its deployment. Our goal is to reduce these repeated modifications. We observe that the DRAM commands and memory controller structures of many DRAM techniques are similar. Our key idea is to use these similarities to compose a set of primitives for implementing diverse DRAM techniques. We propose Terracotta, a new framework with two flexible components: (i) custom command extensions that let DRAM vendors define new commands within a single, standardized interface, and (ii) a programmable memory controller that system designers can program to support new DRAM techniques post-silicon. Together, these enable deployment by configuring the memory controller instead of modifying the interface and controller. ” Find the technical paper here . October 2026. events.title: CDC ‘closely monitoring’ suspected pneumonic plague case
events.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is “closely monitoring” developments in a suspected case of pneumonic plague that led to the death of a researcher in Russia. “At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC posted on X . Paul Friedrichs, a retired military medical officer who worked as the inaugural director of the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy under former President Joe Biden, said Russian officials could help alleviate the worst fears if they disclosed what the researcher was working on, when she developed symptoms, and when she was treated with antibiotics. “What would really make me have trouble sleeping at night is if they continue to refuse to release really basic information,” Friedrichs said, adding that one key piece of information that should be released is the genomic sequence of the pathogen that killed the researcher. “It is understandable that people will assume the worst in a scenario when it would be so easy to disprove that the worst is occurring.” Still, the biosecurity expert cautioned against projecting onto the Russians how the US would handle a biosecurity incident. “The Russian culture and the Russian government bring security forces into all sorts of things that we would never, in normal circumstances, think about involving security agencies or military forces” in, Friedrichs said. “Assuming that their actions would look like ours, and then assuming because their actions don’t look like ours, it must be something nefarious — that’s a bad assumption.” — David Lim

events.title: A brutal winter heating bill is coming for some homes
events.summary: Americans could pay far more to heat their homes with oil this winter than last, a new analysis reviewed by Axios shows, as volatile energy markets and the Iran War deepen the affordability crisis. Why it matters: Heating bills are eating into household budgets before winter sets in, with stark divides between fuel types. By the numbers: Families that heat with oil could pay about 50% more this winter than last, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), up from its 31.3% projection in mid-September. The average cost of heating a home with oil is expected to rise by about $878, costing over $2,600 this winter. By comparison, the Energy Information Administration's Winter Fuels Outlook released Tuesday projects electricity bills will rise 4% nationally, while natural gas bills will fall 9% and propane spending will drop 3%. EIA expects a smaller increase on heating oil than NEADA, projecting a 21% increase in household expenditures. Northeastern households will feel the pain most acutely: about 82% of home heating oil is consumed in the region, where some states lack robust natural gas pipelines, according to NEADA data. Just 3% of U.S. households use oil as their primary heat source, compared to about 45% using natural gas and 43% using electricity, NEADA says. The big picture: Heating oil prices are rising as global oil markets falter because of the wars in Iran and Ukraine and as refinery activity declines. "Those trends really reflect the worst-case scenario of this war, and they are going to feel it this winter, and it's unfortunate," Mark Wolfe, executive director of the NEADA, tells Axios. What they're saying: Because of the cost, some families will cut back on food or medicine, borrow from payday lenders, or turn the heat down to unsafe levels to cover their heating bills, Wolfe says. " With low-income families, sometimes states will move money around to help them, but they'll go without, " Wolfe says. Between the lines: States can put more money toward heating assistance, but they have fewer tools to protect heating-oil customers than households served by regulated gas and electric utilities, Wolfe says. States can require utilities to offer discounts, affordability programs or winter shutoff protections, but they generally don't apply to independent heating-oil dealers. Zoom in: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey declared a State of Energy Emergency Monday over rising winter energy costs, unlocking nearly $150 million in relief and expanding assistance to middle-class households that heat with oil. Rhode Island has also declared an energy affordability emergency and directed $28 million in reserves toward winter electric-bill relief, and Maine Gov. Janet Mills announced $40 million in automatically applied electricity discounts for low-income residents. Zoom out: The energy affordability crisis is compounded by the Trump administration's attempts to dismantle the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP. The administration fired LIHEAP's federal staff at the Department of Health and Human Services in April 2025 and proposed eliminating funding for the program. LIHEAP is still running, but state administrators are operating without dedicated federal staff. The White House referred Axios to HHS, which said it "will carry out its responsibilities for funding Congress has made available" and that "HHS has the staff and capacity to distribute these funds in a timely manner." The bottom line: Winter is coming, and Americans need to prepare for both the cold — and the prices — to bite. Go deeper: How to save money on your electric bill this winter

events.title: 7 things passengers should never do on a train, according to an etiquette coach
events.summary: Fall is a popular time for train travel, but passengers shouldn't forget to pack their manners. Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images Inconsiderate passengers can make traveling an especially stressful experience. Etiquette expert William Hanson shared seven things travelers should never do on trains. Hanson said travelers should avoid talking on speakerphone and placing their bags on seats. Each fall, travelers fill trains to catch some of the US' best foliage views . But whether you're taking a scenic ride or a regular rail journey, inconsiderate passengers can quickly spoil the experience. To make sure you're not one of them, Business Insider previously spoke with British etiquette coach William Hanson to learn some of travelers' biggest etiquette faux pas on trains. From placing bags on empty seats to blasting music, here are seven things travelers should avoid doing. Don't talk on speakerphone. Passengers should avoid using cellphones to avoid bothering other passengers. Jacob Silberberg/Getty Images Hanson said he understands not wanting to keep your phone pressed to your face for long periods of time, but that it doesn't excuse talking on speakerphone . "It explains it, but it doesn't excuse it," he told Business Insider in a 2024 interview through his partnership with Trainline, a European train booking app. Hanson added, "If we were all doing that, let's think we were all on our phones, on the speakerphone making calls in a carriage, it would be a cacophony. You wouldn't be able to hear anything." Although Trainline said its research found that only one in 10 people reported feeling bothered by others on their phones, it's more polite to just wait until you disembark to catch up on your calls. Please, don't place your feet on the seats. Don't put your feet on seats on public transport. Spencer Platt/Getty Images for Fortune Magazine And no, it's not better if you take your shoes off . "Your socks — or heaven forbid you're not even wearing socks — your feet still have germs," Hanson told Business Insider. "And it is not your own personal seat. It is a seat that is shared by numerous passengers on numerous rail journeys." Bags don't belong on seats, either. Do not put your bags on open seats. Erik Gonzalez/500px/Getty Images Trainline reported that over a third of people think spreading out over multiple seats is the most annoying behavior from fellow passengers. Hanson recommends keeping your purses or small bags in your lap, on the floor in front of your seat, or in designated luggage areas. "The only time you can have a bag on the seat next to you is if you're basically on an absolutely deserted carriage and there are clearly numerous seats for people to go and sit on," he said. If you do come across another passenger's bag occupying your designated seat, Hanson recommends keeping the conversation reasonable. "If you are reasonable, they will be able to move their bag," he said. Try to avoid eating overly fragrant foods, like oranges. Take foods on board that won't bother other passengers. Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images Eating on a train is perfectly fine, especially during long journeys, but Hanson recommends being mindful about your snack choices , especially ones that are particularly fragrant or might be loud. One option he discourages people from bringing is oranges. "However delicious an orange is and full of vitamin D, it can actually be quite objectionable as a smell if you are not the one eating it," he said. Instead, try to stick to options like sandwiches , sweets, nuts, dried fruit, or other fresh fruit, such as grapes. Be careful not to play your music too loudly in your headphones. Keep the volume down, so other passengers can't hear it. Edward Berthelot/Getty Images "Some headphones leak when they're too loud, making your favorite playlist a public nuisance," Hanson wrote for Trainline's " Mind the Manners " guide to train etiquette. "I hate to say it but not everyone will be a fan of your audio tastes." Trainline reported that loud music is the most uncomfortable train issue for travelers. If you're traveling with a pet, don't expect everyone to be comfortable. Pet owners should be thoughtful of other passengers. Anastasiia Voloshko/Getty Images Most trains in the US permit pets on board, although it depends on factors including the company, the size of your pet, and the length of your journey. If you are able to take your pet on board, the important thing to remember is that others may not love your furry friend as much as you do. Trainline research found that 25% of people are uncomfortable sitting next to a dog. Hanson recommends that those traveling with their dogs be proactive in opening the lines of communication and asking fellow passengers about their comfort levels. "If you do see some hesitancy and there are many other empty seats to go and sit in that are not reserved, you're going to move," he said. He added that context in these situations is important, too. If the dog owner is the second to arrive, it would be their responsibility to move; but if the dog owner is already seated and someone new comes along, it would be their choice to sit or go elsewhere. The simplest advice? "Talk and be reasonable," Hanson said. "We as humans, we mood match. So, if you go in all guns blazing, then you're going to get a similar reaction back." And finally, try to let people off the train before you board. Travelers should let passengers come off the train before boarding. Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images This tip doesn't need much explanation, and yet it remains a common nuisance for travelers, commuters, and locals alike. "There will be more room for people when you get on if the people have come off the train first," Hanson said. He added, "If you're standing by the doors anyway, you can get on, and there's often a beep or a signal before those doors close. So everyone just needs to just remember: It will be fine." Editor's note: This story was originally published in September 2024, and most recently updated in October 2026. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq reach record closing highs as focus pivots to earnings
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange on Oct 6, before the closing bell, in New York City. - US stocks hit record closes as oil steadied and Treasury yields eased, shifting attention to third-quarter earnings. - The S&P 500 and Nasdaq reached all-time highs, while the Dow stayed about 5% below its August peak. - AI-linked shares and strong company news lifted markets, as traders cut bets on another Fed rate hike and watched inflation risks. NEW YORK - US stocks ended higher on Oct 6 as crude prices steadied and US Treasury yields eased, offering some reprieve from concerns that have preoccupied investors in recent weeks, and allowing markets to turn their attention to the approaching third-quarter reporting season. The broad rally pushed the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq to all-time closing highs. The blue-chip Dow remains just over 5% shy of its record closing level reached on Aug 5. When oil prices stabilise or move lower, “that causes yields to move down because there’s less anxiety about energy-driven inflation, which in turn is helping lift stocks higher,” said Oliver Pursche, senior vice-president at Wealthspire Advisors in New York. “This has been the narrative of the market for the last couple of weeks.” Six of the “Magnificent Seven” group of AI-linked megacap firms advanced, bolstering gains, while small-caps lagged their larger-cap counterparts. The AI trade is very much alive, with the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index gaining ground. Expenditures on AI-related infrastructure were reflected in international trade data, which showed imports of capital goods rose by 4.4% in August. The Commerce Department’s report showed the US trade deficit grew by 13.7% as imports rose to a record high. On monthly and annual bases, imports have grown by 4.3% and 28.4%, respectively, reflecting robust domestic demand that could exacerbate inflation pressures, particularly amid war-related supply constraints. Even so, financial markets are currently pricing in a diminishing probability of 19.4% that the US Federal Reserve will implement its second consecutive rate hike at this month’s monetary policy meeting, down from 50.9% a week ago, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. Fed rate hike bets have been responsive to oil prices, which have surged amid the Iran war, threatening to morph into broader price pressures. But supply worries eased after the Group of Seven countries reached an agreement to release emergency diesel and crude stockpiles, helping to stabilise front-month WTI and Brent crude futures. “We don’t expect (the Fed) to do anything at the next meeting,” said Tim Ghriskey, senior portfolio strategist at Ingalls & Snyder in New York. “But I think they’re in a gradual hiking cycle.” “High oil prices have hit a broad range of consumers,” Ghriskey added. “That’s one of the reasons for the recent Fed hike.” The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 253.14 points, or 0.49%, to 51,521.04, the S&P 500 gained 45.00 points, or 0.58%, to 7,818.95 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 122.48 points, or 0.45%, to 27,599.79. Of the 11 major sectors in the S&P 500, all but healthcare gained ground, with utilities leading the way. Third-quarter earnings season kicks off next week, with a number of high-profile financial firms expected to report on Oct 13. Analysts currently expect annual S&P 500 earnings growth of 30.6%, in aggregate, for the July-to-September period, led by an expected 114.7% jump in energy earnings, followed by a 66.5% estimated surge in tech results, according to LSEG. Marvell Technology climbed 5.8% following the chip designer’s 2028 revenue forecast hike due to strong demand for its data center chips. Chipmaker AMD gained 2.8% after CEO Lisa Su said it plans to substantially increase its chip supply in 2027 to meet booming AI demand. Constellation Energy jumped 12.3% after Alphabet entered into a 3,590-megawatt power deal with the company. Option Care Health soared 32.7% after drug distributor McKesson and private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice agreed to buy the infusion therapy provider in a deal worth about US$5.8 billion (S$7.4 billion), including debt. Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.93-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 258 new highs and 219 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,394 stocks rose and 2,378 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.01-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 23 new 52-week highs and 2 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 61 new highs and 182 new lows. Volume on US exchanges was 16.50 billion shares, compared with the 17.51 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days. REUTERS

events.title: Silicon Valley’s AI wunderkind launches Underdog, the most private Instinct/Muse competitor yet
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When self-taught coder Sigil Wen was 17, he moved to Silicon Valley and lived in an AI hacker house with famed AI researcher Andrej Karpathy. While there, he hacked and coded alongside other people who would become the biggest names in AI, like Perplexity founder Aravind Srinivas and OpenAI researcher Noam Brown. He tested early versions of AI tools that would later become well known, including a chatbot shared by Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann that would become Claude, an image generator from David Holz that would become Midjourney, and what would become OpenAI’s GPT-3 and the image generator Stable Diffusion. Prominent investor and entrepreneur Naval Ravikant hired him for Airchat, Ravikant’s now-defunct rival to the Clubhouse social network. For fun, he figured out how to get GPT-2 running on his Apple Watch. “It was a magical time,” Wen told TechCrunch. Now a Thiel Fellow — the program from investor Peter Thiel that invites young founders to pursue projects instead of college — Wen on Monday launched an invite-only beta of Underdog, one of the most private AI assistants Silicon Valley has yet to offer. The model runs wholly on-device, meaning the user’s data remains on devices they already own, currently Macs and Windows PCs, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions coming soon. Underdog is powered by Husky, the inference engine Wen built to run AI models quickly on a user’s own hardware. Wen says it moves less data between a computer’s main chip and its graphics chip than rival on-device engines. Underdog has other security features baked in, too, like encrypting the keys to the email and other accounts that users authorize Underdog to access. Underdog is, however, using much smaller models than today’s state-of-the-art ones hosted in data centers. It currently uses a 27-billion parameter reasoning model fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B. Wen argues that this model compares favorably with Claude Opus 4.6 in some benchmarks , or what was considered top performance six months ago. He says that means it can handle the everyday tasks that people want an AI assistant to do, like shopping research or answering math homework questions. “You don’t need to sacrifice your privacy for the capability because they’re just as capable,” Wen says. He adds that small on-device models will continue to grow more capable over time. Perhaps the most interesting thing about Underdog is its early business model. The app will be free at first and never ad-supported. Since the AI runs on users’ machines, Underdog doesn’t have the giant overhead of paying a provider for inference. “I don’t have to charge you a subscription to run this because my costs are so super low,” he said. Instead, with Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison as one of his angel investors, he’s borrowing a play from the fintech era. Underdog will take a tiny percentage of payment transactions that the AI assistant makes using Stripe’s secure payment rails, something like an interchange fee. In this way, the AI assistant never has to mine your data. It is as aligned with you as your bank or credit card providers. This runs contrary to the business motivations of many of the other players in AI assistants, whose privacy policies allow them to collect data on users that they may sell to advertisers or other third parties, or use to train other models. That kind of data collection could be a particularly treacherous trade-off for users of an AI assistant, which may need access to the most intimate details about you in order to be useful, from medical conditions to financial data to data on your kids. As Wen wrote in what he calls his AI manifesto , “Why should using AI require surrendering your private information?” He tells TechCrunch: “I honestly want to build Underdog for myself. I’m building a product that I would be proud for my future children to use.” The startup behind Underdog is named Conway Research, and Collison isn’t its only big-name investor. Conway is backed by Andreessen Horowitz via partner Chris Dixon, as well as Khosla Ventures, Hummingbird, SV Angel, the Anthology Fund (the partnership fund between Menlo Ventures and Anthropic), and a prominent list of angel investors that includes Vercel founder Guillermo Rauch, Noam Brown, and Deedy Das, among others.
