events.title: OpenAI’s human rights lead: What the military could do with AI ‘keeps me up at night’
events.summary: In June, Sarah Yager took an unusual role at OpenAI, becoming the company’s first human rights and responsible deployment lead. She’s focused on military applications, given her 30 years of experience in this area and OpenAI’s partnership with the Department of War (DoW). Yager spoke about her role on stage Tuesday at the ScaleUp:AI conference in New York City, where she mentioned her concerns with military institutions adopting AI, particularly in armed conflict. “Everyone is very worried and rightly so,” Yager said. “This keeps me up at night: ‘What is the military going to do with AI when it comes to targeting? And what about autonomous weapons? And where is all of this going?’” Militaries throughout the world are rapidly incorporating AI into their operations as they develop new weapons and autonomous systems like drones and robots. Yager now has a chance to grapple with the difficult questions this poses from inside one of the most powerful AI companies in the world. “I have always wanted to go into places and persuade people where human rights was not necessarily the dominant idea,” Yager said. “With apologies to my OpenAI colleagues, I am now in the belly of the beast, and it’s actually a very comfortable place for me to be because what I love to do is persuade and discuss and debate and hopefully move the needle.” OpenAI approached Yager for the job shortly after the company signed a contract with the DoW in late February to deploy advanced AI systems in classified environment, a high-profile deal that followed a public falling out between the DoW and Anthropic. Anthropic wanted to put guardrails around how the military could use its technology, specifically banning mass public surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, which the DoW would not agree to. The DoW then labeled Anthropic a supply-chain risk, while OpenAI swooped in and took the contract, claiming it was successful in getting the DoW to agree to similar guardrails. The idea of working at OpenAI was not “an immediate yes” for Yager, she said, due to suspicions that the company might be hiring her as a “branding exercise,” as the on-stage interviewer put it, implying she could make the company look responsible—a figurehead without actual influence over the technology. But Yager did her due diligence in talking with employees, particularly “the younger generation who are very worried about what they are creating and who’s at the wheel,” and felt compelled to take the position to see if she could make a difference. Since joining, she’s had some success influencing the direction of the technology, and also some concerns about where it’s going. The use of AI in military applications has proved tricky, with the U.S. military nearly targeting a Chinese military ship based on an inaccurate, AI-generated intelligence report, CNN reported last month. Yager has been able to work directly with researchers and engineers to improve the models, such as making sure they have appropriate responses to basic international agreements, including the laws of war, established in 1949 at the post–World War II Geneva Conventions. She brought in international experts “to literally sit at keyboards and put in prompts for really high stakes engagements,” and had engineers tweak the models based on the response. “That had never been done before, so that was extremely gratifying,” said Yager. She thinks AI companies are trying to “reinvent the wheel” on questions such as defining humanity and morality. “Societies have already figured out a lot of those things, and it’s called human rights. That should be the baseline,” she said, referring to the Geneva Conventions agreements. “I do not want an AI company telling me what is good. If we allow the industry to determine what is good, then it’s a free-for-all.” Yager also implied she was a bit put off by the debate within Silicon Valley around whether AIs, and particularly the new agent technologies, should have rights. This is something OpenAI asked her during her interview process. She said “no” at the time, and reiterated she was focused on human rights, but she has since thought more about the question. Now she feels more open to the “extremely important” conversations about “where agents fit into the legal structures, the labor structures, the tax structures,” but notes that these questions are not a matter of rights. “This is not at all comparable to human rights, and I would really love if we could just get back to the human of human rights,” she said. The crowd—mostly suited businessmen—began to clap. “Big round of applause for that,” said the on-stage interviewer. Another one of her concerns is the relatively insular demographic groups building AI. For example, last week President Trump gathered dozens of tech industry leaders in Washington to discuss AI safety. All the signatories of the voluntary safety accord were men, and as photos of the broader group present at a lunch event reveal, all of the attendees were men, save for AMD CEO Lisa Su. “Men are awesome, but it was a very male photograph of who is going to be making the choices about AI,” Yager said. “One problem with that is that AI is fundamentally shifting the power balance between people all over the world. You did not see affected communities up there.” Yager noted the government is rapidly adopting AI. She’s helping oversight bodies, such as the Government Accountability Office and the Office of Inspector General, build tools to keep tabs on what it’s doing. That accountability mechanism “feels important for democracy,” she said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: The '60 Minutes' ratings roller coaster is on the upswing under top editor Bari Weiss
events.summary: Bari Weiss has put her touch on "60 Minutes" since taking over CBS News last fall. Leigh Vogel/Getty Images for Uber, X and The Free Press Ratings for this week's episode of "60 Minutes" rose again. Audiences seem to be warming to Bari Weiss' revamped version of the longrunning CBS News telecast. CBS leadership had told employees that the "60 Minutes" relaunch was "a big moment" for the network. "60 Minutes" is finding its footing in the flagship CBS News program's first full season under top editor Bari Weiss . About 10.2 million viewers tuned into Sunday's "60 Minutes" episode, according to Nielsen audience data. That's up modestly from the 10.15 million who watched the third episode of last year's season, according to Nielsen data. The second installment drew 6.8 million viewers, up from 6.45 million viewers for the comparable episode in 2025. CBS's Sunday newscast was off last week as CBS hosted MTV's Video Music Awards on Sunday night. This week's solid viewership number is an encouraging sign for Weiss after she relaunched "60 Minutes" under new top producer Nick Bilton in mid-September. The episode featured a segment on AI in the workplace and an interview with Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina. The iconic newscast saw ratings slide 20% in its season debut, from about 10 million viewers to 7.9 million. However, the lead-in from the NFL game prior to the premiere had also been lower than last fall's opener, which can have a significant impact on the "60 Minutes" rating. CBS said that the "60 Minutes" debut approximately tripled its social media reach from last year. The "60 Minutes" debut had a similar viewership pattern as last year's, a Business Insider analysis found, which suggests that the ratings decline was because viewers didn't give Weiss' reboot a try. "60 Minutes" has undergone substantial turnover since Weiss and Bilton took over. Four correspondents left the program , including Scott Pelley and CNN's Anderson Cooper, while Ross Douthat joined as a correspondent from The New York Times. Bilton, Weiss, and CBS president Tom Cibrowski had said in a memo that the program's reboot was "a big moment for 60 Minutes and CBS." Pelley, a "60 Minutes" veteran, had questioned Bilton's qualifications in a staff meeting and accused Weiss of "murdering" the storied broadcast. Bilton fired Pelley and told staffers that he was hopeful for "60 Minutes" despite what he had called a "trying and difficult" start . Weiss said after Pelley's dismissal that she was "only interested in working in a newsroom that is built on trust and mutual respect." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Permanent daylight saving time could be a public health time bomb
events.summary: President Trump is pushing hard for the US Senate to make daylight saving time permanent so, among other things, golfers can stay on the course longer, but it may not be such a bright idea. New research out of Canada suggests that, even if Americans would get an extra hour of daylight in the evening, the ill health effects of permanent daylight saving time could outweigh the benefits. A paper published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal on Monday reviewed evidence on the health effects of permanent daylight saving time (pDST) as several Canadian jurisdictions move to stop changing their clocks. It finds that the opposite approach - adoption of permanent standard time (pST) - would actually be better for people’s health. Sorry, night owls and after-work social butterflies, but the science simply isn’t with you on this one. “Permanent DST preserves later evening light that may facilitate commuting, recreation, social participation, and some economic activity, but it also prolongs darkness on winter mornings,” the authors note. Prolonged morning darkness doesn't really jibe with the inner workings of the human body and light’s essential role in regulating the circadian rhythm. Sure, no one wants to drive home from work in the dark, but we really need morning light to get us functioning properly. Our circadian rhythms, the authors explain, actually run on a slightly longer schedule than a full day - 24.2 hours. For that reason, we rely on natural sunlight to keep us synchronized with the world around us. Morning light is some of the most important, the authors note, because it jump starts that rhythm, wakes us up and gets us moving. Evening light, on the other hand, delays the circadian rhythm, messing with our sense of “social time” and making it tougher to get to sleep and wake up rested in the morning. The effects of later evening light can show up in sleep, mood, education, and work productivity, the authors noted, and we don’t even need pDST to see some of those associations - we can just look at time zones. Move from east to west in the US or Canada and you’ll get some considerable differences in when the sun rises and sets in a particular time zone - in some cases, sunrise and sunset can differ by more than an hour of clock time across a single time zone. In one study cited by the Canadian analysis, residents on the western side of US time zones, where the sun sets later, got around an hour less sleep a week. The study also estimated that an additional hour of sleep per week was associated with around 5 percent higher long-term earnings. Similar results turned up in a German study, the team noted. Another study found that workers on the western end of US time zones ended up working fewer hours, too. On the educational front, an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores in a Florida study “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions.” “Ending biannual clock adjustments may eliminate transition harms that last a few weeks, but the health effects of permanent time are likely to be chronic,” the authors noted. “The preponderance of health evidence favors pST, which would align with the recommendations of sleep and chronobiology societies worldwide.” This isn’t the first time researchers have concluded such. British sleep scientists concluded much the same in 2024, which led to their recommendation to permanently kill DST in favor of a permanent shift to Greenwich Mean Time. That isn’t stopping the US from plowing ahead with plans for pDST, though. The Senate passed a measure to enshrine DST in 2022, but the House never acted on it. This time around, the House has passed its own bill to enact pDST, but the Senate is dithering, leading President Trump to go so far as to post the personal cellphone number of one Republican holdout on social media, Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR), who is opposed to the measure. “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton explained in a post on X following Trump’s doxxing. He’s right, too: The US has twice enacted pDST - once during World War II, which ended after the war, and again in 1973 as an energy saving measure. Congress curtailed the experiment later in 1974 following public backlash over dark winter mornings. The US isn’t alone in trying and failing at enacting pDST, either, as the Canadian paper points out. Russia adopted pDST in 2011 and reversed it in 2014. Chile tried and reversed it as well. In those cases, the reasons for reversing course varied, but concerns included dark winter mornings, disrupted sleep and body clocks, safety, and public dissatisfaction. It’s unclear whether the US government’s latest attempt at enacting pDST will succeed despite political resistance and scientific evidence that it’s a bad idea, but the researchers sure seem to hope not: They note that, if the US makes such a change, Canada will likely be pressured to conform. At the end of the day, we might all be better off just dealing with a couple of clock changes and some short-term sleep disruption. ®

events.title: Meet Alexis Wilkins, the country singer and political commentator engaged to FBI director Kash Patel
events.summary: Alexis Wilkins and FBI director Kash Patel are engaged. Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images FBI director Kash Patel is engaged to Alexis Wilkins after three years of dating. Wilkins is a conservative political commentator and country singer who lives in Nashville. Their relationship has made headlines for their age difference and reported use of government resources. On an episode of " The Katie Miller Podcast " released in December 2025, FBI director Kash Patel said that an engagement ring for Alexis Wilkins, his longtime girlfriend, was "definitely coming." Months later, Wilkins shared that the ring had arrived. Patel, 46, and Wilkins, a 27-year-old conservative media personality, political commentator, and country singer, announced their engagement on Sunday after three years of dating. Patel previously called Wilkins "a true patriot and the woman I'm proud to call my partner in life" in a November 2025 post on X . Their relationship has made headlines for their 19-year age difference and use of government resources, such as Patel's trips on government jets to Wilkins' performances and Nashville residence. An FBI spokesperson told Business Insider that the FBI has "explained publicly, numerous times," that Patel complies with all Office of Management and Budget rules related to personal travel. "The Government Accountability Office documented in 2013 that the FBI Director is a 'required-use' traveler under executive-branch policy because of security and communications needs. That requirement extends to personal travel," the spokesperson said. "This policy long predates Director Patel: use of a government aircraft is not a special travel arrangement created for him." When reached by Business Insider, Wilkins directed questions to her representatives, who declined to comment. Here's what to know about Wilkins and her relationship with the FBI director. Alexis Wilkins was born in Boston and grew up in Arkansas, but her family also spent time in England, Switzerland, and Los Angeles. Alexis Wilkins at the Nashville movie premiere for "REAGAN." Danielle Del Valle/Getty Images for REAGAN Movie In a July 2025 interview on " The Megyn Kelly Show ," Wilkins said that Arkansas was "my favorite place that I lived" and "the place that I spent the most time growing up." She also had a brief career as a young actor while living in Los Angeles, appearing in two episodes of "Modern Family" in 2009 as well as other TV shows and films, including a small role in the 2011 Adam Sandler movie "Jack and Jill," according to her IMDb profile . She graduated from Belmont University, a private Christian university in Nashville, in 2020. Belmont University. John Greim/LightRocket via Getty Images Wilkins earned a BBA in business administration and management from Belmont University. Wilkins told Kelly on "The Megyn Kelly Show" that, in college, she received an "F" in a comparative politics class from a professor who "had it out for me" because of her conservative views, and that she successfully advocated for the grade to be changed. "Getting the grade was just an indication that I was exemplifying that I wasn't being indoctrinated," she said. A Belmont University spokesperson confirmed that Wilkins earned her degree in 2020, but said the school "cannot speak to any student's specific grade or educational record," citing the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. "What we can affirm is that Belmont faculty are committed to delivering a rigorous, high-quality education in which grades are determined on a range of objective criteria, and our classrooms aim to provide a respectful environment where diverse viewpoints can constructively engage," the university spokesperson said. Wilkins said that her college experience led to her career in political advocacy and communications. Alexis Wilkins during a discussion ÒHow to be a Charlie Kirk: Communicating Well and Defending TruthÓ during the National Religious Broadcasters summit at Gaylord Opryland & Convention Center in Nashville on Wednesday, Feb. 18, 2026. Wilkins previously worked as a media personality, spokesperson, and writer at PragerU , according to her LinkedIn page . She also began hosting " Between the Headlines ," a Rumble show where she discussed news items and conservative issues, in 2023. The latest episode was posted in January 2026. In 2025, she worked as press secretary for Republican Rep. Abraham Hamadeh and as director of strategic communications at Women For Gun Rights, The New York Times reported. Wilkins now serves as a board committee member at the National Rifle Association, a visiting fellow at the nonprofit public policy organization Independent Women, and does communications work for Real American Freestyle Wrestling. She also serves as an ambassador for Turning Point USA . She has released music as a country artist. (Photo by Jason Kempin/Getty Images) Jason Kempin/Getty Images Wilkins released three singles in 2020, a Christmas single in 2021, and two singles in 2022 before releasing her first six-song EP, "Grit," in 2023, which debuted at No. 12 on the iTunes country album charts. Wilkins told Miller on "The Katie Miller Podcast" that she wrote her first song when she was 6 years old and began touring after graduating from college. She also said that she is working on new music and has written love songs about Patel. She met Patel, who is 19 years her senior, at a party at country singer John Rich's Nashville home in late 2022. Patel was confirmed by the Senate 51-49, with Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) the only Republicans voting to oppose him. Patel has been a hard-line critic of the FBI, the nation's most powerful law enforcement agency. events.title: Texan company plans to build new outback town for gas workers
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Dunmarra Development Land plans to build village in remote NT for gas workers A digital render of a 120-unit cluster in the planned village, called Dunmarra, in the remote NT. ( Supplied: Dunmarra Development Land ) Dunmarra Development Land has published plans to build a 600 hectare "petroleum services precinct and workforce village" near the Beetaloo Basin. It would house up to 3,000 workers and provide a range of services which could be used by the public. It is understood no planning or environmental applications have been made at this stage. A Texan company has plans for a new "workforce village", which could house up to 3,000 gas workers in a remote part of the Northern Territory. Dunmarra Development Land has published plans online, which say thousands of people could be housed at its 600 hectare "petroleum services precinct and workforce village". It would be located just south of the Dunmarra Wayside Inn in Birdum, about 600 kilometres south of Darwin, and include supermarkets, a medical clinic, airstrip and sporting facilities, with all open for public use. At full capacity it would provide 23 unit complexes as accommodation for a "rotating workforce", with services provided in the "town centre". A worker at Tamboran's Beetaloo site, which recently started supplying gas to the energy grid. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Drilling companies and gas industry contractors would also be able to lease commercial lots to base their business operations at the precinct. The website does not state how much construction would cost or how long it would take to build, but it does say it would not be permanent. Dunmarra is close to the Beetaloo Basin, a massive gas resource which the industry and NT government say could provide a long-term gas supply for energy markets both domestically and overseas . The company is owned by Kit Sheffield, a relative and business associate of Bryan Sheffield, an American businessman who invested in Tamboran Resources's project in the Beetaloo, which recently produced its first gas . "Gas development in the Beetaloo brings drilling, completions, civil and logistics crews to a region with almost no serviced land and no workforce housing," the website said. "Dunmarra puts the workshop, the bed and the mess in one place, on the highway, with gas and an airstrip at the fence." If fully built, the development would be one of the biggest settlements in the NT and dwarf pre-existing towns in the area such as Elliott, Daly Waters and remote communities. Kit Sheffield was contacted for comment. Barkly Regional Council Mayor Sid Vashist said he was unaware of the plan before he was contacted by the ABC. Sid Vashist says local government has not been contacted about the plan. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) He said it was important the development supported existing towns in the region like Elliott and did not reinforce the industry's reliance on fly-in fly-out (FIFO) workforces. "This is literally a huge township that's going to be proposed and created, which could be bigger than Tennant Creek at this stage," Cr Vashist said. He said it was important to have long-term plans for developments built due to the resources sector to ensure they thrive after the lucrative industry departs. "Towns like Tennant Creek were built on mines, but when the mining left, the socio-economic profile of the residents in this town reduced quite significantly, which has been a huge challenge," he said. It is understood no environmental or development applications have been lodged with the NT government. events.title: SEC Seeks Final Judgment Against Former Western Asset Co-CIO Ken Leech in Cherry Picking Case
events.summary: Search Filings Search Filings Full Text Search Latest Filings Mutual Fund Search Variable Insurance Products Search SIC Codes CIK Lookup Public Dissemination Service (PDS) Search Assistance Submit Filings Submit Filings EDGAR Filer Management Portal EDGAR Filing Portal Online Forms Management Portal EDGAR Next Forms Index Filer Support & Resources Data & Research Data & Research Data Library Statistics & Data Visualizations Structured Data Investment Management Data Open Data at the SEC Rules, Enforcement, & Compliance Rules & Regulations Rulemaking Activity Submit Public Comments Staff Guidance No-Action, Interpretive, and Exemptive Letters Self-Regulatory Organization Rulemaking Public Petitions for Rulemaking Enforcement & Litigation Litigation Releases Administrative Proceedings Administrative Law Judge Orders and Initial Decisions Trading Suspensions Distributions to Harmed Investors Receiverships Compliance Examination Priorities Risk Alerts Compliance Outreach Program Proposed Rules What's New Whistleblower Program Featured Topics Featured Topics Crypto Task Force Cybersecurity Market Structure Analytics Saving and Investing for Military Personnel Saving and Investing for Teachers SEC-CFTC Harmonization Initiative Treasury Clearing Implementation About About Mission Commissioners Divisions & Offices Division & Office Directors Advisory Committees Budget & Performance Reports & Publications Commission Votes Contact the SEC Careers The Securities and Exchange Commission today moved for entry of a final judgment by consent against Stephen Kenneth Leech II, the former co-chief investment officer of registered investment adviser Western Asset Management Company LLC, whom the SEC previously charged with a multi-year cherry-picking allocation scheme. As alleged in the SEC’s November 2024 complaint , from at least January 2021 through October 2023, Leech placed trades and then routinely delayed allocations until near or after futures markets set daily settlement prices, allowing him to observe price movements and disproportionally allocate hundreds of millions of dollars in realized and unrealized first‑day gains to favored portfolios and a similar amount of realized and unrealized first‑day losses to disfavored portfolios. Without admitting the allegations in the SEC’s complaint, Leech consented to entry of a final judgment, subject to court approval, that would order him to pay a $3 million penalty, impose an officer-and-director bar and permanently enjoin him from violating antifraud provisions of federal securities laws. Leech also agreed to a forthcoming associational bar against him. In June 2026, the Commission instituted settled public administrative proceedings against Western Asset, ordering the firm to pay a $100 million civil penalty and establishing a Fair Fund to distribute money to affected investors in the disfavored portfolios. “The conduct by Leech and Western Asset was an egregious breach of fiduciary obligations to their clients,” said Brent Wilner, Associate Director of the SEC’s Los Angeles Regional Office. “Together, the resolution with Leech, if approved by the court, and the SEC’s prior settlement with Western Asset will return $103 million and provide meaningful relief to harmed investors, and reinforce that advisers must put clients first, every time.” Also in June 2026, Leech pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in the Southern District of New York to obstruction of justice charges related to false and misleading testimony he provided to the SEC during its investigation; sentencing will take place in the coming weeks. The SEC acknowledges the assistance of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York and the FBI. events.title: After working at Trader Joe's for 3 years, I still come back for these 8 underrated items
events.summary: I love quick, protein-packed meals, so I always add chicken nuggets to my Trader Joe's cart. Jasmine Ascencio I worked at Trader Joe's for three years and tried many products, from snacks to frozen meals. Now, I still return to buy my favorite easy weeknight dinners and pantry staples. I always stock up on overnight oats, chicken nuggets, dolmas, and coconut water. Some Trader Joe's items are impossible to resist. As someone who used to work there, I know this better than anyone. Even after three years acquainting myself with products behind the scenes, I still keep coming back for some of my favorite groceries, from customer favorites to hidden gems. As someone who is neurodivergent, I tend to look for quick, frozen staples and easy-to-make meals . I don't often cook fancy dishes unless I'm feeling particularly inspired — for instance, if I just found an enticing recipe on TikTok. Luckily for me, Trader Joe's has a wealth of products that make for simple, affordable meals. These are the ones that are always on my shopping list. Trader Joe's overnight oats are my go-to for a quick breakfast. caption TK Jasmine Ascencio I've tried overnight oats from several brands and found many to be either too mushy or too sweet. These, however, are perfect. Whenever I go to Trader Joe's, I'll grab a few to keep in my fridge for early mornings. There are several flavors I love, from peanut butter to vanilla, but I always look forward to the pumpkin one that's stocked in the fall. The frozen hashbrowns are a cult favorite, and I've come to understand why. captionTK Jasmine Ascencio When I worked at Trader Joe's , customers would constantly ask if these were in stock. I didn't understand the hype … until I tried them. Now, I almost always keep a box of hashbrowns in my freezer. They crisp up perfectly in the air fryer and make a great base for avocado "toast" with a fried egg. I always buy Norwegian sourdough rye chips to pair with tuna salad. caption TK Jasmine Ascencio I first tried this combo after a customer recommended it. I've sworn by it ever since. The rye chips add the perfect crunch and saltiness to any creamy tuna salad, and they're thick enough not to break easily. Trader Joe's dolmas are one of my favorite pantry staples. caption TK Jasmine Ascencio A customer once convinced me to try Trader Joe's dolmas, and I've been hooked ever since. You can eat these little grape leaf-wrapped rice rolls right out of the can! They're packed in soybean oil and make a great snack or side dish with hummus or tzatziki. Whenever it's in season, I buy this horchata-inspired ice cream. caption TK Jasmine Ascencio Trader Joe's horchata-inspired ice cream is creamy, cinnamon-y, and has just the right amount of cookie pieces (my weakness). In my opinion, it perfectly matches the classic drink's flavor. This is another product that's only around in the summer months, so whenever I see it in the freezer case, I don't hesitate to add it to my cart. Trader Joe's refrigerated chicken nuggets are the ultimate work-from-home lunch hack. caption TK Jasmine Ascencio These chicken nuggets crisp up quickly in the air fryer and are easy to eat as a quick meal or snack. Sometimes, I toss them on a salad for extra protein. They've saved me from ordering takeout more times than I can count — and the spicy ones are great, too. The squiggly knife-cut-style noodles are a delicious alternative to instant ramen. caption TK Jasmine Ascencio Compared to other instant noodles I've tried , these have a chewy, bouncy texture that I love. Also, don't get me started on the sauce — it's spicy, garlicky, and nutty in the best way. I always keep a few packs on hand for lazy lunches or late-night snacks. I'm terrible at staying hydrated, but these coconut waters help. caption tk Jasmine Ascencio As someone who lives off coffee, I'm always looking for ways to stay hydrated. Trader Joe's organic coconut water is refreshing, not too sweet, and not too pricey. Every time I visit my local store, I buy as many as I can. Curious what's in other shoppers' carts? Keep reading our Trader Joe's diaries . This story was originally published on July 31, 2025, and most recently updated on October 6, 2026. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Google backs 'existing nuclear plants' as data centres strain US energy grid
events.summary: Google has said that its data centre growth , fuelled by the artificial intelligence boom, led the company to reach a power-purchase agreement involving the upgrade of six nuclear plants in the US. An essay posted to Google's corporate news detailed the agreement made with Constellation , which operates the "largest fleet of nuclear facilities in the US". Through the PPA, Google says it is essentially enabling more than "1.5GW of new nuclear capacity for the US energy system from increasing the power output of existing reactors and bringing dormant facilities back online". Technology companies continue to come under criticism in the US over the rise in data centre construction. The centres cause energy demand to surge in some areas and lead to an increase in electricity prices for consumers. "As our data centre investments in the US continue, so does our commitment to revitalise the nation’s energy supply, support local jobs and economic opportunity, and bring new reliable electricity capacity to strengthen US grids at no cost to other ratepayers," Google said. The company said that as part of the PPA, Constellation had agreed to use the technology company's agentic AI "workflows across its core operations to accelerate uprate planning, streamline construction and optimise plant output". Nuclear criticism Google is the latest among Big Tech firms to support nuclear reactors in the US, although the moves have not always been welcomed. Critics say that many of the reactor deals include large loans from the US government, meaning citizens are paying for nuclear energy centres. On Monday, the US Department of Energy announced the latest such deal "of up to $4.2 billion" to modernise nuclear plants in Ohio and Pennsylvania. "By getting more power out of the nuclear plants we already have, we can deliver more affordable, reliable, round-the-clock energy for American families and businesses," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said. There are also concerns about safety. Constellation's PPA with Microsoft in 2024 involved the rehabilitation of one of the Three Mile Island reactors in Middletown, Pennsylvania. In March 1979, the core of TMI Unit 2 was partially exposed, prompting a temporary partial evacuation of the area and a lengthy clean-up around Middletown that continues to this day. Although it is Unit 1 of TMI, closed in 2019, that is being rehabilitated, energy safety groups have continued to express concern. And in Covert, Michigan, efforts to restart the Palisades nuclear reactor, which closed in 2022, are also under way. The owners of Palisades, Holtec International , had hoped to restart the reactor by this year, but a series of incidents have cast doubt on that goal. In September, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission confirmed that it was investigating an incident related to a "tipped fuel assembly" that occurred while the reactor was being fuelled. On Tuesday, however, Google did not appear concerned about the potential for opposition as it promoted its endeavour with Constellation. "This builds a more affordable energy future for everyone," the company said. It said it was providing guaranteed revenue that Constellation "needs to invest in upgrades for 11 of their nuclear reactors, while ensuring other grid customers bear none of the associated costs".

events.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
events.summary: Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers. It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory. The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network. Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings to add to its existing catalogue of hit franchises which includes Indiana Jones, Mission: Impossible and Shrek. The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover. Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry. "From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said. Films and streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you Published 8 hours ago Asked about the merger after it had been finalised, US President Donald Trump described the deal as "great". "They're terrific people and it's going to be a great company," he said. Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive. Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology. Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News. Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation". "While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said the company has high debts at a time when interest rates are high. "The combined entity, now called Skydance, needs to cut costs and make bigger profits to be able to get the debt down to more manageable levels," he said. "The fact Tom Cruise movie Digger, Warner Bros' last release before the merger, has been a major flop is a reminder of how the film industry is not a guaranteed ticket to riches." While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning. Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away. Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide". US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead . As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS. Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount. Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained. Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons. Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours. The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick.

events.title: I spent a week alone in Europe and learned 9 lessons about solo travel
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter traveled solo during a train trip through Europe. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I had plenty of experience traveling alone before I went to Germany and Austria. But solo travel in Europe was a different beast. I learned how to tame it. I thought I knew what I was in for. I thought I had it all figured out. I'd taken 30-hour train trips up and down the East Coast, spent seven nights sailing the Caribbean on one of the world's largest cruise ships , and traveled by rail to Niagara Falls , Montreal, and Quebec City — all by myself. So I was pretty used to traveling alone by October 2022, when I went backpacking through Europe . I took a two-week train trip through Germany, Austria, Italy, and Switzerland. I spent the first half of the trip by myself, and a friend joined me for the second half. That first week alone in Europe made me realize that I'm still learning about the art of solo travel . When planning my trip, I learned that some countries are safer for solo travelers — particularly females. Brandenburg Gate in Berlin. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When I travel alone, nothing is more important to me than safety. In my research ahead of my trip, I found that some countries are generally safer than others for solo travelers. The migration firm Global Citizens Solutions releases an annual study about the safest destinations for women traveling alone, based on gender equality, crime rates, and community security initiatives. Both of my solo destinations, Austria and Germany, made the 2025 list, though only Austria made the 2026 list, which included 14 countries. When I visited Austria, I stayed in the heart of Vienna, which allowed me to explore the city streets into the night. In my experience, people kept to themselves, and I didn't doubt my safety while exploring after dark. When I visited Germany, I stayed in an Airbnb in Neustrelitz, a quaint town outside Berlin. I found it relatively easy to figure out the local train system and get to and from Berlin each day. I felt safe walking around on my own in both places. If you're traveling solo, researching your destination beforehand is a must, but your safety is never guaranteed. So stay aware of your surroundings along the way, and use your best judgment throughout your trip. Taking public transit immediately made each destination feel less intimidating. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I live in New York, where I take the subway pretty much everywhere. Still, I was nervous about using public transit in foreign countries where I didn't speak the primary language or have a good sense of where things were. I didn't have to be. I may have felt uneasy stepping into the underground world of Berlin's subway system, but it was no different from my home city. The platform looked the same, with signage identifying the coming trains. I thought both Berlin and Vienna had great transportation systems, and taking trains and trams helped me get a better sense of each place. Public transit apps made it easier to get tickets and plan trips. When I was riddled with self-doubt about navigating these cities, taking public transit gave me a real sense of competence as I stood among local commuters. Booking a stay within city limits made exploring alone easier. The street where the author found a hotel in Vienna one morning. Joey Hadden/Business Insider On solo trips , being intentional about where you stay is important. For this trip, I booked a combination of Airbnbs inside and outside the cities to give me a chance to see what life is like in the heart of the metropolis and the surrounding areas. Commuting to small villages with a travel companion later in the trip felt like a little adventure each time, where we could plan and recap our days. But when I was alone, these treks felt more mundane, like I was wasting time and energy I could have spent exploring the city. In Germany, I booked a stay at a tiny home hotel in Neustrelitz and commuted to and from Berlin by train, about an hour and a half each way. While I was glad I got to experience Neustrelitz, staying far from the city center made my days in Berlin shorter. When I got to Vienna, I stayed in an Airstream trailer in the heart of the city. This made it much easier to explore from morning to night. Though it wasn't as quiet as Neustrelitz, I left Vienna feeling like I had a better sense of the city than I did in Berlin. While staying outside the city can be an adventure, I recommend that first-time solo travelers stay in the center to make their trip easier. I spent one week alone in Europe before a friend joined me, but I surprised myself by wishing I'd booked a longer solo trip. The author prepares to board a train in Europe. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My first week in Europe was tough. Getting used to navigating and exploring on my own took some time. Without someone else to share the process with, I found the first few days difficult to fully enjoy. But by the end of the first week, I felt settled into the nomadic lifestyle and confident in my abilities to navigate cities independently. In fact, I left Europe wishing I had given myself more time alone to truly immerse myself in these new places. Each challenging moment I faced allowed me to grow. To those planning a solo trip to another country, I recommend giving yourself at least two weeks to explore — especially if it's your first visit. After finding your footing that first week, the second week will feel even better. When I'm alone, my headspace can make or break a trip. So, I learned to stay in the moment, celebrate small wins, and not dwell on mistakes. Joey Hadden/Business Insider My trip wasn't perfect. There were times when I went to the wrong train station, got caught in the rain, and struggled to sleep. Dwelling on these mishaps made it harder to overcome them and get back to enjoying myself. Early in my travels, I made a conscious choice to push through and focus on what I could control, like buying an umbrella, arriving at stations early, and taking extra time to sleep. These small wins boosted my spirits. When I arrived in Vienna on an overnight train from Berlin, I was exhausted and hadn't slept. I knew I needed rest, but I couldn't check into my Airbnb until 3 p.m. I started going into random hotels to book a room. By the third hotel, I had booked a safe, comfortable place to doze. I framed this as a small win to celebrate. I got out of my head by focusing on positive problem-solving and found exactly what I needed. My trip was full of little victories like this, from finally getting to my Airbnb in Neustrelitz on the day I arrived in Berlin to finding a delicious food cart next to a park while exploring Vienna. Being dehydrated and tired made it harder for me to stay positive. I learned that it's important to prioritize health when traveling solo. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Sleep makes everything better. events.title: Imported pork 'hiding in plain sight' on Guzman y Gomez menu
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Imported pork 'hiding in plain sight' on fast food giant Guzman y Gomez menu Topic: Food and Beverage Processing Industry Guzman Y Gomez has been criticised by Australian farmers for using imported pork in its products. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville ) Mexican fast-food giant Guzman y Gomez is importing tonnes of pork to serve in its burritos and tacos across Australia. GYG says it's a proud supporter of Australian farmers but local producers say the company should be more transparent about where their meat comes from. The pork industry is pushing to introduce import label rules, similar to those required for seafood. Mexican fast-food chain Guzman Y Gomez (GYG) is under fire for advertising the use of Australian produce while importing hundreds of tonnes of Danish pork each year. The company has confirmed it sources pork from Australia and Denmark for its burritos, tacos and other products. Rob Farmer from Australian Pork Limited (APL) said the fast food chain's practices were a "very good example" of "imported meat hiding in plain sight". GYG uses Australian and Danish pork in its burritos and tacos. ( ABC Rural: Annie Brown ) "They're serving imported pork in a pulled pork burrito and the customers have no idea. "It's not currently a requirement to call it out on the menu," Mr Farmer said. APL is pushing for labelling laws similar to those that now apply to Australian seafood , requiring food chains and restaurants to declare where their product is from. "It's just extremely inconsistent out there at the moment," Mr Farmer said. "You go into a McDonald's and you've got Aussie beef on the packaging of a Big Mac and you go to a different chain and you don't get anything." GYG has defended its decision to use imported pork, saying it depends on "seasonal quality, availability and pricing". "At GYG, we're a proud supporter of Australian farmers, sourcing hundreds of tonnes of fresh, high quality produce every week," a spokesperson said. "We prioritise Australian fresh produce and Australian-manufactured goods, from our chicken and beef to the avocados, and the tomatoes." Imported pork is used by fast food chains and restaurants. ( ABC Rural: Annie Brown ) The company said it was also focused on providing customers "fresh, clean food without compromising on price". Seasonality claim doesn't wash with farmers Northern Victorian pig producer Tim Kingma is disappointed GYG uses imported pork. "Australian pork producers have some of the strongest rules around animal welfare, around our labour and around our environment," Mr Kingma said. "And we think we produce a great quality product." Tim Kingma wants more transparency in pork labelling. ( Supplied: Tim Kingma ) Mr Kingma has questioned GYG's statement about fresh, quality produce, saying it "can't be fresher than buying local". He says he is confused by the company's comments about seasonal availability. "That reasoning doesn't wash at all," Mr Kingma said. "There's definitely not 'seasonal' for the pig industry. My production is weekly like the rest of the Australian pig industry." Australia allows the importation of pig meat under strict biosecurity conditions to protect local herds from the transmission of exotic diseases. In 2025, Australia imported 167 thousand tonnes of pork and pig meat products worth just over $1 billion. A large proportion of the bacon and ham sold in Australian shops is imported. ( ABC Rural: Brandon Long ) Pig farmers estimate that over 40 per cent of pork consumed in Australia comes from overseas. It's used in food service, restaurants, fast food chains and pubs, as well as processed small goods such as ham and bacon. Research commissioned by APL earlier this year shows Australian consumers would back more detailed labelling. "Nine in 10 Aussies want pork origin labelled on the menu," Mr Farmer said. "Almost two thirds, in fact, say they'd be happy to pay a little bit more for it …so we know that there's that preference, but they're not able to make that informed choice." The Federal Agriculture Minister, Julie Collins and her department have been contacted for comment.

events.title: Boomers' dividend stocks take beating from bond yields, with retirement income on the line
events.summary: The rapid rise in bond yields led by the 10-Year U.S. Treasury has made dividend stocks less attractive as income investments. This market dynamic has hit stock prices hard in sectors that income-seeking investors such as seniors rely on, from real estate to utilities and materials. Giving up on dividend stocks is not a strategy, experts say, but neither is a desperate chase for higher yields. Dividend stocks like utilities are being pummeled amid bond market chaos and the rise of the 10-year U.S. treasury , raising questions for seniors about how to continue meeting their income needs. While dividend stocks are only part of a diversified portfolio for older investors, many boomers often depend on dividend stocks and funds for at least some of their income. When returns are rocky, it can, understandably, cause some consternation. Many dividend funds are giving back some of their gains from earlier in the year when bond rates were lower, said Timothy Chubb, chief investment officer at Girard, a Univest Wealth Division, in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania. Sectors including real estate, utilities, and materials have seen stock prices plummet as bond yields become more attractive and dividend stock yields less attractive on a relative risk-reward basis. For all the concern about bonds, inflows into bond ETFs have been rising. Consider the iShares 20+ Year Treasury ETF ( TLT ): it has taken in over $3.2 billion in net inflows from investors over the past month, according to ETFAction.com. To be sure, there is a split in the market between investors who continue to pile into ultrashort bond funds, which had record inflows near $20 billion in September, according to Morningstar. And those investors making a bet that the worst in the bond market is over and the yields are too attractive to pass up. TLT's inflows were its largest monthly inflows on record as its yield hit the highest since 2002, according to Dow Jones data. Boomers, however, shouldn't necessarily give up on dividend-paying stocks. Instead, they should consider several strategies that can blunt the impact of rising bond yields on their income-stock portfolios. Here are a few. While it can be tempting, financial advisors and strategists caution older investors that before doing anything else, the most important thing is what not to do: simply chase yield. "The worst thing that a retiree could do is sell a high-quality dividend payer at depressed prices to chase income somewhere else in the stock market just to get higher yield," said Chubb. Instead, investors should focus more on fundamental earnings growth. In the short term, dividend yields of these companies may look less attractive, but that can change over time as dividends rise and the stock price is likely to be steadier as well. "I'd much rather get a company going up 4% to 5% with another 3% in dividend yield than chasing an 8% dividend yield for a business that's in decline," he said. Be selective about stocks, sectors that can beat inflation Boomers who are buying individual dividend-paying stocks should look at the quality of the company by asking several questions, according to Chubb. Are they able to increase their dividend, and in a way that beats inflation? Is the company growing? Are they borrowing debt to fund the dividend, or are they funding it through the cash flows of the business? The higher-yielding the company, the more debt it has or the more risk that a dividend could get cut in the future, he said. And the more interest rates rise, the more highly levered companies face greater financing risk. "It really comes down to the underlying business," he said. With dividend ETFs, consider the strategy fund managers employ. ETFs that focus on the highest-yielding dividends in slow-growth sectors such as utilities and consumer staples can be hit harder when rates move higher. So investors might want to look more closely at funds that seek dividend growth versus those that are more focused on high yield. One example of a high-yield dividend fund is the Invesco S&P 500 High Dividend Low Volatility ETF ( SPHD ), which tracks an index that selects S&P 500 stocks that offer the largest dividends while seeking to minimize volatility. This fund had a one-month negative return of 7.59%. It's up around 4% year-to-date. Consumer staples (18.5%) and utilities (14%) are the No. 2 and No. 3 sectors in the ETF by weight after real estate (20%), according to Invesco data through Sept. 30. Other high-dividend yield funds haven't been hit quite as hard. Vanguard High Dividend Yield Index ETF ( VYM ), for example, chooses securities based on current yield, with only the highest-yielding companies selected, according to ETF Database. That fund has a negative one-month return of 3.85%, though it's up about 11% for the year to date. Its top sectors are financials, industrials and technology, according to Vanguard data as of Aug. 31 (it has not provided a more recent portfolio disclosure).

events.title: Meta Muse popularity lifts AMD stock to fresh highs as AI agents juice CPU sales
events.summary: The personal agent boom is lifting the fortunes of AMD and Intel, which have outperformed their megacap tech peers this year and over the past month. As leading developers of central processing units, the longtime rivals are finding a major role in the AI market, which had been dominated by Nvidia. "As more agents are created and developed, and more people start to use them for more tasks, it's going to start to shift the workload away from GPUs and onto CPUs," said Ryan Shrout, president of Signal65. The personal AI agent boom is giving Advanced Micro Devices and Intel new life after the companies spent years watching Nvidia and its GPUs dominate the artificial intelligence market. The central processing unit, or CPU, was once the primary workhorse of a computer server before Nvidia's graphics processing units took center stage with the launch of ChatGPT and the start of the generative AI era. Now CPUs are back, lifting the fortunes of market leaders AMD and Intel, whose chips specialize in powering long-running agents that can work for hours on their own. Last week OpenAI released its AI agent Dots, following the lead of Meta , which debuted Muse in early September. Muse caught on so quickly that it topped the Apple App Store in less than two weeks . Well before that, AMD and Intel were already huge winners in the stock market this year due largely to surging demand for CPUs, but they've picked up steam in the past month, jumping 32% and 21%, respectively, as of Monday's close beating all of tech's megacaps. The rally continued on Tuesday, with AMD jumping almost 3% to a fresh high of $649.42. AMD's growing strength in both CPUs and GPUs has pushed the company into the trillion-dollar market cap club. "As more agents are created and developed, and more people start to use them for more tasks, it's going to start to shift the workload away from GPUs and onto CPUs," said Ryan Shrout, president of Signal65, which consults on AI hardware and costs. Users learned about the power behind the new agents by asking them. Muse tells users that it runs on an AMD-powered computer, while Dots said it runs on a virtual computer powered by AMD's EPYC-branded CPU. A Meta spokesperson told CNBC that the company designed its system to use whatever kind of CPU is available. "We take a diverse approach to our hardware and are largely CPU-agnostic by design, which gives us the most flexibility in acquiring capacity," the Meta spokesperson said in a statement. OpenAI similarly uses multiple CPU providers, meaning AMD isn't the only game in town. Most servers at hyperscalers — Amazon , Google , Meta and Microsoft — use CPUs made by Intel or AMD. But nearly every major cloud provider is also developing custom chips of their own, typically based on Arm technology. Arm announced its own CPU for agents in March, with Meta as the debut customer, and its stock price has more than doubled since. Earlier this year, Nvidia released Vera — a fully redesigned central processor — along with an entire rack filled only with the CPUs . The chip giant says it built the new Vera CPUs specifically for agents and expects CPUs to be a $200 billion market by 2030. But it's one part of the chip industry where Nvidia isn't currently the favorite, analysts say. "It's just a new product and they're going to be competing against a lot of different players," Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview, adding that he believes AMD currently has the "best product." CPUs are driving a healthy portion of AMD's growth. Revenue in the company's data center business more than doubled to $6.7 billion in the quarter ended in June, accounting for almost 60% of total sales. " The conversation has changed quite a bit over the last eight to 10 months in terms of agentic usage," said Dan McNamara, AMD's senior vice president and general manager of compute and enterprise AI. McNamara added that CPU sales are going to "really ramp." Muse, Dots and even coding software like OpenAI's Codex use AI models to plan tasks that can run autonomously. The agents need their own computer that can run for hours or even days in the background, explained Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman. GPUs are still needed for inference, or processing an AI model, but an agent also needs a CPU. "CPUs are actually performing the workflows while GPUs are doing the thinking," Newman said. Meta and OpenAI use virtual machines, which partition a server into several lighter virtual computers, so one server can support scores of users. Some AMD EPYC processors have up to 192 CPU cores. According to benchmarks and the agents themselves, Muse's virtual computer uses two cores and Dots uses nine. Benchmarks and queries show Dots using an AMD EPYC 9V74 CPU, which is available from resellers for under $3,000. The EPYC 9D25 reportedly used by Meta for Muse costs even less on the secondary market.

events.title: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
events.summary: British Airways is building what it says is the world's largest business class on its Airbus A380 jets, the world's largest passenger plane. A high-end travel boom has airlines from budget carriers to large, international icons introducing new first-class cabins and other pricier seat options. British Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business-class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers. The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub. British Airways will outfit its Airbus A380, the world's largest passenger plane, with a monster 106-seat business-class cabin, up from the current configuration of 97 business-class seats. First class will also be refreshed and will include 12 suites, down from the current A380 configuration of 14. Premium economy class will grow to 84 seats from 55. Standard economy seats will shrink to just 215 from 303. British Airways said the 106 business-class suites, with sliding doors, will take up the entirety of the A380's upper deck. Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers' appetite for more luxurious trips. British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines , last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson told CNBC in a recent interview that customers are seeking high-end options on long flights, like its Perth-London nonstop. "There is absolutely a customer who wants this and is prepared to pay a premium for it," she said. Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase. The prices can be even higher if they're selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights. Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification. British Airways' overhaul of the cabins on its 12 A380s is also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane's largest user, Emirates, in late 2021. events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Cloud provider Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation, marking what could be its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. Coatue Management and Blackstone are leading the round. A letter to investors reviewed by the Journal shows Lambda’s backlog grew from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September. While that might look like a hearty increase in demand, much of that increase appears to be driven by a $35 billion commitment from one company: Anthropic, which signed a deal with Lambda in late August. That means Lambda’s valuation, which has climbed significantly since its 2025 funding round , could be leaning heavily on Anthropic’s ability to keep paying. Still, with reliable GPU capacity so scarce, investors are clearly still willing to bet on companies that provide it, especially ones with large contracts with a major AI lab. For neoclouds like Lambda, demand isn’t so much the problem as is the cost of meeting it. Data center buildouts are largely funded by debt — of which Lambda just raised an additional $1 billion last week — and lenders are getting choosier about who they offer cash to and under what circumstances. Lambda’s decision to raise more now not only sets the tone for its IPO pricing, but also gives it access to more capital before the scrutiny of public markets arrives. If and when Lambda does IPO — the company was reportedly meant to debut this year, but has pushed that back amid market uncertainty — it will join other Nvidia-backed neoclouds, like CoreWeave and Nebius , that now depend on the health of their stock to fund their data center buildouts. British neocloud Nscale filed for an IPO last month and is expected to begin trading soon. Lambda, Coatue, and Blackstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment. events.title: Tourists must pay and book ahead to see iconic Twelve Apostles
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts From April, visitors will begin paying a fee to visit the Twelve Apostles. ( Supplied ) A booking system has gone live for tourists to visit the Twelve Apostles on the Great Ocean Road. Visiting the Twelve Apostles remains free until April 2027. A new $126 million visitor centre will open on October 16. Tourists wanting to visit one of Australia's iconic natural wonders, the Twelve Apostles, will now have to book ahead and pay an entry fee . Each year, more than 2 million people travel down the Great Ocean Road to visit the remaining seven limestone rock stacks that rise out of the Southern Ocean, about four hours' drive west of Melbourne. The Victorian government has revealed from October 16, visitors will need to book ahead to enter a newly constructed $126 million visitor centre and see the sights. In April, the government will start charging tourists an entry fee. Local residents and traditional owners will be exempt from paying. Acting Regional Development, Local Government and Territories Minister Catherine King said the new visitor centre would support sustainable tourism along Victoria's south-west coastline. "The redevelopment is already playing an important part in the local economy and will encourage even more visitors to spend time in the region, boosting local jobs and businesses," Ms King said. The government said the new booking system would help manage overcrowding at peak times, with money collected from the entry fees used to help fund visitor infrastructure and environmental projects. Port Campbell Community Group secretary Marion Manifold said the group was opposed to the fee as "we believe public land should not be commercialised and should remain in public hands". "If funds are required we prefer an airport tax on visitors into Australia," Ms Manifold said. "It's a good aim but in the past we believe very little money has come back to the Port Campbell national park and believe this is not likely to change." Before: The Twelve Apostles before the 2005 collapse of a sea stack . . After: and after. (Reuters: Parks Victoria) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition She said the group was worried about what the expected increase in visitation would do to the area, highlighting the effect on local infrastructure, including water, sewerage systems and parking. "The crowds, traffic congestion and bus parking also has a wider impact on Great Ocean Road towns and small communities," Ms Manifold said. "The government's aim to increase numbers at the 12 Apostles to 6 million will compound any current issues. "No data has been provided to show how this is sustainable and what the effects it may have on the environment." Minister for Regional Development Michaela Settle says the project is an "absolute game-changer." "What we see here is a centre that will bring visitors in, it will get them to stay longer, to adventure a little further and to see everything that this extraordinary natural coastline has to offer," Ms Settle said. Ms Settle was unable to confirm what the entry fee would be, but said it would be "really small." "The fee is going entirely to the Great Ocean Road Coast and Park Authority," Ms Settle said. Chair of Great Ocean Road Coast and Parks Authority Libby Mears said the centre would bring around 100 new jobs. "The Great Ocean Road Coast and Park Authority [has] employed 40 new people and certainly [will] increase in the peak season," Ms Mears said. "Our food and beverage provider has also employed a significant number, and we have outside ground staff as well." "It is amazing for local communities and local people.

events.title: Singles tax costs thousands of dollars a year
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Singles struggle to afford housing as cost of living rises Louise Taylor faced affordability issues when looking for somewhere to call home. ( ABC News: Lottie Twyford ) Single-income households can struggle to meet housing costs, and older women are one group at risk of housing insecurity. The singles tax refers to extra costs people pay when they can't split expenses like couples can. Housing experts say Australia also has a lack of affordable, suitable dwellings for singles. By her 70s, Louise Taylor had hoped her house would be more than a roof over her head; somewhere she could happily call home. But after "knockback after knockback" trying to find a rental on the private market five years ago, she has been forced to accept her small duplex, north of Brisbane, is all she can afford. "I was at desperate times and I went, 'You know what, I don't care, I just have to do it'," she says. "I was so grateful … then I'm looking around thinking, 'Where am I going to put my lounge room?'" Ms Taylor is the first to acknowledge she is one of the lucky ones and is currently on the housing waitlist. She has also contacted other housing organisations to see if they can help. Louise Taylor is living in a modest duplex north of Brisbane. ( ABC News ) On the pension, she fears the next rent rise and that, if it gets any more expensive, she believes she will have no choice but to move in with her adult daughter. She is also scared that if she cannot afford to rent a house on her own, she may have no choice but to move into a share house. Ms Taylor believes she would have had more success finding a rental, and more power on the private rental market, if she had been applying in a couple. Singles tax costing people hundreds of dollars a month That concept is known as the singles tax — the idea that single-income households do not enjoy the same cost-sharing benefits when it comes to things such as rent and bills as a couple does. Australian Bureau of Statistics data suggests a single person spends more than $770 extra on living costs a month compared to a person in a couple. Better Financial Planning's Michael Khouri says a single person also has to take on more of the mental load managing finances. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Brisbane financial adviser Michael Khouri said there was also the time and effort factor to consider, as well as that inability to share resources. "If somebody's single and they're trying to do everything themselves, they're usually a bit more time-poor," he said. He said he also sees people who have just come out of a separation struggling to fund separate homes — either renting or buying — especially as the cost of housing continues to rise. "Fifteen years ago, I'd find that probably half or maybe, say, 30 to 40 per cent of their expenses was housing, and now it's just getting higher and higher." Louise Taylor says her two-bedroom duplex is more like a one-bedroom home. ( ABC News ) More than half of Australians living alone are women, and about half of those women are 65 or older. Older women are also a growing group at risk of experiencing housing distress or homelessness. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare reports that women and girls make up 60 per cent of the people seeking assistance from homelessness services. And the number of homeless women over 55 has surged, with earlier census data pointing to an approximately 40 per cent increase over the decade from 2011 . Single, older women at risk of housing insecurity Maggie Shambrook says many older women are reluctant to describe themselves as homeless. ( ABC News: Elizabeth Pickering ) The Housing Older Women Movement's Maggie Shambrook said many women who fell into that cohort were living invisibly — couch-surfing or living in vans as they searched for an affordable, suitable home. Some empty-nesters want to move into smaller homes but say the cost of doing so keeps them in their large properties. Ms Shambrook said systemic issues including having worked in lower-paid professions or participated in unpaid caring work, along with the difficulty of building an asset base, contributed to this. And as Ms Taylor had experienced, there was also the issue of finding something suitable and affordable for a single person, especially as they aged. "Your mobility does change as you get older … your ability to navigate obstacles becomes less and less," Ms Shambrook said. "Mould, poor fittings and, in hot weather, no good ventilation, that's a serious issue.
