events.title: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer. But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job. Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog. However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity. What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction. For instance, TechCrunch has seen a han d ful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. ( NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.) But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences. The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out. It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into. To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post. This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0 In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds. Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology. For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests. Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.” “While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained. United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.) Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp , eBay , Zillow , Pizza Hut , Adidas , and various airlines .

events.title: I take about 15 solo trips a year. These 6 must-have products make traveling alone easier.
events.summary: There are a few products I swear by when traveling alone. oatawa/Shutterstock I swear by a few items to help make my solo trips more convenient. My portable tripod allows me to capture photos of myself without relying on help from strangers. My other must-haves include a lotion applicator for my back, a first-aid kit, and a portable charger. As a travel writer , I'm often taking off by myself — as often as 15 times a year. Because I typically travel without a partner, I make sure to pack a few essential items to make my trips easier, safer, and more enjoyable. Here are seven things I never leave for a solo trip without. Having a tripod means I don't have to rely on strangers to take pictures for me. Kelly Magyarics I like to take pictures of myself traveling, whether to post on social media or send to my boyfriend. I'm not into selfie sticks, and unfortunately, I can't always rely on strangers to take photos for me. So, having a cell phone tripod is a good compromise. I love my Toneof universal cell phone tripod because it easily slips into my carry-on luggage and expands when I need to snap a picture. It also includes a rechargeable remote control for the shutter. A first-aid kit is a must-have when traveling alone. I supplement my first-aid kit with over-the-counter medicine. Carol Yepes/Getty Images When I get injured or start to come down with something while traveling alone, there's no one to run out to the drugstore to get medicine or first-aid supplies for me. Sometimes, I'm not even in an area with a drugstore nearby, so I make sure to bring along any items I may need. My first-aid kit is stocked with bandages, cleansing wipes, gauze, tick removers, nosebleed plugs, sting relief, burn ointment, and a thermometer. I also pack some over-the-counter medicine for pain, gastrointestinal issues, motion sickness, and congestion. My portable speaker doubles as a white-noise machine. Kelly Magyarics When I'm traveling by myself, I always carry my LectroFan Bluetooth speaker with me. The sound is incredible considering its tiny size, and it has several white-noise settings to drown out noisy neighbors or street sounds. When I'm feeling lonely, I also like to use it to have a solo dance party in my room. A portable charger is always good to have on hand. Kelly Magyarics One of my biggest concerns when traveling alone is my cell phone battery running low. After all, I need my phone to navigate cities, book Uber rides, make restaurant reservations, and research tourist attractions . That's why I always carry a USB portable charger with me. This lotion applicator helps me avoid getting sunburn in the areas I can't reach. Kelly Magyarics Since I often travel to tropical places , I prefer to pack bottles of sunscreen lotion since the coverage is heavier than spray. But it's tricky to apply the lotion to my own back and shoulders. Foam-brush applicators are clunky to pack, but luckily, I found a cloth applicator from Steugo that folds up and doesn't take up much room in my suitcase. I pour some lotion onto the fabric and then use the handles to rub it onto my back as if I'm drying myself with a towel. I rinse or hand-wash it between uses and throw it in the washing machine once I return home. Having a portable wash bag allows me to do my laundry. Kelly Magyarics I never check my luggage, and being a single traveler means I can bring only one carry-on with me. Even though I can fit a lot in my bag, I sometimes need to re-wear and freshen up my clothes. Because hotel laundry service is often expensive, I bring my own Scrubba portable wash bag with me. To use it, I fill the packable bag with socks, underwear, and T-shirts and then add water and a laundry sheet. Then, I deflate the bag and rub my clothes along the inner washboard before rinsing, wringing, and hanging my garments to dry. events.title: Emmy Awards leave broadcast TV for Prime Video in 2027 under six-year deal
events.summary: Amazon's Prime Video will become the exclusive global home of the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal beginning in 2027. The Emmys will stream live and free in more than 240 countries and territories, with no Prime subscription required. The agreement ends the Emmys' long-running broadcast network rotation among ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. The Emmy Awards will leave its long-running broadcast network rotation for Amazon Prime Video in 2027 under a six-year exclusive global streaming deal, the e-commerce giant and the Television Academy announced on Tuesday. Under the agreement, Prime Video will stream the annual awards honoring the best in TV for free to all audiences, including nonsubscribers, in more than 240 countries and territories. Prime Video's rights to the Emmys will begin with the 2027 ceremony. NBC, owned by Comcast , aired the 2026 ceremony on Sept. 14. Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. In the release, Prime Video was named as the "permanent home" for the Emmys, in contrast to the rotating agreement in place years prior. The switch ends the traditional "wheel-deal" setup to broadcast the awards, where ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox took turns hosting the Emmys each year. The system has been in place since at least 1994 , with the most recent eight-year contract expiring this year. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement. "Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year," he said. The decision to move the 70-plus-year-old awards show to streaming reflects a broader trend in a shifting media landscape as Americans continue to ditch broadcast and cable TV for streaming service subscriptions. Streaming services have pushed further into live events in recent years, securing entertainment and sports rights alongside broadcast networks, and even winning rights that were previously exclusive to networks. In December 2025, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences announced a deal with Alphabet's YouTube and YouTube TV for media rights to the Oscars, taking over from ABC in 2029. Netflix has exclusively aired the SAG Awards since 2024.

events.title: Chancellor plans major intervention to help poorer UK households with rising energy bills
events.summary: Exclusive: Officials working on further radical changes that would change how much energy companies could charge customers John Healey is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget, after ministers became alarmed at forecasts that show bills rising by hundreds of pounds in January. The chancellor is working on plans to spend more than £1bn to help energy consumers, the bulk of which is likely to go towards increasing the discount given to households on certain benefits. Sources say final decisions have not been made, but Healey is set to rebuff a call from the energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether. Energy officials are working up more radical changes to bills, however, which could be implemented after the budget and would change how much companies could charge customers, rather than subsidising their bills. If approved, the energy discount will form a major plank of the budget, which government sources say will be low-key but focused on reducing voters’ cost of living. The chancellor is facing a cash crunch as he looks for money to fund an additional £4.7bn in defence spending and rebuild his fiscal buffer, which has been eroded by higher borrowing costs. He is likely to raise taxes to pay for the additional spending, and is rumoured to be looking at higher bank taxes in particular. Government sources had previously insisted the VAT cut to electricity bills which Andy Burnham announced soon after becoming prime minister would be the last support to be offered this year. But they have become increasingly concerned by forecasts showing that the Iran war will push the energy price cap up by as much as £442 in January – entirely eroding the impact of the VAT cut. As a result Healey has been considering submissions from the energy department on how to ease the pressures on households in the coming months. The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits. Healey is understood to be considering increasing this by a further £100, which would be funded by taxpayers, rather than bill-payers as the existing discount is. Fahnbulleh, meanwhile, has been pushing for more sweeping action to reduce bills for all consumers by as much as £120 by removing all levies. Under the energy secretary’s proposals, the levies, which fund renewable energy and efficiency schemes, would be paid for through taxation instead. She told the Guardian last week: “If we want a system that is resilient, if we want a system that can cope, if we want a system that ultimately can deliver the diversity of energy that we want, what is the fairest way in which we pay for it? “That is both across the exchequer versus our bill-payers, and then within our bill-payers. So we have to ask that question. Every other country is asking that question, and ultimately we’ve got to come to a fair deal.” Removing levies from bills would reduce inflation, but would cost as much as £3.2bn and would be difficult for the government to unwind should energy costs come down in the future. Officials in the energy department are working on more radical proposals for after the budget, meanwhile, including proposals to reduce tariffs for poorer households or those that use less energy. Burnham told the Labour conference last week: “British businesses and bill-payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. Within 10 years, I want those costs to be in line with our neighbours. “This means reforming a broken energy market so it better serves the public interest.” A so-called “social tariff” would force energy companies to charge poorer households less for each unit of electricity they consume than richer ones. Creating such a scheme, however, would involve a large amount of data collection from tax authorities, the Treasury and energy companies – an exercise likely to take far longer than the next few weeks. An alternative plan, known as a “rising block tariff”, would also vary the tariffs that energy companies can charge, but by consumption levels rather than income. The idea, which was proposed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) thinktank when Fahnbulleh ran it, would charge consumers less for a set amount of “essential” use and more once their consumption crossed that level. Alex Chapman, head of economic and environmental policy at NEF, said: “A serious price spike is coming, and without action, bills will exceed the peak of the last crisis. The government must use the budget to put in place both targeted support for the most vulnerable and, critically, a safety net for all.” He added: “Repeated crises have exposed the flaws in our privatised energy system – these can only be fixed by fundamental reform.

events.title: I had 5 kids headed to college. I took a demotion so they could go tuition-free.
events.summary: The author took a demotion for the tuition benefit. Courtesy of Melania Murphy My husband and I blended a family of six kids. Five of them were nearing college at the same time. To make tuition affordable, I took a lower-paying job at a college with tuition benefits. I spent years questioning whether I had given up too much, but the decision changed all our futures. I recently took a career demotion , but not because I lacked ambition. I made this choice because five of our kids were headed to college, and the math was impossible to ignore. When my husband and I married, we blended a family of six children in a western suburb of Chicago. Five were in high school at the same time — two seniors, a junior, a sophomore, and a freshman. We were thrilled to have a big family . We were also staring at the possibility of five college tuition bills arriving almost at once. We found a solution that seemed too good to be true My husband and I both believed college had changed our lives. We wanted our children to have that same chance, but we also knew we could not simply write checks and hope for the best. We expected them to work, apply for aid , and have skin in the game. Still, we did not want them starting adulthood buried in debt. Then I heard about a benefit that seemed too good to be true. Some colleges offer free or deeply discounted tuition to employees and their children. It was the first practical solution we had found. At the time, my marketing career was still young. I had gone back to school after years at home raising kids and was trying to build momentum. My husband had already spent two decades building his career in the office supply industry, so if one of us was going to chase a college job for the tuition benefit, it made sense that it would be me. I found a job that offered a tuition benefit, but it was a step back in my career After months of searching, I was offered an entry-level, data-entry job at a small liberal arts college about eight miles from our house. The tuition benefit was fantastic — my kids would get free tuition if they attended the school where I worked or one on a list of small liberal arts colleges across the country — and it would start right away. The salary, though, was hard to swallow. Taking the job meant accepting a salary that would cut my pay in half and a title that felt like I was taking three steps backwards. On paper, the decision made sense. One year of tuition for one child could cost more than the pay cut. Multiply that by five kids, and the financial logic was obvious. Emotionally, it was not that simple. I had worked hard to create a professional identity after years of being known mainly as someone's mom. Now I was choosing lower pay, a lower title, and work that did not reflect where I wanted my career to go. I told myself I was doing it for the kids, and I was. But that did not erase the sting. For years, I wondered whether I had given up too much. I thought about the salary I had walked away from, the career momentum I had slowed, and the ego I had to set aside every time I explained why I had taken the job. Still, parenting often requires a kind of math no spreadsheet can capture. You add up income, debt, opportunity, pride, fear, and hope. Then you make the choice you believe will give your children more options, even if it costs you something no one else can see. The author earned her master's degree while working at the college. Courtesy of Melania Murphy The decision to take a demotion changed our lives In the end, the decision changed all of our futures. Over the years, the tuition benefit covered 17 years of college for our kids. I earned my master's degree while working at the college, too. Eventually, I moved into an assistant director of marketing role, and one year, my total rewards statement showed my tuition benefit was worth 350% of my salary. Our kids took different paths. One was not ready for college right after high school, but later returned to work on his degree. Two went on to earn master's degrees. Two built careers outside the fields they studied, but their degrees still opened doors. Our youngest, who was not yet in grade school when we married, is now finishing her degree. Parents make quiet sacrifices all the time. Some look dramatic from the outside, but many do not. Mine looked like a smaller paycheck , an entry-level title, and years of wondering whether I had set aside too much of myself. But now looking back, I don't regret it. When I eventually left the college, one of our sons said, "We had a good run. Thank you for all you've done for us." That was when I understood the tradeoff differently. The demotion had not made my life smaller. It had helped make all of our futures bigger. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Hackers obtain counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large services
events.summary: Attackers hijacked three top-level domains and used their control to mint counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large organizations, Google said Tuesday. The attackers launched a series of attacks on the .gh, .sl, and .as country code top-level domains (ccTLDs) and then modified authoritative DNS records for selected domains within those namespaces. By controlling those DNS records, the attackers were able to pass automated domain control validation checks and obtain unauthorized certificates for “several Google domains” and “several leading global brands and widely used online services.” Google said it updated Chrome to block all certificates it identified as unauthorized, and worked with the issuing certification authorities to ensure the unauthorized certificates for Google properties were revoked. Certificate issuance: The weak link in the chain TLS certificates are the cryptographic credentials that underpin authentication and encryption protections for websites, mail servers, and other Internet infrastructure. These x.509 certificates use a digital signature to bind a domain name such as google.com to a public key. The public key is publicly available, while the private key is held only by the website operator. When a connection shows that the keys match, the visiting party knows it’s connected to the authentic site rather than an impostor. Possession of unauthorized certificates allows attackers to cryptographically impersonate the affected infrastructure. Read full article Comments

events.title: What can I do to protect myself after 'Asos hacked' message?
events.summary: The message, which Asos says people should not engage with, popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on Tuesday If a strange-looking message from Asos popped up on your phone on Tuesday, you may be worrying what it could mean and whether you need to do anything. The online retailer has emailed customers apologising for the "unauthorised push notification" containing an external link, adding that they should disregard the message and not click on it. Here's what has happened, and what those who may have been affected are being advised to do. On Tuesday morning, Asos users across the UK were sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company. "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message read. Later that day, Asos said it took immediate action to restrict the apparent hackers' access, was investigating and working with advisers and relevant authorities on "next steps". Data storage company Snowflake told the BBC its investigations had "found no compromise" of its platform. At this stage it isn't clear what information, if any, has been accessed. On Tuesday evening, Asos told customers it may include "basic personal information including name and contact details". "However, we don't believe that any payment-card information or account passwords have been impacted," it added. While those who received the pop-up message will undoubtedly be concerned, it does not mean your phone has been hacked. Don't click the link: The hack notification included a link to a Telegram account - Asos and cyber security experts say not to click on it Change passwords: It's worth updating your password, including across other sites that use the same one as your Asos account. The advice for a strong password is to mix numbers, symbols and upper and lower case characters, and avoid using the same password across multiple accounts Turn on two-step verification for important apps like banking and email: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls this "one of the most effective ways to protect your online accounts from cyber criminals". You can usually turn it on by going into the security settings in your account Monitor transactions: Keep an eye on your online transactions for anything unusual According to Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at global cyber-security firm Check Point, "the biggest immediate risk may be what happens next". She says criminals know people will be searching for information online and expects there to be "attempts to exploit that confusion". Her advice to Asos customers is not to be "scared and frightened". But she says they should be "extremely suspicious" of emails, texts or messages claiming their account has been compromised, offering a refund or asking them to click a link to reset their password. People should hang up the phone if they receive any calls from someone they think might be posing as Asos or another organisation, says Which? spokesperson Kat Cereda. The consumer rights expert says they should contact the organisation themselves afterwards through separate means. It's been less than 24 hours since the notification popped up on people's phones, and there are a number of unanswered questions. It isn't yet clear who is behind the message, what their motivation is, how many people received the notification or how many may be impacted Wilson, from the cyber-security firm Check Point, says there's still "an awful lot" we don't know. Asos said its website and app were operating "as normal, and customers can continue to shop with confidence on ASOS as normal" as of Tuesday night. It said protecting customers "is our priority", and it will provide a further update "as soon as we have confirmed more information". People should visit Asos's official website directly for updates. events.title: Amazon wins global rights to stream Emmys in six-year deal
events.summary: Theagreement replaces the "Wheel Deal" system, which rotated the gala among major networks like ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. Amazon Prime Video has secured exclusive global rights to stream the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal, ending the ceremony's run on traditional US broadcast television. Starting in 2027, the agreement replaces a rotation of the gala among major networks like ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. The ceremony will instead stream live for free worldwide each September, with no Prime Video subscription needed. Official terms were not disclosed. The BBC has contacted Amazon and the Emmys for comment. The move is another indication of how live events are shifting to digital platforms as viewing habits evolve. The Oscars, for example, are moving to YouTube live globally starting in 2029. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, said the existing setup had become out of sync with modern television. "The shows driving the industry forward largely originate on streaming platforms, yet the awards themselves were tethered to broadcast television," Proulx said. "That's why a leading streaming service like Prime Video makes sense for the Emmy's next act." Cris Abrego, chair of the Television Academy, said the deal gives the ceremony "unprecedented global reach", allowing audiences in more than 200 countries to watch live. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Abrego said in a statement issued by Amazon. Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said the platform is honoured to serve as the "global home" for the ceremony, adding that streaming the show for free delivers " the best entertainment to our customers worldwide." The agreement marks a milestone for Amazon, giving Prime Video its first marquee entertainment broadcast after building a live profile centred on sports, including the NFL's Thursday Night Football, NBA, and UEFA Champions League fixtures. Amazon's latest earnings highlighted strong gains in live viewership , external , including record ratings for its inaugural NBA season, which peaked at 6.5 million viewers for Game 7 of the Eastern Conference Semifinals. The Emmys deal positions Amazon directly alongside Google, whose video platform YouTube holds the upcoming Oscar rights. YouTube relies primarily on an ad-supported model, whereas Amazon is leveraging free live access to draw massive global audiences into its wider ecosystem. Like its live sporting events, the free broadcast will allow Amazon to build a substantial global advertising footprint. Moving exclusively to Prime Video is significant for the Emmys, ending a rotation across the major legacy broadcast networks that has been in place since 1955 and marking the first time the gala will leave traditional broadcast television entirely. First held in 1949, the Emmys honor achievements in acting, writing, and production, serving as a primary showcase for the global television industry. events.title: President Trump ranks 12th among the country's richest real estate moguls. Meet the other billionaires in his industry.
events.summary: Donald Trump owns the Mar-a-Lago Club. Win McNamee/Getty Images; Joe Raedle/Getty Images Forbes estimates that several US real estate moguls are worth billions more than Donald Trump. You may have shopped, worked, or even lived in a building owned by one of these magnates. Their portfolios range from office buildings and malls to student housing and rental properties. Real estate has been the source of some of America’s biggest fortunes, including that of US President Donald Trump . However, despite his extensive property portfolio, Trump ranks 12th among the country’s richest real estate moguls. These magnates rarely own only residential properties . Their portfolios often span some of the country’s biggest office buildings, malls, hotels, and logistics hubs. In several cases, they also hold stakes in sports teams and other assets. This ranking was compiled from the Forbes 400 list for 2026, which provides an estimated snapshot of the net worth of the 400 richest people in America as of September 4. Forbes estimated each person’s net worth using sources including interviews and asset valuations, while accounting for debt and charitable giving. In some cases, Forbes lists individuals as “and family” to indicate that some of the wealth is held by immediate family members. Here are America’s richest real estate moguls, ranked by net worth. 15. Robert Faith — $6 billion Bloomberg/Getty Images State: South Carolina Robert Faith founded Greystar in 1993. He is the chair and CEO of the real estate company, which specializes in rental housing properties, including senior housing and student housing. 14. Annette Lerner & family — $6.1 billion Annette Lerner. The Washington Post/Getty Images State: Maryland Annette Lerner's husband, Ted Lerner, built a real estate company in 1952 after she gave him a $250 loan. The firm, Lerner Enterprises, is one of the largest real estate owners in Washington, DC. After Ted Lerner died in 2023, she and her children inherited his estate. 13. Mitchell Morgan & family — $6.7 billion Hilarie and Mitchell Morgan Sean Zanni/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images State: Pennsylvania Mitchell Morgan is the founder and chair of Morgan Properties, which specializes in apartment complexes. The firm owns over 97,000 units across the US. 12. Donald Trump — $7 billion Brendan SMIALOWSKI / AFP via Getty Images State: Florida While Donald Trump’s presidency has added billions to his net worth, largely through crypto , according to Forbes, much of his fortune remains tied to real estate. His portfolio includes golf clubs, resorts, and commercial skyscrapers. 11. Rick Caruso — $7.1 billion Paul Archuleta/Getty Images State: California Rick Caruso built his fortune through Caruso, the real estate company he founded. The firm developed shopping and mixed-use destinations such as The Grove and The Americana at Brand. 10. H. Ross Perot Jr. — $7.4 billion Bloomberg/Getty Images State: Texas Ross Perot Jr. founded Hillwood, a real estate development firm, after borrowing against his billionaire father's fortune. The company's portfolio includes residential and commercial developments, as well as logistics hubs. 9. Herb Simon — $7.7 billion Stephanie Augello/Getty Images State: Indiana Herb Simon founded the company that would eventually become Simon Property Group in 1960 with his brother. The real estate investment trust owns hundreds of properties around the world, such as malls and mixed-use spaces. Simon also owns stakes in the Indiana Pacers and Indiana Fever. 8. Edward Roski Jr. — $8.1 billion FREDERIC J. BROWN/AFP via Getty Images State: California Edward Roski Jr. is the chair of Majestic Realty, which his father founded in 1948. The commercial real estate development firm counts Walmart, Amazon , and UPS among its tenants. 7. Ty Warner — $8.2 billion Jimi Celeste/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images State: Illinois Ty Warner created the Beanie Babies line of stuffed toys, the profits of which he invested in real estate. His portfolio includes the Four Seasons in New York and Las Ventanas al Paraiso in Los Cabos. 6. Leonard Stern — $9 billion Donald Bowers/Getty Images for Green Beret Foundation State: New York Leonard Stern is the chair and CEO of Hartz Mountain Industries, which has an extensive portfolio of real estate holdings, including industrial warehouses. 5. Igor Olenicoff — $9.1 billion Igor Olenicoff has a net worth of $9.1 billion. Bloomberg/Getty Images State: Florida Igor Olenicoff founded Olen Companies in 1974. The firm's portfolio includes over 8 million square feet in office space and over 17,000 luxury apartment units. 4. Neil Bluhm — $9.9 billion Bloomberg/Getty Images State: Illinois Neil Bluhm cofounded JMB Realty in 1970, which became one of the largest real estate developers in the US. Bluhm expanded beyond real estate into casinos and private equity, cofounding Rush Street Gaming and Walton Street Capital. 3. Jeff Greene — $10.1 billion Bloomberg/Getty Images State: Florida Jeff Greene became a billionaire betting against the mid-2000s housing bubble, using credit default swaps tied to subprime mortgage securities before the 2008 financial crisis. 2. Donald Bren — $19.8 billion Jay L. Clendenin/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images State: California Donald Bren is the chair and principal shareholder of Irvine Company, a real estate development firm. The company's portfolio spans new home villages, hundreds of office buildings, and the MetLife Building. 1. Stephen Ross — $21.5 billion Stephen Ross Taylor Hill/WireImage State: Florida Stephen Ross founded Related Companies, a real estate development and lifestyle firm, in 1972. He then founded Related Ross, a real estate development firm focused on West Palm Beach, in 2024. Ross also holds stakes in the sports and wellness industries, including the Miami Dolphins, the Formula 1 Miami Grand Prix, SoulCycle, and Equinox Fitness. events.title: Some public transport trips are more expensive in Adelaide than anywhere else
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ABC NEWS analysis found that train journeys are generally cheaper in Adelaide than Sydney, except for trips shorter than 10km. ( ABC News ) Cost of living pressures and recent price increases to Adelaide's public transport fares poses a budget challenge to people living on low incomes. ABC News analysis has found that Adelaide Metro fares are currently among the nation's most expensive, and are the most expensive for short journeys. Amid a cost-of-living crisis, some Australians have turned to public transport in an effort to curb the pinch at the petrol pump. But for many, public transport is a necessity that enables them to undertake the basics of everyday life. "Public transport is the only way that I can access things like engagement with employment opportunities, education, culture, public events and health appointments," Ann-Maree Anderson told ABC News. She rents in Mount Barker, an Adelaide Hills town about 30km south-east of the CBD. Ms Anderson has recently graduated from university, volunteers for poverty outreach groups and is associated with the Anti-Poverty Network, and has recently shifted from Austudy to the Jobseeker support payment. Analysis shows high expenses in Adelaide Governments across Australia have introduced a range of measures to reduce public transport fares. Tasmania offers free public bus travel, as did Victoria before introducing a half-price fare until the end of the year. The NT government has offered free buses for several years and Queensland's LNP government recently legislated the universal 50c fare introduced by Labor in 2024. Other states and territories have introduced various measures to trim fares, such as age-based free travel and other fare discounts. The SA government pointed to three measures introduced this year to address cost-of-living pressures. "By slashing the cost of 28-day student passes and expanding the Seniors Card, millions of more dollars have stayed in the pockets of South Australians," a government spokesperson said. "The government also put a three-month pause on annual increases for MetroCARD public transport fares to provide cost-of-living respite for commuters during the early impacts of the conflict in the Middle East." An analysis of single fares by ABC News showed Adelaide commuters, including those like Ms Anderson, were currently paying the second-highest fares in the country, behind Sydney. For short trips, Adelaide's fare prices were comparatively the most expensive in Australia. That's because Adelaide Metro uses a network-wide fare system, charging commuters with a single tap of a metroCARD or payment card. In Sydney — which has the most expensive public transport fares in Australia — those short trips of fewer than 8km on a bus or tram, or 10km on a train, are charged at rates lower than Adelaide's standard fares. The SA government's delay to its annual fare rise meant prices grew roughly 3.3 per cent in line with CPI on October 1. Certain fares, including regular and concession metroCARD single trips were raised above CPI though, as were regular 14-day MetroCards, and both 14 and 28 day concession MetroCards. Adelaide's public transport system uses a single tap fare structure applied across its whole network. ( ABC Radio Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton ) Fare reductions can get people on board, sometimes Transport strategist Elliot Fishman, who is the director of the Institute for Sensible Transport, said public transport provided practical means to reduce household spending and the need for more than one car. But when it came to reducing fares, there have been varying results for boosting use of public transport. Dr Fishman's group analysed the fare reductions taken by the Victorian and Queensland governments. Dr Elliot Fishman believes that fare reductions in Adelaide may not have the same impact as fare-cutting initiatives in Melbourne. ( ABC News: Wayne Hammond ) In Queensland, he said "there was a small increase in usage, but a lot of the increasing usage came from existing public transport users". In Melbourne, the program had seen a "13 to 20 per cent increase in public transport [usage] compared to before those fare reductions". "For the increase in patronage, it was more effective for the government to reduce and eliminate the fares than it would have been to provide an increase in the quality of the service to try and get the same boost," he said. Dr Fishman said Brisbane's Bus Rapid Transit system and Melbourne's rail-heavy network moved large numbers of people each day, were primed to benefit from fare subsidies.

events.title: Chinese company to face Australian privacy probe over 'pervert' glasses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australian regulator launches probe into Chinese smart glasses company amid privacy fears Carly Kind says her office has a "range of concerns" about Shenzhen Qingcheng. ( ABC News: Scott Kyle ) Chinese software company Shenzhen Qingcheng is being investigated by the Australian privacy commissioner following an ABC investigation. It revealed last month more than a dozen serious security flaws in the company's app and website used in the glasses for sale in Kmart, Big W Marketplace and Amazon. The privacy commissioner is urging retailers to reconsider selling the product for now. The Australian privacy commissioner has launched a formal investigation into the Chinese software company behind an influx of cheap smart glasses to Australia. It is the most significant action authorities have taken so far to address mounting community concern over the devices nicknamed "pervert glasses" by their detractors. In August, Attorney-General Michelle Rowland took the unusual step of asking the regulator to prioritise the issue amid calls for an import ban . A recent ABC investigation found more than a dozen serious security flaws in the HeyCyan phone app used in smart glasses sold by Kmart, as well as online platforms such as Big W Marketplace and Amazon, among others. Cheap smart glasses leaving Australians' data exposed Independent testing finds a hacker can access cheap smart glasses without a password. Independent testing of the low-cost glasses found Australians' sensitive data, including email addresses, dates of birth, images and videos, were left exposed to hackers. It also found the devices could be hijacked by nearby attackers without a password using only a Bluetooth connection, and that data was in some cases being sent to Chinese servers. "The ABC's reporting … raised the prospect that there haven't been reasonable steps taken to secure [user] information," Privacy Commissioner Carly Kind said. She said her office had "a range of concerns" about the practices of the company, Shenzhen Qingcheng Future Technology Co (Shenzhen Qingcheng), including about the possible use of facial recognition technology. Smart glasses, which look like ordinary glasses, allow the wearer to capture images, video and audio with the press of a button or verbal command. It is not always clear when they are in use. The regulator also made preliminary inquiries with Meta, Google, Kmart, and an importer called BDI Technology over their supply of similar tech in Australia, but none of the other companies is the subject of a formal investigation. Shenzhen Qingcheng was the only company which opted to ignore the regulator completely, Ms Kind said. "The company did not respond at all to our multiple attempts to obtain information … [and] did not even acknowledge receipt of our communications," she said. "It does suggest that some of the fundamentals may not be in place, for example, compliance teams that are appropriately staffed. "We would normally expect pretty prompt attention [to] be given to any outreach from the regulator". An influx of cheap smart glasses have made their way into Australia. ( ABC News: Scott Preston ) A formal investigation means the privacy commissioner will now have the power to compel Shenzhen Qingcheng to provide information about how it is complying with Australian laws. If the company continues to ignore the regulator, she can seek a court injunction to limit the supply of its products. Shenzhen Qingcheng could theoretically face fines of hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars if ultimately found to have interfered with the privacy of Australians. "The Australian Privacy Act provides for really, really considerable monetary penalties in the form of $50 million per contravention … and that can be applied per individual," Ms Kind said. "That would be what we would be shooting for, should our concerns be borne out". In the meantime, the regulator has urged retailers such as Kmart to reconsider selling the product at all. "We have written to the Australian Retail Council and to other retailers, putting them on notice that this company is under investigation," Ms Kind said. events.title: More than $1.2b announced for NSW regional road upgrades
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NSW and federal governments announce more than $1.2b for regional roads The upgrades will support the movement of freight, including wind turbines and associated parts. ( Supplied: Port of Newcastle ) More than $1.2 billion in combined state and federal funding has been announced to upgrade regional roads in NSW. The works are expected to include wider shoulders and intersections, as well as new turning and overtaking lanes. The governments said new and improved rest stops and pull-over bays would also be added as part of the project. A road corridor used to transport wind turbines between Newcastle and Dubbo will be among the regional routes to share in more than $1.2 billion of new funding for vital upgrades. Other projects include the corridor between Muswellbrook and Armidale, and the route between Euston and Tocumwal in the state's south-west. The Albanese government is tipping in $674 million, while the Minns government is investing $610 million. When added to previously announced contributions, it takes the investment from both governments to $1.74 billion. Federal Transport Minister Catherine King said the upgrades would ensure the state's supply chains were not disrupted. "Our export industries and freight operators are the backbone of the Australian economy, and they rely on safe and reliable roads," she said. NSW Roads Minister Jenny Aitchison said the corridor between Newcastle and Dubbo was especially important in light of the Great Western Highway's closure due to a structural failure at Victoria Pass. "[The Golden Highway] is quite important because it doesn't have that more fragile geological infrastructure that we see across the Great Dividing Range," she said. "Also it connects Dubbo and the broader Central West with the second largest city in New South Wales." Jenny Aitchison says the upgrades will support the movement of all kinds of freight. ( ABC News: Romy Stephens ) It has also been an important route for transporting massive wind turbines and generators to the Central West Orana Renewable Energy Zone (REZ). Pauline Hanson's One Nation party has been critical of the REZs, citing the impact on regional roads, among other concerns. However, Ms Aitchison said the upgrades were not solely focused on supporting the renewable energy industry. "It is important for freight of all kinds, whether it's agriculture, mining or anything else," she said. Ms Aitchison said the upgrade, helped by a new cash injection of $294 million, would also include improvements to John Renshaw Drive and the Hunter Expressway. The state and federal governments said the regional road upgrades would include wider shoulders and intersections, as well as new turning and overtaking lanes. New and improved rest stops and pull-over bays would also be added as part of the project, along with additional heavy vehicle facilities, they said. More than $680 million of new money will be invested in the Muswellbrook to Armidale corridor, taking the total investment in the project to $849 million. Ms Aitchison said the upgrades would include key sections of the New England Highway. "People are looking for better productivity. That requires the roads to be wider and to allow more opportunities for passing from general traffic," she said. In the state's south-west, the corridor between Euston and Tocumwal will receive $310 million in new funding for upgrades along the Sturt and Newell Highways, as well as Kidman Way. Premier Chris Minns said better roads would lead to a stronger economy. "This investment will make roads safer for local families, improve travel times and make it easier for businesses and freight operators to get their goods where they need to go," he said.

events.title: I’ve Covered Death Row Cases for Nearly a Decade. What Happened to Christa Pike Wasn’t an Anomaly.
events.summary: The death chamber in Huntsville, Texas Joe Raedle/Getty Images Over the course of two hours, witnesses watched and listened as Christa Pike cried, whimpered and snored through Tennessee’s attempt to execute her. By the end of it, executioners had given her two doses of the state’s lethal injection drugs. Her arms were swollen and blistered, and one had turned purple, her attorneys said. And she was still alive, marking what legal experts say is the first time a prisoner in the U.S. has survived one dose — let alone two — of lethal injection drugs.  Even if the outcome was unprecedented, what went wrong was not. Pike’s was the third Tennessee execution in 14 months to go awry. But as a reporter who has covered death row for nearly a decade and witnessed several executions, I know the state is not alone. The factors behind the breakdowns in Tennessee have popped up again and again across the country — and show how easily another botched execution could occur, even as soon as the ones planned Wednesday in Texas and next week in Florida. Here’s what we know about Tennessee’s attempt to execute Pike: The procedure started more than nine hours late, delayed by last-minute legal fights. Then, inside the death house, executioners struggled to find a vein, jabbing Pike with at least seven needles, according to her lawyers, one of whom watched in dismay. As the caustic barbiturate finally started flowing into the IV lines, Pike did not fall into sedation quickly. Instead, witnesses said, she sang with her spiritual adviser. Then she said her arm felt like it was about to burst open. “Does this happen like that?” she asked.  Like Pike, many aging death row prisoners have medical problems that can complicate efforts to kill them, potentially turning what are supposed to be relatively quick deaths into agonizing, drawn-out procedures. Even when prisoners are healthy, several states have faced questions about the competence of their execution teams, as both the American Medical Association and American Nurses Association have strongly opposed their members taking part in death penalty procedures. And death penalty states across the country shroud their executions in such secrecy that it is often difficult or impossible to confirm the age, source or sterility of the drugs. “The types of failures that went into this botch happen all the time,” said Robert Dunham, director of the Death Penalty Policy Project. “There is nothing in the execution process that states are incapable of getting wrong.” The Tennessee Department of Correction declined to comment, though hours after the attempted execution the agency said in a statement that it had “followed every step” of the state’s established protocol, which “has been consistently effective.” On Saturday, the head of the agency resigned . Meanwhile, Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement that he had ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the execution previously scheduled for December would no longer take place this year. His office didn’t respond to a request for comment. On Friday, Pike’s lawyers filed a motion asking a court to order the agency to preserve any evidence related to the state’s failed effort to kill their client. In a statement, they said the filing “details the serious complications that occurred during the execution attempt, many of which Christa and her attorneys had warned the State and the courts about months earlier.” Pike remains in the hospital where she is receiving critical medical care, they said. After several days on a ventilator, intubated and unconscious, on Tuesday afternoon her attorneys said she was awake and speaking. “Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” they wrote in a statement. “We continue to ask the Governor of Tennessee to commute Christa Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.” Unhealthy Prisoners By the time the Tennessee Department of Correction strapped her to the gurney last week, Pike had been on death row for 30 years. She had been sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer , a fellow Job Corps student in Knoxville. Pike was 18 at the time and, like many people on death row , had a history of mental illness and childhood sexual abuse .  Now 50 years old, Pike has faced an array of health problems, which her legal team had repeatedly warned could lead to a bungled execution. During a three-day hearing in August , Pike’s attorneys argued that her small veins and a blood disorder would make it harder and more painful to put in the IV lines to administer the lethal dose. The Tennessee Supreme Court did not agree , calling their arguments “speculative” and rejecting their request for a stay. Tennessee’s execution protocol relies on pentobarbital, a caustic barbiturate that slows down breathing and has been used to treat seizures, sedate people before surgery and euthanize animals. But its use in putting to death humans has drawn scrutiny. After relying on the drug for all 13 federal executions during the first Trump administration, the Justice Department under President Joe Biden said there was too much uncertainty about whether it would cause “ unnecessary pain and suffering ” and decided to stop using it “unless and until that uncertainty is resolved.” This year, President Donald Trump’s DOJ reversed course and readopted its use. Despite supply difficulties and repeated lawsuits from death row prisoners arguing that using pentobarbital is cruel and unusual, several states still use it, including Georgia, Missouri, South Carolina and Texas, where I witnessed five executions in the late 2010s as a reporter for the Houston Chronicle. Four of the condemned prisoners said the drug burned. Two said they could taste it. One said he could “hear it going through the vein.” But all of them stopped moving within minutes and were declared dead in under an hour.  Tennessee prison officials have not offered an explanation as to why Pike’s attempted execution was so drastically different. Initially, Pike’s attorneys and several death penalty experts raised the possibility that the drugs may have been too old or degraded to work as intended. Yet in Friday’s legal filings, Pike’s lawyers focused on the way the drug was administered, saying it was “abundantly clear” that Tennessee prison officials either didn’t know that the IV lines were out of place or didn’t realize her veins had been so badly damaged that the highly alkaline liquid started leaking out into the surrounding tissue of her arm. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology in Atlanta and one of Pike’s medical experts , said that meant there wasn’t enough of the drug in her bloodstream at once to kill her. “It just got into her arms, and most of it stopped there,” he said.   Like Pike, many people on death rows nationwide have significant health problems often compounded by old

events.title: Disease outbreak prompts salmon company to inject fish with antibiotic
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Salmon company Tassal will inject fish with antibiotics ahead of expected marine heatwave summer Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The salmon industry's preferred method to combat the disease Piscirickettsia salmonis, the antibiotic florfenicol, cannot be used. ( Huon ) Seafood giant Tassal will begin injecting salmon in a Tasmanian pen with the antibiotic oxytetracycline. The industry has been grappling with how to prevent mass fish deaths during the past two summers. The federal regulator is assessing the industry's request for a florfenicol permit after its use was suspended. A salmon company will begin individually injecting diseased fish in Tasmanian waters with an antibiotic this week, in what it says is a new practice for the state. Tassal, the Canadian-owned seafood giant, said it will use oxytetracycline (OTC) to treat a bacterial outbreak in fish at a lease in Tasmania's south, in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel, on Thursday. The announcement follows the salmon industry's controversial use of the antibiotic florfenicol last summer , which was dispersed in the water with salmon food. Both antibiotics treat disease in farmed salmon caused by the bacteria Piscirickettsia salmonis, which has led to mass fish deaths when waters warm during the summer months in recent years. Tasmania's salmon producers have been hit hard over recent years by a bacterial disease in waterways, resulting in large amounts of dead fish. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) The resultant dead fish and the proliferation of antibiotics in the marine environment have made the industry the subject of the ire of environmentalists, swimmers, recreational fishers and the wild fisheries sector . And the head of the industry body Salmon Tasmania said he expects some wild fisheries to be closed during summer, should aquaculture companies be granted approval to use the antibiotic florfenicol again. Tassal waiting for approval to use banned antibiotic again Ahead of last summer, the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) approved the industry's use of florfenicol in southern Tasmanian waters. The APVMA retracted the licence in March, citing an "unacceptable risk of residue exposure to non-target species". In the first three months of this year, the industry used more than five tonnes of florfenicol trying to control a disease outbreak that killed 9,000 tonnes of farmed fish. The fallout from the bacterial outbreak has emboldened opponents of the industry. ( Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation ) In a statement today, a Tassal spokesperson said the company was waiting for approval to once again use florfenicol to treat disease outbreaks. "Florfenicol in feed is the most effective option, and while we await a permit for it, we're using OTC where required," they said. OTC has been used by the industry in the past, but the spokesperson said this would be the first time it is used to treat fish at sea. They said about 10 kilograms of OTC would be used in the first pen on Thursday, with fish individually anaesthetised, injected and then monitored for recovery. 'Huge amount' of antibiotics at fish farm concerning, say Greens, expert Almost 3 tonnes of the antibiotic florfenicol were used at one Tasmanian salmon farm lease in just two months, with information on its use across eight other sites yet to be released to the public by authorities. Despite the preference for florfenicol, Tassal said direct injection of OTC uses "a fraction of the medicine needed for medicated feed and is expected to deliver a more targeted treatment". Tassal rival Huon Aquaculture tried to use OTC to overcome disease outbreaks in coastal pens last year, but ruled it "largely ineffective" before the first florfenicol approval. At the time, the industry argued florfenicol had a range of advantages over oxytetracycline because it required lower dosages, lower levels were excreted by fish, and it had lower toxicity for aquatic organisms. Before the use of florfenicol was approved last November, salmon company Huon trialled oxytetracycline, but found it "largely ineffective". ( Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan ) Animal welfare a top priority, industry says John Whittington, the chief executive of industry body Salmon Tasmania, said he was bracing for a marine heatwave this summer. He said across the industry, fish were being bred and fed for resilience to warmer waters, and would be vaccinated against disease before being released into pens.

events.title: Meta joins with group of companies to tame ‘chaos’ of doing business with AI bots
events.summary: Walmart, Meta and OpenAI Chairman Bret Taylor’s startup Sierra are building a set of tech standards to make it easier to do business with AI bots. As Meta’s Muse and other buzzy AI agents like Instinct see a boom in popularity, some companies have struggled to figure out what's happening inside their walls. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists,” said Taylor. A month after Meta's launch of Muse, the personal agent that quickly turned into a viral sensation, a group of companies is coming together to try to simplify the process of bringing the technology into the business world. Meta, Walmart , Stripe and a handful of other companies are publishing what they're calling a "personal agent protocol." It's an open standard meant to dictate how artificial intelligence agents can interact with businesses. Enterprise AI startup Sierra, co-founded by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, is part of the group. Taylor, who's also chairman of OpenAI and is leading the initiative, told CNBC in an interview that companies have a lot of work to do to figure out how and when personal agents are able to access information. "Companies will know when it's a personal agent versus an actual person. For a lot of companies there's a risk: you don't want just a random bot that isn't acting on behalf of a person to have access to this service," Taylor said. “It is kind of chaos until such a standard exists." Meta's Muse has become the most popular and buzzy version of personal AI agents since hitting the market in early September. It soared to the top of Apple's App Store and remains there, ahead of ChatGPT. However, Amazon is among the companies that have blocked Meta's agents, citing worries of website scraping. Amazon also blocked Perplexity's AI agent and sued the startup in November, alleging the company took steps to "conceal" its AI agents so they could continue to scrape Amazon's website without approval. Perplexity called the lawsuit a "bully tactic." For the new standard, Taylor compared it with the experience of logging into other websites with Google or Facebook credentials, technology he worked on when he was tech chief at Facebook. He said the practice will help with authentication so that businesses know if they're dealing with a bot, and will provide visibility into what personal agents are actually doing through these websites. David Singleton, vice president of engineering and consumer products at Meta Superintelligence Labs and former technology chief at Stripe, highlighted security. In order for agents to work well, he said, customers need to share credit card and personal information, and the new standard creates some level of visibility and control. "We're defining rails that we hope personal agents and business agents can run over for the future," Singleton said, comparing it to email. "If you think about email, it works great because it is a standard that everyone can use to talk to each other, and we think this is going to be quite similar." Singleton said Muse already has millions of users in the U..S and it's "growing rapidly." "What we're finding is that people love using Muse for all kinds of things, things like signing their kids up for classes, finding and buying the best gifts, scheduling that dentist appointment that you have been putting off for six months," he said. "We need a mechanism to have it go faster and smoother." While OpenAI and Anthropic aren't on board now, Taylor said he expects the AI giants to participate, and indicated he will be "really disappointed" if it's not being used by competitors. "The whole point of this is to be an open standard," Taylor said.

events.title: How event contract bundles are boosting volume on prediction markets
events.summary: Combo contracts, similar to parlays on traditional sportsbooks, are increasingly making up a large share of prediction markets' notional volume as traders seek potential high payouts. But those contracts are a very small portion of transactions on prediction market platforms, putting into question if notional volume is still an accurate reflection of where trader activity is on event contract exchanges. The way combo contracts are counted follows federal regulatory guidance governing how exchanges measure volume activity. The growing popularity of a combo contracts on prediction markets is leading to soaring volumes, even as they makes up only a small amount of total activity on the platforms. Combos, or multiple contracts stacked together that only pay out if all of them win — similar to parlays on traditional sportsbooks — have exploded in popularity. Last month, combos accounted for more than 50% of notional volume on Kalshi , driven by the start of the NFL season . Combos are overwhelmingly made up of combinations of multiple sports contracts. As rival Polymarket worked to expand its U.S. exchange this year, combos were a priority following the domestic platform's official launch in May . Combos are now nearly 50% of daily volume on Polymarket U.S., helped by growth during the NFL season. But while combos hold a large share of volume, they actually aren't where most speculators on prediction markets execute their trades. That's because of how the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal regulator overseeing prediction markets, requires exchanges to report volume. The multi-leg contracts are "helping [Polymarket and Kalshi] claim a higher number with lower realistic cash output," said Chris Park, a researcher and founder of MSR Decode, a research firm analyzing prediction market data. When a trader places a trade on a prediction market, no matter the cash they put down, platforms measure it as $1 of notional volume. All event contracts have binary outcomes between $0 to $1, and no matter what price a speculator pays to place a trade, someone has to take the other side of that order and make $1 in total volume. But combos can have payouts that are much greater than $1, meaning someone can put very little money down, pennies in some cases, and it will be measured as potentially thousands of dollars in volume thanks to the market makers who take the other side of these high-payout trades. A CNBC analysis for trades on Kalshi on Sept. 27 showed this in practice. On single contracts, the average amount of cash placed on a trade was less than 47 cents. But on combo contracts, that average per contract was about 9 cents. Similarly, while combos comprised 58% of Kalshi's trading volume in September, they made up less than 13% of the total transactions on the platform, according to data on Dune. Other than sports, combos trump other categories for notional volume on Kalshi, with over 35% total volume share. Details on how combos are measured is not always clear to the public, but their effect on total headline volume numbers can make platforms look as though they're growing faster than they are. The rising popularity of prediction markets' sports-related event contracts has hurt traditional online sportsbooks — including FanDuel parent Flutter Entertainment, and DraftKings — whose stocks have plunged 70% and 45%, respectively, over the past year. But some note that investors may be confusing activity numbers that aren't exactly comparable. "I have spoken to investors who see the notional number and compare it to [the] handle in sports betting, and then make the argument that. you know, these prediction markets have already exceeded [the] scale of sports betting," said Ian Moore, an analyst at Bernstein. A "handle" in a sportsbook measures the total dollar amount wagered, while prediction markets count both sides of a trade. "When a client buys a deep out-of-the-money contract or a combo, prediction markets may have dollar volumes anywhere between 20 to 100 times greater than sportsbooks because CFTC reporting requires one thing and sportsbooks report the same activity differently," said Rich Jaycobs, an independent advisor to prediction markets seeking regulatory approval from the CFTC. "Same basic bet, same basic idea, but you're getting a completely different perception of activity." Kalshi said its notional volume doesn't overstate activity. "If people are more interested in other measurements, they can look at other metrics," said spokesperson Jack Such. While notional volume is the standard metric for prediction markets, some have suggested looking instead at taker volume as a better measurement. That's because "takers" scoop up liquidity from market makers, rather than provide it, and thus can be a better yardstick of where activity is on exchanges. Polymarket agrees with that approach.

events.title: All 27 James Bond movies ranked, according to critics
events.summary: Sean Connery posed as James Bond on the set of "Goldfinger." Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images The first " James Bond " film, "Dr. No," turned 64 this month. To commemorate this anniversary, all 27 "Bond" films are streaming at their new home, Amazon Prime. "Bond 28," whenever it comes, will be the first without longtime producers, the Broccoli family. 007 fans, rejoice: Every film starring the world's most famous spy is finally streaming in one place, the franchise's new home, Amazon. Longtime "James Bond" producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli ceded creative control of Bond , James Bond, to Amazon MGM Studios in February 2025, so it makes sense that Bond's films would live there. Wilson had been involved with Eon Productions, the original studio behind "Bond," since 1972, and Broccoli's family had cinematic stewardship of the franchise since it began in 1962. Amazon officially acquired MGM in 2022, but the studio hasn't produced any 007 content since then; it hasn't even picked a successor to Daniel Craig after his 2021 exit. The Broccoli family's fierce protectiveness of the character was widely believed to have stalled franchise development, but that could change now that Amazon MGM Studios has full creative control. Announcements have been slow, though — all we know is that "Bond 28" will be directed by Denis Villeneuve . In honor of the new James Bond, who's hopefully coming our way soon, we used Rotten Tomatoes to see how all 27 films in this storied franchise stack up, according to critics. 27. "Casino Royale" (1967) "Casino Royale." Columbia Pictures Rotten Tomatoes score:   26% The lowest-rated Bond movie by critics is 1967's "Casino Royale," starring David Niven as the titular spy. This version of "Casino Royale" is a parody of spy films, rather than a straightforward Bond caper. It's also one of two films about James Bond that wasn't produced by Eon Productions. "Casino Royale" also starred Peter Sellers, Ursula Andress, Joanna Pettet, Daliah Lavi, Barbara Bouchet, and Terence Coop in double roles — all of them play different versions of Bond. Woody Allen also appeared as Bond's nephew, Jimmy. "Unfortunately, after the introductory sequences, 'Casino Royale' begins a downhill slide. It gets progressively sillier and more incoherent until it's impossible to keep any of the plot elements straight. Worse, with only occasional exceptions, the humor ceases to be funny, and the whole production degenerates into absurdity," wrote James Berardinelli of ReelViews. 26. "A View to a Kill" (1985) A matte shot of English actor Roger Moore as 007, clinging to a fire engine ladder in a publicity still for the James Bond film 'A View To A Kill', 1984. Keith Hamshere/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   36% Roger Moore's seventh and final outing as 007 was also his worst, according to critics. The film sees Bond travel to San Francisco to save Silicon Valley from a former KGB agent played by Christopher Walken. His bodyguard and lover, May Day, was notably played by Grace Jones. The classic "Bond girl" was played by Tanya Roberts, of future "That '70s Show" fame. "It's not double-oh-seven anymore, but double-oh-seventy, the best argument yet for the mandatory retirement age," wrote The Washington Post's Paul Attanasio. 25. "The Man with the Golden Gun" (1974) Actors Roger Moore and Christopher Lee on the set of "The Man With The Golden Gun". Sunset Boulevard/Corbis/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   40% "The Man with the Golden Gun" starred Moore as Bond and legendary actor Christopher Lee as the titular man with the golden gun, Francisco Scaramanga. Meanwhile, Bond's love interest, Mary Goodnight, was played by Britt Ekland. Bond and Scaramanga engage in a game of cat-and-mouse for much of the movie, as no one knows what Scaramanga looks like, outside the fact that he has a third nipple. "If you enjoyed the early Bond films as much as I did, you'd better skip this one," wrote Nora Sayre of The New York Times. 24. "Octopussy" (1983) Actor Roger Moore, left, and Actress Maud Adams, stars of the latest James Bond film 'Octopussy' pose for a photograph during filming on set at the Nene Valley Railway (NVR) Peterborough, Cambridgeshire, U.K, on Monday, September 6, 1982. Bryn Colton/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score:   41% Let's get it out of the way: Yes, this movie is really called "Octopussy." Its titular character, a successful businesswoman and jewel smuggler, was played by Maud Adams. Bond and Octopussy have personal business: Years earlier, Bond arrested her father for treason. The two form an uneasy alliance to defeat an exiled Afghan prince, Kamal Khan, played by Louis Jourdan. "It's an easy film to hate (and often paints a big target on its back encouraging you to do so), but it works perfectly as a piece of entertainment, where the good ultimately outweighs the bad," wrote Jake Tropila of Film Inquiry. 23. "The World Is Not Enough" (1999) Irish actor Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 in the James Bond film 'The World Is Not Enough', 1999. Here he visits the offices of a Swiss banker in the opening sequence. Keith Hamshere/Getty Images Rotten Tomatoes score: 51% Critics think the worst Bond film starring Pierce Brosnan is 1999's "The World Is Not Enough," Brosnan's third. Bond shares the screen with an American nuclear physicist named Dr. Christmas Jones. Equally improbable, she's played by Denise Richards. His  other  female costar is Elektra King, an oil heiress played by Sophie Marceau. The classic Bond villain, Renard, an ex-KGB agent who became a terrorist, was played by Robert Carlyle. "What do the James Bond series, the Chicago Cubs, and Master P's No Limit empire have in common? All owe their considerable commercial success more to loyalty, marketing, and tradition than to quality," wrote Nathan Rabin for the AV Club. 22. "Die Another Day" (2002) "Die Another Day." MGM Distribution Co. Rotten Tomatoes score:   55% Brosnan's fourth and final appearance as Bond, 2002's "Die Another Day," saw him get overshadowed by Halle Berry. "Die Another Day" plays as a classic early 2000s film: heavy on the CGI and the product placement. But it's notable for its casting of Berry as Jinx Johnson, an NSA agent, whose entrance in an orange bikini remains iconic over 20 years later. "Die Another Day" was also the first Bond movie in 39 years to not feature Desmond Llewelyn's Q as the head of the British Secret Service's fictional research and development division — in other words, he provided Bond with all of his nifty gadgets. Llewelyn died in 1999, just a few weeks after the premiere of "The World Is Not Enough." He was replaced as Q by John Cleese for "Die Another Day," which would end up being Cleese's only appearance as the character. "In a year when 'Austin Powers' has scoffed at 007 as a jo
