events.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
events.summary: Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery. The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance. Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom. Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch. HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS. Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time. While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability . The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings. Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come. While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes". Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger , Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years. For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year. That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas. The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year. If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein. Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date. "Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said. "Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift". Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema. As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas. Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year. Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground. Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods. Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken". "It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts." A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years. The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022. Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities". She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network." Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts. "Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added. CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount. The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

events.title: Kalshi launches transparency features on its election contracts ahead of midterms
events.summary: Kalshi is launching three features on its election contracts to provide traders with more transparency on how active its markets are. Kalshi's election markets will have a Brier score, which will measure the accuracy of its market's probabilities versus actual outcomes. The platform is also launching an activity feeds feature, where it shows individual trades happening on election contracts live. Kalshi decided to provide these additional features after noting election traders were participating on markets covering local races over national ones. With less than a month until midterms, Kalshi is launching three features on its election contracts to ensure traders have more transparency on how active and accurate its markets are. First, the platform will provide tags that indicate which election markets are low volume, which Kalshi defines as those with less than $10,000. Prediction markets experts have warned prices in low-volume markets can fluctuate widely, while spreads between buying and selling can stretch. Second, Kalshi's own election markets will have Brier scores, which will measure the accuracy of the market's probabilities versus actual outcomes. Finally, the platform is launching an activity feeds feature, where it shows individual trades happening on election contracts live. Kalshi decided to provide these transparency features after noting election traders were participating on markets covering local races over national ones. Kalshi's co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour called the midterms the "first meaningful prediction market election," noting the platform's election markets have grown six times faster than football markets this year, compared to the year before. Kalshi's internal data also indicates that more people are viewing their midterm markets than those who are trading by a ratio of five to one. In July, the prediction markets platform released a "Midterms Hub," which allows anyone to view traders' odds on markets tied to U.S. Senate and House of Representatives races. events.title: The 10 safest states in the US — and the 10 least safe
events.summary: Maine ranked as one of the safest US states to live in. : Dukas/Universal Images Group via Getty Images WalletHub released a report ranking the safest states in the US. States were ranked based on 52 safety indicators, including work safety and emergency preparedness. Vermont and Massachusetts scored the highest. Mississippi and Louisiana scored the lowest. Safe to say , safety comes in many forms beyond crime. The ability to prepare well for an emergency situation is a form of security, as is the number of emergency responders available nearby. One's financial well-being amid fear of job loss and inflation is also relative to one's sense of safety. A report released by the personal finance website WalletHub on Monday evaluated all 50 US states, ranking them from the most to least safe. For each state, WalletHub examined 52 indicators across five categories: personal and residential safety, financial safety, road safety, workplace safety, and emergency preparedness. The personal and residential safety category included factors such as crime rates, emergency responders per capita, and neighborhood watch groups per capita. To evaluate financial safety , WalletHub looked at factors such as unemployment rates, median credit scores, identity-theft complaints per capita, and poverty rates. The road safety ranking was determined by each state's rates of traffic fatalities and DUIs, road quality, and share of uninsured drivers, among other factors. WalletHub's workplace safety ranking included examining the number of fatal occupational injuries per 100,000 full-time workers and the presence of Occupational Safety and Health Act plans. Finally, the emergency preparedness ranking looked at states' histories of climate disasters. WalletHub used data from sources such as the US Census Bureau, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Department of Labor, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the Crime Victims Center, among others. Here are the 10 safest states in the US, and the 10 least safe states. 1. Vermont Montpelier, Vermont. Erika Mitchell/Getty Images WalletHub ranked Vermont as the safest state in the US. Vermont's unemployment rate is 2.7% — one of the lowest in the country — which helped it place fourth in the financial safety ranking. It's also the state with the second-fewest reported identity theft complaints per capita. The state's road safety ranking was the third-highest in the US, with the second-best road quality and the fifth-fewest traffic fatalities of any state. Its workplace safety ranking also made the top 10, placing sixth overall. Vermont placed 16th in the personal and residential safety ranking and 11th in emergency preparedness. 2. Massachusetts Boston, Massachusetts. Thomas Roell/Getty Images As the second-safest state in the US, Massachusetts ranked in the top 10 of nearly every category of WalletHub's analysis. The state placed second in the personal and residential safety ranking, with low crime rates, including the eighth-fewest thefts and fourth-fewest murders of any state, according to the WalletHub report. Massachusetts also placed second in WalletHub's road safety ranking, eighth in financial safety, and ninth in emergency preparedness. Its workplace safety ranking was the lowest, coming in at 23rd overall. 3. Maine Portland, Maine. Sean Pavone/Getty Images Maine's low crime rate propelled it into the top three safest states in the US. With the fewest mass shootings between 2024 and September 2026, the third-fewest murders per capita, and the fewest aggravated assaults per capita, it ranked fourth in personal and residential safety. Maine ranked 16th in financial safety with an unemployment rate of 3.4% and the 12th-lowest poverty rate in the US. It ranked 8th in road safety, 21st in workplace safety, and second in emergency preparedness. 4. New Hampshire Portsmouth, New Hampshire. travelview/Getty Images New Hampshire was ranked the fourth-safest state in the US, but it had the highest financial safety ranking of any state. It placed third in personal and residential safety and fourth in emergency preparedness. New Hampshire's road safety and workplace safety rankings were lower, at 12th and 41st, respectively. 5. Connecticut Hartford, Connecticut. SeanPavonePhoto/Getty Images/iStockphoto Connecticut's personal and residential safety ranking was the highest of any state. It placed 21st in both the financial safety and the road safety rankings, 25th in workplace safety, and 15th in emergency preparedness. 6. Utah Salt Lake City, Utah. Sean Pavone/Getty Images Utah was ranked No. 1 in road safety, No. 3 in emergency preparedness, and No. 4 in workplace safety. It placed 26th in financial safety and 35th in personal and residential safety. 7. Minnesota Minneapolis, Minnesota. Sean Pavone/Getty Images Minnesota's workplace safety ranked second, road safety ranked sixth, and financial safety ranked seventh. The state's personal and residential safety and emergency preparedness both ranked 23rd. 8. Indiana Indianapolis, Indiana. Nicholas Klein/Getty Images WalletHub ranked Indiana 7th in personal and residential safety, 25th in financial safety, 11th in road safety, 10th in workplace safety, and 28th in emergency preparedness. 9. Rhode Island Providence, Rhode Island. tupungato/Getty Images/iStockphoto In Rhode Island, the state's personal and residential safety and emergency preparedness were both ranked eighth-best in the US. It placed 20th in financial safety, 16th in road safety, and 39th in workplace safety. 10. Hawaii Honolulu, Hawaii. rebelml/Getty Images/iStockphoto Hawaii rounded out WalletHub's list of the top 10 safest states in the US, placing 10th. Hawaii performed well in financial safety, with the second-highest ranking of any state. Personal and residential safety ranked 20th, road safety 26th, workplace safety 22nd, and emergency preparedness 13th. Keep reading for the bottom 10 states, which were ranked the least safe in the US. 41. Georgia Atlanta, Georgia. Alex Slitz - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images Georgia ranked 34th and 35th in personal and residential safety and road safety, respectively. It placed 47th in financial safety and has the second-highest share of uninsured people. 42. Alabama Birmingham, Alabama. : Joe Sohm/Visions of America/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Alabama ranked 36th in personal and residential safety, 34th in financial safety, and 31st in road safety. It ranked 40th in emergency preparedness. The state tied in the lowest unemployment rate with Vermont, North Dakota, Hawaii, and South Dakota. 43. Colorado Denver, Colorado. Justin Edmonds/Getty Images In Colorado, personal and residential safety ranked 46th among US states. The state placed 19th in financial safety, 41st in road safety, and 38th in workplace safety. events.title: The internet is having a field day with Amazon's 'About You' customer dossiers. Here's how to see yours.
events.summary: Amazon wants to connect you to the right product. Some customers shared screenshots of the tool saying they have skinny legs and flat butts. Getty Images Amazon's "About You" feature offers observations about your purchases and conversations with Alexa for Shopping. It can be a little snarky, shoppers said. One posted a screenshot showing the AI thinks she "has flat buttocks." Here's how you can find out what Amazon thinks about you — tell us what you find in the comments below! Amazon wants to use AI to match shoppers to the right products. Some users say their tool is doing a great job cosplaying a judgmental aunt. The e-commerce giant launched its "About You" feature — basically a customer dossier — earlier this year, pitching it as an editable list of preferences that Amazon has inferred to help shoppers navigate its vast marketplace. With a few clicks, shoppers can pull up Amazon's profile of them, see the conclusions it has drawn, and correct or remove details they don't want shaping their recommendations. The tool has renewed attention on social media, particularly on Threads, where it's now trending. Amazon users say its observations have been enlightening — if not a touch snide. "I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me," one shopper wrote, while including a screenshot of Amazon's About You apparently saying she "has flat buttocks." "I'm literally speechless," they said. View on Threads Another customer said that Amazon determined she "has a husband" — and that the "husband has skinny legs." A third said the page had identified a rather specific habit: "Uses phone in the shower to read Kindle books." "I mean yes but wtf," the shopper wrote. View on Threads Amazon introduced About You in May as part of a broader AI shopping push . The company says the recommendations come from customers' purchase histories, searches, saved lists, product reviews, and conversations with Amazon's Alexa for Shopping assistant. Amazon has offered personalized shopping recommendations for years. About You is different because it gives customers an unusually direct view of the profile behind those suggestions — and, in some cases, an invitation to discover what Amazon thinks their purchases and Alexa conversations say about them. Those sometimes sharp remarks — and the order of their importance — seem particularly illuminating to some social media users. "Has cats," one shopper said the bot observed, then "treats cats as biological children." And then, finally, "has husband." Another person on Threads posted a screenshot of the tool saying she "does not trust people easily" under a list of "Interests & Hobbies." View on Threads Meanwhile, on Reddit , a shopper said the system recognized that they do "not know what truffle is supposed to taste like." How to see your Amazon 'About You' profile The feature is available in Amazon's Shopping app, on mobile web, and on desktop. In the app, you can find what Amazon thinks about you by tapping the following: Account Shopping preferences About You Shoppers can view and edit personal details that shape their recommendations by tapping on each observation. Several Business Insider reporters spent Tuesday morning checking their own profiles. The results were mixed: One account incorrectly identified an editor's partner's name while correctly clocking their slow-but-steady kitchen-appliance upgrade. Another reporter said Amazon groked her preference for organic produce. What does your Amazon "About You" say? Drop the observations in this story's comments section, and we might include them in a future story! Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Hark releases an AI personal assistant with a focus on privacy
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. From Muse to Instinct to Dots, tech firms are hunting for the user experience that will make an AI personal assistant a must-have product. Hark , a startup founded less than a year ago by serial founder Brett Adcock, is throwing its hat in the ring today with the wide release of Hark Pro. Users can access the service for free, with a subscription tier for heavy users. The company sees its mission as building a user interface for AI, not creating AGI or curing cancer. The foundation is a model trained specifically for computer use, and that’s what Hark Pro does — it uses your computer for you. That’s perhaps a less ambitious claim than some frontier labs are making, but a little humility goes a long way in winning over users. And rather than an app, Hark’s goal is to create an operating system for the AI computers of our future. Hark Pro is a full-screen experience with a kind of homepage, featuring a central chat dialog and a feed populated by prompts for actions you might need it to take and visualizations the company calls “panels” that offer mini-dashboards for things you’re interested in. The background is a piece of custom imagery tailored to the weather and time where you are. Like other AI assistants, users configure it to access their digital life — email, calendar, hard drive, credit cards, etc. Then, it can take on digital tasks as well as fielding classic chatbot questions. Abidur Chowdhury, a former Apple staffer who leads design at Hark, demoed the product for me. It proactively asked him about expenses he needed to approve, emails he needed to respond to, a meeting with this reporter, and, of course, pointed out that he needed to book a flight for a trip and offered to take care of it. (“I know the flight thing is put to death,” he admits, grinning.) That does get at the challenge with these apps: One of the harder things for users is actually coming up with useful tasks they are capable of accomplishing. Chowdhury says he was impressed when the AI assistant recently recognized that one of his colleagues needed to renew their car registration at the California DMV, and handled it through the agency’s website. One notable UX choice that Hark makes is showing the user how the agent navigates the web in a small window, an action most AI assistants perform without it surfacing in the app, which Chowdhury says is intended to build trust with users that the agent is doing the right thing. That matters because part of Hark’s pitch is that they are not Meta or OpenAI — “we’re not here to like sell you ads and steal your data,” Chowdhury says. To truly leverage these models, users will need to share their entire digital lives. Beyond very real cybersecurity concerns , will users be comfortable with a company like Meta having its products create detailed profiles of their friends and family? Asked about that kind of profiling, Chowdhury says that “we are doing work to understand you, and be helpful for what you need, but it’s really like task-related — it’s really about how Hark can help take something off your plate and be useful.” What sets Hark Pro apart from its competitors, Chowdhury says, is its effort to fully subsitute for your computer, but also his belief that it just works better. “Please compare it to the others, be critical,” he says. “It might not be faster than Muse, but it will give you a better result, and it will work end-to-end instead of asking you to take over at a point.” One open question is what kind of model best suits the AI personal assistant. Hark’s is explicitly trained for computer use, which makes it faster and cheaper at those tasks, but it’s not clear how much it is trading away the broader knowledge and capability of a frontier LLM. This software is only half the promise of Hark; Chowdhury made his name designing devices at Apple and Hark promises to release an AI-native device to support its software in 2027. They’re still cagey about the form it will take, with Chowdhury bemoaning the “creep factor” of wearable cameras. “I will give you this: The first product that we’re building is a product that’s never ever existed before,” he says. We’ll have to wait and see if this is mere hype and Hark puts out some retread tech instead of a truly novel product. “It’s so hilarious to me that you have AI now, you have a chatbot, and you type stuff in with a keyboard,” Chowdhury says. “Fifty years later and the future of computing is still a terminal.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: DOJ moves to strip citizenship from 40 people
events.summary: President Trump's Justice Department moved to revoke citizenship from 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in recent months, representing what Attorney General Todd Blanche called the "largest denaturalization effort in modern history." The big picture: The Trump administration has made denaturalization a priority, moving personnel to pursue more cases and setting a goal of 250 cases by this month. Driving the news: The DOJ filed 40 denaturalization actions in district courts spanning coast to coast between Aug. 21 and Oct. 2, according to a Monday statement . "Every single one of these individuals lied their way into U.S. citizenship," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said in a statement. Context: Denaturalization cases have a high burden of proof, and to revoke someone's citizenship, the DOJ must file a revocation action in federal district court. The general grounds for revocation, per U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, are illegal procurement of naturalized citizenship or lying to get it. "For civil revocation of naturalization, the burden of proof is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence which does not leave the issue in doubt," per USCIS. Zoom in: Individuals named in Monday's statement had been convicted of or pleaded guilty to an array of offenses, including conspiracy to commit money laundering, sexual abuse of a minor and aggravated sodomy. What we're watching: The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for specifics on how many actions had been filed since the start of the second Trump administration. In April, the New York Times reported that the DOJ had identified 384 foreign-born Americans whose citizenship the department wanted to revoke. The following month, Axios' Brittany Gibson reported that USCIS lawyers had been temporarily moved to U.S. attorneys' offices to work on denaturalization cases. events.title: Leaked audio: What David Ellison told employees at the first Skydance town hall
events.summary: Media mogul David Ellison has completed Paramount's acquisition of WBD. Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images David Ellison addressed Skydance employees for the first time at a companywide town hall. The Paramount-WBD merger closed on Tuesday. "This is an incredibly exciting day," Ellison told staffers. Skydance CEO David Ellison welcomed Warner Bros. Discovery employees and thanked Paramount staffers for their patience at the combined company's first-ever town hall. "This is an incredibly exciting day," Ellison said at an employee-only meeting, according to an audio recording obtained by Business Insider. "I want to start with the most important thing I can say to all of you: Thank you." Ellison addressed workers at 1 p.m. ET, hours after sending a companywide memo announcing that the $110 billion Paramount-WBD merger had closed . Bruno Mars' hit song "I Just Might" played in the moments before Ellison took the stage. "It is humbling to be in this room," Ellison said at the start of his remarks. He then reflected on Paramount's long journey toward buying WBD, saying it "caps off a long-term plan that is three years in the making." "Let me be honest: It was not easy to get here. At times, it was downright ugly," Ellison said, before adding that he'd "do it all over again in a heartbeat." The Skydance CEO, along with co-CEO Ynon Kreiz , unveiled the company's four top priorities in a Tuesday memo: win in storytelling, become the most technologically capable media company , lead in a crowded market, and earn trust every day. Skydance has a wide array of media assets, including the Warner Bros. studio and Paramount Pictures; streamers HBO Max, Paramount+, Pluto TV, and Discovery+; and TV channels CBS, CNN, HBO, HGTV, TLC, and Discovery Channel. "For the first time, we have the studios, the franchises, the libraries, the talent and scale all under one roof to compete with anyone in the world," Ellison said. "It is incredibly exciting." The combined company has the scale and firepower to "go toe to toe with the biggest competitors," Ellison said, though he emphasized that size isn't everything. "We didn't do this deal simply to get bigger," Ellison said. He added that "we're going to invest aggressively in great storytelling." Skydance will take on Hollywood powerhouses like Disney and Netflix, as well as tech giants like Amazon and Google's YouTube. "We're not just competing with traditional media companies anymore," Ellison said. "We're competing for people's time and attention with some of the largest and most sophisticated technology companies in the world, companies with enormous scale, global reach, and virtually unlimited resources." Ellison said that Skydance is "going to embrace technology — not just as a buzzword or as a side project, but as a fundamental capability of this company." Kreiz is tasked with managing the merger integration and running day-to-day operations, while Ellison will form Skydance's creative and tech strategies. "We are not here to preserve the status quo. We are here to build for what comes next," Ellison said of himself and Kreiz. Before the merger, Paramount and WBD staffers said they were uneasy about cross-company competition  as the two media powers joined forces, a move Ellison has told investors will lead to $6 billion in cost cuts. The company has said that layoffs won't be the source of most of the savings. "Bringing together two companies of this size and complexity will require difficult decisions," Ellison said. "There will be changes, and there will be impacts. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I can promise you is that we will move through those decisions as quickly and thoughtfully as we can." CNN star Anderson Cooper later joined Ellison onstage and said that there was "a lot of concern and fear" about potential changes at the news giant, even though top executive Mark Thompson is staying on. The Skydance CEO responded by promising not to interfere in CNN's coverage and to focus on journalism. Ellison's company had a long, winding path to buying WBD. Paramount initiated a rival bid for WBD , which had previously signed a deal with Netflix. After winning the bidding war for WBD, Paramount was sued by 12 states as well as the Writers Guild of America, before settling those lawsuits and pledging to boost its domestic production, among other concessions. During his remarks, Ellison shouted out Makan Delrahim, the company's legal chief, who had served in the Department of Justice during President Donald Trump's first term. "None of us would be here if it was not for Makan," Ellison said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I've been to Italy 16 times. There's one city I always recommend to first-time visitors.
events.summary: After visiting Italy 16 times, Bologna is the city that stands out to me the most. emicristea/iStock I've traveled to Italy 16 times, but my favorite city in the whole country is Bologna. Not only does it have incredible food, but it's also full of stunning architecture. Plus, Bologna is just a short train ride away from Milan, Venice, and Florence. I've been to Italy 16 times, and if you give me an opening, I can work it into just about any conversation. But surprisingly, it wasn't Venice, Rome, or the Amalfi Coast that made me fall head over heels for the country. It was Bologna, the capital of northern Italy's Emilia-Romagna region. Bologna has it all — food, wine, art, history, architecture, and the kind of energy that makes you seriously consider missing your flight home. Sure, seeing the Colosseum is cool, but I prefer eating perfectly made tortellini with a glass of pignoletto in Bologna. Here's why I always recommend tourists add Bologna to their itinerary, even if they can only spare one glorious, carb-loaded night. Bologna's food is truly unlike anything else I've ever had. Emily Cappiello Every Italian I know tells me their region's cuisine is the best, but I'm here to tell you that Bologna is home to the best food I've had. I fell hard for the mortadella, the tortellini, and the Bolognese, and I've spent practically every trip to Italy since chasing those foods. One of my favorite things I did in the city was wander through the Quadrilatero, the city's historic market district, where butcher shops, cheese merchants, and specialty food stores practically demand that you stop every few feet. When I was there, I grabbed a mortadella sandwich and a glass of Lambrusco, then sat in one of the stunning cobblestone alleyways to people-watch. The region is also well known for producing Parmigiano Reggiano , which always seems to taste freshest here. For a traditional Emilian dinner, I always recommend A Balùs. The Bolognese was the best pasta dish I've ever had in all of Italy, and the sardines served on bread with butter literally melted in my mouth. The city's got history, too. wjarek/iStock Bologna isn't just a city where you eat extraordinarily well. It's also a place where visitors can stumble into hundreds of years of history while walking off lunch. One place that particularly moved me was the Archiginnasio Municipal Library, which houses rare books , centuries-old manuscripts, and other special collections. Although, in my opinion, it might not be as visually impressive as the Trinity Library in Dublin, knowing that some of these manuscripts date back more than a thousand years made this place feel pretty extraordinary to me. It's a university city, but it doesn't feel like a typical college town. Artem Bolshakov/iStock One of the city's highlights is the University of Bologna, which dates back to 1088 and is widely recognized as the oldest university in the Western world. But Bologna isn't a typical college town where the bars are packed with rowdy students and every night feels like a fraternity party. Instead, the city has a much more sophisticated energy. I saw students mingling with professors, artists, young professionals, and longtime residents, creating this incredible mix of old-world Italy and youthful enthusiasm. I also loved visiting the Piazza Verdi, a square filled with students catching up with friends after class. I still can't get over how stunning the architecture in Bologna is. Joaquin Ossorio-Castillo/iStock One of the unique things about Bologna's design is its porticoes. I love these eye-catching archways that line the streets, many of which date back to the 12th century. In fact, Bologna has about 38 miles of porticoes, with the most famous being the Portico di San Luca, a pathway that extends for about 2 miles and has more than 600 arches. Bologna is ridiculously easy to visit, even if you only have one night. Emily Cappiello I always recommend Bologna to travelers because they don't have to sacrifice seeing other parts of Italy to go there, since the city is one of the country's main railway hubs. By train, Florence is only 30 minutes away, Milan is about an hour away, and Venice is just about 90 minutes away. Overall, I think Bologna is one of Italy's greatest culinary and cultural destinations, and I couldn't recommend it enough. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Young voters struggle to afford housing. But they don't expect help from political candidates
events.summary: Pennsylvania has lower housing costs than the national average, but voters are still feeling the squeeze of rising mortgage and rent payments. A new CNBC and SurveyMonkey survey found that one in five Americans who rent or have a mortgage spends at least half of their pre-tax income on housing. The Nov. 3 midterm election will be held against the backdrop of average 30-year fixed mortgage rates topping 7.5%. ALLENTOWN, Pa. — Mortgage rates are climbing sharply , home prices continue to gain and inflation in the broader economy is hitting consumers, leading housing affordability to weigh heavily on both renters and potential homebuyers. In Pennsylvania — a swing state where House races could help decide control of the next U.S. Congress — renting or owning a home is cheaper than the national average, but the share of income needed to do either has also risen along with the rest of the country. In 2019, it took 20% of the median income to rent a home and 18% to own. Today it's 22% and 24%, respectively, according to Cotality. "For that person trying to get an apartment, person moving from an apartment to a starter home, starter home to a larger home, each and every one of those cohorts is reporting that it's a challenge right now, and it's something that is weighing on them in a very important political place," Lehigh University political science professor Christopher Borick said. Americans, especially renters, feel financially stretched by housing costs, according to a new CNBC and SurveyMonkey Quarterly Money Survey , released Oct. 5. It found one in five Americans who rent or have a mortgage spend at least half of their pre-tax income on housing, while 49% spend between 25% and 49%. Standard guidelines from banks and lenders say consumers should spend 28% to 30% of their income on housing. The cost of housing is now the top political issue — even higher than the cost of food or protecting democracy — among U.S. voters aged 18 to 34, according to the most recent CNBC All-America Economic survey . Going into the midterm election , the average rate on the popular 30-year fixed mortgage has jumped well over 7.5%, according to Mortgage News Daily. It hit a low of 5.99% days before the war with Iran started. For buyers of a median-priced home of around $450,000, that means an increase of roughly $300 in the monthly payment since earlier this year. Home prices, while cooling from their big gains in the first years of the Covid pandemic, were still up 1.8% in August year over year, according to the latest read from Cotality. Home prices are up close to 60% since the start of the pandemic. Combined with sharply higher mortgage rates, potential buyers are increasingly sidelined. Sales of existing homes in August were down from the year before, coming in at an annualized rate below 4 million. "This figure of 4 million is about as low as we can go. It tells you there is an extreme affordability problem," said Norm Miller, a real estate economist and professor emeritus at the University of San Diego's Knauss School of Business. The share of median income needed to rent or buy a home has increased nationwide, with homeownership seeing the biggest leap. In 2019, it took a national average of 24% of the median income to rent and 21% to own, according to Cotality. Today, it takes 26% of the median income to rent and 28% to own. For some markets, especially metropolitan areas on both coasts, those numbers are significantly higher. A separate report from Apartment List finds 52% of the nation's renters are cost-burdened, meaning they spend more than 30% of their income on housing. This spiked dramatically from 2019 to 2022, as rent prices rose sharply in the first years of the pandemic. More than 22 million households in the U.S. are rent-burdened, a new record. The Lehigh Valley, Pennsylvania's 7 th Congressional District, where 19% of residents are young, is one of several toss-up races in the state. It ranks 8 th nationally among House races where young voters could most influence the midterm elections, according to Tufts University's CIRCLE Youth Electoral Significance Index . In that district, a household needs $67,481 per year to afford a typical two-bedroom rental without spending more than 30% of income on housing. The corresponding "housing wage" is $32.44 an hour, according to the most recent National Low Income Housing Coalition's congressional-district profile. "We've seen a change in the landscape in terms of the cost of housing, access to rental markets, that has really leveraged some of the other broader concerns that we've seen in the area of affordability in a pretty potent way," Borick said. "So when you talk to voters and residents in the area, and you ask them about the things that are driving their concerns right now, housing is always really close to the top of the list.

events.title: Morrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s
events.summary: Odds are good the CMA would approve of a supermarket merger. But does Sainsbury’s need Morrisons? W ould competition regulators really smile upon a combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons? One must assume the two companies believed the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would give a thumbs up if asked, otherwise they would not have initiated their now-aborted merger talks . It’s easy to list the arguments the duo could make. First, the combined market share of Sainsbury’s (15.2%, on the latest numbers from Worldpanel analysts) and Morrisons (8.4%) would still be less than that of mighty Tesco (27.8%). It would not be a case of leap-frogging the market leader, which was Sainsbury’s big idea back in 2018 when Asda was in its sights . Second, Aldi and Lidl are a stronger force in the land. Together, the German discounters represent almost a fifth of the UK market and, since they’re backed by serious international buying muscle, their role as the country’s grocery price police might not be affected one jot. Third, since Morrisons has already sold its petrol stations, the CMA needn’t worry about the touchy issue of fuel. Fourth, at a push, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons could argue that the UK’s food security ( a growing political worry ) would improve if the latter’s 18 food-processing factories were housed within a stronger company that could boost local production. So, yes, one would probably bet that the CMA would ultimately approve some version of a deal. But what version? How many store disposals would be demanded? The CMA, as in 2018, would presumably conduct a site-by-site analysis of drive-times to judge local competition. The regulatory instinct, one suspects, would be to err on the side of intervention in light of the overall national picture. Never mind Tesco’s size, it would still not be a simple decision for a competition regulator to sanction a supermarket setup in which half the trade, or thereabouts, would be in the hands of just two companies. Would a deal still make sense after the CMA’s remedies? It’s impossible for Sainsbury’s and Morrisons to know until they go through the process. That’s the distraction factor for Sainsbury’s. Does its chief executive, Simon Roberts, really want to spend a year bogged down in regulatory back-and-forth? In the Asda episode, the effort sucked the life out of his predecessor’s reign. It’s not as if Sainsbury’s is struggling today. The group is winning market share, profit margins are stable, there’s enough spare cash for share buy-backs and the strategic headaches of its bank and Argos have been solved by selling both . While it would be preferable to square up to Tesco’s buyers on more equal terms, life ain’t bad. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Round at private equity-owned Morrisons, the calculation will be different. Five years after buying the chain for £7bn , owners Clayton, Dubilier & Rice’s thoughts will be turning to how to exit a tricky investment. A disposal will surely look easier than a stock market flotation and the list of potential suitors is short: Sainsbury’s is indeed the obvious candidate. All of which says Sainsbury’s can afford to do nothing, or wait for the terms of any deal to improve. It was the party that walked away from the talks, reported the FT. That’s not a surprise. If a relative bargain is possible, the hassle of a CMA process might be worthwhile. But this is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s.

events.title: Anthropic expands Claude Startups program in bid to snag founders and fast-growing companies
events.summary: Anthropic announced it's expanding its Claude Startups program, which gives members access to thousands of dollars' worth of Anthropic's Claude products and credits. The expansion marks the AI company's latest push to deepen its ties to founders and fast-growing companies. Anthropic said startups that were founded within the past five years or funded within the past two years are able to apply. Anthropic on Tuesday announced it's expanding its Claude Startups program, the artificial intelligence lab's latest push to deepen its ties to founders and fast-growing companies. Claude Startups initially launched in May, and thousands of companies are already participating, according to Anthropic. The company is opening up the program to more organizations, and members will get access to thousands of dollars' worth of Anthropic's Claude products and credits to help them build. "Startups are often the first to push Claude to its limits," Beth Robertson, head of startups at Anthropic, told CNBC in a statement. "When a new model ships, they're ready that same day to take on projects that used to seem out of reach. Claude Startups gives founders credits, tools and direct time with our team, so more companies can build this way from the start." The vast majority of Anthropic's revenue comes from its business customers , and it has spent much of the last year trying to fend off rivals like OpenAI and Google , which both offer their own programs for startups. As it gears up for what is widely expected to be a blockbuster initial public offering, Anthropic is working to ensure that the next generation of businesses will be built using its products. Claude Startup members can receive up to $45,000 worth of discounts and credits through the Claude Startup Stack, which Anthropic described as a "set of benefits for the tools a startup runs on." Additionally, eligible organizations can access a one-time $1,000 application programming interface, or API, credit, as well as a free year of Claude Team for up to five premium seats. Anthropic said members can also meet with the company's applied AI team through virtual office hours and connect with other members of the Claude Startup community at events. Startups that were founded within the past five years or funded within the past two years are able to apply, Anthropic said. events.title: Alito plans to stay on Supreme Court, even if Democrats regain Senate: Report
events.summary: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito plans to remain on the court through at least next summer, even if Democrats regain majority control in the Senate from Republicans in November's midterm election, he says in a new report. Bloomberg reported Tuesday that Alito, 76, has ruled out retiring during the brief lame-duck session of Congress after the election, when Republicans would still hold their Senate majority through early January even if they lose control for the next Congress. If Democrats are the majority in the next session of Congress, they may block any Supreme Court nominee of President Donald Trump, a Republican. Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito plans to remain on the court through at least next summer, even if Democrats regain majority control in the Senate from Republicans in November's midterm election , he said in a new report. If Democrats are the majority in the next Congress, they may block any Supreme Court nominee of President Donald Trump , a Republican. "I intend to stick around through this term," Alito told Bloomberg, referring to the court's current term, which began Monday and which will end in late June or early July. Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' "I made that decision many months ago," said Alito, whose first book, "So Ordered: An Originalist's View of the Constitution, the Court and Our Country," has just been published. Alito was nominated to the Supreme Court in 2005 by then-President George W. Bush, another Republican. Alito is one of six conservative justices on the nine-member court. Three of the other conservatives — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — were nominated by Trump. Bloomberg reported that Alito, in the interview, acknowledged that the idea of retiring had crossed his mind. But he also said, "I don't feel mentally or physically decrepit," according to the news outlet. In a recent interview with CBS News , Alito said he considered retiring this year. "It's something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term," he told CBS. Democrats in the Senate are still stung by then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell blocking the Senate from considering the nomination by then-President Barack Obama of Merrick Garland for the Supreme Court in 2016. That block, which McConnell claimed was because there was not enough time to consider the nomination that was made in March, opened the way for Trump to appoint Gorsuch after he became president. McConnell, R-Ky., after the death of liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg in September 2020 also orchestrated the swift confirmation of Coney Barrett shortly before the presidential election that year, which ended with Trump's defeat and led to President Joe Biden, a Democrat, taking office in early 2021.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Oh lawd it is coming ... to Hugging Face later this month AMD bets $8.2B that worlds matter more than words in AI 8 days ago French dev aims to solve bots' blindness so they can understand GUIs 8 days ago Dutch government turns to NixOS for a sovereign desktop 8 days ago DeepSeek's new model sets a template for powerful LLMs that run lean 25 days ago The search company that plants trees just launched a Linux browser to help Europe battle big tech September 4, 2026 Another week brings yet another open weights model and this one is huge — or at least it is for Europe's AI flag bearer Mistral, which has taken to calling the 1 trillion-parameter large language model (LLM) Le Chonk. Its product name is Mistral Large 4 , which is a lot less fun than the cat-meme-inspired "very official" moniker Le Chonk. Nonetheless, the LLM is the French model-dev's biggest open weights release ever. At a trillion parameters, Le Chonk is squarely in frontier territory, and like most modern frontier models, it is multimodal, reasoning, and employs a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture with about 49 billion active parameters to keep serving costs low. Mistral didn't offer any guidance on hardware requirements in its release blog, but the model is still small enough to run reasonably on 8-way GPU boxes like Nvidia's HGX B300 or AMD's MI355X. We know far more about the hardware the model was trained on. According to Mistral, this Chonker was trained using roughly 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs — or around 52 NVL72 racks — in Mistral's own datacenters located in Europe on a corpus spanning more than 160 languages using a combination of supervised pre-training and reinforcement learning. Sovereign AI remains a major focus for Europe and Mistral is clearly cashing in on demand for frontier class models trained and run within Europe's borders. The model itself is currently in preview, but you won't have to wait long for its weights to drop. Mistral expects them to be live on Hugging Face and other model repos within the month. Early testing by independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis puts Le Chonk at a major disadvantage relative to OpenAI or Anthropic's flagship models. In the AI guru's intelligence leaderboard, Mistral Large 4 preview sits between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and OpenAI's entry-level GPT6 Luna models. Having said that, Mistral's latest model outshines the United States' most capable open weights model, Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling , by a significant margin. So when it comes to non-Chinese LLMs you can actually download, Mistral does quite well. As you'd expect, Mistral's own benchmarks tell a far rosier story. Across coding, agentic, finance, and legal benchmarks, the model build shows its latest LLM trading blows with some of the top Chinese offerings from Alibaba, Moonshot, Z.AI, and DeepSeek. You can find their charts here , but as always take them with a grain of salt. One area Mistral is particularly proud of is Le Chonk's performance in cybersecurity workloads. The company claims the model is one of the strongest performers in cybersecurity benchmarks like Artificial Analysis' new Cyber inde x. This is a dig at proprietary American models from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which have a tendency to refuse cybersecurity-related tasks that could be perceived as adversarial. As we previously reported , this is potentially problematic for customers trying to use AI models to red-team their own systems in order to identify vulnerabilities before someone else finds them. "Provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies," Mistral wrote in a blog post .

events.title: Google told to halt work on datacentres in Finland over environmental concerns
events.summary: Order on two construction sites comes after Google failed to carry out environmental impact assessments Google has been ordered to temporarily stop work on two datacentres in Finland after failing to do the necessary environmental impact assessments on its construction sites. The planned datacentres in Muhos and Kajanni are part of a €13bn (£11bn) project across multiple sites in northern Finland by the technology company amid huge demand for space to house online infrastructure. It comes after it emerged that Tuike Finland Oy, the company representing Google , had felled 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest in Muhos without completing an environmental impact assessment (EIA). In Kajaani, the company has reportedly been logging across just under 200 hectares (494 acres) of land. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation said the sites had been reduced to “sand”, blaming the oversights on the “overheated” market for new datacentres. On Tuesday, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) said it had issued a notice to the company to “immediately suspend” – by 23 October at the latest – “preparatory measures that significantly change the environment” of the two sites until the environmental impact assessment had been completed. Google has until next Wednesday to submit a written explanation. The EIA is ongoing and expected to be completed later this year. But Google has gone ahead with “extensive preparatory measures”, including removing trees, stripping topsoil and constructing site roads, LVV said. Tommi Muilu, the head of the environmental department at LVV, said: “In our opinion, the measures in question will change the environment and cause impacts, the identification and assessment of which are among the key objectives of the EIA procedure.” The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment If Google does not comply, LVV said it would consider enforcement proceedings and a fine. In response, Google said in a statement “we understand the concerns” and that it had “fallen short of our own high standards”. The company added: “We will study the LVV’s findings and follow their guidance. We acted in good faith under the Forestry Act, and ran nature surveys and put in place measures to protect high-value areas. As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares (321 acres) at Muhos.” Tapani Veistola, the chief operating officer at the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, said the malpractice across two sites appeared to be a “systemic problem”. The site at Muhos, he said, was “not a forest any more. It is a sand area.” One of the reasons behind it, he said, was the enormous demand to build datacentres in Finland, which is leading companies to work as fast as possible and overwhelming small municipalities. “The main reason behind everything is the overheated market situation that makes companies speed up processes so much. Also a lack of expertise in municipalities.”

events.title: China moves to register AI digital humans
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts China moves to register AI digital humans as sector attracts more than 1.3 million companies China has issued some of its first official credentials to AI digital humans. ( Douyin: Yuri ) A pilot program in Beijing is issuing identification cards for AI digital humans. The ID states a name, birthday, address and facial features, and allows the digital human to own a digital currency wallet. Digital humans are widely used in Chinese media with the market estimated to be worth $10 billion in 2025. Yuri was just one year old when thousands of fans gathered in Shanghai to watch her sing live. Appearing as a female adult on a 100-metre-wide screen in a concert hall on the Bund, she sang in Mandarin and English, and changed her outfits in an instant. Except Yuri is not a real human — she is an AI-generated virtual idol. Earlier this year she became the first Chinese digital human to receive a government-based official identification card that states her name, birthday, address and facial features. The official identity allows her operators to open a digital currency wallet for her business and secure commercial partnerships in industries including fashion, gaming and automotive. The pilot program in Beijing also made her the first licensed AI artist in the country. Yuri is the first digital human in China to receive digital artist certification. ( AFP: CFoto ) According to a 2025 report from the Communication University of China there are least 1.3 million firms in China linked to the digital human sector. Last month, Beijing issued a new practice guide for broadcasting and online video services, urging them to register their digital humans. It comes as multiple government agencies rolled out plans to regulate the avatars following President Xi Jinping's initiative to develop "new quality productive forces" and strengthen the country's self-reliance on AI. Supporters argue it would protect intellectual property and curb online scams, while critics say it strengthens state surveillance in the metaverse. More than one million firms are actively linked to the digital-human sector in China. ( Supplied: Johnsmith.ai ) Digital humans have been widely used in China's broadcasting, online streaming, micro dramas, e-commerce and propaganda. The market was estimated at 48 billion yuan ($10 billion) in 2025 and rapidly expanding. It started from people using digital avatars to conceal their identities in vertical videos or live streaming as a way to keep their opinion anonymous. With the development of machine learning, digital humans have evolved from script-reading anchors into AI-generated influencers who can interact with users in real time. Yuri, who has 100,000 fans on Little Red Book, or RedNote, has become one of China's most popular AI influencers and is considered a pioneer in generative AI-created virtual idols. A human team develops and maintains her system and manages her interactions with fans. In comparison, the voice or face of many other digital influencers are adopted from real humans, according to the Chinese Digital Human Influence Index Report. Yuri has 100,000 followers on Chinese social media. ( Supplied: Douyin, Bilibili ) AI digital humans have gained significant traction in China's lucrative live-streaming industry, because it offers 24/7 companionship at low cost. Beijing has also deployed its own virtual humans to convey political directives and deliver ideological and history education to Chinese Communist Party (CCP) members. Dozens of local government agencies are also rolling out their digital human officers to respond to public inquiries. Last year Beijing deployed two digital humans to discuss the annual Government Work Report — its annual policy statement. It marked the first time AI avatars had been used for the country's biggest political meetings. While the use of AI humans is growing, the industry has also drawn increasing scrutiny. State-owned media has reported that AI digital humans posing as doctors had been used in videos to promote false medical advice. Earlier this year an advertisement featuring an AI digital human influencer was taken down after netizens questioned how she could claim a pair of contact lenses were "comfortable". An advertisement for contact lenses featuring AI digital human Fang Taozi has sparked controversy in China. ( Weibo: Lan Jing Xin Wen ) Chinese celebrities have also had their faces and voices used without permission to create pornographic deepfakes and unauthorised online commercials.

events.title: Pacific's undersea treasure is worth billions, but some say we'll never see it
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Underwater explorers question viability of deep-sea mining gold rush Experts are concerned the economic case underpinning the deep-sea mining industry does not stack up. ( AFP ) Few people on Earth have seen a polymetallic nodule 4 kilometres under the ocean, but Rob McCallum is one of them. "They are anywhere between the size of a potato or a baseball and they are black," he said. Mr McCallum is a divemaster and founder of EYOS Expeditions, a firm that specialises in deep-sea diving operations. Rob McCallum has been to the bottom of the Mariana Trench and explored the wreckages of the Titanic and Bismark battleship. ( Supplied: Rob McCallum ) He has explored the depths of all five of the world's oceans, including the Mariana Trench, and has made trips to the wreck of the Titanic and the Bismarck. He has also descended into the Clarion–Clipperton Zone — a vast area of the Pacific that's been identified for prospective deep-sea mining projects. This area contains countless polymetallic nodules formed over millions of years. They contain valuable critical minerals including nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese, used to create batteries for phones and cars. Mr McCallum likens them to nuggets from Australia's gold-rush era. Mr McCallum likens polymetallic nodules to nuggets from Australia's gold rush era. ( AP ) Billions have been invested in exploration and research into deep-sea mining, as governments and companies position themselves to tap into a new source of critical minerals. United States President Donald Trump last year signed an executive order to accelerate seabed mining in US and international waters, arguing it could help secure supplies of critical minerals and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers, primarily China. In August, the US went a step further by announcing plans to sell deep-sea mining leases in US-controlled waters around the Marianas and American Samoa. Donald Trump was given a gold replica of a deep-sea nodule by the chairman of American Ocean Minerals. ( AFP ) Meanwhile, mining companies have forecast billions in potential profits, with royalties flowing to Pacific nations willing to open their waters to the emerging industry. But Mr McCallum, and other undersea experts like him, question the viability of the industry, fearing the only winners will be early investors and the companies selling the machinery needed to mine the ocean floor. Commercial deep-sea mining is not yet legal but the International Seabed Authority (ISA) is in the process of finalising a framework that would govern the environmental, financial and regulatory requirements of the industry. Under the draft regulations, companies would need to demonstrate they have the technical and financial capacity to carry out proposed mining operations. "You're operating at pressures that are hundreds of times greater than atmospheric pressure on the surface, so as you go deeper, subsea engineering gets more complicated and incredibly more expensive," Mr McCallum said. Seabed nodules are collected by robotic collector vehicles before being transported to the surface through a riser system. ( ABC ) The nodules have to be physically gathered from the ocean floor by robotic collector vehicles before being transported to the surface through a riser system like a massive vacuum hose. No commercial-scale system exists yet, although industry leader The Metals Company successfully tested a prototype system in 2022, lifting more than 3,000 wet tonnes of nodules — including moisture soaked into the porous material — to the surface. The company described the process as "a marriage of mining and offshore oil and gas technology". But that amount was only a fraction of the 1.5 million wet tonnes the company forecast as its initial annual production rate in a 2025 pre-feasibility study. A polymetallic nodule collector is lowered into the water from one of The Metals Company's ships. ( The Metals Company ) Victor Vescovo, an American investor and technology developer with a background in metals processing, believes the targets deep-sea mining companies are forecasting are unrealistic. "It's human psychology to see nodules lying on the sea floor and say, 'Wow. That's free money. We just need to pick it up,'" he said. Like Mr McCallum, Mr Vescovo is one of the few people on Earth to have operated machinery at extreme depths, having personally piloted submersibles to the deepest points of all five oceans. events.title: The Anthropic researcher whose resignation made waves last month says he was 'working to automate' himself
events.summary: AI researcher Jacob Coxon testified about AI risks before New York City lawmakers. Adam Gray/Getty Images Jacob Coxon, the ex-Anthropic researcher whose resignation made headlines, warned of AI risks at an NYC council hearing. "At my last job, I was, in some sense, working to automate myself," Coxon testified. Automating AI research could soon leave humans unable to control its outcomes, Coxon said. Automated AI research is on the horizon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher said, warning it could leave humans totally unable to control what comes next. Jacob Coxon, the 27-year-old who publicly resigned from Anthropic last month after working as a capabilities researcher, made the comments before New York City lawmakers on Monday as he sounded the alarm that AI could threaten humanity's survival. Coxon testified that automating AI research has become "the primary goal" of top frontier AI labs. "At my last job, I was, in some sense, working to automate myself," Coxon said at the New York City Council hearing focused on AI risks. "When I was at OpenAI, we had milestones for an automated AI researcher, around 2027, 2028, and we are on track or beating these expectations," he said. "That's a matter of months from now, not decades or even five years." Coxon said that once AI can conduct its own research, "humans will be much further out of the loop than we are today, and today is already not great." Speaking from what he called firsthand experience, Coxon said that the majority of the code written today is written by AI. "And people do not check it that carefully anymore," he testified. OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Coxon's remarks on Tuesday. Coxon was among a panel of AI-industry whistleblowers to testify at the hourslong hearing, which also included testimony from representatives of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google , and Meta . "This hearing is not about stifling innovation," City Council speaker Julie Menin said at the outset of the proceeding, explaining, "the true intent of this hearing is to ensure that innovation happens responsibly." In his testimony, Coxon told council members that his experience inside Anthropic and OpenAI convinced him that the firms were moving ahead without adequate safeguards in place. "It is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," Coxon said, adding, "From my experience, the companies are being extremely reckless given the stakes." When Coxon announced his resignation from Anthropic on X in a now-viral post, he said neither Anthropic nor OpenAI was "acting responsibly," and alleged both were "gambling with our lives." During Monday's hearing, Coxon called for more transparency from AI labs and a slowdown in the development of rapidly advancing technology. "The companies run on a startup mindset: move fast, break things, fix them later. That works for a photosharing app. It does not work for building the most powerful technology ever built," he testified. Days after Coxon's resignation, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a new, nearly 4,000-word essay urging the AI industry to slow down. "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote. "Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain." In response, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an X post, "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier. This has been a primary topic of discussions we've had at OpenAI in recent weeks." events.title: AI tools flood into underground cybercrime markets
events.summary: Hackers in underground cybercriminal forums are on shopping sprees for new AI tools , according to research shared first with Axios. Why it matters: AI is making once-specialized hacking capabilities cheaper and easier to buy, potentially transforming far more criminals into dangerous hackers. By the numbers: Advertisements for AI tools on underground forums and platforms surged from fewer than 50 per month in late 2025 to more than 1,400 by February, according to a report from Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center. Sellers offered access to ChatGPT Plus accounts for as little as 10 cents and jailbreak prompts to trick models into breaking their safeguards for 32 cents, per the research. Halcyon studied nearly 4,000 posts across 77 Telegram channels, 20 dark web forums and five specialized underground markets between October and May. Threat level: Companies are already losing millions of dollars to the types of cyberattacks enabled by the tools found on these underground markets. "It really goes to show you how cheap it is to conduct these activities ... which should be scary for organizations," Cynthia Kaiser, head of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of FBI Cyber, told Axios. The big picture: Cybercriminals have completely commercialized the sale and creation of these tools, often modeling software-as-a-service subscription models and online storefronts, per the report. Some sellers are now offering AI tools they tested and promoted on traditional dark web forums through easier-to-manage storefronts hosted on Telegram. "It shouldn't have been shocking to me," Kaiser said. "But what we should take away from this is also how much cybercriminals have learned throughout the years about how to sell and package — and they applied this really quickly to the AI models." Zoom in: Hackers are selling four types of AI tools: Jailbroken and stolen AI services, including prompts that allow users to strip the safety guardrails from mainstream models for as little as $10. Identity fraud and phishing tools that make impersonating real people quick and easy. Access to models trained on malicious data to aid cybercrime, such as the popular WormGPT that's designed to write phishing emails and malware. AI-augmented malware and infrastructure, including a system that can call as many as 120 people at once as part of a scam operation. Flashback: In 2023, hackers could only tap a handful of one-off tools. Now, there's a robust marketplace. Still, AI is largely helping criminals perform discrete elements of existing attacks more cheaply and efficiently, Kaiser said. "What you're not seeing for sale is an agent that does it all for you and has this amazing success rate," she said. What to watch: Halcyon didn't find evidence of criminals selling AI systems capable of running fully autonomous cyberattacks. Even in AI-enabled malware and infrastructure, Kaiser said, much of what researchers are seeing involves coding assistance, infrastructure and other individual tasks rather than AI creating and deploying malware on its own. events.title: Asos confirms hackers sent 'unauthorised' notification to app users
events.summary: Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers. Dozens of people told the BBC they received the strange "ASOS HACKED" message from the clothing and beauty store's app on Tuesday morning - with some saying it left them "scared" to open the app. The notification was addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams in what cyber security experts said looked like a "brazen" extortion attempt. Asos acknowledged the "unauthorised customer notification" on Tuesday afternoon, saying some "basic personal information" may have been accessed. In an email to customers on Tuesday night, the company apologised and urged customers not to engage with the notification. And it said the website and app are "operating as usual" promising customers they can "shop with confidence" while it investigates the incident. The company has not as of yet informed the UK's data watchdog, the Information Commission's Office (ICO), about any breach. Exactly how many Asos customers received the notification on Tuesday remains unclear, but Google's Play store says the ASOS app has been downloaded to android devices more than 10 million times. The British retailer has a substantial global footprint - serving around 17 million customers each year across more than 150 markets. Some Asos app users in Australia, France, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland had also received the notification, according to local reports on Tuesday. Hackers seeking to pile pressure on potential victims by informing their customers is rare, as most extortions happen in private, so this incident may go down as a significant moment in cyber-attack history. Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, called it a "deeply serious" and "brazen" attack whereby the hackers had apparently "turned Asos' own app into their ransom note". But she told the BBC that Asos customers should not be "scared and frightened" - encouraging those worried to change their passwords, avoid clicking on the notification's link and be cautious about possible scam emails or texts. What can I do to protect myself after 'Asos hacked' message? Published 7 hours ago The message popped up on many Asos app users' home screens on Tuesday morning Users of the Asos app appeared to have received the alarming notification at around 10:00 BST on Tuesday. Headlined "ASOS HACKED" and addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams, it said: "We have fully compromised the Snowflake instance." "Engage with us, or we will leak it," it added, before linking to a Telegram channel. The message left many ASOS customers confused. "At first I thought it was an ad or a fun promotion like 'ASOS HACKED get 50% off everything for a limited time only'," Jodie, an analyst from Edinburgh, told the BBC. "Then I read the rest of the message which clearly showed that it wasn't an ad and instead a message to IT." Jodie's concerns about what the Asos incident might mean for data she has shared with the platform, like her address, are shared by other users "My main concern is that my information, such as bank information, home address, telephone number, has been compromised," said Erin, a student at the University of Sheffield. She told the BBC that while her friends have expressed similar concerns about a potential data leak, her sister did not receive the notification on the Asos app. "So the question is what is the extent? Are all customers affected even if they didn't get the notification? It's poor from Asos on all fronts." Asos said in its statement that it took "immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms" on Tuesday - adding it was working with specialists within and outside the company, as well as relevant authorities. It said it does not believe payment-card information or account passwords were impacted, and that its site and app are "operating as normal". "Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate," it said. The BBC understands the National Cyber Security Centre has offered assistance to Asos. Meanwhile Snowflake - whose tools are used by dozens of firms to collect, analyse and store data - told the BBC its investigation was ongoing, but it had so far found "no compromise" of its platform. The company's services have, however, been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years. Snowflake has previously been linked to cyber incidents targeting Ticketmaster and Santander. According to cybersecurity expert Jen Ellis, Snowflake collects data from multiple sources for analysis, and an "enormous" firm like Asos will have lots of data about how people shop globally. However Dan Bird, from cybersecurity firm Horizon3, said the message implied the apparent hackers' access had gone beyond the Snowflake database.

events.title: Roll-out begins for passport-free airport e-gates
events.summary: The new system will be 25% faster than having to show your passport, officials said Passengers arriving into the UK will be able to pass through airport e-gates without showing their passport under a new contactless system, the government has announced. On Tuesday, East Midlands Airport became the first airport to offer the new technology before it is rolled out to all UK airports by early 2027, the Home Office said. The system uses facial technology so as passengers approach the e-gate, their photo is taken and then checked against immigration, travel and passport information and, if verfied, the barrier opens automatically. Testing showed the new contactless system was up to 25% faster than using a passport, according to officials. If further checks are needed, travellers will need to put their passport on the reader or may be directed to a Border Force officer. Officers will continue to monitor all e-gates and offer assistance, while passengers should keep their passport with them at all times, the Home Office said. East Midlands Airport said they expected a 'smoother, swifter and simpler' passenger experience Phil Douglas, director general of Border Force, said: "This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country. "By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK's robust border security. "Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families." Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, the trade body for the country's airports, said the move was "excellent news for the passenger". She added: "It is vital that we have the fast, efficient borders that arrivals into the UK now expect, and we will work closely with our members and government officials to ensure a smooth rollout." Steve Griffiths, managing director of East Midlands Airport, in Castle Donington, Leicestershire, said: "We're delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force. "As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers' journeys smoother, swifter and simpler. "This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area." Standard e-gates are currently available at Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, East Midlands, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted.
