events.title: Scoop: Senate GOP to send $5m to shore up Graham in South Carolina
events.summary: The main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates plans to inject $5 million into the South Carolina campaign as an "insurance policy" to help GOP nominee Darline Graham , a source familiar with the move tells Axios. Why it matters: The GOP's concern that a Senate seat in blood-red South Carolina could be in play shows just how bad the political environment is for Republicans, who face a rash of troubles in states long considered conservative strongholds. "It's an insurance policy. We're going to be there for Darline," said a Republican briefed on the plans for the Senate Leadership Fund. The shift to spending in conservative South Carolina comes after Senate Republicans announced they no longer were financing ads in swing-state North Carolina, where the GOP's Michael Whatley is lagging behind former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in polls. Democrats, meanwhile, are reallocating resources in a way that reflects their optimism four weeks before Election Day. Democrats' main Senate super PAC canceled roughly $1.1 million in ad reservations in North Carolina, based on their belief Cooper is well-positioned to flip the seat now held by retiring Republican Thom Tillis. Zoom in: Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was appointed to her seat in July at the urging of President Trump , a friend of her brother's. Graham faces a host of challenges: She's a relatively poor fundraiser compared to her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who is outspending and outraising Graham, according to the South Carolina Post & Courier . Unlike her brother, Graham shields herself from the press and has shown a relative lack of mastery of foreign policy, which tripped her up during a GOP primary debate. Graham won that primary over Rep. Ralph Norman with 52% of the vote after getting help from Trump. It left some bad feelings with Norman, who endorsed her but briefly suggested he would mount a write-in campaign for the Nov. 3 general election. Zoom out: Voter anger over high prices and Trump's sagging popularity have helped to create a political landscape in which the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC is having to play defense across the country. It's trying to shore up GOP incumbents and challengers from Alaska to Ohio to Texas, where it recently plowed in $131 million over 17 days to boost Ken Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico. "We're not taking anything for granted. We won't be caught flat-footed in any of these races," the source said. The money for Graham will be spent mainly on TV ads to "remind voters that Andrews is a Democrat." Democrats haven't won a statewide race in South Carolina since 2006. By the numbers: Closer-than-expected polling from two firms that typically survey for Republicans sparked concern last week in GOP circles. A survey from Trafalgar showed Graham pulling 43% and Andrews 42%, a statistical tie. InsiderAdvantage also produced a poll showing a 1-point race that's essentially tied, with Graham at 46% and Andrews at 45%. Earlier in September, GOP-leaning Rasmussen Reports showed Graham up by 5 points. Catch up quick: Andrews' campaign has been under the radar compared to that of Jaime Harrison, the Democrat who challenged Graham's brother for the seat in 2020. Harrison raised $100 million for that race, but because he was the state's former Democratic Party chair, it was easier for Republicans to make the race a partisan contest. In contrast, Andrews is running as a "mom and a doctor." Her campaign was largely financed with $3.6 million in campaign contributions bundled by 314 Action Fund, a political committee founded to elect Democratic candidates with STEM backgrounds. What they're saying: "South Carolinians don't know who Darline Graham is or what she believes — she avoids reporters, avoids voters, and lies about Annie rather than doing her job," an Andrews spokesperson told Axios. A Graham spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment. Trump gave a preview Monday of the bare-knuckle attacks to come when he took to Truth Social and used a slur for transgender people to attack Andrews while accusing her of a host of liberal positions. "South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her," Trump wrote . The 314 Action Fund jabbed back at the president in a statement late Monday, calling Trump "perverted" and saying that he "has resorted to name-calling and juvenile insults because his candidate can't win on the issues." Axios' Hans Nichols contributed to this story.

events.title: Longevity guru Bryan Johnson: "People really want me to die"
events.summary: LOS ANGELES — Bryan Johnson , the face of the longevity movement who believes he may never die, announced recently that he had an incurable autoimmune disease — and his critics cheered, he told "The Axios Show" in an exclusive interview Monday. "I mean, I think people really want me to die. Now I get it. It's funny. It's ironic. I push a lot of buttons that people don't like," he said. The big picture : As Johnson himself acknowledged, there's an irony in the founder of the "Don't Die" movement watching people celebrate his diagnosis. But Johnson sees his diagnosis as rocket fuel for his mission to promote longevity, rather than a setback. Catch up quick: Johnson, 49, has autoimmune gastritis (AIG), a chronic condition in which the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach lining. Johnson said "there was joy all around the world" after he announced his diagnosis in July. He spends millions of dollars a year on extreme health interventions, documenting the experiments for an online following that has ballooned to roughly 8 million across platforms including YouTube . When asked if any of his interventions could have fueled his AIG diagnosis, he said: "No. I got diagnosed with hypothyroidism when I was 21 years old. The thyroid and the stomach are very closely linked in immunology. I probably have had this thing for about 30 years." The intrigue : Johnson views the diagnosis, which might appear to undermine his campaign against aging, as just another test of it. In his view, his efforts to do more than manage the disease can help prove the efficacy of his ambitions. "I like the challenge. I'm up for it. I think it's good timing. I'm going to get diagnosed with something at some point. Why not this?" Friction point: Johnson, who calls himself the "most measured person in the world," spends over $2 million a year on his personal health and longevity treatments. He has an entire medical concierge team and a makeshift doctor's office in his home. Experts say the cause of the disease is unknown, and that Johnson's proposed effort to reverse it is experimental. Zoom out: Johnson made his fortune founding Braintree, which bought Venmo and was later sold to PayPal for $800 million. He now runs longevity businesses including Blueprint and Immortals, alongside neurotechnology company Kernel and venture fund OS Fund. Between the lines: One common critique of intensive health tracking is that more testing can uncover more abnormalities, not all of them meaningful. Doctors warn that false positives and incidental findings can trigger a "cascade" of follow-up tests and treatments that can bring added cost, stress, and in some cases, harm. Johnson is a full-throated fan : "I personally appreciate information. I want to know because when you find things early, you're much more likely to be able to address them." He also said his process doesn't feel addictive to him, adding that "the biggest addiction in the world is to make money." The bottom line: The face of the longevity movement sees the hit to his public health record as another potential achievement in his quest to live forever.

events.title: 7-Eleven exits India amid mounting competition
events.summary: 7-Eleven is a global chain of convenience stores best known for quick grab-and-go snacks, beverages, and household staples, often operating 24 hours. 7-Eleven closed all 31 stores in India by September 30 due to tough competition from local retailers, after expanding to about 60 locations since 2021. Seven & i Holdings, 7-Eleven's owner, confirmed the closures but plans to explore options to re-enter the Indian market long term. Rival Lawson plans to enter India in 2027 and aims to have around 100 stores by 2030, showing ongoing interest in the market. TOKYO – All 7-Eleven convenience stores in India shut down in September, according to its Japanese parent company on Oct 6, as media reported the retail giant struggled to compete with local rivals. “We confirm that our master franchisee, Reliance, which operates 7-Eleven stores in Mumbai and Pune, closed all 31 stores on Sept 30,” Seven & i Holdings, the owner of the world’s biggest convenience store chain, said in a statement. After signing a licensing agreement with India-based Reliance Retail, the brand launched its first Indian outlet in Mumbai in October 2021, eventually expanding to a peak of around 60 locations, a Seven & i Holdings spokesman told AFP. Seven & i Holdings declined to comment on why the shops were closed, but the Nikkei and Yomiuri dailies, Japan’s national daily newspapers, reported that the company had struggled against severe competition from local Indian retailers. Seven & i Holdings has not given up on its business in India in the long term, it said. “While our aspiration to serve customers in India remains, we look forward to exploring several options to advance our presence in the market over the long term,” Seven & i Holdings said. Its rival Lawson reportedly said it plans to open its first shop in India in 2027 and to expand its business there to around 100 shops by 2030. AFP

events.title: Wall Street on track for record profits
events.summary: Data: NYSE/Intercontinental Exchange via the New York State Comptroller; Chart Emily Peck/Axios; Note: 2026 projected by the comptroller if first-half growth continues at current pace. First-half 2026 profits were $45.9 billion. Profits are for broker-dealer operations of NYSE member firms and are not adjusted for inflation. Wall Street profits are blowing past expectations this year, the New York State Comptroller's office finds in a new report. Why it matters: Profits are on track for an all-time record, a sign of how the AI boom is fueling dealmaking and how volatile markets are helping trading. By the numbers: In the first half of this year, Wall Street firms raked in $45.9 billion — that's 51.3% more than the same period last year, and already more than the $45.3 billion forecast for the entirety of 2026. If growth continues apace, annual profits could exceed $90 billion. Zoom out: That's far more than 2025's record $65.1 billion and rivals the 2009 record even after accounting for inflation, the report says. Stunning stat: The fees that firms earn from underwriting — helping companies sell new stocks and bonds — rose 68% in the first half of the year, compared with the first half of 2025. Zoom in: That tracks with a 76.5% increase in global equity issuance, a large chunk from the SpaceX initial public offering . Plus, there was also an 11.3% increase in debt issuance, with the AI hyperscalers among the biggest borrowers. Yes, but: It's anyone's guess as to whether the second half of the year looks like the first. There are plenty of market headwinds blowing: the Iran war, higher inflation and interest rates, the potential for the AI bubble to burst among them. The intrigue: Wall Street appears to be thriving despite fears over the city's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani. The big picture: The securities industry makes up a big and growing share of the city and state's tax revenues, but local business and politics aren't significant profit engines. Those instead are driven by national and global markets — it's been a huge year for stocks, the SpaceX IPO was the biggest ever, M&A hit a record and war-driven volatility juiced trading. What to watch: The big Wall Street banks are set to release third-quarter earnings numbers next week — that's the first big test of whether the pace is holding up.

events.title: Latino group bets on bilingual AI to cut voter confusion before the midterms
events.summary: A national Latino civic engagement group is turning to an AI app to help voters cut through an increasingly complicated election system — in English or Spanish. Why it matters: Nearly 39 million Hispanics can vote in this year's midterms, and their political loyalties are increasingly up for grabs. Hispanics have added 5.25 million eligible voters since 2022, more than any other racial or ethnic group, according to Pew Research Center. The Latino electorate remains highly fluid: About 1 in 7 Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 now say they want Democrats to control Congress, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll . How it works: Mi Familia en Acción launched Nubi last week, a bilingual AI-powered app that answers questions about voting, voter registration, citizenship and Know Your Rights information. Users can ask questions in English or Spanish about where and when to vote, early voting, mail ballots and registration. Nubi operates in all 50 states and can tailor information to the local or district level. Unlike a general-purpose chatbot , Mi Familia en Acción president and CEO Héctor Sánchez Barba tells Axios that Nubi doesn't search the open internet for answers. The organization feeds it information from sources it considers reliable, with human review and guardrails around what the AI can answer. If Nubi doesn't have an answer, Sánchez said, it is designed to say so and direct the user to a trusted source or partner rather than invent a response. State of play: Nubi represents a five-year effort to marry Mi Familia en Acción's traditional organizing with technology. The organization launched a more basic chatbot about two years ago before developing the current AI version. Mi Familia en Acción financed development itself, Sánchez said, though he declined to disclose the cost, calling it a "very big investment." The organization says it plans to keep updating Nubi as voting rules, court decisions and government policies change. Zoom in: The goal is to turn a complicated search across election websites into a conversation. A voter could ask whether they're registered, whether they can vote by mail, where their polling place is or what early-voting options exist. Nubi then walks the user through basic questions before giving a locally specific answer. The tool is updated regularly and eventually could expand its answers on questions involving immigration enforcement or problems a voter encounters at a polling place. What they're saying: "People don't need to be a constitutional lawyer to find information about how they need to vote," said Sánchez, adding that the goal is to put reliable information in one place. He stressed that Nubi is nonpartisan and doesn't recommend candidates or causes. Sánchez also said the technology won't replace door-knocking and other traditional organizing, but could extend civic information into rural or overlooked communities that organizers rarely reach. Zoom out: Nubi arrives as Latino voters play an increasingly large — and less predictable — role in American elections. Pew projects Hispanics will account for 16% of eligible voters in 2026, nearly double their 9% share in 2006. Latino voters are also fragmenting into competing political identities rather than moving uniformly toward either party. In May, 52% of registered Latino voters surveyed in 17 competitive House districts said they were undecided or could change their minds.

events.title: Scoop: Gun safety groups jump into midterms with $10 million assist for Democrats
events.summary: Everytown for Gun Safety , a group that advocates for stricter gun laws, is teaming up with House Democrats on a $10 million ad campaign to boost former gun safety advocates now running for Congress, Axios has learned. Why it matters: That's a significant sum at a moment when Democrats are raising alarm bells about being outgunned financially in the midterm elections. The candidates boosted by the campaign are all former volunteers for Moms Demand Action, which is part of Everytown. The candidates include: JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Pia Dandiya of Florida, Christina Bohannan, Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James of Iowa, Christina Hines and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, and Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania. "For nearly two years, a MAGA House has rubber-stamped the Trump administration as it tore up federal gun safety laws, and flipping these eight seats is how we put a stop to it," Everytown president John Feinblatt said in a statement first shared with Axios. "There's a Moms Demand Action volunteer on the ballot in every one of these districts, and we're partnering with House Majority PAC to turn them into majority makers." Mike Smith, the president of House Democrats' main super PAC, House Majority PAC, said in a statement: "Every seat on this map is a chance to put a check on a Trump administration and a MAGA House that have spent two years putting the gun lobby ahead of American families." Between the lines: The money will go to fund TV and digital ads focused broadly on "public safety," referencing not just gun control but drug trafficking, immigration, crime, and police funding. The Bohannan ad says she is "running for Congress to put public safety first. That means working with both parties to secure our border, hire more police officers and keep illegal guns and fentanyl off our streets." The Cognetti ad mostly focuses on her broader anti-corruption message but lauds how "she got millions for police and cut violent crime by 80%" as mayor of Scranton. The other side: "House Democrats have fully embraced the radical socialist agenda of abolishing prisons, releasing criminals back on the streets, and defunding the police," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement. "Voters won't buy their lies about Republicans who have fought to protect our communities." Editor's note: This article has been corrected to clarify that Moms Demand Action is part of Everytown (not another gun safety group).

events.title: Inside Trump's new AI playbook
events.summary: President Trump's newly minted "Super Intelligence" task force faces a daunting mandate: reconcile fiercely divided cabinet factions to forge a tech policy that keeps pace with the blistering AI race. Why it matters: The task force brings the administration's scattered AI work under one roof, but it also makes it likely that any new rules will be forged in the crossfire of competing internal camps. In an interview, Task force co-chair Scott Kupor rejected the assertion that the administration is asleep at the wheel on AI policy, arguing that rigid, static legislation would risk becoming instantly obsolete. What they're saying : "The worst thing for us to do would be to assume a static set of knowledge that allows us to put a regulatory schema in place that then has unintended consequences," said Kupor, a Silicon Valley veteran who is currently serving as director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, akin to an HR director for the federal government. "Look, we live in D.C.," he said. "There's nothing that's not political in this town. People have different views and that's totally fine. Our obligation is to demonstrate to the American people that this is good and also that we take the anxieties and the concerns seriously." "At the end of the day there is no daylight between the president and anyone else, which is we need to win," he said. Kupor was the first employee hired by venture giant Andreessen Horowitz. Between the lines : The group's makeup highlights the competing fiefdoms driving Trump's AI strategy , with some working on model approval and coordination and others continuing to voice deep skepticism about pro-regulation forces in the industry. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trump Chief of Staff Susie Wiles have worked behind the scenes to encourage some oversight, including through the voluntary model-review process that already exists. Managed within the Commerce Department, the reviews have already been used for top models at Anthropic, OpenAI and now Google, sources tell Axios. On the other end of the spectrum, figures like David Sacks and the Pentagon's Emil Michael represent an approach that is wary of the potential for a slowdown in model development or new regulation to reduce competition for frontier companies. Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and the new AI czar , is expected to bring cohesion to the group's collective work, much as he does with the myriad intelligence agencies. The entire committee is set to operate under Trump's explicit marching orders: Innovation cannot be bottlenecked, and America must stay ahead while finding a safe path forward, Kupor said. Kupor suggested one outcome may be that AI regulation is divided among different federal agencies, although it is too early to know what the group — which will do its work over 120 days — will ultimately recommend to the president. His primary area of focus initially will be to seek input from stakeholders in the energy, manufacturing, security and financial services industries. Kupor said he expects Clayton will keep close tabs on the intelligence community and the committee will continue to stay in close touch with the AI companies. Zoom in: The administration is leaning hard into corporate self-policing to manage the risks. Kupor and other officials believe that third-party audits and direct reporting to corporate boards carry severe securities law implications that rival traditional government oversight. The bottom line: The task force's goal isn't to draft a bureaucratic "PhD dissertation," in Kupor's words. But it remains to be seen whether streamlining existing efforts without new legislation will satisfy Americans who are increasingly anxious about AI safety.

events.title: The most-watched election in U.S. history
events.summary: The 2026 midterms are shaping up to be the most intensely observed, recorded, dissected and challenged election in American history. Why it matters: A small army of partisan and nonpartisan observers will show up. So will a surge of Justice Department monitors, organizers looking for signs of ICE and citizen journalists broadcasting their search for illegal voting in real time. Between the lines: More nonpartisan observation can bolster confidence in elections, studies show . But officials worry that activists expecting to find wrongdoing could misread routine events. Election officials have been raising concerns that "vigilante citizen journalists" could interfere with the election, said Andrew Walchuck of Common Cause, a nonprofit organization that's also recruiting nonpartisan election observers. "I worry that people are going to go in and claim they're seeing things that they aren't," said Andrew Garber of the Brennan Center. "Just minor, innocuous things that are going to happen as millions and millions of ballots get cast and counted, then it gets spun into something nefarious or untrue," Garber said. The intrigue: After the 2020 election, claims from observers and activist sleuths helped fuel challenges to the results. It was then channeled into numerous lawsuits from the Trump campaign. The cases were almost all dismissed or denied relief in court. Influencers and online activists can turn real-time claims about wrongdoing into national controversy before officials can weigh in or push back — including while votes are being cast or counted. "What gives me concern is that we have an administration that is trying to spread conspiracy theories and spread lies about our elections and... [then] having more people out there with that purpose behind their work troubles me," Walchuck said. The other side: "Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of voter fraud continues to pile up. Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable," Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement. This year there have been more than two dozen federal charges against people for voting when they're not eligible and about 160 arrests, according to the Justice Department . A review from the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan organization, says instances of illegal voting are "extremely small." Zoom in: The DOJ plans to train 1,000 election monitors to deploy across the country, one of the largest-ever efforts from the agency. It builds on a significant increase in observers in 2024 . The Senate Democrats have spun up their own arm of election observers, using office staff to monitor the polls. That's in addition to a new 50-state-plus-territories recruitment program by a coalition of Democratic state parties, aiming to recruit at least 10,000 election watchers. The Republican National Committee is building on its election watch network set up in 2020 to counter perceived voter fraud. GOP partisans have signed up in record numbers to be poll workers and the party is hosting virtual and in-person trainings for observers and challengers. A network of anti-ICE activists is transitioning ICE watch trainings into poll watching trainings, responding in part to the Trump administration saying ICE could make arrests at the polls. When asked in September about deploying agents, Trump told TIME magazine he hadn't thought of it. Zoom out: These efforts will coexist with a slew of nonpartisan observing efforts, ranging from voter protection groups to international election observers. There will also be state party and campaign staffers who regularly monitor the polls for concerns. These are typically more mundane, including monitoring accurate opening and closing times for polling locations that can be remedied with quick litigation. The rules and terminology for observers vary by state laws , which also govern how close an observer can be to voting machines or tabulation processes and how to document concerns about malpractice. The bottom line: "Having questions and wanting to understand more about the election process as a sort of curious citizen is a good thing," said Avery Davis-Roberts of the Carter Center, which monitors elections internationally and will have volunteers in five states in November. "And we hope that people will use observation and the findings of our observation as a way to better understand how the process works and maybe have some of those questions answered."

events.title: Our Reporter Spent 10 Weeks Gambling on DraftKings. Here Are 5 Things He Learned.
events.summary: Bankrolled by ProPublica, reporter Jake Pearson tested online gambling guardrails by mimicking the betting patterns of a problem gambler for 10 weeks. Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Jake Pearson/ProPublica, Chris Alcantara/ProPublica. Online gambling has surged in the U.S. since the Supreme Court allowed states to legalize sports betting in 2018, prompting public health concerns about gambling addiction and calls for stricter consumer protections. Online sportsbooks such as DraftKings and FanDuel have touted “responsible gaming” features as evidence that they are taking appropriate steps to protect consumers from spiraling out of control. Reporter Jake Pearson put these safeguards to the test. Bankrolled by ProPublica, he mimicked the betting patterns of a problem gambler for 10 weeks, consulting a panel of addiction specialists, recovering gambling addicts and professional sports bettors for advice. He found that the safety features were overpowered by the app’s product design and promotions that pushed him to continue gambling. Pearson detailed his entire journey, which you can read here . Here are five takeaways from his investigation. 1. Sports betting is ubiquitous. The industry relies on very active losers. Today, nearly a quarter of all Americans , and half of men ages 18 to 49, say they have an active sportsbook account, according to the Siena Research Institute. But that rapid growth has come with consequences: About a quarter of active sportsbook account holders surveyed by the organization this year said that they’d lost enough on a bet that they’d have trouble meeting their financial obligations. Gamblers who lose frequently are the bettors sportsbooks are most interested in, Matthew Gaskell, a British psychologist and expert on gambling addiction, said. Gaskell noted that a relatively small number of active losers account for a substantial amount of sportsbooks’ revenue. A 2024 study out of Connecticut found that 1.8% of problem gamblers in the state accounted for 51% of sports betting revenue . What Does Your Data Reveal About Sports Betting Apps? Help ProPublica Find Out. If you’ve bet on sports with FanDuel or DraftKings, you can help ProPublica understand how these apps work. Use our browser extension to download your betting history, then upload your files. Share Your Experience DraftKings says its responsible gaming system provides adequate safeguards to protect customers from spiraling out of control. “I think as a business, as an industry, we’re doing a good job of educating people, of raising awareness, of making tools and resources available, of monitoring accounts,” Lori Kalani, DraftKings’ chief responsible gaming officer, told Pearson. But policymakers aren’t so sure. Lawmakers from Colorado to Massachusetts are now proposing stricter consumer protections. 2. DraftKings has adopted responsible gaming tools. They require users to opt in, limiting their effectiveness. DraftKings’ responsible gambling safeguards include in-app notifications that encourage gamblers to take a break after they’ve lost money and “time reminders” that tell users how long they’ve been on the app. The app also features a responsible gaming center that allows users to set a budget, track their spending or opt into tools like those that allow them to limit the amount of time and money they spend in a 24-hour period or enact more severe restrictions such as a multiday “cool off.” But this system largely relies on users to have the wherewithal to opt into the tools — something that experts say can be difficult for someone struggling with gambling addiction. DraftKings told Pearson that if a customer’s behavior raises too many red flags, the company will proactively close an account. Yet it wouldn’t specify how often this actually happens. Screenshot by Jake Pearson/ProPublica Pearson’s experiment mimicked the behavior of a problem gambler to see when — and if — the company’s safeguards would stop him. The first in-app responsible gaming prompt Pearson received came more than a week after he began gambling on the NBA playoffs, when he’d already lost roughly what a minimum-wage worker in New York City earns in a month. It told him that he’d hit $2,500 or more in deposits and said to “visit our Responsible Gaming Center anytime to set limits for yourself and access tools for safer play.” But the app’s warning wasn’t triggered by Pearson’s reckless betting. It was legally required. When New York legalized mobile sports betting in 2023, lawmakers required the apps to notify users when they hit $2,500 in total deposits. The pop-up gave Pearson two options: set limits or “I understand.” He clicked the latter and was back in action. Even as Pearson exhibited red flag after red flag, according to our panel of experts, his subsequent warnings from the app followed the same pattern. DraftKings says millions of customers have visited its responsible gaming center, but the little data available publicly suggests only a small percentage opt into these tools. Just over 8% of active DraftKings users in Massachusetts were using them as of April, a company official told state regulators this summer. The official added the number was trending up. Kalani says her 51-person team manually reviews user accounts suspected of problem gambling. Yet even after Pearson deposited $21,600 into his account in less than eight weeks and exhibited just about every sign of compulsive gambling, he didn’t register for a manual review under the company’s criteria. 3. The design of online sports betting platforms can encourage users to gamble more.  Online gambling companies have created sophisticated technology products designed to squeeze maximum engagement out of users, just as social media companies like Meta did years earlier with users of Facebook and Instagram, according to Darragh McGee, a researcher at the University of Bath. Indeed, Pearson found that the app’s design encouraged him to keep betting. Pearson found the app’s quick-tap deposit buttons increased automatically. Screenshot by Jake Pearson/ProPublica. Debit card number redacted by ProPublica. As he gambled more, he found that the app’s quick-tap deposit buttons increased automatically, making it even easier to mindlessly transfer large sums from his bank into his DraftKings account. And while DraftKings’ safety warnings were sporadic, he was getting up to six push notifications a day notifying him of rewards and betting opportunities. DraftKings told Pearson it sent him 32 responsible gambling prompts over 10 weeks of gambling, including emails that every DraftKings customer gets. Pearson counted in-app notifications about his betting 14 out of the 71 days he gambled on the app. 4. Perks can also help encourage users to bet more. events.title: Crypto PACs’ House targets raise eyebrows
events.summary: The News The cryptocurrency industry’s leading network of super PACs is under scrutiny after revealing it will back 19 House Republicans but only 13 House Democrats. Fairshake, which emerged as a kingmaker last election cycle, said three members from each party would receive $1 million ahead of November. But it did not provide a breakdown for the rest of its spending, even as skeptics pointed out that its list contained more Republicans than Democrats in tough races. “The absence of [North Carolina Democratic Rep.] Don Davis is the most dangerous thing, because that’s a Dem who’s in a swing seat who’s not getting love,” despite backing the industry’s top legislative priority, one cryptocurrency executive told Semafor. Last cycle, “there was at least the argument that Dems had driven them to this; this time, it’s been two years of going hard in on [President Donald] Trump.” Know More Hill Democrats privately grumbled about Monday’s announcement and the group’s decision not to support Democratic backers of cryptocurrency legislation like Davis and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet, D-Mich., who represent swing districts and stood to benefit from outside spending. The vast majority of lawmakers on Fairshake’s list represent safe districts, facing only token opposition in their general elections. And the three Democrats named by Fairshake as receiving $1 million represented districts that have been competitive in previous elections but who are expected to win re-election this year. Fairshake, which a spokesperson noted “has always been and always will be an issue-focused organization,” spent more in Democratic primaries than Republican ones this cycle. But Monday’s announcement is nevertheless fueling speculation that it could give the GOP a boost in Senate races by not spending against Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, despite her vote against the cryptocurrency bill. “It’s completely full of sh*t,” another cryptocurrency executive told Semafor after Fairshake announced plans to spend against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, last month. “The fig leaf of bipartisanship is no longer fooling anybody.”

events.title: Polls show how AI is changing the workplace
events.summary: As AI adoption spreads across the US workforce, new polling suggests that its benefits have so far been concentrated among those likely to hold upper-level positions. Twenty-eight percent of US employees say they use AI at least weekly, according to a two-year study from Jobs for the Future, The Families & Workers Fund, and Gallup, while 54% say they haven’t used it at work. Use of the technology on the job is much more common among those with college degrees and those in managerial roles. Speed is the most common benefit that AI users point to, with 63% saying the technology helps them do their jobs faster. Among those in the highest paid positions — people earning $10,000 or more a month — seven in 10 say it’s accelerating their work, while fewer Americans who earn less say the same. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Democrats press White House on still-secret AI framework
events.summary: Two Democratic senators want answers from Trump administration officials on industry influence on the still-unreleased AI regulatory framework, part of the AI executive order President Donald Trump signed earlier this year, according to a letter shared first with Semafor. “We are concerned that the Trump administration is accommodating the interests of Big Tech CEOs rather than addressing the safety and security risks posed by increasingly sophisticated AI systems,” Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., wrote in the letter addressed to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House cyber adviser Sean Cairncross, and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, among others. The letter cites reported industry influence over what eventually became the executive order. It also highlights Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s central role in shaping the more recent White House AI accord, pointing to the administration’s “cozy relationship” with and “deference to industry executives.” The letter is the latest indication that Democrats are not giving up on a sustained push for answers from the administration on what is still a mysterious, voluntary framework for AI companies to submit their highest-level AI models to the government before release. Should the party gain power back in Congress, its demands will have more teeth. “The American people deserve strong guardrails set by democratically elected officials, not a toothless framework shaped in secret by a handful of billionaires,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote Monday, pressing for answers to five questions by Oct. 19. They asked for details on meetings and correspondence between industry and government officials leading up to the release of the executive order in June. They also want to know whether independent evaluators or other stakeholders beyond industry were consulted, and demanded a description of the pre-deployment testing process established under the framework.

events.title: Trump administration presses Congress for anti-fraud legislation
events.summary: The Scoop The White House has formally sent Congress proposed legislation that would impose mandatory minimum sentences on those convicted of fraud involving federal benefit programs, according to a copy of it seen by Semafor. The proposal, sent to House and Senate leadership on Sunday night, follows President Donald Trump’s call over the weekend for lawmakers to crack down on “fraud in Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security programs.” The administration’s language would establish a range of mandatory minimum sentences based on the amount of loss involved in fraud schemes, according to the document. The proposal would also bar courts from placing those sentenced under the provision on probation or suspending their sentences. People found responsible for less than $40,000 in losses would face at least one year in prison; those responsible for between $40,000 and $250,000 in losses would face at least two years in prison; and violations involving $100 million in losses or more would result in at least 20 years in prison. All violations would carry a maximum sentence of life in prison. It’s unlikely that Congress would be able to take up and pass the legislation during its post-election session after the midterms. With Democrats poised to take the House majority next month and the Senate also in play, the proposal also faces a steep climb in 2027. Also included in the administration’s legislative proposal is language that would hold “any officer or employee of the state” personally liable if they knew about alleged fraud and “willfully, intentionally, or recklessly” ignored it. Such officials could also be financially liable for damages up to the “amount of all loss resulting” from the fraud, or if that loss exceeds $1 million, up to three times the amount. Know More Trump in recent months has empowered Vice President JD Vance to pursue fraud across the US, as he and other Republicans have sought to campaign on a familiar message of stopping waste, fraud, and abuse. The administration has pursued a number of high-profile fraud claims, most notably in Democratic-led states such as Minnesota and California. This is the latest crime-related push from Trump, who won his presidential election in part on a law-and-order message. The proposal now sits with Congress, where lawmakers will have to decide whether to take it up.

events.title: Trump expands access to tax-exempt diesel
events.summary: President Donald Trump is expanding access to tax-exempt diesel while simultaneously pledging a swift end to the Iran war, an implicit acknowledgment that his administration is running out of ways to significantly stem the conflict’s economic fallout. “It’ll end very quickly, and prices are going to come down very sharply,” Trump said at the Nebraska rally Monday night, where he signed the executive order on so-called red-dyed diesel. “You might say, ‘Please, please, sir, it’s going down too fast.’” Later, he again promised to pay every American $5,000 if Republicans come out ahead in the midterms, warning of a “1929 South economic depression” if Democrats win. Republicans are cool to the checks idea, and despite Trump’s promises to wrap up the war, his administration has no clear way out of the conflict. — Eleanor Mueller

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Staff in AI, Cyber, SAP and Testing told the consultation is over, with notices due Friday Google teams with nuclear power giant to give reactors a tune-up 2 hours ago Anthropic Claude subscription plan provides more value than OpenAI's, study says 4 hours ago Permanent daylight saving time could be a public health time bomb 4 hours ago European AI flag bearer Mistral's new open weights model is 'Le Chonk' 7 hours ago Trump Mobile customers' data dumped - and some never even received their gold device 7 hours ago KPMG has offered staff facing redundancy £100 to waive their legal rights to appeal or to bring claims over the loss of their job, according to sources. As The Register revealed last month, the consultancy is laying off around 4 percent of the workforce in the UK, equating to some 200 humans being forced to look for new employment in an uncertain job market before Christmas. Staff within the AI, Cyber, SAP, and Testing teams are at the sharp end of the corporate job cutting exercise. On October 1, those at risk were told the consultation process is over and KPMG will inform them of their fate by email on October 9. In a message to staff, seen by The Register , KPMG said: “The collective consultation process has now formally concluded. The firm's original proposal remains unchanged. Employees will be notified on Friday 9th of October 11-11:30am by email if they have been selected for redundancy.” In addition to exit terms that some at KPMG previously described to us as insulting , The Reg understands the consultancy is offering £100 in exchange for employees' existing contractual confidentiality and other post-termination obligations. Some staff see it as a gag order. “The firm's original proposal remains unchanged,” one insider claimed, “offering marginally above statutory terms alongside a nominal £100 consideration for employees to waive their legal rights to appeal or bring claims. “The prevailing consensus among staff [is that] this approach is arrogant and disgraceful, particularly given the decision to dismiss personnel right before the holidays while withholding their earned annual bonuses,” the source added. Annual bonuses are discretionary, performance-based, and typically paid in January. KPMG has not communicated with staff on bonuses for 2026 but we understand anyone under notice (given or received) is not eligible for a payout. Instead, a spokesperson re-sent its earlier statement: “As our market evolves, we are adapting where we are focusing and how we are set up to make sure we have the right skills in place to best serve our clients. To respond to these market dynamics combined with low levels of attrition, we are proposing reductions in some of our advisory client-facing teams and will support our colleagues throughout this process. ” The latest job cuts come six months after KPMG expunged 600 roles across the UK org chart, and is indicative of the financial pressures facing the big four accountancy and consultancy giants. events.title: UK events firm that hosts arms fairs and comic shows sold to rival for £2bn
events.summary: FTSE 100 firm Informa to buy Clarion from private equity group Blackstone A British events business that hosts arms fairs and conventions for comic book fans has been snapped up by a FTSE 100 rival for more than £2bn. Informa has struck a £2.24bn deal to buy the London-based events organiser Clarion from the private equity group Blackstone The takeover will add more than 100 events to Informa’s portfolio – from the defence and security exhibit DSEI held at London’s ExCel, to the comic book and pop culture themed Awesome Con in Washington. DSEI, which is held every two years in London as well as in Germany and Japan, has also attracted protests. Last year, hundreds demonstrated outside the four-day fair in London in protest against Israel’s three biggest arms companies present at the event. Elbit Systems, Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries have supplied the Israel Defense Forces; the latter two are state-owned. Clarion’s portfolio also spans travel shows, classic car meet-ups and events for the technology, gaming, design and technology industries. Its Classic Motor Show event in Birmingham next month is billed as the “world’s largest vehicle club gathering”. Stephen Carter, the Informa chief executive, said the company was “accelerating the focus” on its core live events business, as it also laid out plans to spin off its academic publishing arm, Taylor & Francis. Informa, which is headquartered in London and employs 14,000 people, hosts big industry events around the world, including London Tech Week and the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity. However the FTSE 100 group’s shares have been flat so far this year as it was forced to reschedule several events in the Middle East because of the conflict in the region. Last year Carter, who has led the group since 2013, moved his residency from the UK to the UAE and retired from the House of Lords. Informa makes more than a third of its revenue in India, the Middle East and Asia. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The academic publishing business made about $1bn (£760m) last year. Informa said that it had launched a formal process to separate Taylor & Francis, and that it would “review all options”. The outcome of the review will be reported alongside its full-year results in March next year. Taylor & Francis, which was founded in London in 1852, joined Informa in 2004. It publishes journals and books about science, medicine, technology and engineering. Informa told investors on Tuesday that in order to fund the Clarion deal, it will raise £940m through a share placing, which will include an offer for armchair investors through the broker RetailBook. The takeover is expected to accelerate Informa’s growth and bolster its earnings per share from 2027, the company said. Shares in the business, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, rose by 1.4% in early trading on Tuesday.

events.title: We're saving £100 a month for our kids but they won't get it until they're 57
events.summary: Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices now Richard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them. The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules. , external So the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083. Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing. "Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow." 'We don't eat out as often as we used to' Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council. He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended. In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18. The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life. Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past. "We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain. "And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids." 'I want to retire earlier so this will help' Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600. The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show. One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open , external as in the same period a year earlier. Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023. While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more? Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years. "The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help." Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says. Hugo Thompson is happy to wait until he is at least 57 to access the pension fund For parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity. "Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound." It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children. In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts. Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half. Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three. Wally Luckeydoo says he is giving his children a "financial head start" "My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally.

events.title: UAE's e& returns to its original Etisalat name as it focuses on AI growth
events.summary: UAE telecoms group e& is to return to its original Etisalat name, four years after it changed the company's name, as it looks to boost growth in the artificial intelligence era. “Etisalat is the name we are taking forward – a name that reflects our heritage, our strategy and our ambition for the AI era,” the company said on Tuesday in a filing to the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange, where its shares trade. The move was announced in the presence of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court. It was revealed as the Abu Dhabi-based company marks 50 years since its formation. Today, I witnessed a new milestone in the journey of “Etisalat” as it celebrated 50 years of achievement and launched its vision for the next chapter. A national institution that has accompanied the UAE's development and helped build its digital capabilities. Etisalat continues… pic.twitter.com/rzHR7uYSJW — منصور بن زايد (@MansourBinZayed) October 5, 2026 Etisalat was rebranded as e& in 2022 amid plans for the company to transform into a global technology investment conglomerate. “Etisalat means connection. For 50 years, that purpose has guided what we build and the role we play,” the company said. “Today, it carries even greater significance as we bring connectivity, digital capabilities and infrastructure together to enable new opportunities.” The telecoms company is pushing for AI-led growth, with the launch of a strategic project to develop and expand digital infrastructure capacity within the UAE and abroad. The project includes plans to expand international connectivity capacity to more than 500 terabits per second by 2030 – more than 25 times the current capacity – in addition to developing diverse routes to enhance connectivity efficiency and reliability, delivering advanced, low-latency performance, it said in a statement. The move comes after the company reported a 9 per cent increase in its second-quarter revenue, as it expanded its customer base across international markets despite uncertainty caused by the Iran war. Revenue in the quarter rose to Dh19.2 billion ($5.2 billion) year-on-year, with its overall customer base increasing by nearly a third to hit 251.5 million. In July, the company also agreed to sell its entire stake in Vodafone Group for $5.95 billion as it refocuses on its core businesses.

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters No, this is not GRUB of the meatball variety Sweden is the home of bork, and what better way to mark it than with a huge example of digital signage that shows a GRUB message instead of an ad? Spotted by eagle-eyed Register reader Alexander, the GRUB in question is sadly not the delicious meatballs for which a well-known Swedish furniture maker is famed, but rather the bootloader familiar to Linux fans, usually when something is working as it should (since we can't imagine much call for selecting from multiple operating systems in the world of digital signage). GNU GRUB (the GRUB is short for Grand Unified Bootloader), according to GNU, "is responsible for loading and transferring control to the operating system kernel software." In this case, the user has some options. UEFI firmware is one. Some options for DMS are another. DMS might mean Dank Material Shell, unless you know better. It's an attractive enough desktop, but it seems like overkill for something that slings ads for the few seconds Stockholm commuters raise their gaze from their devices. Some enticing possibilities are on offer. Hitting "e" will edit the commands while "c" will drop the user into the command line. That's assuming, of course, that the user is carrying a keyboard to attach to the stricken screen, something we're sure every Register reader has in their backpack, but not something civilians would necessarily keep on their person. GRUB has featured in this column before , appearing on a UK bus after a filesystem became a bit poorly (motion sickness can clearly affect computers as well as commuters), but this is a wall-sized example of the breed. Judging by the passengers on the escalators opposite, it appears that nobody is rushing to the aid of the stricken signage. That's probably for the best – leave it for a few seconds (by the looks of things), and it'll have another go at booting. Still, it's always good to see GRUB putting in an appearance in a section often dominated by Windows and Android whoopsies. events.title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
events.summary: A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters. The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said. Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents. The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said. There were £1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the £1.18bn detected the previous year. At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024. Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters are targeting much bigger payouts. "As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them." Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers." He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg". Macbooks, fishing equipment and Lego sets One of the most notable fraudsters identified by the ABI last year was a man found by IFED to have fabricated reports of stolen high-value Lego sets , external . The man's scam claims to Axa Insurance during 2021 and 2022 also included other high-value items such as MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles and fishing equipment, IFED said. In 2023, IFED said it found collectible Lego sets matching the ones claimed to have been stolen displayed in the man's living room during a search. Alongside his prison sentence handed down last year, he was also ordered to repay the £14,000 he had claimed. Other cases highlighted by the ABI included a man jailed for 20 months for manipulating women he met on dating sites into participating in staged car crashes, and a man sentenced to four and a half years for submitting over £300,000 worth of fraudulent travel medical emergency claims. In general, the ABI said motor insurance remained the area where insurers identified the most fraudulent cases, accounting for 55% of all scam claims. Meanwhile, the ABI's figures found that exaggerated loss remains the most common type of insurance fraud, with 26,900 cases identified. This is when someone deliberately attempts to increase the cost of a claim beyond its true value, the ABI said. events.title: Advancing The CFET-Based Device Roadmap: Novel Integration Modules And Standard Cell Configurations
events.summary: Key takeaways: From the A7 logic technology node onwards, industry may likely transition to CFET-based transistor architectures which enable 4.5-track (4.5T) and below standard cells. Progress in CFET enablement is backed by two complementary R&D tracks, with imec pioneering many of the underlying innovations: the development of CFET-specific process modules, and a design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) exploration of scalable standard cell configurations. Part 1 of this two-part article presents two optimized CFET-specific modules: (1) a backside contact module; and (2) a gate-stack integration module that enables multiple threshold voltages in nanosheet and CFET devices. Part 2 covers imec’s latest CFET DTCO studies. A novel scalable architecture for sequential CFET is presented that enables split-gate and common-gate device options, key in advancing both the logic and SRAM scaling roadmaps. Another DTCO study presents improved routability at the back-end-of-line (BEOL) level to support the scaling of CFET standard cells. CFET technology moving forward, backed by integration efforts and DTCO studies The semiconductor industry is going through a major architectural transition, with gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors replacing FinFETs in advanced logic nodes of 3nm and beyond. GAA nanosheet transistor technology offers scalability down to the A10 logic generation, where it enables 5.5-track (T) standard cells – the track being a measure for the standard cell height. For the A7 node, options are becoming increasingly diverse to meet the growing diversification of application needs, driven by the AI revolution. According to imec’s latest roadmap, one option is to design systems around imec’s CMOS 2.0 scaling paradigm. With CMOS 2.0, a system-on-chip (SoC) is partitioned into heterogeneous, functional tiers each optimized using the most suitable technology, and reconnected using 3D interconnect technologies. For other use cases, GAA nanosheet technology may be pushed to its ultimate scaling limits, with power delivered from either the frontside or the backside. But industry may as well transition to complementary FET (CFET) device architectures. By stacking p and nMOS transistors on top of each other, standard cells can be further scaled down to 3T, thereby extending the classical CMOS logic roadmap to at least the A3 technology node. Fig. 1: Imec’s logic technology roadmap. Imec and its industrial partners are working to make CFET-based devices manufacturable. In recent years, they laid the groundwork for key integration approaches, categorized as monolithic CFET (mCFET) and sequential CFET (sCFET) [1,2]. Both approaches start from the vertical stacking of Si/SiGe layers from which the n and pFETs are fabricated. With mCFET, the vertical device structure with common top and bottom gates is patterned and processed in a single sequence of process steps. The patterning, deposition and selective removal of materials around and in between the high-aspect ratio device structure requires considerable effort in terms of module development. sCFET, on the contrary, patterns the top and bottom devices independently using dedicated masks. With sCFET, the individual process steps are simpler compared to mCFET but some critical steps need to be executed twice – for top and bottom separately. sCFET additionally involves two wafer flips, distorting the wafer and challenging the precise alignment of front-to-back device connections. Pending further progress in alignment accuracy, mCFET is believed to offer the fastest path to industrial adoption. Progress in CFET integration is complemented with design-technology co-optimization (DTCO) studies that examine CFET device architectures from a circuit level perspective [2]. These studies aim to identify scalable standard cell configurations and performance boosters that offer the best tradeoff in terms of power, performance, area and cost. In this 2-part article, we report major progress in CFET device integration, and we discuss CFET scalability using DTCO studies. In part 1 [link], two process modules were presented that are essential for both mCFET and sCFET device flavors: (1) a backside contact module, and (2) a gate stack integration approach that enables multiple threshold voltages (V t ) in nanosheet and CFET devices. In part 2, a scalable architecture for sCFET is introduced, allowing both split-gate and common-gate configurations. Besides progressing the logic roadmap, DTCO work shows how this split-gate architecture also benefits CFET-based SRAM scaling. Finally, improved back-end-of-line (BEOL) routability is demonstrated, supporting the scaling of CFET standard cells. The reported results are achieved in the framework of the imec-hosted European NanoIC pilot line, which is targeting the development of beyond-2nm systems-on-chip. CFET development, which is centered on CFET-specific designs, process steps, modules and baseline flows, has been selected as one of the key enabling technologies for extending the logic roadmap into the ångström era. This will help Europe to remain at the forefront of next-generation semiconductor innovation and manufacturing. A novel architecture for sCFET: Split-gate device architecture enlarges CFET’s scaling potential Earlier DTCO studies have already demonstrated the scaling potential of CFET technology across subsequent logic nodes – a prerequisite for the semiconductor industry to adopt the new device architecture. For mCFET, for example, imec previously identified the double-row (DR) CFET architecture as the most optimal way to integrate mCFETs into an A7 standard cell [3]. A double-row CFET standard cell contains two rows of stacked devices with a shared vertical signal via in between, and power walls at the cell boundary (see Figure 2). Later, layout inefficiencies were addressed, resulting in an optimized version of the double-row CFET: the half-height double-row (hDR) architecture. At IEDM 2025, additional scaling boosters such as the integration of hybrid channels were introduced to support aggressive area scaling targets towards A3 [2]. Common-gate and split-gate devices: The challenge of offering both flavors with one device architecture The process flow for fabricating mCFET devices inherently offers common-gate devices: the gates of n and pFETs are structurally connected to one another. This works well for 90-95% of all basic logic gates – think about an inverter circuit (or NOT gate) that performs the logical operation of negation. But for other logic circuits, such as flipflops and multiplex gates, independent control of n and pFET metal gates is desired. One way to address this need is to leave one polarity of the stacked CFET device unused (for example, only using the nFETs, and removing the pFETs). events.title: While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution | Charlotte Hill
events.summary: While British children go hungry, we waste 1.1bn meals a year. Bring on the redistribution revolution Food businesses and the government must make redistribution a key policy to address food insecurity. We know the surplus food is out there Charlotte Hill is chief executive of the food redistribution organisation Felix H ow often does this happen? You open the fridge and find some ingredient you meant to use but didn’t get round to, and even though it’s still edible you think perhaps it’s just easier to throw it away. In the UK it’s estimated that an average household wastes about three meals a week , or 156 meals a year. Household fridges are one thing. But across the food sector, more than 1bn meals’ worth of easily accessible surplus food is wasted each year in the UK for the same reason: because it is easier to throw it away. That equates to 470,000 tonnes – enough to feed every child in the UK three meals a day for a month. When so many people are struggling to afford food, that is a staggering amount – and what’s even more shocking is that it is good quality and nutritious. We hear a lot about grocery stores and restaurants throwing out perfectly edible food, but they are just a small part of the problem. The vast majority of food waste , about 850m meals, comes from farms, followed by food manufacturing facilities with 178m meals, another 71m from the hospitality and food service sector, and finally 12m meals from the retail sector. When I say easily accessible, I mean this is food we have the capacity to rescue and get to people. The organisation I head, Felix, is a food rescue charity. We recover edible surplus food that would otherwise go to waste and get it to more than 8,000 organisations that do amazing work to feed people in need. This food sustains lunch clubs for older people where friendships are forged and isolation is addressed. It supports food pantries, where families can access a weekly bag of shopping for just a few pounds. And it can provide meals in homelessness shelters and refuges. But with food insecurity rising, so too is the need for the food we recover. So we must rescue more of that billion-meal surplus. In our food system, unavoidable surplus food is generated at every stage of the supply chain. On farms, unpredictable weather, grading standards and mismatches between harvest volumes and buyer orders contribute to the enormous quantities of edible produce without a home. But we are working with farmers to ensure this food is getting to people’s plates; almost half the food we gave out last year was fresh fruit and vegetables. In manufacturing, production overruns, packaging changes and quality control measures create surplus that cannot be sold through normal channels. But there are bright spots – and an incredible example is the food manufacturer Premier Foods. When their noodle nests don’t pass quality control, we take them and use a partner organisation to repack and label them. We are doing a similar project with 2 Sisters Food Group, a huge manufacturing company that uses late-night surplus factory capacity to repack breaded chicken with minor visual defects. We are also working with supermarkets such as Asda, Co-op, Ocado, Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Waitrose. They give us a huge amount of stock that we get straight back out to every part of the UK. So many companies are doing their bit, but the reason many are not is economics. It is cheaper for a business to waste food than to give it to people: the corporation tax system does not reward food donation in the same way it does a financial one. In addition, public subsidies for alternative disposal routes – such as turning food waste into animal food or biogas – provide profit. This creates a market that actively pulls surplus away from human consumption. We must change this. That is why Felix has started the Redistribution Revolution. Felix, City Harvest, Community Shop, The Bread and Butter Thing, His Church, Feeding Britain, Neighbourly and the wider Felix and Xcess Networks have formed the Food Redistribution Partnership UK, working together to rescue more food. Backed by the government, we have launched a national programme to redistribute surplus food that aims to triple the amount of food we redistribute over the next decade. According to our research, about 1% of all excess food in the UK food system is redistributed by charities. France redistributes about twice that , while the US does three times more. Our revolution needs food businesses to make redistribution the default route for all surplus food, and view it as an opportunity for social good. We need philanthropists to invest in the infrastructure required to store and move the food. And we need the government to change the tax system and make it more financially viable for companies to get food to people.

events.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
events.summary: OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments. The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox. "We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said. Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation. Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present. An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind. When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake. "In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said. "The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough." Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents. "Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party." OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia. The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said. Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to. This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours. The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations". "We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well." Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI. "We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee. The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models. An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard. "In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association. Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.
