events.title: DeepSeek set to raise at least $15 billion in Tencent-backed funding
events.summary: DeepSeek’s funding sets the stage for one of the most highly anticipated Chinese market debuts in years. DeepSeek is set to raise at least 80 billion yuan (S$15 billion) in Tencent-backed funding, exceeding its initial target ahead of a planned IPO in early 2027. The company plans to build a massive AI data centre in Inner Mongolia using 160,000 Huawei AI chips, aiming to advance its large language model technology. DeepSeek's founder prioritises pushing AI technology boundaries over monetisation, reflecting China's ambition to compete globally in artificial intelligence. DeepSeek is close to securing at least 80 billion yuan (S$15 billion) in its latest round of funding, blowing past its own capital-raising target ahead of a landmark initial public offering in early 2027 . Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) and WeChat-operator Tencent Holdings have committed among the largest amounts in the current financing, which closes soon, sources familiar with the matter said. DeepSeek initially sought about 50 billion yuan, but interest outstripped expectations after the successful release of its latest AI model, the sources said, asking not to be named as the details are not public. Based on term sheets signed, the final tally could approach 100 billion yuan, they added. The company is riding high after the release of the V4 Flash large language model, which reset expectations for cost versus performance against leaders Anthropic and OpenAI. That caps a strong run for founder Liang Wenfeng , whose start-up has forged a reputation for technical breakthroughs since a 2025 model that matched the capabilities of Silicon Valley offerings at a fraction of the cost. As with other artificial intelligence players, DeepSeek requires huge amounts of capital to bankroll its ambitions in a potentially revolutionary technology. The company plans to deploy at least 160,000 of Huawei Technologies’ top accelerators at a massive data centre it is building in Inner Mongolia, which may create one of the largest known clusters of Huawei AI chips. It has publicly released software created with Huawei to program AI chips, a foray into a new arena in close partnership with the hardware leader . Rival Moonshot, meanwhile, is also targeting an early 2027 IPO after closing funding at a US$50 billion (S$64 billion) valuation. Liang pledged in at least one meeting with investors in 2026 that he will keep developing open AI models while pursuing a broader goal of achieving artificial general intelligence. The hedge fund manager made it clear his main goal was to push the boundaries of the technology rather than monetisation, Bloomberg News has reported. While discussions around the current deal are near an end, details may still change in final talks, the sources said. DeepSeek had originally targeted a valuation of about 500 billion yuan in its financing. A CATL representative declined to comment, while Tencent had no immediate comment. DeepSeek did not respond to an e-mailed request for comment during a Chinese public holiday. DeepSeek has drawn enormous interest from would-be investors because it is one of a clutch of companies that sit at the heart of China’s effort to compete globally on AI. Once the round closes, the next step should be to restructure the company to prepare for an IPO, the sources said. Tencent, which also landed the biggest investment in the start-up at 10 billion yuan in a previous round of financing, aims to integrate AI into its platforms. CATL may be eyeing an increasingly lucrative business of supplying components to the industry, including for data centres. The AI lab’s capital-raising had attracted its share of controversy. DeepSeek briefly suspended the deal after comments widely attributed to Liang about US-Chinese AI competition went viral on social media. Chinese media outlet Yicai reported in July that the billionaire entrepreneur had talked about a reliance on Nvidia chips and China’s persistent lag in AI sophistication relative to the US. Liang’s net worth more than doubled to around US$36 billion when DeepSeek closed its first round of external fund raising this summer. The AI start-up grew as an offshoot from his hedge fund High-Flyer, which provided much of the initial support. Liang contributed again in the previous 50 billion yuan round, which valued DeepSeek at roughly 350 billion yuan at the time. BLOOMBERG

The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what 1 day ago OpenAI is now offering API customers the option to watermark the output of certain models in order to comply with the letter of Europe's AI Act. And within a few weeks, the biz plans to apply a form of digital watermarking – like it or not – to eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union. But unlike rival Anthropic, it isn't applying its watermarking technique to content generated outside of Europe, though API customers can choose to have the marks applied to content made anywhere. Moreover, OpenAI is using technology that misses a fair number of instances of AI-generated text and can easily be tricked. The EU AI Act requires generative AI service providers to make model output identifiable in a way that's readable by machines. Anthropic was the first major AI company to announce its approach to AI Act compliance, which involves the application of Google's SynthID-Text algorithm. It's doing so globally. Microsoft and Meta have been working on similar technology for image-based AI because the EU is not the only market in which people have raised concerns about content provenance and the potential to use AI-generated content to produce misinformation. OpenAI already applies other content provenance signals to AI-generated images, audio, and video. In keeping with the letter of the AI Act, OpenAI is now offering a text watermarking approach called textGrain [PDF] that "adds an invisible statistical signal to the model’s word choices. Our detector looks for that signal to assess whether a passage contains an OpenAI watermark." Large language models predict word tokens one at a time from a probability distribution of potential words. By picking a different word to emit periodically – ideally a synonym – the resulting text deviates from the statistical pattern produced by an unbiased model. A watermark detector, which OpenAI is making available only to approved researchers and organizations, should flag that vocabulary divergence. That's the theory, but in practice results vary. The target error rate is one percent, but in short passages of 200 words, the detector may only flag 80 percent of the watermarks, compared to 95 percent in a 400-word passage. The results are also worse in texts that are functional, like passages about math or code, as substitutions are more likely to introduce errors. The textGrain paper does not address the likelihood that a statistically altered word choice might alter the meaning of a given passage. That's a possibility if the algorithm were to alter some salient fact or figure. Anthropic's approach, which also replaces certain output words though using a different algorithm, brings similar risks. In any event, OpenAI's watermark is easily defeated by word substitution. In tests on 400-token passages, swapping out 10 percent of the words with synonyms reduced watermark detection from 92 percent to 66 percent. And when replacing 25 percent of words, the watermark signal could only be detected in 17 percent of cases.

events.title: Nvidia-backed start-up Reflection unveils open AI model to rival China offerings
events.summary: The AI model is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks. Reflection AI, founded by ex-Google DeepMind researchers, launched Beam, an open-weight AI model rivaling leading US and Chinese options for business and coding tasks. Beam matches China's GLM-5.2 in reasoning benchmarks and is cost-effective, with more technical details due in October. Backed by Nvidia, Reflection secured major deals with SpaceX and Nebius, supporting US efforts to promote AI exports and counter Chinese tech influence. SAN FRANCISCO – Reflection AI, an artificial intelligence start-up from two former Google DeepMind researchers, has unveiled a new open-weight model that it says rivals leading options in the US and China. The model, called Beam, is designed to perform well for business customers and developers on coding and AI agent tasks while costing less than many competitors, the company said on Oct 5. It said Beam scores comparably on advanced reasoning benchmarks to GLM-5.2, a flagship open model from China’s Z.AI. Reflection intends to release more technical details about the model later in October. While China is still widely viewed as behind the US in AI, Chinese developers like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI have gained ground by offering cheaper and customisable open model. Top US firms, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have primarily focused on closed or proprietary offerings as they work to build up their enterprise businesses. Reflection emerged from stealth in 2025 with a focus on developing open AI models. The firm is backed by Nvidia and other investors. It has held talks to raise US$2.5 billion (S$3.2 billion) at a valuation of US$25 billion, the Wall Street Journal previously reported. The start-up has also struck billion-dollar deals with Elon Musk’s SpaceX and cloud provider Nebius Group to secure computing power to develop its models. The model release stands to boost the American government’s efforts to export the US and its allies’ AI abroad. Earlier in 2026, Reflection was part of a US-brokered deal to build sovereign AI in Korea. Officials are planning to cobble together more of these deals promoting exports of US tech, which are designed to prevent the spread of Chinese alternatives. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Australian consumer confidence plunges to worst level since 1990s after RBA rate rise
events.summary: Key indicator dropped about 20% after the Reserve Bank last month announced the highest interest rates since 2011 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian households are the most persistently pessimistic they have been since the early-1990s recession, after a fourth rate rise this year. Confidence among Australian consumers has plunged about 20% since the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted interest rates to the highest levels since 2011, according to the Westpac–Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index. The survey, conducted between 28 September and 1 October, showed the confidence index dropped by 4.7% to 80.4% in October – the worst level since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict in early April. But for respondents surveyed after the RBA call on 29 September, the index dropped to 67.2% – the lowest level since the late 1990s. That was broadly in line with the weekly ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer survey, which fell about 5% to 67.1 points. Westpac’s head of Australian macro-forecasting, Matthew Hassan, said sentiment had been extremely weak for the longest period since the “disastrous” recession of the early 1990s. “Australian consumers remain stuck in a cost-of-living nightmare that seems to have no end in sight,” Hassan said. “The latest RBA move looks to have badly rattled consumers. Responses over the course of the survey week show a very sharp deterioration after the decision was announced.” Assessments of family finances and buyer sentiment were the biggest categories affected. Expectations about the economic outlook fell less sharply, but assessments about the economy in the next five years were back to lows not seen since August 2020, shortly after Melbourne’s second lockdown and before jobkeeper subsidies were expanded. AMP economist My Bui said the decline was unsurprising given the September rate hike and rising fuel prices. “On our calculation the weekly petrol bill for a typical Australian household has gone up by $20 versus the beginning of the year,” Bui said. “The worry with declining confidence is that it tends to correlate with household spending on a per capita basis: the downtrend in confidence over the past 12 months suggests consumption per person will likely fall further into contraction this year.” Mortgage holders were the most pessimistic home ownership subgroup given rising borrowing costs at 77 index points. Those who own their home outright experienced the largest decline in sentiment in the month, as the housing market downturn extended for a sixth month. Renters were the most optimistic, unchanged at 84.8 points. Hassan said fears of job losses were rising, with unemployment expectations ticking up 1.9% higher. But there are still signs the labour market is holding strong. Citi analysts Josh Williamson and Faraz Syed said “job vacancies have increased to a two-year high of 122 points, which accords with business sentiment expectations of positive employment growth”.

events.title: Irish budget tackles childcare and energy costs
events.summary: Childcare subsidies will be increased in new budget The Irish government has used its budget to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs. Taxes on heating oil and gas will be cut and then frozen for the lifetime of the government. Temporary tax cuts on petrol and diesel, which were introduced earlier this year , will be extended. Childcare subsidies will be increased which will be worth up €2,220 (£1,882) per child per year. Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers and Minister for Finance Simon Harris Finance Minister Simon Harris and Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers announced a budget package worth a total of €8.65bn (£7.33bn), €7bn (£5.93bn) on spending and €1.65bn (£1.40bn) in tax changes. Harris raised the threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax from €44,000 to €46,500 (£37,307 to £39,418.05). He said that, alongside other changes, a single person earning €50,000 (£42,395) a year will pay €700 (£593.25) less in personal taxes. Harris added that the government had heard "loud and clear" the importance of an income tax package for middle earners. "People are working hard and doing their best. They need the government to work with them and we get that." Ireland collects more taxes than it spends on services Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services. Harris said the government expects to run a surplus of €6.7bn (£5.7bn) this year and a surplus of €9.5bn (£8.1bn) in 2027. Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments. A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has previously criticised the government for not saving more. Harris said an extra €1bn (£847m) of the surplus would be invested in 2027 on top of the already planned transfer of €4.8bn (£4.1bn). €11m to support cross community projects in NI Other new measures announced on Tuesday include a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK's stock and shares ISA. It will allow people to invest up to €50,000 (£42,395) tax free, with sums above that taxed at a flat rate of 1% a year. There will be a new €15m (£12.7m) fund to help keep rural pubs open, with the details of grants and eligibility to be developed in coming weeks. Chambers restated the government's commitment to fund a range of cross-Irish border projects through the Shared Island Scheme. These include the Narrow Water Bridge and a teaching block at Ulster University in Londonderry. He said there would also be €11m (£9.3m) for the Reconciliation Fund, which supports cross community projects in Northern Ireland and additional money for next year's Belfast Fleadh. events.title: Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
events.summary: Keith Ely remembers the Brunel Centre's heyday but is looking to the future The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide. "It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973. Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw. Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling. Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left. That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year . But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space. "It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me." The Debenhams store in the Grafton Centre in Cambridge closed in 2021 In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema. There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre. This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country. So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls? "There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre. "The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet." Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, Before the Brunel Shopping Centre was built in the 1970s, people in Bletchley would travel to Aylesbury or Bedford to shop Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, The centre initially had little natural light, before the roof was replaced with glass Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, In 2021 Milton Keynes City Council was awarded £22.7m from the government's Town Deal Fund to redevelop the site Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, Boots Opticians, the last remaining store in the centre, is already closed on Wednesdays Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE , external found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres. Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres. Dr Kardi Somerfield says centres that have leisure businesses can "extend the day" and attract customers into the evening "It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton. Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds. Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops. "The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open." The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses. Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing. Characters from TV show The Flintstones were at the opening of the Weston Favell Shopping Centre in 1974 But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down. Market Walk in Northampton is t o become a leisure and entertainment space . "Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use. This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton. Footfall – the number of customers entering the building – has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg. "We are still relevant today," he says. "Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got." What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities. Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible. Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store. Silhouette Youth Theatre currently holds sessions in the Emmanuel Church, inside Weston Favell Shopping Centre George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Death of a star may not be game over for the inner solar system after all Google launches first datacenter satellite and research that finds orbiting bit barns can work 5 days ago Boeing's Calamity Capsule gets another shot at the ISS taxi business 7 days ago Starship finally makes orbit but engine trouble cuts the victory lap short 7 days ago Astronomer watches Starlink satellites sinking to build a ‘planetary barometer’ 11 days ago Google's TPUs to catch some rays in orbit next week 12 days ago When yellow dwarf stars like our sun die, they swell to an enormous size and destroy their inner planets by either crushing them with massive gravity or evaporating them with astounding heat. While these suns later settle down to become a white dwarf, the process is nearly always game over for planets in an inner solar system. Or maybe not, according to a paper published on Monday titled “Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf.” As explained by NASA’s Hubble Mission team, the paper’s authors pored over Hubble Space Telescope observations of white dwarf star HS 0209+0832 from 1999. According to the paper, data from those scans “revealed the presence of carbon, aluminum, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere, as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified.” The authors of this paper used new techniques to identify the mystery matter, and concluded that there’s plenty of the element niobium present in what looks like a gas giant orbiting HS 0209+0832. In NASA’s post, co-author Nicholas Stone, a theoretical astrophysicist at the University of Wisconsin, pointed out that “Niobium and other elements heavier than iron are astronomically special because, unlike many common elements, they are not formed in the cores of stars by thermonuclear fusion.” “Instead, these heavy elements can only be synthesized in the exotic conditions that briefly emerge inside dying stars. The presence of niobium is a signpost of these ‘death’ throes, and the expulsion of the dying star's innards into space.” Finding niobium is also notable because, as the paper explains, “the canonical rock-forming elements [are] silicon and iron.” The paper explains that its authors compared the material observed at HS 0209+0832 with all known examples of rocky material around white dwarfs, and to all meteorites in our Solar System, but could find “no compositional matches.” That finding suggests that the niobium-rich gas giant at HS 0209+0832 represents both a secondary planet – which are rare – and a body composed of material we’ve not previously seen becoming a planet. It also shows that planets can form close to a star after the hellish red giant phase. Oh, and let’s not forget that HS 0209+0832 is also an exoplanet, a class of body humanity first spotted in only 1992. The paper suggests the niobium gas giant is about the size of Jupiter, but that the white dwarf is blasting away its atmosphere and perhaps creating “a comet-like tail of material that would form a disk around the white dwarf star and fall back on to its surface, leading to Hubble detecting the niobium when studying the star” Co-author Jamie Williams, from the Department of Physics at the University of Warwick, told NASA he thinks the niobium world will stick around. “If the second-generation planet is there, I think it is likely to survive. Eventually the white dwarf will cool and then maintain a consistent temperature, with the planet in its stable habitable zone for millions of years,” Williams said.

events.title: Banks still refusing credit cards, watchdog says
events.summary: The Government of Jersey said whether credit cards were offered to islanders "remains a commercial decision" Islanders are still struggling to get credit cards despite personal data changes to make it easier to apply for one, a consumer council has said. The changes which came into force on 30 July meant the government could securely share personal data with UK credit reference agencies, which had been seen as the main barrier to successful applications . However, the Jersey Consumer Council said several providers had still refused applications and called for the government to work closer with businesses and banks. A spokesperson for Jersey's government said it had "engaged with providers throughout this process" and whether products were offered in the island "remains a commercial decision". Carl Walker from the Jersey Consumer Council said credit card companies may need convincing to bring their business back Carl Walker, from Jersey Consumer Council, said credit card companies would need to be reminded of the change which had allowed more information to be shared. "The last time they were involved... Jersey was slamming the door shut, so they have switched off and turned their attention elsewhere," he said. "We're pushing the government to write them an official letter to say this piece of legislation has now changed, Jersey's now open for business... and then leave it up to them whether they decide they to come back or not." Listen to the latest news for Jersey A spokesperson said the government had "successfully delivered a project to share islanders' data with credit reference agencies". "This was a key issue identified by the industry as an obstacle to providing credit cards in Jersey," they said. "It remains a commercial decision for providers to decide whether to offer their products or services, including credit cards, in Jersey. "The government has engaged with providers throughout this process... and will continue to do so." Follow BBC Jersey on X , external , Facebook , external and Instagram , external . events.title: ‘It really hammers people’: Scottish islanders hit by highest diesel prices in UK
events.summary: Inhabitants of the Hebrides and Shetland tell of how fuel costs are putting the squeeze on commuting, services, food and more A s fuel prices reach the highest level in the UK since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Scottish islanders are feeling the pain more than most. On the mainland, the price of diesel has soared to a record high of 200.01p a litre, bringing the cost of filling an average family car to more than £110, according to the RAC. Petrol has risen by a third since the start of the Iran war at the end of February, averaging 174.71p – increasing to 195.64p in motorway service areas. In the Hebrides and Shetland, prices at the forecourt have jumped even higher, with some fuel stations selling diesel for more than 220p a litre during the initial rise. While European governments appear to have staved off a US export ban that could have sent prices even higher, in Shetland the lack of competition and the cost of shipping to remote areas have made it the most expensive place in the UK for fuel. The ramifications for island life have been immediate. Adam, 43, who lives in North Uist in the Outer Hebrides, said diesel had reached £2.28 a litre on the island, making his 45-mile round commute particularly expensive. He and his wife have diesel cars that they need for work and transporting their three children. “You accept that things are more expensive, especially food because there’s more distance to travel and we are further from distribution centres. Same with getting things delivered here because you have to drive more miles. But when something like the price of diesel skyrockets, it really hammers people here more than other places around the country,’” he says. In between work and dropping children off with his wife, Adam says they really rack up the miles. To cut costs, Adam says the family is having to buy the cheapest food they can, given that food prices are also dependent on the price of diesel that haulage companies pay. “It’s come down a bit in the last week or so. I never thought I’d look up at a £2.18 diesel price and think: ‘Oh, quick, I better fill up now.’ It’s really bad. Although people think of this place as really tiny, you’re in your car all the time. I average 15,000 miles a year, and my wife does even more because she’s a health visitor. She gets the same mileage as someone who’s a health visitor in the central belt, yet we pay a lot more,” he says. About 26,000 people live in the Outer Hebrides, most on the largest island, Lewis and Harris. Adam says rising prices have also hit accessibility to public services, which are already difficult to reach for islanders. “The Scottish government say they want to help repopulate places like this but in reality, they are not offering much practical support. For example, my daughter had a referral to a paediatrician for a hearing test so I had to take her to Stornoway for that. It involved booking ferries, driving more than 100 miles and staying in a hotel. We can claim some money back from the patient travel scheme but they only offer you £40-£50 for a hotel. Because of the costs getting there, the NHS stops being free at the point of use because we can’t be treated locally,” he says. Bob, a postman who lives in Shetland, said that people in the North Sea archipelago were frustrated by rising fuel prices while also being a hub for the oil and gas industry. “You are resigned to it. It’s always been slightly more expensive than everywhere else, so you have to pay the prices. What can you do? Fuel poverty has always been an issue up here. It’s ironic in a sense given we are near where a lot of the oil and gas arrives from the North Sea. Yet, we are paying higher prices than anyone else. It’s the same with the windfarms,” he says. Bob says that islanders often have no other choice but to drive, especially when getting to work. “Most jobs are in Lerwick so unless you live in town, you need to drive. There is a bus service but people who work don’t use it much because it’s difficult to make their hours,” he says. “I only ever drive small cars. I have a Fiat 500 so it’s not too bad. But an awful lot of people have big 4x4s up here because of the weather. Diesel prices will be having a big impact on them.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Ryan, 25, from the Isle of Benbecula in the Outer Hebrides, says the soaring costs mean many islanders are having to cut back. “A lot of family and friends up here are taking fewer journeys than they would normally outside work. For a lot of people, it’s a case of just going to work and going to the shops. Even those journeys are not short. The Western Isles span 130 miles. South Uist itself is about an hour top to bottom. A lot of us easily get through a few tanks a month on fuel. It’s a lot of the money that’s getting spent up here,” he says. Ryan works in a nearby hotel and is paid close to the minimum wage.

events.title: UK regulator FCA to investigate how it handled Epstein whistleblower who took his own life
events.summary: British banker Simon Andriesz helped to expose alleged ties between late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick A top UK regulator has launched an investigation into how it handled a whistleblower – who highlighted alleged ties between the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and the US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick – after he took his own life. The British banker Simon Andriesz died late last month aged 57, the campaign group Transparency Task Force, of which he was a member, confirmed over the weekend. Andriesz had formerly worked as a managing director at BGC Group, the financial brokerage where Lutnick had been chief executive. He had accused the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) of failing to hold his former employer to account for alleged wrongdoing, and had been wrongly told he did not qualify for whistleblower protection. The banker had spent years raising concerns about his former employer: first in regards to accounting irregularities – which he raised internally at BGC in 2016, a year before he was sacked – and then in 2020-21, when he reportedly told the FBI that Lutnick had undeclared business ties with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Lutnick has since said he had no “personal or professional relationship” with Epstein. He was named Donald Trump’s commerce secretary in late 2024. Andriesz, who had been living in Cornwall, later unearthed an email chain in the Epstein files that suggested Lutnick and Epstein had discussed the prospects of a startup business they were both involved in, in 2018. Epstein died in jail in August 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. However, Andriesz told the BBC’s File on 4 Investigates this summer that authorities in the US and UK had failed to hold BGC and its parent company, Cantor Fitzgerald, properly to account, or protect him from potential retaliation. He also later accused the FCA of mistreating whistleblowers, and raised concerns about the toll that whistleblowing had taken on his family, career and health. The FCA had also given Andriesz misleading information, saying he would not qualify for whistleblower protection because his identity had become known. The regulator apologised to him and said that further guidance and training would be provided to its whistleblowing team. The FCA confirmed it had now tasked a new board member to investigate how staff handled Andriesz’s concerns. “We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz’s death,” an FCA spokesperson said. “Our thoughts are with his family and friends. Since expressing our condolences, we’d asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future.” However, the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) on investment fraud and fairer financial services is concerned that the FCA is being allowed to “mark its own homework” and called on the regulator to pay an independent party to “forensically and objectively evaluate its handling of whistleblowers”. The APPG’s chair, the Labour MP John McDonnell, said: “It is vital that this time a truly independent and non-conflicted organisation carries out the work needed. If the FCA refuses to respond positively, the APPG will consider all alternatives, including conducting its own call for evidence from whistleblowers who have interacted with the regulator.” Lutnick has not been accused of any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein, and has previously said: “I unequivocally condemn the conduct attributed to Jeffrey Epstein and everyone who participated in his illegal activities. The survivors of his crimes deserve our respect and support.” A BGC spokesperson said: “BGC has long disputed Mr Andriesz’s allegations but does not intend to relitigate these matters at this sad time. BGC is sorry to hear this tragic news and expresses our condolences to Mr Andriesz’s family.” In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org , or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

events.title: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess | Gaby Hinsliff
events.summary: Burnham’s surprise EU-turn could deliver the Tories from a generational mess Badenoch would never have reopened the door on Brexit, but now that the PM has, it suits the Conservatives to let him walk through it T here’s no way on earth it should have worked, but somehow he may have got away with it. Last week, the actor Richard E Grant became the first contestant on The Traitors – a show whose only unbreakable rule is never to let anyone know you’re the murderer – to gleefully announce within minutes of being selected that yes, haha, it’s him! Yet even then many of his fellow contestants seemed to like him too much to recoil. And that, roughly speaking, is now Andy Burnham’s Brexit strategy. After years of Labour politicians – not least Burnham himself, in the Makerfield byelection , without which he would not now be prime minister – trying to hide their real feelings about Brexit, Burnham has decided just to tell the truth and hope people roll with it. Leaving hasn’t worked, he said bluntly last week in Liverpool , and Britain should consider the alternatives. If you’re a leaver who suspects him of being out to unwind Brexit – well, yes, he is. This bold strategy seemingly surprised much of his own cabinet , an early lesson in how he likes to work for those who hadn’t studied his Manchester operation closely enough. But the oddly muted initial response to what would once have been a seismic shock suggests it’s wrongfooting some opponents, too. Nigel Farage has been the only one to react with unfettered glee . Reform’s next manifesto is basically now written for him: save Brexit, stop the boats and don’t vote for Restore because it can’t win. Things are more complicated for the Lib Dems and Greens, who, having pitched themselves as the only real pro-Europeans on the left, are now stuck with trying to take credit for pushing Labour into doing the right thing. But it’s the party currently holding its conference in Birmingham that faces the most interesting dilemma. Kemi Badenoch doesn’t mention Brexit much these days – only elected after the referendum, she seems to regard the generational Conservative trauma of that period as history now – and it gets only brief mentions in The Right Way , the 95-page personal essay she says would form the bedrock of a Tory government. In his platform speech on Monday, the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, chose to focus on accusing Burnham of supposedly dragging Britain back to the 1970s, rather than back to 2015. On this they echo much of what’s left of the Tory vote, who are more interested in tax, the costs of doing business, small boats and what exactly Labour has against labradors in pubs than in relitigating the Brexit deal. Yet the Conservatives are still promising to reverse any Labour unravelling of Brexit, regardless of how that affects the economic growth Badenoch simultaneously insists is everything to her. It makes no intellectual sense, which arguably didn’t bother previous Tory leaders. But it’s a mistake for one pitching herself as a rigorous thinker, approaching power with the same robustly worked-through theory of the world as Thatcher in the 1970s. Growth is now Badenoch’s rationale for everything, from scrapping the Environment Agency – accused of being a drag on developers, although that’s precisely what some rural Tory voters like about it – to giving parents earning over £100,000 free childcare (on the grounds that, currently, high earners will cut their working hours rather than lose that nursery place). It’s her defence for some potentially unpopular choices, her alpha and omega. Yet by ignoring the ongoing damage Brexit is doing to trade and GDP, Badenoch is chopping her self-professed growth mission off at the knees. In her 1976 essay The Right Approach , which Badenoch’s treatise consciously echoes, Margaret Thatcher declared that her party “has always been outward-looking, while concerned with the security, the economic interests and the honour of Britain”, and lambasted Labour’s lack of enthusiasm for the then European Community. The context now is obviously different, but Thatcher in 1976 was still a pragmatist arguing for Europe “to concentrate on what is practical and what is attainable”, where Badenoch in 2026 is an ideologue. The Tory brand remains toxic despite its leader’s relative popularity mostly because voters got sick of endless Brexit-related drama consuming Westminster, while none of the practical benefits materialised. There’s no point dangling policies such as free childcare for bankers over the remain-voting former Tory shires without acknowledging all that. But if she can’t bring herself to do so, then Badenoch’s next best bet is to let Burnham rescue her party from a dead end of its own making. Though they would never have opened this door, in truth it suits the Tories to let Burnham walk through it, while blaming him for whatever goes wrong.

events.title: World Bank says Middle East economy to contract 2.1% in 2026 due to Iran war
events.summary: The World Bank on Tuesday lowered its 2026 forecast for the economies in the Middle East , saying the region's overall GDP will contract by 2.1 per cent for this year. The revision was the latest downgrade the World Bank has forecast for the region as the Iran war continues to constrain energy supplies. Economists had previously lowered their 2026 forecasts from 3.6 per cent in January to 2.1 per cent in April. Global growth, meanwhile, is projected to slow to 2.5 per cent this year, the World Bank had said in June. The seven-month conflict has affected a wide variety of sectors as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz initially choked off much of the region's energy supplies. This also led to setbacks in tourism, aviation and logistics, with uncertainty in financial markets, the World Bank said in its latest Economic Update for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (Menaap). “This conflict is very painful and it has concentrated the losses of the conflict in our region while the global economy and other regions are upgrading their forecasts, and we are downgrading significantly,” Roberta Gatti, Menaap chief economist at the World Bank, said in an interview. Economies in the Gulf Co-operation Council are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue. Economies in the UAE and Saudi Arabia are set to slow from 6.2 and 4.6 per cent in 2025 to minus 1.6 and minus 2 per cent in 2026, respectively, the World Bank said. Qatar is forecast to have its weakest economic performance in five decades, slowing from 1.8 per cent growth in 2025 to minus 20.9 per cent this year after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites. Kuwait's economy is forecast to contract by 14.6 per cent, a downwards revision of 8.2 percentage points from April. The war has hit oil exporters particularly hard, with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks across the region. Oil production in the Gulf dropped from its prewar average of 26 million barrels a day to about 16 million in March, the World Bank said. The IMF's PortWatch monitor showed just three tankers moved through the strait in the seven-day moving average ending September 27. “It's a volume story. It's a quantity story for us. It's a price story for the world,” Ms Gatti said. Oman, which is less reliant on the Strait of Hormuz, is the only GCC member projected to experience positive growth this year, at 3.1 per cent. Iraq 's growth prospects also faced a downwards revision of 3.8 percentage points since April with a negative growth rate of 12.4 per cent. Iraq, which is Opec's second-largest producer, depends on oil for about 90 per cent of its government revenue. Iran's economy also expected to shrink by 7.7 per cent in 2026. The World Bank report works on the assumption that the Strait of Hormuz will gradually reopen beginning on December 31. Under this scenario, economic activity in 2027 for the UAE will rebound to 8 per cent, Saudi Arabia by 6.1 per cent, Qatar by 25 per cent, Kuwait by 20.5 per cent and the GCC as a whole by 8.6 per cent. The UAE has embarked on a “ Zero Hormuz ” strategy to diversify its supply chains, while Saudi Arabia has relied on its East-West Pipeline to move oil to Yanbu Port on the Red Sea. Oil prices have swung wildly since the onset of the war on February 28, with global benchmark Brent crude trading at about $118 a barrel in March and in May. Saudi Aramco chief Amin Nasser credited the East-West Pipeline for keeping oil prices at about $100 a barrel. Mr Nasser also warned it could take up to two years to refill global inventories that were reduced under emergency measures. He was speaking at an energy conference in London on Monday. Oil importers, by contrast, are expected to fare better in what Ms Gatti described as a “reversal of fortunes” compared to the 2022 energy shock after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The World Bank anticipates Egypt's economic activity to pick up at a 5.1 per cent pace after growing by 4.4 per cent last year. It also raised its 2026 forecast for Morocco by 0.2 percentage points to 4.4 per cent, and 0.7 percentage points for Pakistan at 3.7 per cent. Its projection for Jordan remained unchanged at 2.7 per cent, while Tunisia received a slight downgrade of 2.3 per cent growth, 0.2 percentage points lower than its April forecast. Compounding effect Ms Gatti said the Iran war is placing a compounding effect on economies already mired in conflict, harming recovery prospects and contributing to long-term economic pain. Renewed hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah are reversing Lebanon's economic recovery of 4.2 per cent growth in 2025 to a contraction of 6.4 per cent this year. Forecasts for growth in Afghanistan and Yemen were also lowered to 3 per cent and 1 per cent respectively, while the World Bank anticipates Syria's economy to pick up between 8 and 10 per cent this year. The World Bank estimates GDP growth in the West Bank and Gaza will slow from 4.3 per cent in 2025 to 1.5 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 3 percentage points compared to April. The poverty rate in the area remains an estimated 41.9 per cent. It also said Gaza's economy is still in a state of “near-total collapse” despite the October 2025 ceasefire, owing to flare-ups in tensions, continued restrictions and stalled reconstruction preventing recovery efforts. “There were ongoing fragilities and now we see less humanitarian aid. We see a need to keep the attention,” Ms Gatti said. She said the economic costs of fragility were being compounded by the conflict, with reduced humanitarian aid making it important to maintain attention and investment in affected countries to prevent the consequences from being felt by future generations. AI productivity gains The report also said that, despite the conflict, artificial intelligence remains a key avenue for opportunity in the region. Economists said it could boost the productivity of up to 20 per cent of the region's jobs. The World Bank has previously urged developing countries to quickly adopt AI or risk falling behind on the economic gains it can deliver. It said developing economies can avoid mistakes by adopting available tools, adapting them to local conditions and advancing towards frontier AI development. “Some of the complements that are needed to fit the benefits of AI might not require money, but they require political will and vision. You need regulation and ethical regulation for AI to operate well,” Ms Gatti said.

events.title: Community supermarket opens in shopping centre
events.summary: Gina English from the SEK Community Food Shop in Chatham says the store is open to everyone A new community supermarket offering access to affordable and healthy food has opened in a Kent shopping centre. The store run by SEK Community Food Shop welcomed the public to its home on the first floor of The Pentagon Centre in Chatham. Gina English from SEK says the shop is open to all as "in addition to supporting people with food insecurity, people will also be able get wraparound support from us, help with employment, looking at CVs and interview skills. We're also going to help people with budgeting and money management and signposting to other local services". Initial funding to set up the supermarket was provided by Medway Council through the Crisis and Resilience Fund. Shoppers can walk straight into the social supermarket, with no prior booking required, to access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries, including a £1 fruit and vegetable bag. Cost are kept low as the store redistributes surplus food to reduce waste, helping to protect the environment at the same time. SEK already operates two similar stores in Kent. English said: "We've had Ramsgate for about three years, Ashford just for just over a year and across the two shops in the last year alone we saw 55,500 transactions and we were able to save 170 tonnes of perfectly good food from going to waste, so they do work." Rod Taffs and Shirley Graves from Chatham were among the first customers into the newly opened community supermarket Some of the first to experienced the store were Shirley Graves and her partner Rod Taffs who have already filled their basket with bargains. "People want to come down and see what they've got, it's amazing," says Graves. "I've got a box of 20 samosas for £1.50 and a big huge bag of chicken for £6. Times are quite tight at the moment, being pensioners, it's cheap and the chicken is amazing." "That's going to do us three or four meals," adds Taffs. Medway Council leader, Vince Maple, said: "I think most people across Kent and Medway would want to see food not going to waste, so the ability to have good quality food at a reasonable price, helping not just our families and individuals on low incomes but helping all families has got to be a good thing." The shop also has a confidential, soundproofed office pod at the back of the store where customers can seek personal advice and guidance. The SEK Community Food Shop in The Pentagon Centre, Chatham, is open Monday to Saturday between 10:00 and 18:00. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Tells users ‘action required’ – but maybe don’t make that action a Jira ticket, because it has this bug ServiceNow under siege as Atlassian adds to ITSM take-outs May 1, 2026 Atlassian’s new data collection policy protects rich customers while AI eats the rest April 18, 2026 Atlassian gussies up Confluence for the AI era April 9, 2026 OpenAI now gets to decide which type of product assassin it will become March 25, 2026 Atlassian to shed ten percent of staff, because AI March 12, 2026 Atlassian has told its users to patch its datacenter products, pronto, to prevent attackers accessing their files. The Australian collaborationware company on Monday sent users an email that opens with the words “Action required” and points to a security bulletin that explains CVE-2026-21589 . The 9.3-rated arbitrary file access vulnerability is present in the datacenter versions of its Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye products. Atlassian says the vulnerability “allows an unauthenticated attacker to access specific files within the web application root directory in affected versions.” That’s scary because Atlassian warns “In some configurations, there may be sensitive files present that increase your risk.” There’s also some good news in that attackers must know the exact filename and path to exploit the vulnerability, and the mess doesn’t allow anyone to see the contents of a directory. Another piece of good news is that Atlassian has updated its products – so users only need to find a change window in which to upgrade to a safe version of their software. Atlassian advised those who can’t patch ASAP to remove their instances from the internet, if possible. “Instances accessible to the public internet, including those with user authentication, should be restricted from external network access until you can take action,” the company warned. Its advisory also includes mitigations and advice on how to determine if your instances need the fix. Users who made the move from datacenter products to the Atlassian cloud have nothing to do, as Atlassian fixed the flaws in its own SaaS. That state of affairs rather vindicates Atlassian’s 2020 decision to stop developing its low-end server products and require users to shift into its cloud , and last year’s sequel in which it decided to discontinue its datacenter software , too. Atlassian admitted it hasn’t made that migration easy, because it somehow released a lift and shift tool that was worse than an earlier version . In March 2026, Atlassian axed ten percent of staff . The company’s share price was on a year-long slide at the time, as pundits suggested it might fall victim to the SaaSPocalypse, a theory that AI would replace business software. events.title: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
events.summary: It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff? T emperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.” I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues. Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan. Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh. And while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”. For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come. Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this “little treat” economy , eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.” While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque. It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs. It was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer. Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.

events.title: Arizona welcomes new Taiwan representative office, rejecting warning from China
events.summary: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an office in Phoenix to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region PHOENIX -- Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs joined Taiwanese leaders at the opening of an economic and cultural office Monday to aid Taiwanese businesses and citizens in the region, despite pressure from the Chinese government to block it. Taiwanese authorities have said the new Phoenix office — their 14th in the United States — will promote collaboration in technology, especially in semiconductor manufacturing, and better serve a growing number of Taiwanese migrants in the city. After the plans for the office were announced in July, Hobbs received two letters from China’s consulate general in Los Angeles asking her to object to the proposal, according to documents the governor’s office shared with The Associated Press. In a July 3 letter, the Chinese authority called the governor to “refute such an attempt by the Taiwan authorities and stop any political gimmicks to harm the friendship and cooperation between China and the State of Arizona.” The stance was reiterated in an Aug. 21 letter. The letters were first reported by Phoenix radio station KJZZ. Hobbs highlighted Arizona’s ties with Taiwan at Monday’s opening. “Every Arizona elected official should show the courage necessary to support the partnership between Arizona and Taiwan,” Hobbs said. “As our economic partnership grows, we are mobilizing every available resource to support Taiwanese companies expanding here in Arizona.” Beijing claims the island as a breakaway province inseparable from China, while Taiwan considers itself separate from the Chinese mainland and has its own government. Scholars say that local-level collaborations with the Chinese government and Taiwan have become more politicized as U.S.-China relations have deteriorated over the years. Taiwan has been increasing its economic footprint in Arizona, with advanced chipmaker Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, pledging $100 billion to expand its operation in northern Phoenix. That brings its total investment in the city to $265 billion, the largest foreign direct investment in U.S. history. Around 500 Taiwanese engineers are working to ramp up production at TSMC in Arizona, according to Jason Hsu, a former lawmaker in Taiwan and a senior fellow at the public policy think tank Hudson Institute. Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego also said the city is seeing a sort of “baby boom” in its Taiwanese communities, with several labor and delivery rooms even launching Mandarin language programs. events.title: OKX debuts a platform that turns 50 currencies into digital dollars, betting emerging-market investors want stablecoins
events.summary: Crypto exchange OKX launched a stand-alone app on Tuesday that lets users convert more than 50 local currencies into U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins, as the company tries to expand its offerings beyond just being an exchange. OKX Money, which went live at the company’s OKX Now product event in Singapore, is aimed at emerging markets in Latin America, Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East. OKX argues that currency swings, limited banking access, and foreign-exchange fees in those regions make it difficult to “protect savings and spend globally.” “The key gap for people and institutions is settlement,” Haider Rafique, OKX’s global managing partner, tells Fortune. He specifically cites two friction points: A small business shouldn’t wait days for a bank to settle a payment, and a traveler shouldn’t have a credit limit frozen by pending hotel deposits. “I grew up in Pakistan,” he says. “I still have all the receipts of my mom and dad sending me money through Western Union ,” along with the memory of the fees paid from their “hard-earned savings.” OKX Money will allow customers to hold three dollar-backed stablecoins: Paxos’s USDG, Circle’s USDC, and Tether’s USDT. According to OKX, the platform offers up to 10% annual yield on eligible USDG balances; virtual and physical cards with no foreign-exchange markup; and referral rewards. Compared with legacy technologies, “crypto has one moat: We are technologically more advanced than traditional finance, whether it’s money or markets,” Rafique says. OKX Money is the latest launch in a series of new products from the cryptocurrency exchange, sparked in part by a March funding round with Intercontinental Exchange . The owner of the New York Stock Exchange invested in OKX in a deal that valued the cryptocurrency exchange at $25 billion. (The total investment was undisclosed, but Bloomberg reported the figure to be roughly $20 million.) On Sunday, the OKX-ICE joint venture–cochaired by former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo—filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission to launch a separate platform for round-the-clock trading of more than 60 tokenized U.S. stocks. In recent weeks, OKX also introduced an account-protection program, named OKX Shield. In addition to security safeguards, Shield promises to reimburse up to $100,000 for regular users, and up to $500,000 for its highest class of VIP users, in the event of a third-party takeover. The launch comes as crypto platforms have lost an estimated $2.7 billion to hacks this year, according to security firm CertiK, including nearly $388 million stolen from rival exchange Bitget last month through a vulnerability in a third-party security product.  Roughly 97% of global stablecoin market value is tied to the U.S. dollar, a dominance drawing attention in Washington—where officials hope dollar-backed tokens will fuel demand for U.S. assets—and beyond, where several economies are exploring their own alternatives. “Every nation should be thinking about this technology,” Rafique says. “But the question is, what is the world willing to put their money towards?” He says he would welcome an Asian rival to the dollar stablecoin: “If there’s an Asia-based, fiat-pegged stablecoin that has stability, people will absolutely trust it.” In particular, he cites a Singapore-dollar-based stablecoin as something he’d be interested in. Rafique sees the crypto industry at an “inflection point.” Even as Bitcoin has rebounded, he says, liquidity in the altcoin market “is just not there.” Consumers in markets like Venezuela and Turkey once “YOLO-ed” into crypto to hedge inflation and chase fast-rising assets. Yet now, with access to U.S. markets, energy markets, and pre-IPO price exposure, Rafique says emerging-market investors are asking a different question: “Do I really need to bet on the next ApeCoin?” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Moonshot said to be heading for Hong Kong IPO in early 2027 after value hits US$50 billion
events.summary: Moonshot is one of the biggest stars of China’s AI scene, bursting onto the global stage in July with the debut of Kimi K3. HONG KONG – Moonshot AI has closed the final round of private fund raising at a valuation of about US$50 billion (S$64 billion) and is heading towards an initial public offering in Hong Kong in the first quarter of 2027, according to sources familiar with the matter. The Chinese artificial intelligence champion has also begun laying the groundwork to start gauging investor sentiment through early look meetings starting as early as October, some of the sources said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. Moonshot is one of the biggest stars of China’s AI scene, bursting onto the global stage in July with the debut of Kimi K3 , an open model that goes nearly toe to toe with leading platforms from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic on some metrics. Its planned IPO is one of the most hotly anticipated deals in Hong Kong , where fund raising driven by the industry is setting fresh records. The company is considering raising up to US$5 billion in the deal, sources have said. It is unclear how the valuation or the IPO timeline may be affected by tighter oversight of China’s AI industry after regulators opened a data security probe into DeepSeek and Moonshot, according to The Information, adding to broader concerns over governance and safety. Deliberations are ongoing and the timing of the IPO might still change, the sources said. Moonshot representatives did not respond to requests for comment during a Chinese public holiday. The company’s valuation has risen steadily through a series of fund-raising efforts. A previous round this summer valued it at US$31.5 billion. Moonshot’s annual recurring revenue (ARR), a gauge of future sales, is expected to rise to US$2 billion by December from US$1 billion now, sources have said. The firm achieved US$300 million of ARR in June, Bloomberg News reported earlier. The Beijing-based AI lab previously added Bank of America as overall coordinator for the transaction alongside sponsor banks China International Capital, Deutsche Bank and Goldman Sachs Group, sources said previously. The company has filed confidentially for the IPO , they said. Founded in early 2023 by Yang Zhilin, a former Tsinghua University professor who previously worked at Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google, Moonshot counts Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and 5Y Capital as its backers. events.title: Oprah-backed True Food Kitchen files for bankruptcy after expansion
events.summary: Oprah Winfrey had decided to invest in True Food Kitchen and joined the board after dining in its Palo Alto, California, location. True Food Kitchen, backed by Oprah Winfrey, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy due to management turnover, Covid-19 impacts, and a cyclospora outbreak, closing a dozen locations. The chain plans to recapitalise or sell, has secured a US$20 million bankruptcy loan, and ended its ghost kitchen delivery strategy. Founded in 2008 with a wellness focus, remaining locations continue serving health-conscious food with natural ingredients amid restructuring efforts. True Food Kitchen, a health food focused restaurant chain that counts American media mogul Oprah Winfrey among its investors, has filed for bankruptcy after struggling with management turnover and lingering effects of the Covid-19 pandemic. The company said in court papers that it had closed a dozen locations after filing for Chapter 11 protection on Oct 4 and will seek to either recapitalise or sell the business. The chain said it grappled with “significant management turnover, which resulted in frequent changes to expansion strategy, brand direction and menu offering”. The chain has sought permission to end leases in Miami, New Jersey, Southern California, Columbus, Ohio, New Orleans, Chicago, Bethesda, Maryland, Reston, Virginia, Scottsdale, Arizona and Long Island, New York. True Food Kitchen’s advisers have already entered into separate transactions for certain unexpired leases, chief restructuring officer Nathan Cook said in a court filing on Oct 5. Winfrey decided to invest in the restaurant and joined the board after dining in its Palo Alto, California, location, former True Food Kitchen chief executive Christine Barone said in a 2018 interview with Bloomberg. Barone now leads the Dutch Bros Coffee chain; Jeff Chandler was appointed CEO of True Food Kitchen in July. In 2022, True Food Kitchen announced a US$100 million (S$127.9 million) investment round led by new investors HumanCo and Manna Tree and support from Centerbridge Partners. A True Food Kitchen spokeswoman said on Oct 5 that Winfrey remains a minority investor and that Centerbridge is no longer a shareholder in the company. Like most restaurants, Covid-19 era lockdowns significantly impacted True Food Kitchen at a time it was expanding. To offset the loss of in-person dining, the chain used some of its locations as “ghost kitchens” and opened one off-site kitchen for delivery service, only, Cook said in the filing. The strategy, which has since ended, impaired staffing and the dining experience at its restaurants, he said. A True Food Kitchen lawyer told a bankruptcy judge on Oct 5 that the cyclospora outbreak in July “also didn’t help”. True Food Kitchen has lined-up a US$20 million Chapter 11 loan to help fund operations during the bankruptcy. The financing is being provided by an affiliate of HumanCo. The brand was founded in 2008 by wellness author Andrew Weil, who has appeared on Oprah’s talk-show, and restaurateur Sam Fox. True Food Kitchen’s remaining locations are open and serve items that are cooked without seed oil, grass-fed beef, pasture-raised eggs and antibiotic-free chicken, according to court papers. events.title: 'Can I be in the UAE after overstaying my visit visa?'
events.summary: Question : Can a telecoms company impose a travel ban over an unpaid bill? I owe a telecoms company money and haven't paid it for months. I have been sent a message saying that I owe Dh2,930 and that my account is now 190 days overdue. It also said: “We hereby inform you that legal proceedings may be initiated to recover the outstanding amount.” The message was from a credit management company. Can they make a case against me and put a travel ban on me for this? Is there any other action they can take? JC, Abu Dhabi Answer : For an unpaid telecom debt of Dh2,930, a full court case is unlikely, but JC can still face consequences. The account has probably already been cut off, and the company will follow up as he owes it money. Companies can pursue debts in court but, for in this case litigation costs would be disproportionate relative to the amount owed. A travel ban will not happen. Under Article 324 of the UAE Civil Procedure Law (Federal Decree Law No 42 of 2022), a creditor – a person or company that is owed money – can only apply for a travel ban against a debtor if the debt is Dh10,000 or more. Below that threshold, a civil travel ban cannot be issued, regardless of the risk of a person leaving the country without settling their debts. It is common for UAE companies to hand over small debts to collection agencies. That will lead to regular telephone calls, emails and even WhatsApp messages. These companies are licensed and regulated, and there are rules that they must follow. The agency must not overstep by making repeated calls designed to intimidate rather than to communicate, as that constitutes harassment under UAE law. They are only allowed to make contact between 9am and 8pm, and must not disclose information to any third party. That includes calling a place of work and telling anyone the call is about a debt. If the collection agency breaks these guidelines, a complaint can be made, first to the telecoms company, but if that doesn’t stop it, then to the Central Bank of the UAE. JC needs to start making repayments in order to stop follow-up calls and messages. Non-payment of any debt will affect a person’s UAE credit record . This will affect a person's ability to borrow and open financial accounts. Since the change in legislation this year, landlords can now ask for confirmation of a credit score, which can also affect a person's ability to rent a home. Q : I have overstayed my visit visa after my employer failed to arrange a work permit. What can I do? I have a question about overstaying a visit visa. I came to work for a company, and although the team promised me a visa, it never happened. I don’t have a contract, and they have now said they do not want me to work for them any more. What can I do about this? I want to find another job and stay in the UAE. Will I get in trouble or have to pay a fine? MP, Dubai A : The important point here is that MP has been working illegally since arriving in the UAE. From the outset, the employer should have given MP a proper offer of employment and a labour contract, and applied for a residence visa and a work permit. As this did not happen, the company has been employing MP illegally, so she has been working illegally. Sadly, this means that she has no protection under UAE law. This means that MP is unable to make a legal complaint against the company, even if it has broken the law. No doubt the employer will know that this is not permitted, but the company can be reported for breaking the law. Any company that takes on staff without a visa can be fined up to Dh50,000 and may have difficulty obtaining visas in the future. As MP has been in the UAE without a valid visa, MP will have overstay fines. Since February 2026, the UAE has unified overstay fines across all visa types and emirates. They are now the same for all visas, whether tourist, visit or residence visas, and there is no variation by emirate. The fine is Dh50 per day. If an overstay exceeds 30 days, an additional exit permit, known as an “outpass”, at a cost of Dh250 to Dh300, including base and service fees, is required before leaving the country. It is possible to pay the overstay fines and stay in the UAE without leaving the country, provided a new employer initiates the visa process immediately. If not, MP will need to leave and return on an employment entry permit from a new employer. MP should visit an Amer centre, a division of the General Directorate of Residency and Foreigners Affairs, for advice and to find out how much MP owes. Once the overstay fine has been settled, MP can find a new job and be employed with a visa in order to stay legally in the UAE.
