events.title: Solar market set for Africa boom, says report
events.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa’s off-grid solar market is due to expand by 450% by 2035, with more than 35% of installations projected to be in Nigeria, according to a new report by global research firm Wood Mackenzie. Across the continent, persistent failures in national grids and growing populations have already created an off-grid “ shadow ” fuel market, predominantly led by diesel generators. However, the recent rise in fuel prices due to the Iran war, alongside the removal of subsidies in Nigeria and a significant drop in solar panel prices in recent decades, are driving the shift to solar. Outside Nigeria, Kenya, and DR Congo are also projected to be major solar power hubs. For more of the continent to reap the benefits of solar power, however, blended funding models and consistent rural electrification policies will be needed to help bridge the power gap, the report warned. — Paige Bruton

events.title: Budding food scrap pickup services across the US want your coffee grounds and eggshells
events.summary: Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells and carrot tops is a way to reduce the amount of food waste that goes into landfills, where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane DETROIT -- Every Monday, Ricky Blanding drives his Ford Ranger pickup truck around Detroit along a carefully planned route. Blanding hops in and out of the truck, grabbing buckets of food scraps from porches and restaurants, piling those scraps into bins in the truck bed and driving them to a composting site. Blanding is the CEO of Scrap Soils, one of the many budding food waste collection services across the country helping to divert food from landfills and make composting more accessible. It's especially important for those who can't compost at home, who live in cities without municipal curbside pickup or who can't get to a drop-off location. Composting leftover coffee grounds, eggshells, carrot tops and more reduces the amount of food that goes into dumps where it produces the potent greenhouse gas methane. It also ultimately helps create healthy soil for gardeners and urban farmers. Experts say companies like Scrap Soils are an important part of cleaning up the broader food ecosystem. Emily Cassidy, research associate at climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, said composting offers the dual benefits of reducing landfill methane emissions and, once the composting process is complete, returning nutrients to soil. “Because methane has such a big impact on the climate in a short amount of time, the more we can reduce methane, it is like pulling the emergency brake on climate change,” Cassidy said. Beyond mitigating climate change, composting can also improve local food production, she said. “That’s a way that we can see that we’re benefiting the environment, because we’re taking food and then replenishing the ground with those nutrients,” she said. Blanding, a 34-year-old native Detroiter, co-launched Scrap Soils in 2020 to play a local part in solving a statewide food waste problem that mirrors what's happening around the globe . Food waste is a huge source of methane in Michigan landfills, estimates say, and accounts for millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions in the state. In Detroit, more than 70 homes and businesses are signed up for Scrap Soils’ weekly pickups. It's an easier way to compost than making space in one's backyard or driving to a city drop-off site. Home pickups start at $15 per month, while businesses pay $60 per month or more, depending on volume. One of those commercial customers is The Grand Porter restaurant in the Southwest neighborhood of Detroit. “We go through a lot of eggs, so mostly egg scraps, eggshells and the cardboard. We put all of our bread scraps, stale bread scraps, in here,” said Lou Hammer, the restaurant's executive chef, pointing to a large bin with bags of food waste inside. “Some tomato tops, some avocado skins. Probably a few other things in there, too.” “It doesn’t take any extra effort,” she said of the pickup service. “This was going to go in a bag anyway. It’s just going to go in a green bag instead.” After completing his nine-hour, more than 100-mile (160-kilometer) weekly route, Blanding drops off the waste at Scrap Soils' partner, Sanctuary Farms in Detroit. There, everything from apple cores to rotted pumpkins to corn husks is composted into a rich soil additive that's available for purchase. “Food waste has not only become the problem,” Blanding said, “but it’s also the solution to so many issues in climate change.” The company ultimately plans to purchase a larger truck, as well as its own property and equipment for composting. It's fundraising to meet a matching grant through the state. Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Iran live updates: Saudi Arabia says 2 of its airports were damaged in strikes District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' That hasn't been without challenges. As Blanding seeks to grow, he's come up against skepticism that a small team with limited resources can make a big impact. Companies like Scrap Soils also face challenges ranging from gaining visibility to getting people to actually sign up and commit. At the same time, emphasizing what can and cannot be composted, and how to do it correctly — such as removing produce stickers before putting a peel in the bucket — is key to its success, too. “The role of a hauler is very important, and education around composting is also very important,” Blanding said. “Being able to continue to get more engagement and more partnership, those things go far in helping us to expand this tiny effort into something that actually can scale,” he added. Despite hurdles, other independent composting programs and companies are expanding. Examples include the Denver Compost Collective , Nashville’s Compost Co. and Compost Now , which operates in Atlanta and the North Carolina cities of Raleigh, Durham and Asheville.

events.title: Games Workshop seeks IT leader to summon the legions in epic saga battling the forces of ERP
events.summary: Games Workshop is on the hunt for a head of IT to guide the organization through its technological saga for the next two years. The UK-based tabletop games retailer and manufacturer of the globally popular Warhammer figures said that under the fixed-term contract, the heroic individual would take overall responsibility for its global IT and customer technology capability, and report to the Chief Operating Officer. “The role has a broad remit spanning our core technology estate, information security, major systems change and the technology behind our customer-facing digital platforms, including warhammer.com,” the job ad said, although sadly it closed for applications over the weekend. “We need someone who can understand what Games Workshop needs now, anticipate what we will need in the future, and make good decisions about how technology supports the long-term success of the business,” it said. Candidates might want to be aware that, if they are lucky enough to be offered the job and they accept the mission, the battle will not be an easy one. The head of IT will take responsibility for core IT environment and information security, advising senior management on technology, security, risk and investment. They will also support the teams to keep “significant technology programs moving, openly tackling the challenges that come with major change, and ensure that we continue to make rapid progress.” The Nottingham-based retailer and manufacturer is in the midst of ERP and supply chain management systems overhauls that were first mobilized years ago and have been beset with delays and over-runs. Back in January 2021, The Register reported that Games Workshop delayed its Microsoft Dynamics-based ERP rollout and appointed a new integrator, having already hoped to go live in 2020. By September that year, it said project issues were impacting the development of new features in online shopping. In January 2022, it added another £500k to the project budget with no end in sight. A year later, it said the business faced ongoing challenges to integrate new IT systems when it was still heavily reliant on working with its legacy tech systems. “Finishing these projects and upgrading our systems continue to be a key area of focus. We are making some progress but it's costing us more time and money – we will remain cost conscious," it told investors. Around four years later, challenges remain ongoing, according to the latest annual report, published in July, for the year ending in May 2026. It said the group’s main financial system is still being supported by a number of legacy ERP applications for which “we have identified control deficiencies in our previous audits.” These still exist, according to a review of IT systems. The report added that the responsibility for delivering IT had moved to its operational manufacturing and supply chain director, under the COO from June, a decision which “helped bring all of the internal departments together.” “Our Systems Improvement Plan (SIP) is on track with very clear milestones for us all to support and deliver,” it added. Games Workshop is famous for the phenomenon of Warhammer 40,000 — also known as WH40K or 40K — thought to be the most popular miniature wargame in the world. Battles are set in the distant future, leaving the technology department to hope the end of its long-running ERP saga comes before that date. ®

events.title: Adnoc signs Thai LNG deal after Iran war disrupts Gulf supply
events.summary: Adnoc has agreed to supply about two million tonnes of liquefied natural gas to Thailand ’s Gulf Development, boosting the country's access to the fuel as the Iran war disrupts supplies from the Middle East. Deliveries under the multi-year sales and purchase agreement are to start in 2027, Adnoc said on Monday. The company did not disclose prices, the length of the contract or where the cargoes will be sourced from. The agreement builds on a first LNG supply deal between the companies signed in 2025. The latest deal comes as Thailand seeks to diversify its LNG supplies after the war sharply curtailed shipments from the Gulf. Natural gas accounts for more than 60 per cent of the country’s power generation, while about 24 per cent of its LNG imports – about 2.2 million tonnes a year – normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz, almost all from Qatar, according to Thailand-based Krungsri Research. State-controlled PTT has been exploring alternative supplies, including from Oman, Mexico and Canada. The regional war has upended a global LNG market that was already heading into a period of tighter seasonal demand. The strait, through which about a fifth of global crude and LNG flowed before the war began in late February, remains largely shut. QatarEnergy declared force majeure in early March, while an Iranian missile strike on the Ras Laffan complex on March 18 knocked out about 17 per cent of Qatar's LNG production capacity. Cargo cancellations to some Asian buyers have since been extended through November, helping push prices in Asia and Europe towards their highest levels since late 2022. Gulf LNG exports remain far below their prewar pace of about three shipments a day. “This agreement builds on our first LNG supply agreement with Gulf Group and reinforces Adnoc’s commitment to ensuring reliable energy supplies to Thailand and our Asian customers,” said Nasser Al Muhairi, acting chief executive of Adnoc downstream industry, marketing and trading. Gulf Development chief executive Sarath Ratanavadi said the agreement would help to build a “diversified, resilient LNG portfolio” and gave the company greater flexibility to meet demand. The supplies will be delivered through Adnoc Trading and its LNG marketing and trading platform , launched in Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM in July. Adnoc is targeting 47 million tonnes a year of marketable LNG beyond 2030 as it expands its portfolio and trading operations.

events.title: From Scan to Treatment Plan, AI Helps Close Breast Cancer’s Deadliest Gaps
events.summary: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among American women — yet the gaps in care are wide. A majority of women over age 40 skip the recommended annual screening. Radiologists are reading more mammograms with fewer colleagues. And when a diagnosis arrives, the tests that inform treatment can take weeks to return results. Companies in the NVIDIA Inception program for startups are building AI applications to support clinicians at each of these friction points, including imaging, risk assessment and treatment planning. About 40 million mammograms are performed in the U.S. each year, but a projected shortfall of tens of thousands of radiologists over the next decade is straining the system’s capacity to read them. At the other end of the care timeline, treatment decisions often hinge on genomic assays sent off to outside labs — assays that take weeks to process, at a moment when speed and certainty matter most. The companies below are addressing both ends of that gap, and everything in between, accelerated by NVIDIA AI infrastructure. Automated Imaging Delivers AI-Powered Insights For women struggling to find time or a nearby location for breast cancer screening, access is a practical barrier that translates into missed diagnoses. NVIDIA Inception startup iSono Health was built around simplifying this imaging workflow. The company’s FDA-cleared ATUSA platform — a wearable, automated 3D quantitative ultrasound system — captures a standardized breast volume in approximately two minutes per breast, compared with up to 45 minutes for a conventional handheld ultrasound. The system’s AI, trained on thousands of full-breast scans comprising over 1.5 million ultrasound frames, automates image acquisition. It uses NVIDIA GPU acceleration and open source medical imaging technology to deliver a 3D scan that the company says is 28% more sensitive than a handheld 2D ultrasound. Handheld ultrasound depends on whoever holds the probe, so a woman’s scans typically can’t be compared from one year to the next. ATUSA captures the whole breast the same way every time, creating a repeatable view of breast tissue that could help clinicians analyze how a patient’s tissue changes across successive scans, while also reducing operator errors and variability. ATUSA is commercially available through partner clinics across California, Texas, Georgia, Tennessee and Washington D.C., with new sites coming online regularly. “Getting the scan closer to the patient is the first breakthrough,” said Neda Razavi, CEO of iSono Health. “Our vision is to make that scan increasingly informative: helping clinicians see what is there, understand what has changed and make more informed decisions.” iSono Health has developed AI capabilities for lesion detection, 3D segmentation and lesion classification. It next plans to extend its AI pipeline into multimodal diagnostic intelligence spanning 3D ultrasound, mammography, MRI and clinical information. The company has a multicenter clinical study with 3,200 patients underway to further validate the platform’s performance, with lead research sites at UC Davis and Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Finding Cancers, Cutting False Alarms Another NVIDIA Inception company, Whiterabbit.ai, develops AI technology for breast cancer screening. Its FDA-cleared WRDensity software automatically assesses breast density from mammograms and has been used in the care of hundreds of thousands of patients. The company has also developed WRRisk, a clinical decision support software for estimating patients’ long-term risk of developing breast cancer — and is researching a new generation of AI for mammography that could help radiologists detect more cancers while automating the screening of mammograms that are negative for breast cancer. The goal is to reduce the burden on a strained radiologist workforce, accelerate results and reduce avoidable callbacks for patients, and lower downstream healthcare costs. “Every day, breast radiologists face a needle-in-a-haystack problem, trying to find roughly one cancer in every 200 mammograms,” said Jason Su, cofounder and chief technology officer of Whiterabbit.ai. “We hope AI can be a powerful sidekick to radiologists, helping to clear away the hay so they can focus their expertise where it matters most.” Whiterabbit trains its AI models on a cluster of NVIDIA GPUs housed at Washington University in St. Louis, supplemented by additional GPU capacity in the cloud. Inference runs on NVIDIA GPUs deployed directly in the clinic. Predicting Which Treatments Will Work Once a patient is diagnosed with breast cancer, the next question is what to do about it — and the answer depends on predicting how the cancer will respond to treatment. Today, these predictions are limited in scope and accuracy, and often require a separate tissue biopsy with a two- to four-week wait. Ataraxis AI is building clinical intelligence that predicts patient outcomes and response to different therapies using digital data, including pathology slides that are already part of the standard patient workup. “The tools oncologists rely on today to guide therapy decisions were largely trained once, fifteen years ago, and never updated. Our models get stronger every time we acquire more clinical trial data,” said Joseph Cappadona, member of technical staff at Ataraxis AI. “But as we scale our models, the bigger shift is being able to answer more questions to help oncologists personalize therapy across all cancers.” Ataraxis’s AI models analyze digital pathology slides and standard clinical variables to predict treatment response and recurrence risk. One model predicts whether presurgical chemotherapy is likely to shrink a patient’s tumor to the point of response before the operating room. After surgery, another model estimates a patient’s five-year recurrence risk and the likely benefit of chemotherapy as a next step. Both models have been validated across more than 10 institutions and multiple clinical trials, and are in active clinical use. They run on NVIDIA GPUs on premises, in an offsite data center and in the cloud — using PyTorch accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA throughout. Providing Tumor Insights With 3D Visualization Another NVIDIA Inception company, SimBioSys , joined NVIDIA on a recent panel marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month. The company builds AI-powered precision medicine technology that creates accurate 3D models of breast tumors, veins and other soft tissue, delivering important insights to help guide surgeries and influence treatment plans. It has also built a tool to estimate the risk of breast cancer recurrence based on 3D volumetric data from a patient’s breast MRI, tumor pathology and clinical data. “We’re building a platform that now allows us to take multimodal data — imaging exams, pathology results, genomic testing when applicable and other biological inputs — and, using AI, bring that all together,” said Stacey Stevens, CEO of SimBioSys, at the event.

events.title: Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it
events.summary: Anthropic's IPO prospectus leaked this week, and boy was it filled with interesting details. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or YouTube. You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live For starters there's the fact a third of it is all about existential AI risks, then there's the fact that, despite some impressive revenue growth the company still has yet to turn a profit. Combine that with massive capex predictions, and you have an IPO with massive valuation, yet a long, hard road toward anything resembling earnings. Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg editor in chief Matt Rosoff, and enterprise IT reporter Lindsay Clark on this week's episode of The Kettle where they discuss the revelations, what they mean for the state of the AI industry, and just how much distraction from its actual problems Anthropic can eke out by keeping that doomsday narrative front and center. Lindsay Clark (00:36) Thank you. Matt Rosoff (00:37) Thanks for having us. Brandon (00:38) Yeah. So Lindsay, I know we didn't break this story. This was, I believe, a Financial Times exclusive, but what was reported about those IPO docs, in the story you wrote and just how apocalyptically optimistic is this whole thing? Lindsay Clark (00:53) Well we have this scenario where a company, Anthropic, is trying to sell itself by telling people that there's an existential risk to its technology, which I think is a bit of a weird way to go about it. But nonetheless, that's in the prospectus according to the Financial Times. And they also offer some insight into the numbers that are going around. Anthropic is still massively loss-making as far as we know. Brandon (01:22) There was what, I think you said, $8 billion loss on $4.6 billion of [revenue] or something? Lindsay Clark (01:28) That's right, and it says it plans to spend $500 billion or so on cloud computing over the next few years. So I don't know what you make of those numbers, but it's hard to get them to add up in my head. Brandon (01:40) I mean it's interesting just how it's still not a profitable company. But Matt and I were discussing earlier, I was saying that I think it's interesting that Anthropic is pushed ahead with this IPO despite OpenAI pausing it, because I feel like Anthropic has long had this reputation as sort of being the more safety-conscious, the more conservative AI company. But here they are with OpenAI kind of saying, Well, we're gonna pump the brakes on our IPO until we can make sure our models are safe, but Anthropic is plowing ahead. Now there was a report that they had actually turned profitable on an adjusted basis [in] Q2 this year, but that's if you strip out all of the training costs. So I guess if it's just inference alone, without the training costs and without certain other costs, they have decent margins. So maybe there is a path to profitability. Now it looks as if their operating loss last year was almost double their revenue. So if their revenue continues to increase at the rate that it is, which is, it seems like it's going up 4x, 12x per year, something like that, depending on the period you're looking at. If they can't get the expenses under control, the business doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense. Nonetheless, I think they are growing faster because they were earlier to enterprise and they have become more essential to more companies than OpenAI did. And I think OpenAI is still sort of adjusting its business model and maybe not growing at quite the same rate. So that's my suspicion is that those numbers would look even worse. Brandon (04:01) Yeah, so the safety argument is probably just some spackle slapped on top of the bad financials to try to kinda hide it, I guess. If what you're saying is correct. Matt Rosoff (04:12) That's my speculation. It doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense to say, well, we're so worried about this amazing thing that we've built that we don't want to show you our books and we're not gonna go public yet until we have that all figured out. That seems like a strange argument to make. Brandon (04:31) Yeah, I would have to agree with that. So speaking of economic impact, Lindsay, you were talking a bit more in your story about some of the broader sort of economic scope of the AI industry. events.title: Qatar’s luxury market attracts 34,000 visitors
events.summary: Many Gulf events have been postponed or canceled because of the war, but Qatar’s annual bonanza of bling was lively last week. More than 34,000 people attended the six-day Doha Jewellery & Watches Exhibition, and many — unlike this reporter — weren’t lookie-loos. Doha’s exhibition center was transformed into a gallery of coveted gems and timepieces, with the cars at the valet reflecting the wealth of the clientele inside. Shoppers were reluctant to talk, but several said they attend every year because exhibitors (there were more than 50 representing 500 brands) bring in inventory that isn’t usually available in Qatar. One jeweler said sales in a single week were like Valentine’s Day, Mother’s Day, and Christmas all rolled into one. For those seeking iced-out Pateks, or more modest trappings, the exhibition returns in late April. — Mohammed Sergie

They will feed the country’s first LNG export terminal, designed to produce 12 million tons a year in its initial phase. “ No country or company secures its energy future alone ,” Executive Chairman Sultan Al Jaber said in Paris last week. events.title: Gulf SWFs on track for major investments despite war
events.summary: Gulf sovereign wealth funds are on track for one of their most active years of dealmaking ever, even as war disrupts businesses and economic growth. Regional funds are forecast to invest $136 billion by year-end , making 2026 their second-busiest on record, according to consultancy Global SWF. Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala leads with $26.2 billion invested so far this year. Nearly half of Gulf sovereign fund investment went to the US, showing that American assets remain attractive despite the debate about the future of Gulf states’ relationship with their main strategic ally. Gulf funds are major backers of the $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Kuwait’s and Qatar’s funds may also be called on to transfer money to their government budgets to help prop up state finances, hit by the decline in oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz, Global SWF said. That won’t stop the funds from expanding rapidly in coming years, with Gulf funds set to control $8.8 trillion by 2030, up from $6.1 trillion. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes
events.summary: As of Oct. 1, 2026, states must pay more to run SNAP. AP Photo/Allison Dinner The number of people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is falling fast. The program formerly known as food stamps helped roughly 42 million Americans put food on the table in 2025. As of June 2026, the most recent data available, the number of people enrolled in the program in the whole country had declined by almost 13% to 36.4 million . Among those no longer getting benefits are an estimated 1.5 million children . What explains this decline? President Donald Trump says a strong economy has driven down demand for the program. It’s possible that some people have left the program because their incomes rose. But the enrollment decline has a lot to do with the big tax-and-spending package the president signed into law in July 2025 . States are struggling to keep up For example, the law caused some immigrants residing legally in the country, such as refugees and those seeking asylum, to no longer be eligible for SNAP benefits. In addition, more people enrolled in SNAP now may only get up to three months of benefits if they don’t work, engage in training programs or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. These work requirements previously applied only to adults up to the age of 54; that cutoff is rising to 64. Another change is that parents of older children ages 14-17 are now expected to meet these work requirements . All states are phasing in these restrictions, but the number of people getting SNAP benefits is falling much faster in some states than others. That includes Arizona, where enrollment has fallen by almost half , along with Louisiana and Illinois , where it’s down by about one-fifth. And now, states must pay more to run SNAP , which is federally funded but state-administered. In my research on the history of SNAP, I’ve found that changes in the way states run their programs have a big impact on who can get help. States are struggling to adapt to new federal policies. As additional changes roll out, more families may lose access to SNAP. Covering more of the administrative costs As of Oct. 1, 2026, states have to pay 75% of all administrative costs, which include paying staff who manage the enrollment process and maintaining the program’s computer systems. Previously, states paid 50% of those costs. The federal government estimates that states and local governments will pay roughly US$17 billion more in administrative costs over the next five years. In the 2027 fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, California – with the largest population of any state – will be responsible for paying roughly $670 million more to run the program. Wyoming, with the smallest number of residents, will pay about $3 million more . Costs will be shifted to local governments in nine of the 10 states where SNAP is administered by counties. Looming changes tied to ‘payment error rates’ State agencies and some state legislatures are imposing stricter rules and requiring applicants to provide more paperwork documenting their income, expenses and the number of people in their household. Caseworkers in states such as Arizona have reportedly been overwhelmed with the paperwork. Those seeking help have spent hours trying to get through on phone lines and have faced monthslong delays. States are taking these steps to get ready for another change that will roll out in October 2027. At that point, many states will also have to cover up to 15% of the costs of benefits for the first time since the program began in the 1960s. This cost is much larger than the administrative costs and could be staggering for many states . How much a state pays will be based on its “payment error rate.” These error rates measure how much in benefits are paid above or below what families are actually entitled to based on their household size, income and expenses. It is calculated based on an in-depth review of a small sample of a state’s benefits payments each year. These inaccurate payments are generally a result of mistakes on the part of the applicant or their caseworker – they rarely are the result of fraud. The payment error rate includes benefits paid to ineligible participants. It does not include payments never made to applicants who were eligible for benefits but wrongly denied them or incorrectly dropped from the program. Supporters of SNAP argue that this makes states err on the side of denying benefits. Range of rates States with an error rate less than 6% won’t face new costs for benefits. But only nine states had rates that low in 2025. States with an error rate between 6% and 8% will be responsible for 5% of the costs of their residents’ SNAP benefits. States with an error rate between 8% and 10% will have to cover 10%. States with error rates over 10% will have to cover 15%. There’s a weird twist: If a state has an error rate over 13.32% , it won’t have to pay part of the cost of residents’ SNAP benefits for up to two years as they would have had it been in the 6% to 13.32% range. Farm bill politics could play a role To reduce their error rates, states need to invest in more staff, training, technology and better application and verification procedures. But states had little time to do all that. The states’ share of costs slated to kick in as of October 2027 is based on the error rates in the fiscal year that ended in September 2026. Organizations representing state and local governments and social workers are pushing for an across-the board two-year delay. What’s more, legislation known as the “ farm bill ,” which sets policies for agriculture, conservation and food-related assistance like SNAP, is now ensnared in the dispute. Democrats, whose support is needed to pass the legislation in the Senate, would like to see most of the new SNAP changes repealed. Congress aims to pass a farm bill roughly every five years, but the most recent one, which was finalized in 2018, has expired . Short of rolling back all the SNAP policy changes, many Democrats have refused to vote for the farm bill unless it includes a two-year delay for all states in shouldering part of the cost of SNAP benefits. If the Democratic Party holds a majority in one or both chambers of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections, their leverage could increase in these negotiations. The Republican Party’s version of the farm bill now pending in the Senate includes a one-year delay in the benefits-funding changes. But it would increase the states’ burden even more than the policy planned for October 2027. That’s a nonstarter for Democrats. What states can do about all this Meanwhile, there are many signs that a large share of the people who have lost their SNAP benefits are struggling to feed their families. More people, for example, are seeking help from food pantries and banks , which fear they will not be able to keep up with growing demand. It’s hard to predict what might happen next. events.title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
events.summary: By teaching entrepreneurship, colleges can better prepare students for a fast-changing job market and technological disruption. Igor Golovniov/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their unemployment rate hit 5.7% , compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s one of the worst rates in the past 20 years. Meanwhile, roughly 4 in 10 graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic. As an educator for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate? What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok attained that threshold in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly. Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers. I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit. 3 core lessons The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences develop the capabilities students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers. Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech. Making adaptability a core skill: Students need to learn how to be nimble . This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world. To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator . The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape. Understanding customer value: Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech . Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level. Emphasizing fundamentals: Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate. Students in startup training have to deal with uncertainty, resource constraints and customer interaction, all of which will make them more nimble in their careers. David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images The many paths toward entrepreneurship Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value. But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course. That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback. More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, such as Cornell and the University of Washington . At Georgia Tech, we have a playbook that we have developed through our experiences that follows the following principles: Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum: One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out. Build a pathway to business creation: Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, including MIT , Rice University and the University of Texas . But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a learn/make/launch/scale pathway that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them. Offer real venture experience: A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch.

events.title: Hungary’s former foreign minister grilled over ties to China's BYD automaker while in office
events.summary: Péter Szijjártó, Hungary’s former foreign minister, is appearing before a parliamentary committee to answer questions about his dealings with Chinese automaker BYD while in office BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungary’s former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó appeared before a parliamentary committee on Monday to answer questions about his dealings with Chinese automaker BYD while still in office. He left politics in July to take up an executive position with the company. Szijjártó, who served as Hungary's foreign minister for 12 years under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán before an election defeat in April, announced in July that he would resign his seat in Hungary’s parliament to take the job at the world’s top electric carmaker . The announcement prompted accusations of a conflict of interest, and criticism of his central role in facilitating substantial government subsidies for the company while in office. In addition to securing the deal allowing BYD to open its first European factory near the southern Hungarian city of Szeged, Szijjártó also announced in 2025 that the company would locate its European headquarters and a research and development center in Budapest, and receive 20 billion forints ($63.7 million) in government assistance. Upon arriving at the closed-door National Security Committee hearing on Monday, Szijjártó told reporters that there had been “serious misunderstandings” related to BYD’s investment in Hungary. He made no mention of his new position at the company, which he earlier described as an “executive responsible for the group’s external relations and the development of new business lines.” “I consider it a great success that this factory came to Hungary,” Szijjártó said on Monday. “I would also like to point out that the proposed and awarded government subsidies for the construction of the BYD factory in Szeged have remained well within the framework of the usual subsidies for investments of this magnitude.” Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Iran live updates: Saudi Arabia says 2 of its airports were damaged in strikes District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, told lawmakers in July that Szijjártó had helped BYD “with hundreds of billions (of forints) in public money, diplomatic support and state infrastructure,” and that an investigation would be launched to “examine all the decisions, negotiations and state commitments” made by Szijjártó related to the BYD investment. While in office working under Orbán, Szijjártó concluded numerous foreign investment deals with Chinese companies to open factories in Hungary, largely related to battery production for the electric vehicle industry. Orbán’s government hoped the investments would make Hungary a global hub of lithium-ion battery manufacturing, yet decreased demand and other market pressures have so far prevented those investments from paying high dividends. Since taking office in May, Magyar’s government has promised increased regulation and tighter oversight of the battery production sector following some workplace accidents and findings at several plants that showed contamination levels over legal limits. events.title: Washington has picked a side in Ethiopia's new war
events.summary: There is new cause for alarm in the Horn of Africa. A week after a coalition of seven opposition groups announced an alliance to overthrow the government of Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, fighting has broken out across several regions of the country of 130 million people. Led by the Tigrayan People’s Liberation Front, the militias of Ethiopia’s largest regions of Amhara and Oromia have also pledged their support. Early battles have taken place along a critical commercial route leading east to the port of Djibouti, while drone strikes were carried out around the army’s main airbase near the capital, Addis Ababa. The choice of economic and political targets reflects the reality that even though the Tigrayans are weaker militarily than in their previous war that ended in 2022, they can still create asymmetric pressure on the government. Ethiopia’s army is now quickly regrouping and is pushing the TPLF back into Tigray, where government forces have retaken the regional airport and now occupy the capital, Mekelle. As the conflict moves into urban areas, the risk of displacement and civilian casualties grows. And in a region already suffering from aid shortages, and anticipating even greater food insecurity from this year’s El Nino, humanitarians are rightly nervous about a potential catastrophic fallout. But the Tigrayans and their “Alliance for Survival” allies believe they have an ace up their sleeves. A coalition of neighboring states, led by Egypt and including Eritrea, Sudan, and Somalia have reportedly been working in the background to support the Prime Minister’s armed opponents. Abiy’s announcement of building three new hydroelectric dams on the Nile, along with his threatening claims on the Eritrean port of Assab, and his army’s support for the Rapid Support Forces militia next door in Sudan have made him no friends across the region. All would like to see his ambitions contained. With a fully internationalized conflict already raging in neighboring Sudan and long-time foe Eritrea poised to enter the fight on the side of the Tigrayans, the risk that Ethiopia’s conflict converges with existing regional instability and animosities is high. The fallout from a regional war on US priorities from counterterrorism to Red Sea security would be disastrous, which raises the question why isn’t the Trump Administration doing more to stop it? On Oct. 4, the State Department urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to “exercise maximum restraint,” though curiously did not address the current fighting by Ethiopia’s internal armed groups. But back in June, the State Department sanctioned a group of Tigrayan officials for “undermining resolution to the crisis in Tigray” and last week the US ambassador in Addis blamed Tigrayans for their “poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive.” None of this suggests an even-handed approach this time around that would enable Washington to mediate an end to the violence as it did in 2022 to end the last Tigray war. This time, Washington has picked a side. Rubio’s newfound prioritization of commercial diplomacy , reflected in the announcement last week of the sale of $5 billion in Boeing aircraft to Ethiopia’s national airline, speaks to Washington’s focus on economic returns over peacemaking. But that view is shortsighted. Ethiopia’s double-digit economic growth and large infrastructure plans are vulnerable to the threat of nationwide war and regional meddling. The African Union has called for calm , but only Washington has the political leverage to manage a regional crisis. With Red Sea instability occupying more of Washington’s strategic focus, it would do well to prioritize peacemaking and ensure that Ethiopia’s economic potential is not undone by a descent into a region-wide conflict.

events.title: Ubuntu 'Stonking Stingray' beta swims out: Deeper Rust 'oxidization' plus LLM speech-to-text
events.summary: Ubuntu 26.10, “Stonking Stingray,” has entered beta testing, slightly later than planned – it is in fact scheduled to be released on October 15. While many people will stay with the LTS version, there’s some interesting stuff in there. There are already some release notes, but like the OS itself, they aren’t final yet, and there are still some gaps. Canonical does note that the "oxidization" process – exchanging core Unix tools written in C with new Rust replacements – goes further in this edition: now, the stock OpenPGP encryption support is via the Rust-based Sequoia-PGP. Perhaps one of the most daringly different new features is Canonical’s promised LLM-powered Myna speech-to-text tool. This isn’t installed by default, but you can add it, and a choice of speech-recognition models. We found various sets of instructions, including the unofficial “Ubuntu Handbook”. Our geriatric testbed was a little old for this, though, and we couldn't try it. A couple of weeks ago we took at look at the beta of what will become Fedora 45. Both Ubuntu 26.10 and the default workstation edition of Fedora will use GNOME 51, but since the Fedora beta, the final release of the latest GNOME is here: GNOME 51 “A Coruña”. The version in the Ubuntu beta isn’t working completely smoothly. We saw a persistent error about missing themes, and although the OS offered to install whatever was missing automatically, this failed. Since it doesn’t actually say what is missing, we can’t install it ourselves. The problem is only cosmetic: just some missing icons in applications, very similar to what we saw in Alpine Linux 3.16 four years ago. Sadly, problems around GNOME themes are a long standing issue. As we reported earlier this year, the Linux Mint developers are still struggling with them. The occasional missing icon aside, though, Stonking works pretty well. We tried both in a Virtualbox VM and on bare metal on our old testbed Thinkpad W520, and it ran well in both. The new installation program that arrived with the 2024 LTS version works fine, and now makes it much clearer which control is currently selected with an orange highlight. We do wish the window was resizable, though. The testbed machine has two SATA drives and we had to do a lot of scrolling to choose the right partitions. It also failed to use our dedicated swap partition, although we selected it during installation. Although GNOME 51 removed their support for old Nvidia devices in this development cycle, it still picked up and used the machine’s Nvidia-controlled Displayport output. It didn’t work perfectly: GNOME couldn’t report on the model or properties of our Quadro 1000 GPU, or the CPU-integrated Intel one for that matter, but at least the second screen worked. More surprisingly, it even worked in the Fallback session, even though that uses the Metacity X11 window manager – and while logged into to a Fallback session, it could identify both GPUs. GNOME 51 isn’t a very feature-heavy release, but the Settings app has some useful additions, such as the ability to automatically disable the trackpad when an external mouse is connected. In our testing, it picked up and let us configure mouse, trackpad, and trackpoint, each in a separate tab. GNOME 51 no longer supports Wi-Fi networks with the old WEP encryption system, though. Modern Linux continues to move away from being an OS for old and low-end hardware. If the machine is online during installation, the installer fetches any package updates as it works, so the first update post-install is much quicker. However, this doesn’t apply to Snap packages: the .deb package phase of our first update was very fast, but we got various new snaps. One detail we haven’t noticed before is that while a snap application is updating, its dock icon temporarily gets a progress bar to tell you it’s being updated. We did a full install with all the optional extras, so this applied to Thunderbird as well as Firefox. A full installation took a fairly hefty 13 GB of disk space, although to be fair, that included 4GB of swap space – so in real money, it’s about 9 GB, which isn’t too bad for 2026. According to the htop command, it idles at about 1.2 B RAM, which is quite high, but then GNOME is no lightweight. Linux kernel 7.3 is still in development, but at the time of writing it’s up to RC5, and our testing ran without a hitch. The final version may be out before “Stonking” is completed, but if not, users will get it very soon afterwards. We also gave the Kubuntu desktop a very brief try. In this release, it uses Plasma 6.7.5, and ran well – it was fast, smooth, and happily drove both screens of our testbed machine; helpfully, on our first login, it asked where the second display was relative to the first. If you want modern Wayland niceties such as different dots-per-inch settings on different screens, but you also want a traditional Windows-style layout, KDE is currently the way to go. Plasma 6.8 is scheduled for later this month, and totally drops X11 support. It’s likely to be the desktop in Kubuntu 27.04, making it Wayland-only – so 26.10 is probably the last ever version of Kubuntu in which displaying your desktop thanks to X.org is a supported option. We installed X11 support, which is just one command: sudo apt install -y plasma-session-x11 This brings in multiple extra dependencies, which is why we specified the -y switch, but it took just seconds. We logged out, logged back again choosing “Plasma (X11)”, and… Everything looked absolutely identical. Which is how it should be, of course. Both screens were working normally, thanks to the Nouveau FOSS NVIDIA driver. The only visible differences are the classic “wobbly window” effect when moving windows around, and that the title-bar context menu regains the option to “shade” a window: roll it up, leaving only the title bar visible. You can’t do this in a Wayland environment. Under Wayland, htop reports about 1.2 GB in use; under X.org, about 1.3 GB. The resurrected Oxygen theme from KDE 4 is built in, if you want a bit more visual bling, but we preferred the flatter grayer look of the default Breeze theme. The only freeze that we saw in all our testing of the Stonking beta was after logging out of a Plasma (Wayland) session and trying to log back in using Plasma (X11). To be fair, we suspect most people wouldn’t chop-and-change this much. Ubuntu Stonking is shaping up well. Aside from the small theme-related glitches, GNOME worked fine, and KDE didn’t even have those minor issues. The equivalent beta versions of all the official flavors are also available, including both Ubuntu Unity 26.10 and Ubuntu MATE. Despite a hundred other distros, Ubuntu remains the go-to desktop Linux for most people. While Canonical is getting slightly more experimental with interim releases again, this is a mature product now and they’re a pretty safe bet. ®

events.title: Bolsonaro and Lula head to a runoff in Brazil's presidential election
events.summary: Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s veteran President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy BRASILIA, Brazil -- Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, and Brazil’s incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off in a runoff Oct. 25 for the top job of Latin America’s powerhouse economy after neither won a majority in Sunday's vote. The country’s electoral court in Brasilia said neither the 80-year-old incumbent, seeking his fourth non-consecutive term, nor the 45-year-old son of former President Jair Bolsonaro would garner the majority vote needed for an outright win. The court had Bolsonaro with just over 56 million votes to Lula’s 53.7 million, with 99.8 percent of the vote reported. The next presidential term is set to begin Jan. 5. The winner will be in charge of Latin America’s biggest economy and a population of 214 million. A win for Bolsonaro would increase U.S. influence in Latin America. If Lula wins, Brazil will keep its distance from Washington and continue to deepen its relationship with China. Flávio Bolsonaro addressed the press and a small group of supporters, including some wearing green and yellow Brazil jerseys and one woman wrapped in the Israeli flag, outside his Brasilia house. “Brazil wants change, that’s the reading of what happened today,” Bolsonaro said. “It’s the end of the Workers’ Party era,” he added, in a reference to Lula's party. Lula, seeking to be encouraging ahead of an uphill battle to beat Bolsonaro in the runoff, said the result was “unexpected” as he had thought he could win in the first round. “Tomorrow we start a new campaign,” Lula said. “I am very good in the knockout stage. We will see who has the best plan.” Both Lula and Bolsonaro will have three weeks to reach moderate voters who did not support them in the first round. Augusto Cury, a writer who finished in third place with 3.4 million votes, said he would not endorse either in the runoff. Ronaldo Caiado and Renan Santos, two candidates who garnered about 5.3 million votes combined Sunday, have previously said the same. In the campaign ahead, Lula is expected to try to capitalize on the popularity of his social policies and his rival’s many legal woes. While the once widely popular Lula saw his approval ratings plummet during his third term, standing up to the U.S. gave him a boost. And he still enjoys a strong base of supporters who credit his social policies for improving millions of Brazilians’ lives. But the incumbent faces a tough battle because of an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro . Bolsonaro will likely lean into his messaging on affordability and link the president to corruption scandals. He has promised to crack down on Brazilian criminal groups and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy , second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father and bringing him back to politics. Both candidates face image problems: Roughly half of Brazil’s population disapproves of the Bolsonaro family, and roughly half disapprove of Lula’s Workers' Party, according to multiple polls. Four years ago, Lula beat then incumbent Jair Bolsonaro by about 2.1 million votes. While it was a successful night for Bolsonaro, nothing is won yet, said Mayra Goulart, a political scientist from the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. Lula should “look at the votes for Augusto Cury and Ronaldo Caiado and try to reduce abstention,” she said. Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations Suspect in FlyDubai incident was previously identified as security risk: Officials District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Reacting to the result, Alvaro Senra, 65, a history professor and Lula supporter in Rio de Janeiro said he felt “calm but very sad.” He watched the count with friends at a bar. “I think this is the result of conservatives working under the radar, including by neo-Pentecostal churches. But I think Lula can still win,” he said. Earlier in the day, Maria Ribeiro, a 50-year-old cellphone vendor from Brasilia, said she voted for Bolsonaro’s eldest son because she wants freedom to express her evangelical religion. She hopes he follows in his father’s footsteps. “I voted for his father, and I don’t regret it,” she said. The proximity to his father was what worried Lorena Zschaber, a 40-year-old photographer, who watched the results roll in at an LGBTQ+-friendly bar in downtown Rio de Janeiro. During his father’s presidency, “people felt more at ease to discriminate,” she said. “I’m an LGBTQ+ woman, I can’t think of anything worse happening than Flávio Bolsonaro being elected,” she added.

events.title: Spain's PM calls snap election as housing price protests grow
events.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election next month after parliament rejected his proposed plan to tame public anger about the country’s housing crisis. A temporary eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her Madrid home has galvanized demonstrations that have spread across Spain. Soaring property prices have upended European politics from Portugal to Germany, with the issue rising to the top of voter worries in several countries as prices race ahead of incomes. Home ownership in the EU declined last year , data showed. Experts say the continent should take a page from the US: “If Europeans want to meet their housing needs, they will probably have to revisit their zoning systems, just like Americans, ” Works in Progress wrote. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Brazil heads for election runoff with Bolsonaro in the lead
events.summary: Brazil’s presidential election will go to a runoff on Oct. 25, after conservative challenger Flávio Bolsonaro unexpectedly emerged as the favorite in the first-round vote. Polls seesawed in the runup to the election as both Bolsonaro — whose father was banned from running after having led a coup attempt — and left-wing incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva traded corruption allegations, a key issue that defined the race . A Bolsonaro win would confirm Latin America’s shift to the right: The seven most recent elections there have all been won by conservative candidates, most of them friendly to the Trump administration and its ambition of reasserting hegemonic power in the region to counter China’s growing influence. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Wizz Air delays start of Abu Dhabi flights to January due to European security update
events.summary: Wizz Air has postponed the launch of some routes to Abu Dhabi from late October to January following security updates from Europe's aviation regulator. The low-cost airline said last month that it was resuming flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai, alongside routes to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Amman in Jordan. The launch of routes to Abu Dhabi – including from Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Cyprus and Hungary – scheduled to begin in late October, has now been pushed to January 10, 2027, due to latest guidelines from the EU Aviation Safety Agency (Easa), Wizz Air said in a statement to The National . “The continued closure of Iraqi airspace requires longer routings and technical refuelling stops for the A321neo aircraft operating these services. Combined with current fuel prices, this makes the affected routes commercially unviable under present conditions,” the airline said. The UAE services were part of a wider restoration of 12 routes and 49 weekly flights to the Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Jordan over the winter, providing 470,000 seats across services to nine European cities. With Jordan's airspace also placed on the “do not operate” list in Easa's latest conflict zone information bulletin, flights to the country have been suspended until October 25, Wizz Air said. “Affected customers will be informed directly about their options, and we will continue to monitor conditions ahead of the revised launch date,” the airline added. The carrier suspended its European-operated services to the Middle East in late February due to the regional conflict and widespread airspace disruption. The airline was set to resume operations after its low-cost subsidiary, Wizz Air Abu Dhabi, ceased operations on September 1, 2025. Wizz Air Abu Dhabi, which operated for five years from the UAE capital, said in July last year that it would suspend all locally based services from the emirate because of operational challenges and geopolitical instability.

events.title: Euro sinks as fiscal and political worries mount
events.summary: The euro sank to its lowest level against the dollar since May 2025 over Spain’s snap elections added to mounting fiscal and political worries across the region. Investors have grown increasingly alarmed over the eurozone’s debt burden, moribund economic growth, and persistent inflation . France is a particular cause for concern: The spread on 10-year French bond yields above German ones — the European benchmark — briefly surged to more than 150 basis points due to concerns about Paris’ huge debt pile and political uncertainty, with far-right and far-left parties ascendant ahead of presidential elections next year. Previous efforts to corral France’s public finances with spending cuts have, however, been “ economically and socially disastrous ,” a leading economist wrote in Le Monde, arguing that Paris should prioritize “fiscal responsibility, not austerity.” — Prashant Rao

events.title: ‘Enough to go around’: Brookfield’s bullish on AI investing, even if it has to share it with rivals
events.summary: The Scene Wall Street isn’t built for consortiums. Blood feuds flourish, and the pressure to outperform rivals leaves little reason to team up with them on investments. But the sheer size of the AI buildout has competitors playing nice. “There’s enough to go around for all of us,” Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey tells Semafor. Chalk it up to Canadians’ go-along-to-get-along instincts, but the race to shift the cost of the AI buildout — $7 trillion over the next decade, by Brookfield’s estimate — from the hyperscalers themselves to external money managers is making strange bedfellows. Brookfield has a joint venture with Nvidia to buy up to $100 billion of AI infrastructure assets. It’s also in a consortium arranged by the chipmaker to corral another $500 billion alongside Apollo, Blackstone, and KKR — some of Brookfield’s fiercest rivals. Data centers, as well as the hardware inside them and the power plants feeding them, are basically the same as bridges, ports, and other unsexy but economically fundamental stuff that firms like Brookfield exist to build, own, and operate — albeit “on a much larger scale and happening much faster,” he said. There will still be plenty of losers among data-center financiers, he said. For power projects, he’s wary of gas, which is slow to deploy, and keener on fuel cells, onshore renewables, batteries, and nuclear. “If there’s a single narrative that is most starkly divorced from the fundamentals we’re seeing on the ground,” he said, “it’s the idea that the demand for AI infrastructure and the energy and the supply chain that supports it is in some way fragile.” Q&A Tim McDonnell and Liz Hoffman: Is power still the most important bottleneck for digital infrastructure? Connor Teskey: By a very large margin. This imbalance and the capital requirements for energy are going to last through the end of this decade and beyond. But in an environment where all forms of generation are seeing increased demand, we see certain technologies growing the fastest — fuel cells because they’re the fastest to deploy; renewables because they’re the cheapest form of bulk electricity; batteries and energy storage because they provide stability to an increasingly volatile electric grid; and nuclear because it provides your large-scale baseload and energy security. Which offers the best returns? Down-the-fairway, mature renewables — onshore wind and solar, battery storage — are absolutely seeing the most growth and have the most market participants. So maybe your return outcomes are more range-bound. Nuclear is a huge opportunity. There is incredible demand, huge capital requirements, and there are far fewer people who have the expertise in order to invest and help pull those projects off of the ground. Therefore, the return requirements are going to be different. You’re part of the consortium that Nvidia put together. [Nvidia CEO] Jensen Huang has been propping up a huge chunk of the AI buildout. Are we now at a place where investors who do this for a living are stepping in and backfilling that support? If I can play it back to you in a slightly different way, AI infrastructure is growing on a very traditional trajectory that we’ve seen [before]. Initially it’s done by independent capital providers who look to build and hold the assets. Once the asset class grows, you begin to see banks syndicate the financing. Other capital participants come in, whether it’s private credit or insurance. That is exactly what’s happened within AI infrastructure. The only thing that’s different about this one is it’s happening on a much larger scale and happening much faster. I’ve never seen competitors at the same table this often. How do you think about places where you want a deal to yourself versus sharing it — and sharing the returns — with your competitors? We’re seeing one of the biggest energy buildouts in history. We’re seeing global trade rewired with an increasing focus on resiliency and production of critical goods closer to home. These are mega-trends that require far more capital than what has traditionally been available from both governments and even the public markets. So why can you get five or six of the leading players at one table? Because there’s enough to go around for all of us. But if everyone is in this trade, what’s going to differentiate winners and losers? While it’s easy to paint everything with a single wide brush, there is going to be a dispersion of who performs well and who has some disappointing results. To be absolutely clear, we’re not doing every opportunity we see. We are doing the tiniest fraction. And even with that very tight filter, we can deploy a tremendous amount of capital. Returning to the energy supply question, where do you see gas fitting in here? You mentioned lower-carbon technologies, but all the tech companies are scrambling to get their hands on gas turbines. Gas is going to be critically important. But try and order a new gas turbine today, it’s not coming in a decade that has a ‘two’ on the front of it. That’s why today we see the greatest amount of growth in things like solar and batteries. When you look at some of the mounting public pushback on data centers, is that a risk to the pace of energy demand growth ahead? Is there a risk of overbuilding? If there’s a single narrative that is most starkly divorced from the fundamentals we’re seeing on the ground, it’s the idea that the demand for AI infrastructure and the energy and the supply chain that supports it is in some way fragile. Or that there’s a small tweak in model efficiency that’s going to disrupt this supply-demand imbalance we have today. Even if demand , there would still be an imbalance that the current levels of supply are nowhere near servicing. So will it be this way forever? No. But certainly today being a provider of incremental capacity into this supply chain is very attractive. It’s also important to recognize that what we’re building is under 20- or 25-year contracts with the greatest counterparties in the world. We’re going to get a return on our capital in that initial contract, regardless of what the demand environment looks like two or three decades from now. Infrastructure projects historically have a public offtaker, like the Port Authority or municipal water departments. Private companies are on the other side of the AI projects. Is AI fundamentally infrastructure, or are we just calling it that? In the past, economies ran on toll roads and railroads and pipelines that were physical. But as the world around us increasingly digitizes, data is going to need to be increasingly transported, processed, and stored just like every other commodity. So we view this as building the pipelines and the toll roads for a digital era.

events.title: Windows 11 market share creeps upwards as cost of staying on Windows 10 set to double
events.summary: The first year of Windows 10 Extended Security Updates is coming to an end, and Windows 11's market share has ticked up as enterprises weigh up the cost of keeping Windows 10 running a little longer. Windows 11's market share has risen above 70 percent to 71.5 percent, while Windows 10's has dropped to 27.77 percent, according to statistics wrangler Statcounter. Microsoft does not provide official statistics on Windows 11 and 10 usage, so Statcounter's figures should be treated as estimates. They are derived from Statcounter's tracking code, which is installed on over 1 million sites globally. The shares have remained relatively static since a surge in Windows 11 adoption at the end of last year, likely driven by the upgrade wave after Windows 10 dropped out of support on Oct 14, 2025. The Extended Security Updates (ESU) program allowed holdouts to stick with Windows 10, but the first year of that program is coming to an end, and kind old Microsoft will be hiking the prices for year two, at least as far as commercial customers are concerned. ESU licenses cost $61 per device for the first year for commercial users. Microsoft stated that the price would double every consecutive year for a maximum of three years, meaning that a renewal for year two will come in at $122. There are ways around the charge, of course. As well as consumers who can stay with Windows 10 and receive free security updates in return for redeeming Microsoft Rewards Points or using Windows Backup to sync their settings to the cloud, Windows 365 users are also exempt. It's also worth noting that European Economic Area (EEA) consumers receive no-strings-attached security updates. However, enterprises that need Windows 10 security updates must pay for them, as they did with other Microsoft products the software biz moved on from despite large user bases. The rising cost may be prompting some to reassess their estates. This month's uptick, while far short of last year's surge, could signal a sizeable ripple as the economics of keeping Windows 10 devices supported begin to favor Windows 11. Enterprises have plenty of reasons to keep Windows 10 devices: that one weird bit of hardware that won't work with anything else, or a simple case of a refresh cycle not fitting in with Microsoft's demand that old kit be junked to allow new software to run. Esben Dochy, a principal technology evangelist at Lansweeper, told The Register that its data indicated enterprises had been very active in moving off Windows 10 during the first year of ESU, with what is left being much "stickier." He reckoned there would be a "small bump" around the renewal date, and said, "The ESU price doubles for the second year, and that makes the business case for replacing the 'we'll get to it' machines a lot easier," but noted "it's likely that the steep part of the curve is behind us. "The remaining devices are mostly ones where paying ESU is cheaper or simpler than replacing whatever they're bolted to. For those, ESU really is the cost of doing business." The Statcounter figures indicate that that "small bump" could be on the way as ESU costs double, but many of the Windows 10 hold outs seem unlikely to be going anywhere just yet. ®

events.title: The AI boom is making the world’s cheapest smartphones disappear
events.summary: AI data centers are driving demand for memory chips, pushing phone makers to raise prices and abandon some of their most affordable models. The world’s cheapest smartphones are disappearing because AI infrastructure is absorbing the components. Prices of existing smartphone models have risen by about 15% globally this year , while newly launched models are roughly 25% more expensive than last year. A global memory chip shortage, driven by demand from AI data centers, is pushing up the cost of making smartphones. Chinese smartphone makers — which have championed affordable, feature-rich devices and account for approximately 60% of all smartphones shipped globally — have “drastically reduced” their entry-level projects this year as memory-chip costs have risen, Ivan Lam, senior analyst at research firm Counterpoint, told Rest of World . They are instead prioritizing more profitable premium devices. The smartphone price increases vary sharply by region: They have risen by 21% in India, 19% across Asia-Pacific, and 18% in the Middle East and Africa. In the U.S., they have gone up by just 5%. The shift could affect more than consumers looking for cheaper phones. For people who have yet to buy their first smartphone, higher prices could make it harder to get online at all — potentially widening the digital divide. The consequences will also reach the U.S. as more essential services move online and the global supply chain for smartphones becomes more expensive. GSMA, the global mobile industry association, had earlier said nearly 800 million more people will use mobile internet by 2030. But it is concerned that rising smartphone costs would affect this projection and widen the gap of digital inequality, Claire Sibthorpe, head of digital inclusion at the group’s nonprofit foundation, told Rest of World . “We live in an increasingly digital world, and the proliferation of technologies such as AI is creating greater digital divides and inequities,” Sibthorpe said. “Stakeholders are increasingly using AI to provide access to important services, but people won’t be able to benefit without access to an internet-enabled phone and the internet.” In 2025, more than one in four smartphones shipped globally cost less than $150 . That market is now shrinking. Chinese phonemakers including Xiaomi i Xiaomi Xiaomi is a Chinese consumer electronics company that leads the country in smartphone manufacturing and sales. READ MORE , Oppo, Vivo, and Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE have built their businesses around offering affordable phones with increasingly sophisticated features. But the economics of that strategy are changing. What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300.” Ivan Lam, senior analyst, Counterpoint Chinese companies “would rather reduce investment in products below $150 or $200 and put more resources into higher-margin phones, branding, user experience, and AI,” said Lam. In India, Xiaomi raised the price of a 128GB Redmi 15C from 12,499 rupees ($140) at launch last December to 16,999 rupees ($190) in June, a 36% increase. In Southeast Asia, Oppo’s sub-$100 phone shipments plunged 96%, and Vivo moved its main entry-level model above $100 in most markets, according to research firm Omdia . In Africa, where 81% of smartphones shipped last year cost less than $200, shipments of sub-$100 phones fell 34% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. “What used to be below $150 may become below $250, or even $300,” Lam said, adding that he does not expect costs to return to their pre-2025 levels. The memory-chip shortage is unlikely to ease soon, Ramon Llamas, research director in mobile devices at market research and advisory firm IDC, told Rest of World. “ There are three primary manufacturers of memory, and in late 2025, all of them pivoted the vast majority of their supply towards AI centers instead of consumer electronics,” Llamas said. “That left many companies scrambling for inventory. … Scarcity of memory has driven up prices for memory, and those price increases have been passed on to the consumer.” Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology make up more than 90% of the global memory chip market. These companies have entered several partnerships with U.S. AI giants in recent years. S&P Global has estimated that the capital expenditure of U.S. hyperscalers — Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, and SpaceX — will exceed $1.3 trillion in 2027 , up from a projected $870 billion in 2026 and $470 billion in 2025. Shipments of sub-$100 smartphones are already falling sharply. The 173 million sub-$100 smartphones shipped globally last year are disappearing, with shipments falling almost 60% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to IDC.
