events.title: How ProPublica Reporters Became Private School Owners in 24 Hours
events.summary: The only requirement to open a private school in Arkansas is displaying a flag and flagpole, so the reporting team visited the local flag shop in Little Rock. Brian Chilson/Arkansas Times It began as a casual question — and a flicker of curiosity — uttered during a meeting of ProPublica journalists who this year are reporting on publicly funded private schools. We were discussing how, in many states, basically anyone can open a private school wherever they want. No experience, no training, no curriculum required. One of our editors jumped in and asked: What if ProPublica tried to establish a private school? We were intrigued. We are longtime education reporters, not educators. Would that matter? Where, if anywhere, do states draw the line on who is fit to run a school — and in some cases, collect public money to fund their ventures?  We decided that testing the thesis that anyone can open a school would be valuable to our ongoing reporting, particularly at a time when we have found that private schools are growing rapidly across the country — in barns, farms, co-working spaces, people’s homes and parks. These new schools are fueled by taxpayer-funded vouchers and other programs, and our reporting has revealed states have little interest in monitoring them .  We had some inspiration to draw from: In 2015, comedian John Oliver founded a tax-exempt church to show how easy it was for televangelists to avoid paying taxes while soliciting millions of dollars.  Some of us live in Chicago and are well aware of the lore of the Mirage Tavern , a real bar that undercover reporters operated in the 1970s to expose corruption in the city. While that investigation had a substantial impact, and led to a new city oversight agency, it also drew criticism for its deceptive practices.   We drew lessons from that reporting and set some ground rules at the start of our experiment. To be clear, we had no intention of operating schools. We won’t enroll any students.  Most importantly, it would be critical for us to be transparent about who we were in our applications, using our newsroom phone numbers and email addresses. In one state, we even disclosed that we were “journalists exploring opening a microschool.” We also decided we would stop the experiment if it would require doing something illegal or using public resources for our own benefit. Help ProPublica Report on Education Have you had trouble finding a school or using a voucher-style program? Do you have concerns about schools — public or private — in your area? Help us understand how families across the country are navigating their school options. Get in Touch Here’s how we went about the experiment in Arkansas, West Virginia and North Carolina:  First, we partnered with newsrooms in the three states — the Arkansas Times , Mountain State Spotlight in West Virginia and The Assembly in North Carolina — and pursued creating the schools together. No one knows their states better than reporters who live there, so we wanted to work with the experts. Plus, the school applications required local addresses and we reasoned that newsroom addresses, which state officials could easily look up, would be extra transparent.  Then, we came up with names for the schools. We aimed to call them Curiosity Academies to reflect our curiosity as journalists. We succeeded with the ProPublica-Arkansas Times Curiosity Academy and ProPublica-Mountain State Spotlight Curiosity Academy. A word-count limit required us to scrap curiosity for our school in North Carolina. We simply called it the ProPublica-Assembly Academy.   Next, we filed paperwork with each state. That turned out to be easier than working through the legal and ethical questions with our editors, our legal team and our standards editor to design our experiment in the first place.  In Arkansas, we didn’t need permission from the state Education Department, which does not regulate private schools. All it took was filling out a form on the Arkansas secretary of state website, $45 and an American flag to be recognized as a private school business (yes, Arkansas requires all schools to have an American flag — but only public schools also are required to have the Arkansas flag). The secretary of state’s office even emailed us a certificate. The official certificate acknowledging our school Secretary of State/State of Arkansas But when it came to applying for our private school to become eligible for public funds, a process that does add some guardrails, we didn’t think we could do it. In Arkansas, private schools participating in the voucher-like program have to be accredited or working toward it, which often requires creating curriculum and school handbooks. That seemed like a step too far since we weren’t actually opening schools.  However, we discovered that Arkansas allows a subset of schools called microschools to use public money with fewer requirements. So, we decided to apply for public funds as a microschool. That process also took only about 10 minutes. We didn’t need to provide our credentials or a background check, prove our fiscal stability or assure that the newsroom was a safe place for students. (If approved, we would not take the next step and register to receive public money.) Want Your Own ProPublica Academy Merch? Visit Our Store A state employee who reviewed our application, which we submitted in early September, said we missed the deadline for this school year but could apply for next school year. He also suggested another way we could tap into public money. Kaelin Clay, the Arkansas Department of Education spokesperson, said the agency reviews applications to the voucher-like program to determine if the schools meet state requirements. She said microschool families have the “freedom to choose” where and how their children learn. In West Virginia, we spent little time handwriting the required information on notebook paper and submitting it to the state Education Department. We eventually established our school as a microschool after a state employee shared that, unlike the regulations for private schools, we would not need an inspection.  We did need proof of at least a high school diploma, and we shared one of our real college transcripts from the late 1990s with the local school district, which then notified the state of our new school. (We couldn’t find the high school transcript; does anyone keep them?)  In an official statement, a spokesperson for West Virginia’s Department of Education said it “does not approve or deny the operation of microschools for any reason, including the qualifications of the owner/operator.” State law includes no mechanism for oversight of microschools. events.title: BT buys TalkTalk out of administration to keep 2.5M customers connected
events.summary: Former state-owned telco monopoly BT Group has bought TalkTalk's consumer and wholesale businesses out of administration, rescuing services used by 2.5 million customers. BT says it acquired TalkTalk Telecommunications Limited and PlatformX Communications Limited on a debt-free basis. It expects a total cash impact of approximately £400 million in its current financial year, including the acquisition consideration and other costs. BT said it stepped in after a prolonged sale process failed to find a buyer for the consumer and wholesale operations. TalkTalk reported approximately £1.2 billion in revenue over the past 12 months but was loss-making. Separately, TalkTalk Business and UK technology services biz ARO announced plans to merge in August. The UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said a collapse could disrupt emergency calls, hospital communications, and medical alarms. DCMS Secretary of State Lisa Nandy stated: "Phone and broadband services are vital national infrastructure. If TalkTalk services fail, there is a genuine risk to life and public services – including to hospitals, schools, and emergency care." Nandy issued a Public Interest Intervention Notice under section 42 of the Enterprise Act 2002, allowing her to consider the wider public interest alongside competition concerns. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) must report to her by October 19. BT says the businesses will operate separately and continue to compete pending the regulatory review. Kester Mann, director of consumer and connectivity at FDM CCS Insight, said: "Given BT's strong position in the broadband market, it will inevitably also evoke scrutiny from regulators keen to ensure a fair and competitive playing field. This is even more relevant coming just days after competition authorities raised serious concerns over nexfibre's planned acquisition of Netomnia." Last week, the CMA provisionally identified competition concerns in wholesale fixed broadband services over nexfibre's proposed acquisition of Substantial, Netomnia's parent company. BT Group chief executive Allison Kirkby said of the TalkTalk deal: "This is a genuinely unprecedented situation, where millions of citizens and businesses were at risk if TalkTalk had collapsed. Our immediate priority is to stabilise the business and provide a safety net for the households and businesses who rely on TalkTalk." Clive Selley will lead the stabilization and integration planning with immediate effect. Martijn Blanken takes over his role as CEO of BT International. Mann noted: "The deal cements a painful decline for one of the UK's most established and well-known broadband providers. With a clear value-for-money proposition, it should have been thriving amid continued concerns over the cost of living. "But it failed to respond sufficiently to a fast-changing and increasingly competitive market, became burdened with debt following a buyout in 2021, and regularly suffered with poor perception over service. Its demise should serve as a stark warning to any value-focused telecom provider." ® Updated to add at 1244 UTC: A Virgin Media spokesperson got in touch – suffice it to say, competitors are less than pleased: “This has all the characteristics of a stitch up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest. Just days after the competition regulator proposed potentially blocking a logical deal between nexfibre and Netomnia that would accelerate fibre investment and create a genuine, financially sustainable challenger to Openreach, it now appears that rules might be watered down so the incumbent can roll its tanks over competition and further tighten its grip on the market. “The logic simply doesn’t add up. We don’t believe rules should be thrown out the window to allow TalkTalk to fall into BT’s lap without a proper process and we will be raising our concerns directly with government and regulators.”

events.title: A Trump-sized shadow looms over the Supreme Court's new term
events.summary: The Supreme Court 's next chapter begins Monday, with the justices set to decide key questions involving President Trump's immigration agenda, climate -change litigation and gun control in their new term. The big picture: But one of the most closely watched fights may be on Truth Social, rather than the docket, as an increasingly agitated Trump chastises the high court he helped shape. The executive and judicial branches are set for another round in the white-columned ring with a president who moves at breakneck speed . State of play: The court recently agreed to hear two major immigration cases, one over mandatory detention for certain immigrants and another over deporting immigrants to third countries where they lack ties. On the latter, the high court allowed the administration to restart its fast-tracked third-country deportations late last month while it considers the underlying legal questions in December. The court agreed Thursday to take up the detention case, setting the stage to test the Trump administration's legal interpretation that noncitizens who entered the country illegally, but have been living in the U.S., are to be held without bond. While federal appeals courts have been divided on the issue, a vast majority — nine of the 11 — have rejected the Trump administration's interpretation. Flashback: While the Supreme Court shot down Trump's attempt to undermine birthright citizenship last term, it handed him a number of immigration wins and green-lit policies on its shadow docket. Those victories for Trump allowed the administration to end temporary protected status , enforce stricter asylum rules and use a revamped tool to check voters' citizenship . Zoom out: Before those cases come to the bench, the court will hear arguments Monday in a key climate case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants, Axios' Ben Geman reports. The court also added two other cases to its lineup Thursday, on top of the mandatory detention debate: One is about a federal law protecting land use by religious groups brought by a missionary organization, and the other is about military benefits in divorce settlement agreements. Later this year, the court will weigh the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and consider whether Arizona can mandate proof of citizenship for people registering to vote. More disputes over other Trump policies are sure to reach the court this term. Friction point: Though the high court has inflated executive power and gave the president a number of summer shadow docket wins, it also checked some of his most audacious actions last term. He didn't like that. After the justices blocked the administration's pre-midterm attempt to rewrite mail-in voting rules, the president raged against his own Supreme Court picks. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," he wrote on Truth Social. In a recent interview with Time, the president said he regretted nominating them, saying, "I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it's unfortunate what they did." events.title: A Prediction Market About the Past? Sure, Why Not!
events.summary: Would you put money on whether Covid-19 originated from a lab ? How about whether some of the footage from the Apollo 11 moon landing was actually filmed on Earth? Verifact Markets, a new startup that bills itself as a “prediction market for disputed facts,” is betting that people will be eager to weigh in on questions like these. The company’s premise is so quirky it sounds like something a couple of philosophy and economics majors dreamed after too many bong rips in their dorm room: Instead of wagering on the future, why not trade on stuff that already happened? When Verifact Markets launched on Friday, some of the initial topics traders could take a position on included whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide and whether insurance behemoth State Farm “intentionally delayed” claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires . The featured market during beta testing was, indeed, about the origins of Covid-19. (As of writing, the market is still open, with “true” priced at 76 cents and “false” at 32; the majority of participants had put money on the pandemic beginning at Wuhan Institute of Virology.) Verifact Markets is being funded and incubated by Positron Capital Management, the family office of tech investor Peter Wokwicz. He envisions the startup as a way to settle debates over hot-button issues like the amount of energy consumed by AI data centers. “I’m excited, because nobody’s done this before,” Wokwicz says. “We’re not going to shy away from controversial markets.” In a regular prediction market , participants buy financial instruments known as event contracts, which are pegged to whether a specific event will take place in the future. Topics range from which team will win the Super Bowl to what the price of bitcoin will be in 15 minutes to whether the US and Iran will reach a nuclear deal. Someone who buys a “yes” contract on Polymarket that the Bears will start Case Keenum next week will make money if that happens. Similarly, someone who bets “no” on Kalshi that it will rain in Miami tomorrow will lose money if there’s a downpour. Each prediction market has its own rules about how it resolves events, and sometimes things can get messy, like when Polymarket bettors tussled over whether Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky actually wore a suit , or when Kalshi traders revolted over how the platform settled a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader would leave power. Verifact Markets’ setup is even messier. That’s by design, since the platform focuses specifically on scenarios where people disagree on what took place. It lists markets for past events that it considers “disputed” and lets its customers wager “true” or “false” on whether they really happened. People can also submit “evidence” for or against their position, and the company plans to offer rewards for credible documentation that helps resolve markets. If Verifact Markets determines that there’s enough evidence to make a call, it does so. If it still can’t tell, the company will “expire” a market and pay out users based on its calculation of the odds at the time. According to Verifact Markets chief executive and cofounder Rodrigo Aquino, the markets themselves won’t determine whether something is true or false. That means even if all of the customers in a given market voted “true,” that won’t necessarily make it so. Trading prices will be factored in alongside other evidence and documentation that is submitted to the company by users. It is also planning to launch its own research system, which Aquino describes as “patent pending.” When I ask Aquino how the system works, he keeps the answer impressively vague: “We are analyzing, multi-dimensionally, a multitude of data points,” he says, noting that the process is “very mathematical, very quantitative” and also “very secretive.” When I point out that credibly determining how the Covid pandemic started would be a massive news story, resolving a mystery that has eluded scientists for years, Aquino remains upbeat. “It’s doable,” he says. Verifact says that it is currently in talks with market makers about providing liquidity. Right now, the project is so small that it is being bootstrapped by Positron Capital Management. There are a number of ongoing lawsuits in the US over whether prediction markets should be considered financial instruments or gambling, but it’s hard to discern how Verifact would factor into that debate because of its rather odd business model. For the time being, the company is only offering its markets to people outside of the United States as it looks for the most viable legal path forward domestically, as it is not a licensed exchange in the US. But Wokwicz claims he purchased a regulated financial exchange in the last year and intends to roll Verifact into it when he can.

events.title: Oil prices would have hit $200 a barrel if not for East-West pipeline, Aramco chief says
events.summary: Brent crude prices would have reached up to $200 per barrel if Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline did not exist, the chief executive of Saudi Aramco said. The company ​can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million barrels per day available ⁠within days, ​Amin Nasser ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday. “Our system is intact,” Mr Nasser said. Aramco has ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required, he added. Brent crude, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, has been trading around $100 a barrel over the past month, even as more tankers are transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has been playing a vital role as Aramco over the past month boosted crude shipments from its main export terminal at Ras Tanura. The company reacted quickly to a temporary halt to its main cross-country pipeline after an attack last month. Aramco has since brought flows on the East-West pipeline back to about 80 per cent of capacity, meaning it also has more oil to ship from the Red Sea. Aramco has ensured its oil supplies proved resilient throughout the conflict by relying on international storage and working to quickly repair damaged infrastructure, Mr Nasser said. He did not mention reports of recent attacks on the kingdom in his speech. Aramco is looking for alternative crude export routes and additional international storage facilities to avoid relying too much on any single method of reaching global buyers, he added. 'Scarily thin' reserves However, the oil stockpiles that cushion the world from supply shocks have become “scarily thin”, putting markets at risk of worsening unless the Strait of Hormuz fully reopens, Mr Nasser said. He was speaking only days after governments in the world’s biggest economies announced plans to release as much as 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel stocks to ease rising fuel costs. “Until Hormuz fully reopens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify,” he said. “While the squeeze on crude is serious, refined fuel prices have risen even more sharply.” Releasing stockpiles will buy economies some time but will not fix the imbalance between supply and demand, Mr Nasser said. Even after the vital shipping chokepoint at Hormuz reopens, it may take as long as two years for energy-consuming countries to replenish their stockpiles, he said. Gulf producers are working to step up production and exports and have succeeded in boosting crude flows to near prewar levels. The higher flows have provided scant relief for oil markets, which are still pricing in security risks to supply in the Gulf and Red Sea. With inputs from Bloomberg and Reuters

events.title: Strong data. Bad vibes. Voters are judging Trump's economy by prices.
events.summary: President Trump's economic data keeps getting stronger. His economic polling keeps getting worse by the day. Why it matters: The midterms are less than a month away, and the administration is circling the drain on voters' No. 1 issue. It may be too late to change that, but it's also not clear anyone has much of a plan to try. What they're saying: "If I say 'oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union." "It's true that the polls, which have gotten the president's success wrong every time, have been saying that people are looking a little bit depressed about the economy. But if you look at their actions, the actions speak way louder than words," Hassett added, citing spending and default data. The big picture: There is ample evidence the economy is, statistically speaking, relatively strong. 💰 Economic growth is solid and accelerating. 💪 The labor market is relatively stable . 💵 The K-shaped economy is ending as lower-end wages rise. 🛍️ Public and private data say consumers are spending more than ever. Yes, but: People feel lousy. ☹️ The Conference Board's consumer confidence index is at a 12-year low. 🐘 Republican sentiment in particular is eroding at its fastest rate since the Great Financial Crisis, per University of Michigan data. 🪫 38% of voters told the latest CBS News poll their personal finances are fairly or very bad — a reflection, perhaps, of the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for months now. (When respondents were asked what they think about when they rate the economy, 91% said "prices.") 👎 73% disapprove of President Trump's handling of the economy, per the latest AP-NORC survey, the lowest rating he — or President Biden — ever had. (69% say Trump's handling of cost-of-living issues has been worse than they expected in his second term.) Friction point: When voters go to the polls, they don't bring the latest release from the Bureau of Economic Analysis with them. They bring their feelings, and those are very bad. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told " The Axios Show " the administration wasn't going to repeat the Biden-era mistake of telling people how to feel. But Trump himself said last week that Republicans weren't doing a good enough job of messaging . The intrigue: So far, Trump's strategy seems to be the rich-uncle theory, which doesn't appear to be paying off with voters. He continues to promise $5,000 checks for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterms — a $1.3 trillion bombshell that most people don't believe he'll ever pay. On Saturday, he promised seniors $2 billion in Medicare rebates , a big number that works out to about two weeks' worth of premium payments. Between the lines: Some of the tension comes from the nature of the economic boom, an AI-fueled bonanza that nonetheless appears to be leaving many ordinary Americans behind. It's not a K-shaped economy, says Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI, but a "gator economy" — as in an alligator's mouth, where the bottom stays flat and the top is pointing to the sky poised to chomp. The bottom line: There's good reason to think the economy's not that bad. There's even better reason to think voters don't care. Emily Peck contributed reporting.

events.title: Fewer young Americans are ‘thriving,’ poll finds
events.summary: The number of young Americans who say they’re “thriving” is near a low point while the share of middle-age adults who say the same is at a nadir, underscoring the level of relative dissatisfaction among these key demographic groups ahead of the midterms. Only 44% of adults ages 18 to 29 describe themselves as thriving, according to Gallup , 20 points lower than the high measured in 2010. Forty-five percent of adults 30 to 44 say the same; both figures have declined in the years since the COVID-19 pandemic. These declines appear to be tied to increases in rates of depression, among other factors. The share of those ages 45 to 64 is also at a low of 46%, on par with the measure during the 2008 financial crisis. In sharp contrast, those 65 and older are more likely than ever to say they’re thriving, which appears largely driven by satisfaction with their economic situation. — Morgan Chalfant

events.title: Latino men swung hard to Trump in 2024. Now they're swinging back
events.summary: Latino voters, whose dramatic shift toward President Trump helped power his 2024 victory, are moving sharply back toward Democrats ahead of the midterms, two new national polls show. Why it matters: Republicans built pieces of their 2026 strategy, including newly drawn House districts in Texas and Florida, around the assumption that Trump's historic Latino gains would endure. A reversal is complicating that bet in key races. Trump's breakthrough with Latino men was among the clearest signs of a changing GOP coalition in 2024. Two years later, those gains look far less durable, though Democrats haven't recovered all the ground they lost in the last decade. The latest: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll found Latino voters preferred Democratic control of Congress 59%–35% — a 24-point advantage, double the margin the same poll found in 2024. A new CBS News/YouGov poll tells the same story: Hispanic likely voters favor Democratic House candidates 60%–39%. Zoom in: Latino men have undergone a particularly strong political whiplash. Hillary Clinton won Latino men by 31 points in 2016, according to the Edison National Election Pool exit poll , and Biden won them by 23 points in 2020. But in 2024, Trump won them by 10 points. NBC now finds Latino men preferring Democratic congressional control 53%–39%. Stunning stat: About one in seven Latino voters who say they backed Trump in 2024 now want Democrats to take control of Congress. A majority of Latino voters say their congressional vote will be a signal against Trump. Driving the shift: The economic squeeze felt by Latino voters hasn't changed much, but who they're blaming has. Nearly two-thirds of Latino voters say their income is falling behind the cost of living in the NBC poll, almost exactly where that number stood in 2024. But 78% disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living. Democrats now hold a 21-point advantage on handling the economy, after Trump held a 4-point edge over Harris in NBC's 2024 poll. Trump's mass-deportation agenda has also sparked backlash: 67% say Trump's enforcement has gone too far. The enforcement campaign has also become personal: 31% say they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported. Yes, but: Polling voters a month before a midterm isn't the same as measuring who actually turns out. Pew found that Trump's 2024 Hispanic gains were driven largely by changes in who voted that year, not by Biden voters switching to Trump. In the NBC poll, 17% of voters said they or someone close to them was considering not voting in person because of fear of immigration enforcement. Between the lines: Despite all this, Democrats haven't repaired their brand with Latino voters. Their net favorability has actually fallen by one point from 2024, but the GOP's has fallen by 18 points. In 2016, 55% of Latino voters viewed the Democratic Party positively and 24% negatively — a 31-point net positive rating. Today, it's 41% positive and 42% negative. Republicans have still made lasting inroads: Just 16% of Latino voters viewed the GOP positively in 2016, compared with 27% today. But negative views have also risen, from 57% then to 62% now. What we're watching: Both parties are fighting over a large and growing Latino electorate in key races across Arizona, California, Florida and Texas.

events.title: App-makers are having a blast with the iPhone Duo, turning it into a retro Walkman
events.summary: The iPhone Duo isn't even out yet, but developers are already having fun with the new design, creating apps that turn Apple's first foldable smartphone into everything from an accordion to a retro Walkman. Why it matters: Clever apps that couldn't exist on a traditional iPhone could help persuade early adopters to fork over nearly $2,000 for Apple's first foldable. Flashback: It's reminiscent of the early days of the iPhone, when developers turned its giant touchscreen and sensors into virtual versions of familiar objects, such as the lighter apps with flames that flickered and swayed as the phone moved. Zoom in: Among the apps is Duo-Man , a music player that turns the latest iPhone into a portable cassette player modeled on Sony's Walkman. Users open the Duo to choose an album and "insert" a cassette, then close it to start listening. Even the clicks and static are actual recordings from a real Walkman. It's the brainchild of indie app developer Vidit Bhargava, who created it during a four-hour hackathon late last month. "I love the Walkman," he said. "I was just staring at it. I was like, this thing opens exactly like the iPhone Duo. What if your iPhone Duo was your Walkman, and you had to open up the door to change the album, and once you closed it, it would start playing the music?" Bhargava has a particular affinity for the Walkman, having previously altered one of the vintage players to only work when a person is moving. Zoom out: Developers are finding ways to make the fold itself part of the software. The San Francisco hackathon where Duo-Man was born produced 73 submitted Duo projects, ranging from games to music tools and a virtual pop-up book. Accorduon turns the hinge into the bellows of a virtual accordion: The faster you fold and unfold the phone, the louder the instrument plays. Crate , which took first place at the same hackathon where Duo-Man finished second, turns the Duo into a beat machine, where folding controls effects and snapping the phone open triggers a musical drop. Foldtales uses the hinge to create a virtual pop-up book, with castles, trees and other objects rising as the phone opens. Twofold uses the partially folded screen to hide each player's pieces in virtual versions of classic tabletop games. And Delta developer Riley Testut is working on Duo support that could make the foldable iPhone resemble another familiar hinged gadget: Nintendo's dual-screen DS. My thought bubble: Apple is years behind Samsung and Google in releasing a foldable phone. But its large developer ecosystem could help it catch up quick. And the timing could turn out to be fortuitous. Developers are getting a new piece of hardware just as AI coding tools are making it faster and easier to turn a quirky idea into working software. What we're watching: Whether the initial burst of experimentation produces enduring apps — and whether Apple sells enough Duos to reward developers for building custom apps.

events.title: Oklahoma Oil Company Plugs Disposal Well That Posed Threat to City’s Drinking Water
events.summary: The Flying Monkey disposal well in Enid, Oklahoma. Last year, the city asked the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica An Oklahoma oil and gas company plugged a well that disposes of oil production’s toxic byproduct after an investigation by The Frontier and ProPublica revealed that regulators had approved the well in violation of state rules meant to protect public groundwater supplies. The disposal well, named the Flying Monkey, injected oil field wastewater underground and sat roughly a quarter-mile from two municipal groundwater supply sites that served the small city of Enid in northwest Oklahoma. Wastewater injection operations are banned within a half-mile of public water wells unless regulators hold a hearing to ensure that this activity will not pollute groundwater. Regulators at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission did not hold a hearing before approving the well in 2018. The city of Enid filed a complaint last year asking the state to revoke the Flying Monkey’s permit to operate. On Sept. 14, with the complaint still active in the agency’s administrative law court, employees of the Flying Monkey’s current owner — BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings LLC — dropped a cast iron plug into the bottom of the well, followed by more than 200 sacks of cement, to permanently seal it off, according to a report the company filed to the corporation commission. A representative of the state was on site to witness the plugging. Eric Huddleston, an attorney representing BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings, which acquired the Flying Monkey in 2020, said the company decided to permanently shut the well after determining it was “underutilized and operationally unnecessary.” A spokesperson for the corporation commission did not respond to requests for comment, including about the agency’s role in the well’s closure. Enid city officials said they did not know the well had been plugged until our reporter informed them. “This decision is, for lack of a better word, thrilling because this is such a vital issue,” said Frank Baker, an Enid city commissioner. “Our water sources have been put in danger, and for this one well to have been plugged, this is the best possible outcome.” In Enid’s 2025 complaint to the state, its lawyers noted that the Flying Monkey’s original operator, Hinkle Oil & Gas, had incorrectly checked a box on its permit application stating that the injection well was not within a half-mile of a public water supply well. “This was demonstrably false,” Enid’s lawyers wrote. Hinkle previously declined to answer questions about the Flying Monkey. Earlier this year, BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings refiled a permit application for the Flying Monkey, where it acknowledged the proximity of the city’s water supply wells. A building containing one of Enid’s groundwater supply wells sits about a quarter-mile from the now-plugged Flying Monkey disposal well. September Dawn Bottoms for ProPublica The Flying Monkey had a checkered operational history. In the last five years, the state has shut down the wastewater disposal well repeatedly after it failed tests of its structural integrity. These failures can indicate a problem that might allow wastewater to escape, potentially threatening drinking water sources. The well had failed five of these tests since 2021. In early July, nine days after the newsrooms’ investigation published, the Flying Monkey’s owner reported another leak in the well’s tubing. The state gave BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings 90 days to fix the leak or to permanently plug the well. Our investigation identified two other wells in Enid that violated the state distance rule between wastewater injection wells and the city’s groundwater supply sites. Both of those wells, which are owned by other companies, remain active. Read More To Protect Its Drinking Water, This City Has to Appeal to the Oil Regulators That Put It at Risk The proximity of wells to drinking water isn’t only an issue in Enid. Across Oklahoma, the news outlets identified at least 114 injection wells that were located within a half-mile of a public water supply well. More than 300,000 Oklahomans live in communities that rely on these water wells, according to our analysis. Baker, the Enid official, told The Frontier and ProPublica that he hopes the corporation commission will begin to plug other injection wells that threaten public water supplies. “I hope and pray this is an example that we’ll start to see replicated across the state in the near future,” he said. In addition to its request to plug the well, the city of Enid has asked the corporation commission to impose stronger regulations on oilfield wastewater disposal near its water supply, including a wider distance buffer between the injection sites and the city’s water wells. This request comes amid a recent uptick in wastewater injection in the Enid area, according to a legal filing made by the city. The commission previously declined to comment on Enid’s complaint because it is an active case. The case will continue to be heard in the agency’s administrative law court later this year. events.title: Democratic-controlled Senate would confirm ‘very few’ Trump nominees
events.summary: The News The winner of Senate control would snatch one of the biggest tangible prizes of the midterms: control over President Donald Trump’s nominees. If Democrats are in charge, don’t expect many of Trump’s picks to move at all. “If the nominees are as crappy as his present ones, very few of them are going to get through. If he sends us a new [Defense Secretary Pete] Hegseth, I bet he wouldn’t pass the Senate,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told Semafor in a pre-election interview. “It’s the quality of the candidate that matters. Thus far, Trump has a record of notoriously bad candidates.” Democrats are favored to take the House, which would limit big bipartisan breakthroughs on legislation next year. But if Republicans can hold the Senate, they’d at least retain the ability to confirm Trump nominees — most notably, lifetime judicial appointments. Schumer’s comments confirm that Democratic control of the Senate under Trump would turn the battle to confirm Senate nominees into trench warfare, with committee chairmen able to bottle up Trump’s picks easily and Schumer able to simply not put them on the floor. Perhaps a handful of judges would be confirmed, but Cabinet secretaries would face long slogs. There’s also little hope that a Democratic majority would confirm a Supreme Court nominee — should a vacancy arise — after then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell’s blockade of Merrick Garland during the Obama years. “A Democrat-controlled Senate will without any question block every single one of President Trump’s nominees. This includes every cabinet member and every judge who is committed to upholding the Constitution,” said Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo. “[Schumer is] not going to change his playbook of obstruction and opposition.” Know More It’s been more than a decade since the president’s party lost control of the Senate during a midterm election. After the 2014 red wave, Senate Republicans gave former President Barack Obama few lower-level judges, blocked a Supreme Court seat from being filled, and even blocked his attorney general nominee, Loretta Lynch, from confirmation until the Senate passed a human trafficking bill. There’s no way around a judicial nominee blockade, but Trump can lean on acting officials in the executive branch. If Republicans do lose Senate control, look for the GOP to use its blunt confirmation tools — including confirming large tranches of nominees — in November and December to accomplish as much as they can before Schumer takes control again. There are currently 27 judicial vacancies at the district level and 10 nominees to fill those, mostly in Republican states. There are also a handful of nominees ready to be confirmed to federal appeals courts. If Republicans hold the chamber, they will probably prioritize judicial appointments for the next two years.

events.title: Brighter isn't better and more is less. The AI slowdown is nigh, no matter who says what
events.summary: There has been much chilly weather in the sunny meadowlands of AI futures. Fortunately, to use an indecently inappropriate adverb, the rest of the world isn’t really looking, being too busy chewing its nails over the very many other intimations of disaster. Sure, rebel swarms of attack agents breaking out of the labs isn’t a good look. OpenAI delaying its IPO and a new model launch likewise. All these things soak up whatever bandwidth the news media have to AI right now. Putting them in a bigger context, that of promises made and not kept, problems known but not fixed, the observable risk-reward ratios as models develop, we may at last start having a sense of what sort of crisis awaits. Actual crises are frequently triggered by crises in confidence, themselves caused when frameworks of assumption stop standing up to reality and wishful thinking. Thus, the assumption to date is that models will get more powerful and infrastructure more capable, in a way that justifies — demands — massive capex. The economics of giant infrastructure investment when you can’t buy what you need is a great bet in free markets that presupposes that freedom, and yeah, about that. A bigger problem is the idea that more powerful AI is always better. It frequently is, but that’s not good enough, When frontier models have to be kept in LLM jail for uncontrollable dishonesty, not so much. Here, the bigger context is that we’ve known that at heart LLM probability space is entirely relative. There is no ground truth there. Nobody has fixed hallucinations, and now we see the fascinating phenomenon of a machine that doesn’t understand truth but can deliberately lie. If more powerful models are better at that, scratch one assumption. Another huge assumption is that even at the current level of model reliability, agentic architectures are ready to be useful. Those who show all the caution of a chronic gambler on a winning "streak" are as ready to get the brakes slammed on as their opposites. The principal contender for the one true proof of concept that agentic AI is a dangerous fount of unexpected consequence is Meta’s new Muse. It is aimed at low-information credulous users and its star turn is, of course, shopping. The AI use case that’s five years away, and always has been. It’s Meta, so of course it soaks up all the information about you, your online activities and the people you talk to as much as it can. It will soon have ultracute animated Tamagotchi-style pets you can wear around your neck to improve your status as a Meta monitoring post. And we did say it was Meta, so has all the attention to security and careful design you may expect. Which is why it’s already been caught sending people’s physical addresses to strangers, and why when researcher Jonny at neuromatch.social went poking around its infrastructure — each instance runs permanently on its own Linux VM — they found just a ton of fun. Headline party tricks hard-coded. What looks like attempts to train off Claude. And yes, you can get it to run your own things on that VM deep within Meta, which Jonny points out is a botnet paradise waiting to happen. This banger of a bad ‘un is being given away to Meta users, who pretty much define a vulnerable target audience for tech that may not be totally trustworthy. Meta, of course, is dead against AI safety regulation. Place your bets on the headlines to follow. In any case, the upside of using agents as demoed in every keynote is either so trivial and trite — book me a restaurant! — or so catastrophic if it fails — organize my family vacation! — that consumer agents are a bust. It’s just that Meta may be bringing a lot of accelerant to that particular fire. There are other fires, of course, many known about since everything kicked off. Model collapse due to training on data contaminated with output? Still a thing, still no fix a "better" AI might provide. And that habit AI has of retailing everything and paying for nothing, choking off its own training data supply chain and a huge chunk of commerce and culture with it? Very much still a thing. Where AI does make consistent progress is in domain-specific tasks. Science, engineering, mathematics, and coding, if you match a model with enough reinforcement learning with humans who know how to manage them, there are startling results. You don’t get much innovation, not much newness, which is the true driver of progress. Better than humans is highly contextual. Computers have been better at chess for decades, but there isn’t a better chess. Horses run faster than humans, and that’s been useful for four millennia, but we got to peak horses quite some time ago. So the question is, have we reached peak AI, where the cost of future developments don’t match the risk they won’t work well enough to justify? If ChatGPT already writes a perfectly good business letter in a couple of seconds, there is no meaningful improvement to be had for users. Most AI is profoundly annoying, in ways that have nothing to do with the models and everything to do with perverted UX in an attempt to justify growth. That is both unsustainable and a tacit admission that AI hasn’t solved its use case problem. If we are at or near peak AI, is that the crisis that bursts that goddam bubble? Certainly a readjustment, as all bets on the continuous uptick curve are off. AI as it stands is useful enough to power a big industry sector, just in ways that are and remain at odds to how it is marketed and its future fantasies. Trust in AI Max may be shaken, but there's still room for lots of improvement. That slowdown that everyone who isn’t a miscreant is calling for may happen organically, if we escape the smoking-is-good-for-you mentality of the Metans and the Muskovites. That’s still a gamble we shouldn't be taking, but the odds may be better than we thought. ®

events.title: Non-oil sectors in UAE and Saudi Arabia maintain strong growth trajectory despite Iran war
events.summary: The non-oil private sectors of the UAE and Saudi Arabia maintained their expansion trajectory in September, as the Arab world’s two largest economies shook off the effects of the Iran war . The seasonally adjusted Riyad Bank purchasing managers’ index – a benchmark gauge of the kingdom’s non-oil economy – rose to 55.3 in September, from 53.8 in August, well above the neutral 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. The rate of improvement in the non-oil sector business activity last month was the strongest since February and marked the sixth consecutive month of improvements in business conditions. The acceleration last month was largely driven by a marked rise in new order growth, although it masked the softening in the rate of output growth. New orders hit levels closer to the index’s long-run average, suggesting that demand in the kingdom has recovered well after a slowdown in the middle of 2026. Businesses surveyed also referred to gradual improvements in the market that led to increased client numbers and higher spending. “The acceleration was primarily demand-led. New orders increased at their fastest pace since February,” said Naif Alghaith, chief economist at Riyad Bank. The September reading of the PMI index was broadly consistent with the “wider picture of the Saudi economy”, which was driven by domestic consumption, investment activity, government and PIF-related projects. “The strong improvement in new orders provides a positive forward-looking signal for activity in the coming months,” Mr Alghaith said. While the recovery was predominantly driven by the domestic market in September, new orders from foreign customers have now dropped for seven months running. Companies surveyed pointed to the effects of supply chain disruption amid the regional conflict that in some cases led to shipping delays. Gulf states including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, Opec’s biggest oil producer, have faced attacks during the war, which is now in its seventh month. The tourism and leisure, retail, aviation and properties sectors across the Gulf took a hit as Iran attacked civilian infrastructure and regional energy installations during the early days of the conflict. Gulf economies have bounced back gradually, although Iran continues to attack commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, while Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports are under a "maritime blockade" from Yemen's Tehran-backed Houthi rebels. Demand drives UAE Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years in response to higher input costs. Meanwhile, business activity increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand both purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index in September remained stable at 55.3 recorded in August, well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. The latest PMI reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, said David Owen, principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. “Businesses saw customer demand improve, not just in local markets but abroad as well, with new export business rising at the strongest rate in nearly two years,” he added. The improvement in the UAE’s business conditions was mainly driven by a “rapid monthly rise in output”, with the fastest rate of growth since February, before the outbreak of the war. Stronger demand conditions also supported a marked increase in new orders, although the pace of expansion eased from the seven-month high posted in August. The overall new order numbers were also supported by an increase in new business from abroad, which expanded for the third consecutive month and at the sharpest pace since November 2024, PMI data showed. However, as the demand strengthened, companies raised their output prices at the steepest rate since May 2011, which was among the fastest since the survey began. "While the economic picture looks more robust now, selling charges also rose markedly, suggesting that firms are taking the opportunity to boost their margins following a period of strong input cost pressures,” Mr Owen said. “With oil markets remaining volatile, and shipping routes still constrained, input costs and selling charges may remain elevated." Dubai momentum Non-oil private sector business activity in Dubai, one of the biggest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory. The Dubai PMI posted 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, signalling a “solid improvement”, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026 so far. The boost to Dubai’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven a "sharp and accelerated increase in output”, the fastest so far this year. New orders also rose markedly, supported by the strongest expansion in new business from abroad for two years, the PMI survey data showed. Although employment in the emirate increased in September, the backlog of work still increased at a sharp pace. “The rate of output price inflation quickened to the fastest since January 2014 as companies passed on higher input costs to customers,” the survey found.

events.title: HKTDC’s Belt and Road Summit drives momentum
events.summary: [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] The 11th Belt and Road Summit, which took place in Wan Chai on 9-10 September, brought together more than 6,200 top officials, business leaders and senior professionals from 70-plus B&R countries and regions to explore opportunities for further cooperation and partnerships. Co-organised by the HKSAR Government and the Hong Kong Trade Development Council (HKTDC), the signature event gave attendees the chance to promote cross-regional trade and industry collaboration, as well as to accelerate new initiatives and achieve concrete outcomes. Underlining these intentions, the Summit’s broad theme this year was “Advancing High-Quality Development‧Embarking on a New Journey”. Significant results were achieved not just in showcasing over 300 investment projects, arranging more than 800 meetings between potential dealmakers, and facilitating the signing of more than 60 memoranda of understanding (MOUs) and other agreements. Equally notable was the diversity of sectors involved, ranging from finance and professional services to manufacturing and construction; the presence of organisations from the ASEAN bloc, Central Asia and the Middle East, and the interest shown in what Hong Kong can offer nowadays as both a “super connector” and a “super value-adder”. The two-day agenda featured a series of keynote addresses from high-profile speakers plus plenary sessions and informative panel discussions. This allowed participants to share their expertise on policy issues, navigating risk, and creating opportunities for enterprises to expand into international markets at a time of supply chain disruptions and geopolitical uncertainties. There was also an emphasis on innovation, enhancing trade and investment resilience, and helping to transform initial connections into tangible results and lasting ties. For instance, in his opening remarks, Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu noted the importance of a proactive approach to advancing regional exchanges and opening new markets. The former highlighted the immense possibilities in trade, transport, industry, technology, capital investment and human resources that came with reviving the ancient Silk Road in a modern format and establishing comprehensive strategic links. Cosse said it made sense then because the B&R pillars of infrastructure, connectivity, trade facilitation and financial integration aligned with Uruguay’s long-term belief in multilateral cooperation and free trade. And today that commitment to enhancing capital flows and developing joint projects with Hong Kong and other partners in Asia remains as strong as ever. Besides formal plenary sessions and high-powered debates, this year’s Summit also introduced new thematic zones to spotlight Hong Kong’s ability to support the practical needs of enterprises in different sectors. For instance, the “GoGlobal Connect Zone” showed how the city’s professional services expertise has helped Chinese Mainland companies plan for expansion and connect with international markets. There were also roundtable discussions and a one-stop exchange and matchmaking platform to assist with answers and general advice. Separately, the Central Asia Zone featured eight exhibitors from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, showcasing the rapid development and investment opportunities in Central Asia. And the Middle East Zone gave attendees a much fuller understanding of the potential for business and investment in the six countries, covering Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE. Saleumxay Kommasith, the Deputy Prime Minister of Laos, used his special address to illustrate Belt and Road cooperation in practice. He highlighted the impact of the Laos-China Railway, which opened in 2021. Since then, it has carried more than 70 million passengers and transported over 90 million metric tonnes of freight.

events.title: The Agentic AI Super Cycle
events.summary: The biggest technology revolutions of the past were driven by steam engines in the 1700s, railroads in the 1800s, electricity, cars, phones, planes, computers, and the internet in the 1900s. Now we are at the dawn of the Agentic AI revolution, which will be the biggest of them all. A few years ago, Goldman Sachs predicted Generative AI would increase global GDP by about 7% over 10 years. McKinsey had a roughly similar projection. Today, more than half of USA GDP growth is due to AI infrastructure investment. Agentic AI is much more powerful and more economically impactful than generative AI (and any previous industrial revolution) and requires much more compute investment for broad adoption. More than half of GDP in advanced economies is labor, with more than half of that labor being cognitive work that can be made much more productive with agentic AI. So far, coding is the early adopter, with most coders now using agentic AI to generate and validate most code. That makes the coder more of an architect and manager. What’s astounding is that this happened in less than 2 years. Frontier models are now used extensively to generate code for the next frontier model. But how quickly will other fields extensively adopt Agentic AI, and will supply chain constraints be overcome to meet the demand? Recently, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, called for a pacing of the development of frontier models to ensure everyone is building in the right controls and safeguards. AI leaders agree these controls are important. “We’ll make AI that is incredibly safe,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO. Any pacing of model development won’t slow the pace of investment. Dario noted safeguards will involve more training. Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, noted on CNBC recently, “even if we stop today, the amount of intelligence that’s available in the world is massive,” and “there is so much opportunity to drive growth with good ROI (return on investment).” Data center AI CapEx (capital expenditure) will reach ~$1 trillion this year, and is projected to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030 (Source: Jensen Huang, Goldman Sachs Technology Conference). By comparison, world GDP is expected to be $123 trillion this year. AI is expected to go from ~1% to ~3%. Of the world’s top 10 highest market capitalization companies, 8 are major AI players: Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, TSMC, SpaceX, Meta, Broadcom. Collectively they make up almost 20% of the total market cap of the world’s publicly traded companies. Only a couple of these AI companies were in the top 10 a decade ago. Anthropic is expected to join the top 10 market capitalization club later this year. Massive companies like Nvidia are projecting 70% growth in revenues next year at huge scale. It’s natural to think this can’t keep going. But maybe it can. The key factors are: If agentic AI has high ROI; If it has a huge TAM (Total Addressable Market), and If it continues to become more powerful and less costly for years to come. If all those conditions are met, then we are in the biggest supercycle of our lives — and of history. The AI leader companies will get much bigger along with the US and world economies. There will be losers, there will be pauses/plateaus/consolidation, but this is a 10+ year Super 2 Cycle. Data center AI investment offers very attractive ROI The hyperscalers, Anthropic, and OpenAI are ramping AI CapEx because they see rapid demand growth, strong ROI, and because they don’t want to fall behind competition. This is a gold rush. Morgan Stanley in July concluded the major hyperscalers had paths to 25% to 50% ROIC (return on invested capital) for GenAI. These are very attractive returns. Dave Patterson, distinguished engineer and fellow at Google, said at the recent AI Infra Summit that Google recovers its cash outlay for a TPU in 1 year, and in 2 years for its custom Axion CPU. At Goldman Sachs Tech Conference, Thomas Kurian, CEO of Google Cloud, said TPUs paid back twice as fast as GPUs, so even GPUs recover their investment in 2 years. This is a fantastic ROI, although he might be leaving out land and building costs. The reason this isn’t increasing near-term profits already is because Google keeps increasing CapEx spend faster than revenue growth. Amazon senior vice president Peter DeSantis talked at AI Infra Summit about how the company builds the data center and the racks in parallel with building the Trainiums. This accelerates cash recovery, enabling Trainium shipments from the end of the production line to the data center to be in operation (and making money) in a couple months. He contrasted this to most companies that build the chips, then the trays, then the racks, then the rows, then install. That keeps cash tied up much longer before revenue generation. New Street forecasts that hyperscaler negative cash flow will bottom in 2028 at 20% of revenues, but then rapidly turns to a positive free cash flow of 10% of revenues by 2030. AI cloud revenue grows almost 10× from 2026 to 2030! And AI cloud revenue by 2030 exceeds non-AI. TSMC builds >90% of all AI compute devices (GPUs and custom XPUs like TPU and Trainium). TSMC is an extremely well-run company that does its homework thoroughly. At the recent Goldman Sachs Technology Conference, TSMC’s CFO said the foundry thinks we are still in the very early stage of a megatrend. Token costs are dropping fast using advanced processes and packaging, but this leads to increased demand for AI compute. TSMC is building numerous huge fabs and advanced packaging factories to try to keep up. We need a LOT more AI compute at much lower $/token At the Goldman Sachs Tech Conference, Jeetu Patel, Cisco’s president and chief product officer, said that agent consumption of tokens now exceeds consumption of tokens by humans using GenAI, and <2% of humans are now using agents in a power user capacity. So the half of today’s tokens that are agentic could grow 50× when 100% of humans use agents in a power user capacity. And that’s for today’s models. Future models will grow exponentially in compute requirements, but costs are coming down exponentially at the same time. Fig. 1: Agentic token consumption has soared to >50% of total demand. Source: Cisco Goldman Sachs in May projected token consumption will grow 40× from mid 2026 to mid 2030. events.title: Extreme Environments Push Chips To Their Breaking Point
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Orbital data centers, military/aerospace vehicles, HPC experiments, quantum, and advanced manufacturing equipment are all putting pressure on chips to withstand extreme environments. Conditions include any combination of thermal and mechanical shock, radiation, high speeds, noise, vibration, pressure, and humidity. Advanced 4D modeling, simulation, AI/LLM-based design exploration, and physical lab tools are all needed to ensure complex chips and systems can survive. Chips that were once qualified against a limited set of operating conditions are now being designed for environments where multiple stresses hit at once. Radiation, thermal shock, vibration, pressure, noise, and cryogenic temperatures are colliding in applications ranging from orbital data centers and defense systems to particle physics, quantum computing, and advanced manufacturing. That is changing how chips are designed and qualified. AI-enabled design tools, machine learning, and language models can explore more design options earlier, but virtual models still have to be checked against physical behavior. For extreme-environment electronics, the challenge is not just predicting failure modes, but reproducing enough of the real operating environment to trust the prediction. Space is becoming one of the clearest pressure points. The growth of satellite constellations, orbital data centers, space probes, surface explorers, and military space systems is increasing demand for radiation-hardened designs, including at newer process nodes where performance and power benefits must be balanced against survivability. That demand is already showing up in the design ecosystem. “We have seen a major uptick in activity for rad-hard fab processes, particularly in the new process nodes to support orbital data centers,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys . “A lot of this is owing to the Golden Dome (multi-layered U.S. missile defense initiative). The next frontier for the next battlefield is space, and so you’re seeing the investment now accelerate, and we’re going to see a lot more rad-hard designs added.” Beyond national security, governments and nations are competing for global leadership in emerging technologies. For example, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) is working with Morgan State University, Northrop Grumman, and Project Omega on the DARPA-funded Rads to Watts program, which aims to convert Cold War-era radioactive decay into high-density nuclear micro-power radiovoltaic systems for extreme environments, including space, remote sensing, undersea infrastructure, and defense applications. [1] Radioisotopes such as Strontium-90 will be converted directly into electricity to operate for decades without refueling or battery replacement. Researchers achieve this by combining ultra-thin semiconductor layers with high-energy, beta-emitting isotopes. Simulation, characterization, and survivability analysis are essential to ensure these systems can operate in harsh environments. Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory is working with Siemens on a project titled Accelerating eXtreme Environment Specs-to-Silicon (AXESS) that uses LLMs and smaller surrogate models to speed up design exploration, then integrate and co-optimize all stages of chip development for quantum computing, fusion energy, and particle physics. [2] Fig. 1: A Fermilab engineer holds a custom circuit board designed to measure chip performance in cryogenic environments. Source : JJ Starr/Fermilab Each extreme-environment application presents a unique set of physical stressors that the hardware device must account for. “Particle accelerators and research accelerators are a particularly challenging environment because the doses are ridiculously high, and you need the equipment to do its thing while it’s getting damaged by the radiation,” said Hugh Barnaby, leader of extreme environment reliability in the U.S. Department of Defense’s ME Commons SWAP Hub at Arizona State University. “That extends to the medical equipment that’s used in proton therapies for cancer, which uses high-energy electrons. And in semiconductor manufacturing, lithography causes radiation damage. They’re using X-rays now for some of the really advanced technology, like backside power delivery. They have the power distribution on the backside of the chip. They used to use a wafer-analysis technique called LADA (laser-assisted device alteration), but now they can’t because the power is on the backside. They can’t use the lights. So they’re considering X-ray-assisted device alteration lasers (XADA). The problem is, they’re worried about the X-rays causing damage to the material.” Barnaby and one of his students, Jereme Neuendank, found that strange things happen to semiconductors at very low temperatures. [3] “If you combine that with radiation, it gets even weirder,” said Barnaby. ” We had some good theories with models backing them up, and we’re still doing a lot of work in that area.” Lab tools are evolving to study the effects of multiple stressors at once. ASU researchers developed the Rigel DSTAT, which has three rods collectively containing 9,000 Curies (Ci) of radioactive material to simulate the radiation environments found in space and nuclear applications. It also contains a tiny cryostat, which enables devices to be exposed to really saturated, extremely cold temperatures by evacuating a chamber and then filling it with either liquid nitrogen or argon, whose temperatures are about the same. “Then we can do radiation testing at liquid nitrogen, which is 77 Kelvin,” said Barnaby. Fig. 2: This illustrated setup shows how ASU’s extreme environments lab would test radiation and extreme cold together to mimic space. Illustration by Sophia Franz. Source : ASU The tool was ideal for a company designing readout ICs for satellites that would need to withstand cold, radiation, ionizing-dose threats, and low-frequency noise. In particular, random telegraph noise has emerged as one of the biggest reliability problems today, especially in analog/mixed-signal electronics. And that noise problem is exacerbated in the cold. “You want the cold to reduce the noise that comes off of the diodes that are creating the currents, the light detectors,” Barnaby noted. “They like the cold there. But when you’re doing the CMOS, to do the readout of those signals, the random telegraph noise signal does not, at best, improve with cold temperature. We’re still studying that physics.” The applications for these kinds of lab tools are growing. “We have talked to people about doing research in thermal energy exploration,” he explained. “We’ve also been getting into advanced packaging, which means extending into a pretty wide array of reliability issues such as pressure, humidity, high tempe

events.title: Buyer missed one option and got 1% of the cable they needed
events.summary: Every Monday morning The Register kicks off proceedings by asking the same question – “Who, Me?” – the title of the reader-contributed column in which you share your tales of the occasions on which you didn’t quite nail the brief yet somehow found career relief. This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Terry” who told us that in the 1970s he worked for a defense-related company. “I needed 100 meters of RG8 50 ohm coax cable, so ordered it from an ‘accredited’ supplier,” he wrote. “What I didn’t notice was that there was an option for ‘partial delivery’." Terry’s order duly arrived, all one meter of it – plus paperwork explaining that the other 99 meters would be along presently, thanks to the partial delivery option. “Needless to say, the one meter was not enough to span the distance between the two laboratories I was trying to link with an RF connection,” Terry wrote. Offering the partial delivery option cost the supplier their accreditation. Terry later learned that a junior employee at the cable supplier was sacked over the matter, after admitting he thought sending one meter of cable was a jolly jape. “I did not think it was a joke at the time,” Terry wrote. Have you made a procurement error that ended up costing you, or your supplier? If so, don’t short-change your fellow readers! Instead, click here to share your story with Who, Me? Our mailbag is a little short on stories, so contributions of any length are very welcome. ®

events.title: Trump proposal could make it easier to suspend or expel Head Start students
events.summary: The Trump administration has proposed changes to Head Start regulations that would remove rules against suspending and expelling preschoolers It was sometime around Xavier Rogers' second birthday that his mom and Early Head Start teachers noticed a shift in his demeanor. Xavier, usually a happy baby, now mostly wanted to play alone and would sometimes bite and hit other kids in his class. Instead of removing Xavier from his class, his Chicago-area preschool gave the family extra support from a social-emotional and mental healthcare team. “With these supports in place, I feel like he has grown tremendously,” said Xavier's mom, Joanna Isitt, a Head Start teacher herself. Now 4, “he’s become much, much more aware of himself and how he feels and how others may feel.” He's less likely to resort to negative behaviors, and he even encourages her to join him in breathing exercises, saying, “OK, Mama, smell the flowers, blow the candles.” The protections and support Isitt and her son received are part of longstanding Head Start regulations, but they could soon disappear under the Trump administration’s proposed rule change for the 61-year-old early childhood education program. The proposal would eliminate federal guidelines that keep kids who exhibit behaviors like Xavier’s from being removed from Head Start programs. Instead of receiving the help he needed to self-regulate, the little boy could have been told to leave, and his mother could have been left scrambling for alternative care. AP has partnered with The 74 , an education-focused nonprofit news outlet, to cover the impact of the Trump administration's proposed changes to Head Start. The family lives in Illinois, which has its own regulations against imposing exclusionary discipline such as suspensions and expulsions on preschoolers. But some other states, such as South Carolina and Florida, do not. The updated Head Start rules would ask providers to make their own discipline policies by following state and local licensing requirements. Advocates and experts fear Head Start students and families in these places could experience a more punitive reality if the proposed changes take effect. Suspensions and expulsions are associated with negative outcomes, including lower educational achievement, decreased likelihood of graduating high school and depression. “If the state of Florida doesn’t have standards related to suspension and expulsion, and that’s what the administration wants us to go by … I think as a country we should all be very concerned that we’re taking our most vulnerable children and families and potentially putting them in an environment where they’re going to have no protections,” said Wanda Minick, executive director of the Florida Head Start Association. Only 14 states and Washington, D.C., have laws or policies that align with Head Start’s rules around exclusionary discipline, according to a recent analysis by the Children’s Equity Project at Arizona State University. Of those, researchers said, only around half the laws appear to apply to all children under 5, the population served by Head Start. And in only one, Minnesota, do the regulations explicitly include Head Start programs. That means that in 70% of states, Head Start students would be left with fewer guardrails should the rule change pass. Many of the states with flexible rules or no laws end up removing the most preschoolers from their classrooms, while states with tighter regulations suspend far fewer, according to an analysis of 2023-24 federal data by The 74 and The Associated Press. The data captures suspensions for pre-kindergartners who are enrolled in public school districts. South Carolina reported suspending 604 public preschoolers a total of 1,181 times that year, while Minnesota reported zero students suspended. Florida reported expelling 466 public preschoolers, more than any other state. Ultimately, the data shows, some Head Start students would remain shielded from expulsion and suspension, but some would not — simply depending on where they live. The public may comment on the rule change through Oct. 6. These include lower adult-to-child ratios, a required number of monthly mental health consultations, timely developmental screenings and staff breaks. In this environment, “if they were to make it permissible to either reject kids or throw them out, I think a lot of teachers would, because they’re just feeling so much strain,” said Joel Ryan, executive director of the Washington State Association of Head Start.
